With a Linux version now available, I just purchased this game for $1.  I then ran it and proceeded through all 50 levels in one sitting taking 66 minutes.  That may seem short, but it was really a lot of fun, and, having played the whole game, I'd wouldn't have minded paying $2 or $3 for it.
The puzzles are not overly difficult by any means, but, as another reviewer mentioned, the difficulty does increase after level 30.  If anything, this game left me wanting more levels to play through, which is not a bad place to be for such a simple (bit elegant game).
Anyway, it was certainly worth the price, and even if somehow you *don't* like it, you're hardly out a fortune, right?  Kudos to the dev.  I didn't check beforehand, but this game could have a mobile version with no need to change anything about it.
Also, this game screams out for a simple level editor or Steamworks support.  It would increase the value and replayanility of the game enormously, and it would definitely make it a stand-out hit in my opinion.

SOMA is a very interesting psychological horror game.  Well, when I say 'horror', it's not
scary but the atmosphere is excellent and tense throughout.  There aren't too many jump scares and it relies on cranking up the tension to mess with your head.
The story unfolds in a natural way, without huge narrative dumps.  You start the main plot not knowing what's going on, slowly figuring out how it all fits together.  I found my attitude to the overall situation changing as I got more information (as one example, you'll see a survey on a computer a short time into the game.  Compare your answers at that point with how you feel near the end,)
SOMA poses questions along the lines of the Ship of Theseus thought experiment: if you replace an object one component at a time, eventually replacing all parts, is it still 'the same' object?  Except in this case, it's not a ship involved but something more interesting...
The graphics, atmosphere, sound and writing are terrific. The only downside is that it doesn't take too long to complete but the experience makes it worthwhile.
This game is worth your time and money.

Just finished SOMA.
Great ride from start to finish, amazing atmosphere and compeling story that questions morals and humanity.
This is traditional Fricional Games design, gameplay is simple with some detailed enviroment interaction, the game is mostly linear but its sections have enough room for some exploration, puzzle solving feels simple but effective enough in keeping the flow of the game, though some stealth sections might feel repetitive.
The graphics while not a technical wonder like AAA PC FPSs like Crysis 3 still look good and do a great job at introducing and maintaining SOMA's amazing creepy, dreadful, Sci-fi atmosphere (Reminded me of movies like "Sphere" and "The Abyss"), some sections in particular look really good.
The Audio here is quite exceptional and demands you to experience SOMA in glorious 5.1 or even 7.1 surround.
The story here is good and the main reason to play this game, i won't spoil it, i can only say that the writing and production here is good and will captivate your insterest in uncovering the whole plot.
Now is it a scary horror game? Well, it is a horror game that relies more on atmosphere than jumpscares (You still get a hefty dose of them though).
For me, SOMA gets an 8.5/10 and i feel that its 30$  price tag is cheap, unfair and unreflective of the ammount of value that Frictional Games put in it.
Recommend it!

Few games hold true potential to be something amazing. This is one of those games that has amazing moments of suspense, thrill, fear, and fun, all bundled together in a nice package with a bow on top.
The problem is that these moments are absolutely buried beneath what I can only hypothesize as general negligence in the creation of this game. The only way that this product released in the state it's in is with clueless developers, or a forced release date that resulted in a product being shoved out the door way too early.
"But it just came out of beta" is the excuse I've seen given by many trying to justify their purchase and hold on tightly to the fact that an early investment wasn't a mistake.
As someone who backed the Kickstarter, I am wholeheartedly let down at the fact this game is less balanced than a sinking ship. The fact Jason can inconsequentially teleport on top of counselors in plain sight, rapidly break through doors in seconds, can swing faster than a ninja whilst counselors cannot hit me whatsoever (this is a claim. Jason can power-walk through attacks), and is invulnerable during ALL of his interactive animations is completely and totally unacceptable in any form of release.
There is no semblance of balance that went into the creation of this game. I'm under the impression that there was no actual testing was ever in the development process beyond "we can ship it." I'm genuinely♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off that the F13 IP is being treated this poorly. The only thing that works as intended in the "Add to Cart" button on the store page.
At $40 I want something I could at least pretend is functional. Until then, this is on par with the 1989 "Friday the 13th" Nintendo game release.

Skyward Collapse is a very unusual game. An odd duck of sorts.
You control or rather help both oppoosing factions. You are striving for balance, but balance will be impossible to maintain. All your helpful nudges and interventions will get out of control and tip the scale towards either one faction - initially - or complete and utter chaotic powercreep (when you devastate the landscape, unleash minor gods, mythic creatures, wonders and miracles to "balance" whatever imbalance has crept in, trying to delay the inevitable).
Motto: "You are your own worst enemy. Every single one of your problems was caused by you and every solution is a future disaster in the making."
It is a turn-based god game for people who can lose every game (because they all end in disaster). In the end, it becomes a score-hunt or a story-driven experience depending on what kind of player you are.
The UI is minimalistic, I guess, but perfectly sufficient. The game could do better in guiding and explaining things to you (at least I found myself drawn to google after a few games).
I can recommend the (rather cheap) expansion pack, but it will neither make nor break the game for you. If you do like the base game, go get it. If you don't, the expansion won't help. So check out the basic game and if you love it like I do, then get the expansion.
My hourly stats are incorrect, I have played this game quite a bit longer. There is a lot of replayability to challenge yourself ever more (last longer, or more chaos/upheavel). There are also quite few options and game modes to vary the experience.
What kind of gamer will like this? Probably a patient, somewhat puzzle-game appreciatative strategy gamer who cares more about clever mechanics than winning big (or just the spectacular). You will have to rethink your strategy every game and go back to the drawing board to the improve. There is a lot of depth here, but you'll have to think to get there. The game does not hand it to you or guide you along to better strategies.

SOMA is a game that is well written and despite the few flaws was an experience I enjoyed immensely. Tl;dr at the end.
Taking place mostly in an underwater facility of which you know nothing of its function, it eventually opens up to reveal a multi-layered story taking place over different time periods (some spanning weeks, some spanning decades). The plot holds together cohesively and seemingly without effort. In an environment as imaginative as a facility being taken over by (????) and with the mission to save (????) by (????) a (????) into (????), having a plot that is easy to follow is a testament to how inspired the concept was from the get go.
The 'horror' aspects of the game are done moderately well, but if you have played a frictional game the concept is mostly the same. The most interesting aspect is that most of your adversaries have specific rules or 'sensitivities' either to sound, light levels, or even player line-of-sight. I wouldn't say the game is horrifying, however those with thalassophobia (like myself) will find some parts...uncomfortable.
The game shines when taken as an adventure of discovery. You find bits and pieces of the past and future, allowing you to understand what happened to the world, as well as you. There are sequences of moral dilemma and some existential questions if this is something you are looking for. While the concepts are interesting, they aren't quite new. Despite this, the levels are creatively designed, the enemies are interesting, and the story keeps you engaged until the end.
Tl;dr
SOMA is a well written, more-spooky-than-scary mystery that is lots of fun to unravel and may make you consider the benefits of AI and what makes you human. Worth full price, a steal on sale.

SOMA is only comparible to other horror games in the sense that it should be played late at night with headphones. You won't find jump scares or sudden unexpected surprises. You will however find a sense of dread that always starts with almost imperceptible glitch of the display. Is that my graphics card acting up? Maybe the HDMI cable came a bit loose? You hear the sound skip with static and you feel the hairs on your arms begin to tingle. You know what is coming, or at least you think and hope you do. Is that a figure in the distance? What was that in the corner of my eye? Was that a sound of something coming towards me or was that just background noise?
Will it go away or will it find me...?
All in all I would rate SOMA as one of my favorite games of 2015. It makes you think and it doesn't hold your hand. It mostly relies on you, the player, to figure out what is happening and piece it together for yourself. It makes you consider what it means to be human, the nature of consciousness and what makes one life more important than another. It makes you question whether the needs of the many really do outweigh the needs of the few, or the one. It has the mark of any truly engaging piece of fiction: it has stuck with me long after finishing it and continues to do so.
It's that type of a game where you find yourself playing it today and finish it in one batch!

I waited to post a review for Beam.NG because for a while, it was more like a tech demo than a game. I still considered it one of the most fun games I'd played, but it was cumbersome for anyone that wanted to just play a game. The early versions could require as much work as play at times, and obviously a project this ambitious had some problems with performance and optimization.
Now between the mods and the actual Campaigns and scenarios built in, I feel comfortable recommending it without reservation. There is plenty of content right out of the box, and the game seems to scale for lower-end machines much better every time an update drops. I simply cannot speak highly enough of this game at this point. Once you dip your toes into the released content, I challenge anyone not to beg for more.
Luckily, there is an tremendous mod scene. It's not built into Steam (for reasons beyond me, it's discussed on the forums and the official website).
Do yourself a plethora of favors, there is a giant banner that will walk you through the incredibly simple process of adding mods (At the time of writing, there is no built-in manager. Just download and move to the corrrect folder, the game detects them on start-up). Also, anything tagged Alpha or Beta is official content that is just not finished or released into the full game. I have barely scratched the surface and try to stick to official mods for compatibility reasons.
If it runs poorly, wait it out or request a refund :/ I'd recommend a gamepad or wheel for driving but you'll need KB+M for the interface. The latest patch even made it possible to work the UI over Steam Link (360 controller only), as long as I wasn't trying to go to the moon. If it seems too much like work, spend 10m on YouTube and find a decent beginner's guide (the official site also has plenty of great info). I literally cannot think of a complaint about this game, unless it being made so well that it becomes esoteric counts. I don't count it.

I was a little disappointed to find out this game is only one hour, after getting really hooked (no pun intended) on Hook's really unique puzzles. It basically revolves around ideas of circuitry, and making sure you have the right lines connected and/or disconnected in order to slide swords and hooks out without hitting other swords and hooks. It's simplistic, but in it's simplicity there can be a lot of complexity that spawns from it. And this game has a lot of mind-twisting puzzles. But it's sort of looking at your homework assignment, and thinking, "Well, sh**! How am I gonna get through all this!" And slowly, but surely, you inevitably get through your homework and think to yourself, "Well, that was easier than I thought it would be." Except with Calculus... I'll never forget those long nights studying Calculus...
But Hook isn't a very hard game. If you bump the hooks into each other you just go back to the beginning which isn't really punishment, but more of an annoyance as you already know how to get back to where you were in the puzzle. But it does promote being careful in how you play. The game also, as I stated earlier, is only about an hour's worth with only 50 puzzles. I mean, if I'm paying a dollar for a puzzle game like this, I'd expect 100 or even 150 puzzles, since they seem so easy to make (I mean, yes, there's a lot of mental thought put into the puzzles but the programming aspect seems relatively simple).
And, unfortunately, the game has zero replay value. I hear this argument with another puzzle game, Portal, and my argument against that is that the story is what makes the game replayable. Like popping in your favorite film and experiencing all those emotions you went through the first time. However, Hook has no story. It's just 50 puzzles that slowly get more complicated as you play through, but once you know the secrets of the puzzles, that ruins the idea of going back to play again, because there are no extra challenges, no secrets, and only one Steam achievement you can obtain. But, I will admit, the game did grab my attention with its fun puzzles, the music is tranquil and promotes a slower, steadier style of playing the game, and it's very satisfying to hear the swords and hooks click into place properly and the once-complex puzzle getting more and more simple.
It's not a game I'd suggest you buy at full price, but if there's a Steam sale, and this happens to be one of the games on the list- this is a fun little game to waste a free hour you've got. Maybe the developer can use this as a good foundation to make even more unique (and hopefully longer) games.

One of my favorite games in a long time. I've spent more than 60 hours on it in just over a week already, so it's easily worth the money in playtime-per-hour terms. The multiplayer is where the meat of the game is. The single player isn't bad, but should mostly be treated as a super detailed, long-form tutorial rather than some super-awesome story campaign.
The melee combat is absolutely great. I'd explain it as a mix between Dark Souls and a fighting game. Slower, more telegraphed moves focusing on defense/evasion, locking onto a single target at a time, and stamina management like Dark Souls. Unique characters with their own sets of attack combos, 3-area attacks (Top, left and right in For Honor compared to High-mid-low in a normal 2d fighting game), throws, chip damage, unblockable or uninterruptable moves from fighting games.
Dueling is where the game really shines, but I find all of the game modes fun. The 4v4 modes can be a bit screwy sometimes with people running away from fights or grouping up to gangbang people, but the game has a few systems in place to stop it from being too much of an issue - most of the time, at least. There are some balancing issues and bug fixes that need to happen in regards to combat/abilities, but a lot of peoples complaints in this area can unironically be summed up with "git gud scrub" - as the game has a really steep learning curve and high skill cap.
All the other multitude of negative reviews give you plenty of examples of the negatives, though I think they definitely over-exaggerate the problems. However I'll go through the negatives and put my experiences with them just to be comprehensive.
Peer-to-Peer networking:
The game doesn't have dedicated servers. Instead it uses some new type of P2P networking where every game client is also a host, so you're all sending and receiving information to each other at the same time. This prevents there from being a "host," thus avoiding "host advantage" like older P2P games. However it does cause overall higher pings than a dedicated server, and you can still get host migrations if the "session host" - the guy leading the lobby who receives player invites from the matchmaking servers - leaves.
The host migration thing happens sometimes, but not a huge amount, and the vast majority of times only takes a few seconds. I've not really experienced the horrible lag, long matchmaking times or inability to join games tha a lot of others are complaining about. I'm not saying it doesn't happen, but the worst I've experienced is a few matchmaking errors here and there or the matchmaking derp'ing as it tries to throw me into a game that's already full. Which since the queue times are mostly instant for me I just requeue and get into a game right away - I've never had the errors happen more than a couple times in a row before it puts me in a match.
Micro-transactions:
I, personally, am fine with the fact that there are micro-transactions since it means all future DLC is going to be free for everyone. However I do wish they'd have adopted more of an Overwatch or Dota2 model with cosmetics only. As it is things are /mostly/ cosmetic, but there is an aspect of "pay to avoid grinding" to them as well. Which I think is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ in a full price AAA game, but it doesn't really effect gameplay the way they've implemented it.
So I would say it's something I don't like, but since it's still totally optional and doesn't actively take anything away from the game... That I don't really care, I guess. It's a shady business practice that I wish wasn't there, but doesn't hamper my enjoyment of the game in any way.
TLDR:
Overall I think For Honor is a great multiplayer game and would highly recommend it. It has some issues, but nothing that's too big of a deal from my experience.
Final score - 8/10
If it had a proper, good campaign and improved on the few negatives it has it would easily be a 10/10, and I'd say that just multiplayer gameplay wise it's a 9/10 for me, but the overall package I'd say is a fairly solid 8/10 even with its flaws.

Well, we had several people turn up on the stream for this one and, all in all, it was a creepy experience. Let’s get cracking.
I – Story [10/10]
Knock-knock is a indie survival horror game from the twisted minds of Ice-pick Lodge. The player takes on the role of the “Lodger”, the current resident of an unusual house deep in the woods. Lately, the Lodger has been noticing strange things happening; not only in his home, but in the forest surrounding it as well. Things have gone missing, odd noises are heard throughout the house, and something unnatural is coming out of the woods. And, when night falls, it seems as though someone (or something) else is sharing the dark corners of the house with you.
The goal is to stay awake (and sane) until the dawn breaks. The Lodger must wander the rooms of his home by night, evading the unknown and the invisible, all while counting the seconds until the sun will rise. Only during the night can the Lodger solve the puzzle of what’s really going on. Are the “Guests” really there or is he slipping steadily into madness? What has happened to the forest? What has happened to his home? Where can he draw the line between reality and imagination? With multiple possible endings, Knock-knock is a breath of fresh air when it comes to survival horror.
II – UI [9/10]
The user interface is incredibly minimal. There is no real HUD, other than a slight outline in front of certain objects which you can use to hide behind. This did wonders for the immersion level of the game and really helped maintain a spooky atmosphere throughout the story.
However, at a certain point in the game, the game itself becomes timed and a white crack appears at the top of the screen. In some sequences, this white crack can be seen at all times and does tend to take away from the experience as a whole, if only a small amount.
III – Gameplay [10/10]
The gameplay in Knock-knock felt incredibly unique. While the controls were simple (on K&M or gamepad) the game itself can quickly become intense and you’ll find yourself wishing you could sprint. As I mentioned above, the goal of the game is to survive each night in the house while maintaining your sanity. This can be done in a variety of ways and (assuming you play the game at some point) you’ll no doubt decide on a strategy which you deem to be best.
Every room you enter will need to have the light source repaired to turn back on. This takes a small amount of time to accomplish, so you must be vigilant in observing your surroundings. Once the light is repaired, the Lodger may or may not close his eyes briefly. If his eyes close, he is adjusting to the light meaning that there is furniture in the room. Some rooms may allow you to do this more than once, to reveal even more decor inside. Repairing lights is also the only way to seal a “Breach” before some apparition from your nightmares manifests in the house with you.
You can’t reach every breach in enough time to seal it off, so, at some point, you will be dealing with some scary ghouls. You can deal with these guests in a number of ways. Your first option is to hide behind things when they enter a room with you. Your hiding spot may or may not fool them. Assuming it does fool them, they will leave the room and begin to wander off. If it doesn’t fool them, you’ll take a hit to your time meter and lose some time. If that clock goes all the way back, you go insane and repeat the night. (It is also important to note, that time goes backwards ever so slowly while the Lodger is hiding too.)
Another way you can deal with the guests is to evade them, though this can prove difficult in many cases. Certain guests can appear suddenly and block off doorways. While you can move through them, you’ll take a hit on your time meter. Also, if you turn a light on in a room inhabited by a guest, you’ll take a hit. Some guests are even impossible to hide from, like The Invisible One. The key to successful evasion is to learn all you can about the guests; how the move, what they sound like, what the best way to deal with them is, etc.
IV – Content [9/10]
Content-wise, there isn’t a whole lot to Knock-knock and there didn’t need to be. There are a delightfully horrifying amount of different Guests that will come and haunt you during the nights. There are even a number of interesting bits of furniture that you can hide behind when said guests come calling.
The one thing I do wish had been implemented, however, is some sort of upgrade system for the Lodger. Perhaps a skill-tree of sorts that would let you upgrade your movement speed, hiding efficiency, time it takes to repair lights/open doors, etc.
V – Visual [10/10]
The graphics of Knock-knock are simply brilliant. Everything is hand-drawn and absolutely eerie. While the Lodger is a bit of an odd duck, his house and the forest around are wonderful. Not to mention the legion of spooks that are crawling around with you at night. It’s all very visually unsettling at times and I wouldn’t want it any other way.
VI – Audio [9/10]
The music of Knock-knock is great. I got this one off of Humble Bundle and (much to my pleasant surprise) it included the official soundtrack for the game. The sound effects are equally well done, with a few exceptions. One or two of the guests seemed to be overly loud and they make noise constantly until they are encountered by the Lodger and then leave the house. Other than that, no complaints here.
VII – Overall [9.5/10]
Overall, Knock-knock is an extremely fun game and a great addition to the survival horror genre. This one is best to be played alone and in the dark if you want the full experience of it. At full price or not, this is a solid game and a great purchase.

SOMA is a game that is well written and despite the few flaws was an experience I enjoyed immensely. Tl;dr at the end.
Taking place mostly in an underwater facility of which you know nothing of its function, it eventually opens up to reveal a multi-layered story taking place over different time periods (some spanning weeks, some spanning decades). The plot holds together cohesively and seemingly without effort. In an environment as imaginative as a facility being taken over by (????) and with the mission to save (????) by (????) a (????) into (????), having a plot that is easy to follow is a testament to how inspired the concept was from the get go.
The 'horror' aspects of the game are done moderately well, but if you have played a frictional game the concept is mostly the same. The most interesting aspect is that most of your adversaries have specific rules or 'sensitivities' either to sound, light levels, or even player line-of-sight. I wouldn't say the game is horrifying, however those with thalassophobia (like myself) will find some parts...uncomfortable.
The game shines when taken as an adventure of discovery. You find bits and pieces of the past and future, allowing you to understand what happened to the world, as well as you. There are sequences of moral dilemma and some existential questions if this is something you are looking for. While the concepts are interesting, they aren't quite new. Despite this, the levels are creatively designed, the enemies are interesting, and the story keeps you engaged until the end.
Tl;dr
SOMA is a well written, more-spooky-than-scary mystery that is lots of fun to unravel and may make you consider the benefits of AI and what makes you human. Worth full price, a steal on sale.

*** Commentary ***

The game is not perfect. Let's be clear. But the bugs are no where near as common or harmful as people make it out to be. For whatever reason, Gun Media and Illfonic are being held to a totally different standard from other indy developers. The game has just as much woes as a game published by large developlers that spent mega-millions and it's being patched just as timely. This is not a big budget game, and to be an indy, it's really slick.
With a few bizarre exception, the reviews from media sources are good, if not perfect. But reviews from the community are unduly harsh. This highilights the biggest problem, that cannot be stated enough, Jason fans are a toxic community. Bad review from entitled momma's boys who cry when the game is balanced and cry louder when it's not. Scratch the surface on the odd poor media review and you'll discover another whiny fanboi and the low bar of "journalism" in the era of digital publishing.
The game is good, and with the ability to shut "the community" out and enjoy it, it just got much better.
*** Original ***
I'm a backer of this game with all DLC. The launch hasn't exactly been smooth. There are several issues with having enough dedicated servers and the centralized backend database making it unplayable currently. It's not unsual right now that you don't get XP for your playtime, and as I write this I've been "Saving Profile Data" for about 10 minutes.
The game got a very limited closed beta, and it shows. Now that the masses are on board, lots of silly exploits are being discovered and becoming the norm. For example, Jason can trivially about-face to side-step attacks. It's as hilarious as it is frustrating. But far worse, Jason can use his Shift ability to intantly teleport to a counselor and grab them. This was not intended and it seriously imbalances the gameplay. Many within the community defend it, which segues into the real problem with this game:  The single biggest detriment to this game right now is the community.
You should be aware that voice chat is enabled by default, which has lead to incidents of racism, sexism, the expected smack talk, and players revealing of other counselors locations. You can mute other players, but there's no global or permanent mute settings. These still wouldn't help if the others are conspiring with Jason against you, but at least you wouldn't have to hear it. At minimum, the Jason player shouldn't be able to speak or hear the voice chat outside of the lobby. Whoever thought to integrate voice chat as-is needs to be a character in this game so we can kill him in effigy a thousand times over. They should also apply at McDonalds before self-serve kiosks eliminate this career opportunity from them.
Clearly everyone wants to be Jason. However, when they can't be Jason, people will play his mini-me and go after other counselors. Although it could be an interesting and edgy twist, there doesn't seem to be any real penalty for doing it. The only solution is to remove the ability for counselors to attack each others. You can still slam a door in their face and lock it, leaving them outside with Jason. At least then, it's defensible as a self-survival tactic. That's exactly what Chad would do, right?
I decided to back this game after the developers stated they would bring a single player mode. I am hoping they have the wisdom to add both Jason and counselor modes and that this will count for XP, achievements, and the rest. I'm not really interested in the "other people" elements of games, and so far this game isn't changing my mind.
Devs, you're going to have to anger some entitled, gibbering fanbois to make this game fair. If you don't, expect continued refunds, bad reviews, and fated sales figures. I know you want to make this game fun, so don't be afraid to re-engineer Shift to only be usable outside of proximilty to counselors and cease if you get close to one unobstructed.
The visuals are fantastic. The game engine is solid. The play (sans exploits and other abuses) is amazing. I was worried with as much money as I sunk in this, but I'm impressed with what's here so far. The game has A LOT of potential, so I am hoping they work out the kinks. However, I cannot recommend the game currently. There's just too much making it "not fun" to make it worth $1, much less the $40 price tag (and I paid way more than that). There's not even a rudementary practice mode or tutorial to let you get used to the controls and mechanics. Since Steam doesn't let me give a neutral review, I have no choice but to give this thumbs down for now. SOMA is only comparible to other horror games in the sense that it should be played late at night with headphones. You won't find jump scares or sudden unexpected surprises. You will however find a sense of dread that always starts with almost imperceptible glitch of the display. Is that my graphics card acting up? Maybe the HDMI cable came a bit loose? You hear the sound skip with static and you feel the hairs on your arms begin to tingle. You know what is coming, or at least you think and hope you do. Is that a figure in the distance? What was that in the corner of my eye? Was that a sound of something coming towards me or was that just background noise?
Will it go away or will it find me...?
All in all I would rate SOMA as one of my favorite games of 2015. It makes you think and it doesn't hold your hand. It mostly relies on you, the player, to figure out what is happening and piece it together for yourself. It makes you consider what it means to be human, the nature of consciousness and what makes one life more important than another. It makes you question whether the needs of the many really do outweigh the needs of the few, or the one. It has the mark of any truly engaging piece of fiction: it has stuck with me long after finishing it and continues to do so.

NOTE: While I rated this thumbs down, this is actually a Neutral Rating.
So to start off. I will say that the game mechanics are solid. The network code leaves a lot to be desired.
For a multiplayer only release. the shift in priorities shouldve been to network code in the last months up to release because graphically. the game is really good. the frustrating things youll find if you get a ping above 150 are as follows:
- Getting stuck in drawers that you search because of a dip in network connectivity, requiring another player to hit you to get out of it.
-as Jason, having moments where you cant swing your weapon or use any of your abilities. and being stuck like that for the duration of the game until someone hits you. which is unlikely as most people are not going to run up to Jason and hit him.
-acquiring an item and having the act teleport you randomly somewhere else in the room. this can be bad because if its on a bear trap, well, you know what happens next.
And I understand that building a title like this with a small team probably wasnt easy. but id software was a team of 10 to 12 people when they created the Quake series. and i think that another month in a half stress testing the network stability wouldve been a huge help to rectifying these kinds of issues.
As for why its $40? simple. Hollywood wanted their cut and that was likely to cover licensing fees.
If they get single player in, which frankly i hope they do because it would let you test strategies and tactics with Jason outside of a live environment, that will help to justify the price. add better client prediction to the network code in addition to single player? and this game could easily be a AAA title. Right now? it is still technically a multiplayer beta. and when the network isnt garbage, its a fun multiplayer beta. When that status changes, I will be happy to append the review to reflect it. Right now, expect some technical difficulties from time to time, and alt f4s in frustration not because you lost, but because you got stuck in a drawer and couldnt swing your weapons.

A game that truly stands the test of time. I never thought anything could top the smash hit that was Knights of the Old Republic, but I was wrong. The Sith Lords takes everything good about the first game and improves upon it. Some of the biggest would be the ability to use force powers from the start of the game. It was my one and only gripe in the first one. Having to spend those first few hours fighting through Taris before finally able to reach the Jedi and learn the ways of the force again. Another huge improvement is the ability to actually influence your companions and sway them to your line of reasoning. Unlike in the first game where certain companions had to be killed off depending on choices made, this time around you can corrupt or enlighten everyone. Nothing brings out the inner Sith Lord in me more then being able to show my followers the true meaning of the power of the dark side of the force. That is not to say this game does not have bugs and glitches, as it most assuredly does. It was released in a pretty unfinished state with a lot of content cut out. But even with all that, the fact that it's still a game I could never stop playing shows just how great it was. Plus with the restoration mod the game returns to the full glory it was meant to be.
To stop babbling like and idiot and wrap this up before I bore anyone to tears. Let me just say that if you enjoyed the first game, love star wars, or just want to unleash your inner sith lord...or weak jedi scum. Then buy this game and travel to a galaxy far, far away.

It takes hours to find another player on the map, and finding food and water is near impossible since it takes forever to get anywhere. The least you could do is give us a spawn point nearby one of the active lakes. Starting out starving and thirsty makes this an even larger feat, because by the time you reach water or food, you're already pretty much dead and someone kills you with one hit.
I'm overall impressed with the amount of updating and fast fixes, but the game just isn't there yet. Flowing rivers, and intelligent npcs might make the task of playing less tedius, while keeping the game just as difficult as the developers want it to be. We understand you want the map to be large, and the game to be challenging, but there's a point where it goes from challenging to just plain boring from waiting forever. So as it stands for now, my review remains negative.

UPDATE EDIT: Nice! I was finally able to play it, took awhile for me to update my review so my apologies about that. I like the dinosaurs and their skins, very beautiful! However the enviroment could use a lot of work for a new age game. I myself and perfectly content with the way it is now, but I know people who are to hard on graphics so if that's something you really care about then this game probably isn't for you.
You aren't able to play as humans or cannibals yet, but I don't really care to be honest. I'm curious as to how that updates in the future, and how they play seperately. Something that annoys me is the chat option, there should be both a species chat, and a public chat. Not being able to communicate with all players can be difficult and causes a lot of confusion, especially if you are the only one playing as that species.
I really enjoy the way the game plays so far, and was extremely excited to hear that isn't even all the dinosaurs they will be adding. Personally I would like to see an accurate representation of Dilophosaurus for once (sick of seeing the ridiculous Jurassic park version, it's pathetic), so I hope that will be a thing if they do add it. Otherwise other dinosaurs which would be interesting to see if they add them are Leaellynasaura, Ankylosaurus, Triceratops, Giganotosaurus, Microraptor, and Spinosaurus.
One thing that annoyed me though, and still does, is the unfair balancing of some dinosaurs. The raptor class is way too fast, and can kill any slower moving dinosaur without a scratch just by being behind their attacks, even the T-rex and other towering beasts. There literally was no possible way for me to get to them, and some would kill people for no reason at all and wouldn't give it up. The power of some of the dinosaurs seems strangely nerfed compared to others, and are pointless to be whatsoever. Understanding this is early access though, I can safely believe this will be fixed in the future.
Overall it's a wonderful game, and worth my purchase so far.

Where do I start... If you're one of the lucky ones, you will be able to buy the game, launch it, and be able to play immediately. (Don't count on it...) I had to throw out SOS to Steam/Nether for their gut-wrenchingly poor support for Steam-Nether account synchonization.
Game play, game play... It feels like a really *really* poorly done mod for Fallout or Skyrim... E.G. Guns have incredibly boring accuracy mechanics, and melee combat feels like a mod went poorly, and abandoned by the modder -- out of shame.
About 20%~25% of my time is time spent stuck *inside the environment*... Inconspicous walls seem to like to grab characters, and never let them go. Not to mention the half dozen areas that should be "inaccessible" to players, having no real way out... Other than to starve to death, or get mauled by monsters... Which, by the way, means you lose all your stuff (with no chance of getting them back, lest you get stuck in the inaccessible area again...)
The monsters... Probably some of the most, grotesquely boring enemies I've ever experienced in any format of FPS... Probably equipped with the most tragic sense of AI that's ever disgraced the visage of mankind, with even a speck of paying attention you should be able to tell exactly where the monster is going, and what attack it's going to do LOOOONG before it'll touch you.
Player VS. Environment VS. Player
Great concept on paper, but when applied... You only get players who rally up, and camp the buildings and kill you on a whim... Which is totally popular, and legitimate tactic for PVP games... But but for an adventure/survival/exploration/PVP -- it's just a really poorly mish-mash of concepts that are easily dismissed to make it into an entirely PVP game, with basically less-than-spectacular weapon and combat mechanics.
Occasionally character stops sprinting, mid-sprint... Standing there as an open target for whatever nasty beast is drooling after you, or player is trying to kill you.
I made a point to test my theories in PVE, and successfully killed every monster the game had to offer with the basic starter knife... No. I am not a pro at this game, no it was not epic, it was all actually really depressing, and disappointing...
So... With pathetically done environment, extremely lack-luster PVP, monsters that make Rust Bears/Wolves look like IQ-Over-9000 (minus erratic teleporting, which is still quite unimpressive...) and well. All-around lack of content and an otherwise undesirable atmosphere for a game... Not to mention the HUD/social/communications in this game is just... Atrocious...
The character customization offers a massive variety of everything between Vanilla, to... Well. Vanilla.
If you spend money, you might get a single M&M to put on top of it... But they will only provide the color/flavor you don't like.
This isn't even half of the stuff I want to say about this game... But I think the point has been made.
Buy something else...
Play something else...
Don't waste your time on this like I did.

This would be the one game I played in its entirety more times than I can remember. From the first time I played it on the PlayStation back in 1999, I come back to it every now and then when I just want to let myself loose. And it feels great every time, no matter the platform - Nintendo 64, PlayStation or PC. Although, many people were disappointed it's not a true sequel to the original Quake - it is the first entry in the Strogg saga.
Some time in the future, the Earth has been invaded by the Strogg, a race of cybernetic aliens, whose past and origins aren't quite clear. They don't take prisoners, they take unwilling recruits. Dead or alive, they will serve as an extension of the ever growing Strogg army. The Space Marine Corps have decided to show the Strogg they won't just sit around while our planet's population is being decimated by the alien forces, and have launched a massive counter-assault on Stroggos, the invaders' home planet (or, at least, their current home planet).
As the operation goes downhill the minute it started, the player assumes control of Bitterman, one of the few marines left alive on the surface of Stroggos. Armed with whatever he finds along the way (and he will find a plethora of weapons), Bitterman must cut his way through Strogg defenses all by himself, and try and bring the Strogg forces down.
The unique atmosphere of the game will keep you on your toes all along, as the Strogg fall under your sights one by one and you complete objectives sent by the Earth command.
The only downside of the Steam version is the lack of the original soundtrack, a very strong heavy metal score composed by Sonic Mayhem, which really gave the game a unique feel. This is something that should really be rectified in an update or a patch, as playing Quake II without the Quake II music is like riding a horse, naked. It just doesn't work. Since the original game read music directly from the CD, I don't think it's such a big problem to have the OST in a compressed format, along with the game. Or at least have the CD image of the game available for those who purchase it, so they can burn it and enjoy the full Quake II experience.

If you enjoyed any of the 4v4 battle modes in beta, you'll be unhappy to learn that its only gotten worst. P2p connections are still mind bogglingly attrocious with players now learning that they can leave games partway causing host migrations which ultimately don't work, forcing everyone to leave the match. I would estimate 50% of my games have ended with no rewards or exp being handed out because of this. This leaves the 1v1 or 2v2 modes as the only viable PVP options for any progression and at this games AAA price point, I would say its hardly worth.
At this state, I should also mention the countless times I've been met with "Unable to join the match. Error 0043560000" after minutes of queueing.
Get it on sale or get it when the server issues are finally addressed because it really is a fun unique fighter when it works but at in this state, I heartfully regret purchasing on release.
PS: I would just like to add that the devs at Ubisoft have stated "We are very aware that connectivity in general is a very big topic here and you should know it is truly our top priority here on the development team. There are a lot of different topics rolled into a topic as broad as connectivity, such as Matchmaking, NAT, Grouping, Stability, Join in progress, and more, each of which needs consideration when talking about the overall connectivity experience."
It is nice to know that a fix is actively being worked on, but its still a massive slap to the face when a game is released as always online (singleplayer included), only to have one of the most irritating online connectivity issues of games I've played in recent history.

I've had a lot of fun with this title, but it does start to fall apart after long-running games. I experienced massive slow-downs after more than seven or eight generations and various save and load errors. Regardless, the game is great and a great example of the real-time strategy format. I've simply modified my game type selections so I don't end up playing that long during a single session. Considering that it starts to feel like a bit of a grind around that point anyway, I don't mind the sacrifice.
There are a few aspects of this game that make it stand out in its genre. The continuation of your lineage's goals over several generations, for instance, is a unique approach and adds an entire realm of activities outside of your standard economy-driven real-time strategies. Imagine adding the Sims to your favorite RTS. If that doesn't sound like fun to you, no worries, you can play out your life as a lonely hermit who doesn't get involved with the town's social affairs. There are enough game type choices that make this just as entertaining an option.
If you like real-time strategies, and the medeival format entices you, I'd highly recommend giving this game a try; that is, if you can get past the dated graphics. I certainly can. If the latest graphics are a hard requirement for you, skip this one; you won't enjoy it.

NOTE: While I rated this thumbs down, this is actually a Neutral Rating.
So to start off. I will say that the game mechanics are solid. The network code leaves a lot to be desired.
For a multiplayer only release. the shift in priorities shouldve been to network code in the last months up to release because graphically. the game is really good. the frustrating things youll find if you get a ping above 150 are as follows:
- Getting stuck in drawers that you search because of a dip in network connectivity, requiring another player to hit you to get out of it.
-as Jason, having moments where you cant swing your weapon or use any of your abilities. and being stuck like that for the duration of the game until someone hits you. which is unlikely as most people are not going to run up to Jason and hit him.
-acquiring an item and having the act teleport you randomly somewhere else in the room. this can be bad because if its on a bear trap, well, you know what happens next.
And I understand that building a title like this with a small team probably wasnt easy. but id software was a team of 10 to 12 people when they created the Quake series. and i think that another month in a half stress testing the network stability wouldve been a huge help to rectifying these kinds of issues.
As for why its $40? simple. Hollywood wanted their cut and that was likely to cover licensing fees.
If they get single player in, which frankly i hope they do because it would let you test strategies and tactics with Jason outside of a live environment, that will help to justify the price. add better client prediction to the network code in addition to single player? and this game could easily be a AAA title. Right now? it is still technically a multiplayer beta. and when the network isnt garbage, its a fun multiplayer beta. When that status changes, I will be happy to append the review to reflect it. Right now, expect some technical difficulties from time to time, and alt f4s in frustration not because you lost, but because you got stuck in a drawer and couldnt swing your weapons.

Amnesia is a fantastic game from start to finish - thrusting players into the innards of a Gothic castle, bereft of memory or context save for a cryptic message on a note. From there, they must make their way ever forward, navigating darkened passages and puzzles, and piecing together the events of the story through ghostly memories and tattered notes found in the empty rooms.  The non-combat orientation of the game only adds to the tension, as the inability to take hostile action makes the moments when the player encounters a hostile force a truly tense moment- either by virtue of a frantic flight for one's life, or a harrowing bit of hiding. (The sewers and the damn water creature remain the thing that made me the most tense).
What's especially artful, however, is how the environment itself serves as an antagonist to the player, with the very darkness draining the player characters sanity, causing them to hallucinate, and also make more noise due to being frightened, which in turn can serve to draw the attention of hostile creatures that may be nearby. The slow encroachment of the...unnatural substance in the castle is also noteworthy for being altogether unpleasent.
All in all, if you're a horror fan, I'd definitely recommend taking a peek at this game, especially if you've never seen it on youtube.

This is literally DDR with an RPG laid overtop of it. Down to the song menu and difficulties. If DDR doesn't appeal, tread carefully and watch your time played in case you want a refund. I only have a bit clocked as of this review but I can tell you it's DDR with an RPG.

Once in battle, you switch between one of four characters' step charts, and follow the arrows like in DDR; you can stop after activating an attack at a first, second, or third power level. But legitimately, DDR with an RPG inside of it.

SOMA is not a game to be played for scares like Amnesia.  Though those scares can be found here, the true, sublime horror comes from the questions it forces you to ask and perhaps even answer before moving on.  And I can assure you, you will carry all the questions and nagging doubts that SOMA gives you with you for the rest of your life, as they cannot be ignored.  I've already long been contemplating the things SOMA talks about, but having a tool to better explore those thoughts made for an extraordinary learning experience, and an emotional rollercoaster.  Not to mention some horrifying realizations that apply just as much to ME in reality as they do in the game.  10/10, not even kidding.  Any weaknesses it has are eclipsed by the monolithic existential horror it forces you to face and consider, opening your eyes to things you can never forget because they are all too real.  Or maybe it's only as real as you.  That's for you to reconcile with yourself.
NOTE: THERE ARE NO ALTERNATE ENDINGS TO THIS GAME.  Do not make decisions with that assumption and go solely with what YOU think is right or what matches your understanding of what's happening.  The decisions have no effect on gameplay.  They are not meant to affect that.  They're supposed to affect YOU.
<BELOW I DISCUSS UNDERLYING THEMES IN SOMA, HOWEVER IF YOU'RE SMART YOU CAN PRETTY EASILY DEDUCE SPOILERS FROM IT>
What are you?  I mean, YOU, what are YOU?  Can you  transfer your consciousness to another body or is it just a copy with the original YOU being deleted?  Is it even right to delete that original?  How is it "original" or any different from a "right-to-live" standpoint as the copy?  Is there any merit to an original?  Is there even a difference?  With every second either of them remains conscious making two increasingly different people, is that not proof that each collection of memories, even if they are exactly the same, are in fact two distinct entities, therefore both deserving of all considerations for human rights as individuals?  Are YOU only a continued stream of consciousness with moments of unconsciousness constituting the end of the previous being and a beginning for a new one upon awakening with the same memories to continue?  Or are you defined only by the collection of memories, and the lapses in consciousness don't matter?  Even if you somehow managed to keep both continuing streams of consciousness in the copies exactly the same as they progressed, are they the same person?  Or are they two distinct entities that are remaining identical to one another?  Is it ever possible for the original to transfer elsewhere, or is it just up to the perception of those outside, and the original is trapped?  If the original transfers to an exact replica of its brain, is there a difference in "originality" of the copies as opposed to a different method of storage?  How long can these chains go?
This is just some of the♥♥♥♥♥♥this game makes you ask yourself, and it's not the kind of stuff you can just forget about.  It truly can make you reevaluate your entire existence.  And I've never had that before from a game.  Bioshock Infinite was incredibly pretentious and preachy in its attempts to handle somewhat similar ideas, but SOMA does it nigh on flawlessly, and leaves the player to reconcile these things themselves.
Despite some shoddy graphical stability and a few quibbles here and there, I am compelled to give the game a 10.  I've never before experienced something like this from a game, and it'll certainly continue to impact me for the rest of my life.

Basic gameplay is a "dance-off". Your group of 4 vs. the enemies. You can outfit your troupe with different skills and items. After that it's simply "hit the correct colored input buttons on your controller" (or other input device). If you can match and mix your attack types you can also do bonus damage vs. certain elements, e.g. lightning vs. water.
The game is a decent challenge for people who are not used to button combinations, even on easy, because you WILL need both hands (I used the left stick on A,B on the xbox controller to get through the game). You will quite regularly have to combine two different inputs: left/down or up/right or left/right, up/down. I guess, it's possible with a keyboard, maybe even a programmed mouse if that even works or a different input device. I'd have liked to actually try out a real dance mat, but oh well. No place, no time, no money. If you turn the difficulty to medium or hard, be prepared to just feel inadequate. At least there will never be more than 2 button prompts at once, but the general speed those prompts need pressing increases to kinda double the easy mode rate.
It's a good game, got a decent play time, and it's cheap. Only caveat is that you kinda have to like rythm games and dance music (mostly electro, but there's 1 or 2 rock songs and some jazz-y titles).

A really nice top-down 2D ARPG that is reminiscent of Sword of Mana and Legend of Zelda games. This is an indie game developed by maybe 5 people judging by end credits scroll.
Pros:
+ Nostalgic-feeling callback to early-90's games
+ Full controller support and audio options
+ Replayability through harder difficulty mode and different stat builds*
+ Save states
*In order to reach an achievement:
which is impossible to achieve in one playthrough, where having save states helps.
Cons:
- Skill level in art/design of the game leaves some weird choices in full display (Cutscene eyes, character model's feet)
- One or two songs on the soundrtack that are a bit too manic
- Game balance falls off toward the end when you have become a walking apocalypse, though that's not to say it isn't enjoyable.
I feel like this is one of the better options available for people that want a nostalgic-feeling game to play for a few hours. There may not be as many secrets or as much replay value as Shovel Knight, but that was developed by a much larger team, as well as having more inside. I feel like Evil Quest has about 4 hours of content for the main game, but it is easily worth 20+ hours of your time if you are a completionist, or just want to experience the game over again.
Final Verdict:
7.8/10 - Occasional cringy-looking art and crazed fast-paced music are the only complaints to be found with this title.

This game might be a bit friendlier on touch screens, but with a mouse, it's harder to be accurate with clicks, and since timing is one of the things that gets you lightbulbs (a measure of completion in this game), that can get a bit annoying.
And do note that simply beating all the levels in the first world doesn't get you access to the second world.  You have to get 50 lightbulbs out of the 20 levels provided (and up to five bonus levels, though you'll only have up to three to help boost your first world lightbulb count).  Each level gives you up to three lightbulbs -- one for completing it (so that's 20 for getting through the levels), one for completing it fast enough (another 20), and one for completing it in few enough moves (another 20), and you might have up to 9 more possible from the three bonus levels you'll have access to when you have fewer than 50 lightbulbs).  You don't have to get all three lightbulbs at the same time, thankfully, and there are also one-time treasures that you can retrieve (usually taking more time/moves than you'd otherwise need).  But still, out of 69 possible lightbulbs, you have to get 50 of them just to get to the second world.
Thankfully, the first world is relatively easy.  So I found myself with 48 lightbulbs coming out of it, no access to the second world, and had to scrounge a couple more lightbulbs out of one of the extra levels.
Granted, I've never been a huge fan of puzzle games.  So take what I'm writing with a grain of salt or something I guess.
Edit: Okay, it turns out it wasn't that hard to pick up another four lightbulbs from the first world.  Oh well.  Still, now that I've gotten into the second world, I still feel frustrated and annoyed.  Again, I guess puzzle games just aren't my thing, but certainly having me stay this long by keeping the Steam trading cards drip-dripping like this has only increased my dissatisfaction.
(Disclosure: I acquired this game from a promotion offering a free Steam key of this game, at the Indie Gala Store.)

For a 2 bucks game, this one packs a lot of fun. Its mechanics are not great, the combat feel clumsy sometimes and later in the game your character got way overpowered with all the spells learnt and all gear upgraded. Evilquest is heavily based on a NES game called Crystalis and it gets the job done if you're expecting a good old school like game. Same thing with some monsters. There is also some little things in the game that looks like it is unfinished, like the jumping and charged shot abilities. Your character is told to use these features to solve puzzles, but I think only twice I've used the jump and charged shot to solve puzzles.
Overall it's a funny game to play in short bursts, as you can finish it in about 3-6 hours. I took longer because I like to explore every bit of the map and such. Also the funny bits of the game are entertaining, as you play with the villain this time. I'd recommend it for its low price if you like casual Zelda like clones. But if you are looking for a more retro feel and a challenging game, you should probably avoid this one. I'll give it a 6/10.

I had a bit of fun with the game. I enjoyed building up my dynasty. I enjoyed attempting to climb the political ladder while preparing for a revolution. I enjoyed the satisfaction of advancing my station in society. But the game just seems unfinished with broken or strange mechanics, nonsense dialogue, and game breaking glitches.
Building a dynasty is cool. You get married, you have kids. Simple. But having a flourishing dynasty is useless because you're only allowed to control three characters at a time, and if you stop controlling one at any time, they're gone for good. If you have a member halway up the political ladder and you need to control another member of your family so they can start having kids of their own, you're out of luck. You have to make a choice. Do most of my kids end up unmarried and childless, or do I abandon my political career for them?
Some of the broken mechanics involved the game permanently being stuck on pause and reloading a previous save does nothing. Others are the strange way you manage your dynasty, down to the weirdest dialogue. I understand it's a sim, but when my wife and mistress are both referred to as "him", or when people spout off random dialogue during a discussion, it breaks the immersion a bit. Another broken mechanic is the EXTREMELY limited space in which you can build. The maps are small and the slightest hill will prevent you from placing a building. This leaves you with massive wide open spaces in an already tight fit. The only way I found to slightly get around this was to place different buildings in the same spot before they could be built in order to form a grotesque super structure.
But good luck playing the game if you decide to buy it anyway. There's no manual.
Ultimately, I never got to complete the game. The game ended up breaking after I had basically taken over the whole town. Would I play it if it was more polished and didn't feature a stifling dynasty tree? Yeah. It's not a bad concept. They just didn't do a good job of it.

Launch server issues? (probably fixed by time you read this)
===============
Did you hear about the little boy who died in the server room?  His name was Jason.
"Database login failure"
Ok, first off, there have been server issues... in saying that, I've been fortunate and have, in total, had to wait about 1 hour.
Now we've got past that, let's discuss this game, this amazing game.
Background
========
There are 7 counsellors and Jason.  Jason, an axe, spear, pickaxe, fireaxe wielding looney.  The 7 helpless counsellors have to escape by:-
a. Killing Jason - GOODLUCK with that!  More chance of solving a rubix cube in under 5 seconds.
b. Finding a fuse, fixing the phone box, calling the cops and then escaping through one randomly chosen exit
c. Find a battery, keys and fuel then drive a car/boat to one of 2 exits!
Jason meanwhile has 5 abilities, knives and traps.  The abilities, which have cooldowns after use, consist of:-
Moprh - teleport to anywhere on map
Shift - Allows Jason to run faster than Usain Bolt and suddenly appearing whereever you desire.
Sense - Jason can reveal counsellors nearby
Stalk - Turns off the 'I'm chasing you music' and hides him from counsellor mini-map
Rage - This is automatically enabled towards the end, all of his abilities are more powerful, last longer and chances are... you'll die if you don't have an escape route available.
Once Jason has caught up with a counsellor there are SO many ways to dispatch his victim once in his grasp.  I won't spoil them here and I wouldn't watch a video of a kill montage as that'll spoil it.  Just enjoy it!  They're truely gruesome!  It's great!
There are a number of Jason's to choose from, each with different strengths and weaknesses, which affect cooldown times for Jason's abilities, added strength to smash doors down quicker, swim faster etc.  It's all about how you prefer to play.
My counsellor experience
==================
Playing as a counsellor is tricky.  Do you move slowly and silently whilst trying to avoid detection - but remember Jason gets stronger the longer the game goes on or do you run about like a madman, making Jason's senses go wild and sooner or later he'll be honing in on your position!
My advice - a bit of both!  Start running around at the entering multiple cabins, opening as many drawers as possible and if Jason hasn't paid you a visit wait until you hear the first death.  That's when you want to move silently.
Counsellors are easily scared, seeing a dead body or being chased by Jason adds to their fear, which will make it harder to see and remove the HUD.
You can find traps, weapons and other weapons to help defend yourself against Jason.
Chances are... you'll die.. in a horrific way!
My Jason experience
==============
It feels great to be overpowered, but a well skilled counsellor can put up a good fight!  Remember, the longer it takes you to kill the counsellor you're chasing, the others are tooling up and possibly half on their way to the great escape.
Some of the funniest experiences are when the counsellors get a car, you can stop the car - just walk/shift into it.  Dragging a counsellor out of the car window and then forcing his head on your spear is a sight to behold and will provide a laugh a minute!
Only one person can be Jason so there is a 1 in 8 chance... so enjoy it while you can!
Overall
=====
Absolutely loving this game.
Really enjoy playing as counsellor and absolutely love playing as Jason - who wouldn't right?!  The game feels well balanced - sometimes 2 or 3 escape, sometimes none and very rarely everyone.
For £30 - I've spent more money on worse games.  For me, the game is a 9/10, because I love Jason, Friday 13th, the whole hide and seek and the gruesome kills/deaths!  For everyone else - I imagine an 7/10 or 8/10.
If this game sounds of interest to you... then get it!
So to be fair, without bias... this game gets an.......
EIGHT of out TEN
8/10
+Hide and seek simulator
+Jason
+Gruesome kills/deaths
+Balanced

Very enthralling story set in the war in Afghanistan. Instead of taking the Call of Duty-approach of jumping between set-pieces all over the world you jump between a couple of different characters from a few special operations units carrying out small-scale attacks against (mainly) the Taliban. I loved this concept, it had me hooked from the get-go and got me through the entire campaign in one sitting. I played on the highest difficulty level and it lasted about 4,5 hours (well balanced difficulty, punishing you for getting hit instead of relying on bullet-sponge enemies in infinite waves).
The story is a bit on the short side but at the same time completely without filler and loaded with well-written characters and thought out missions. It's more "Hollywood-realism" than power fantasy, meaning the missions feel credible while you never feel like Rambo. You still mow down hundreds of enemies á la the end of "Fury" but the prescense of AI-controlled squad mates make it feel like a team effort. Like previously mentioned, I really liked this take on story-telling and found it somewhat original for the genre.
What I didn't like about the game was how limited the graphics options were. The game deactivates options it considers "out of your league", meaning I could not play this game at anything higher than 1440p "Medium" settings. As in there wasn't any options but "Low" and "Medium". Ridiculous. Fortunately the game still looks great and is very well optimized.
I have not played the multiplayer and have no interest in doing so. The single-player however is one of the better ones I've played from the last decade. I loved it and would highly recommend this game  based on that experience.

You can keep your world thriving by consistently making new cities, consistently placing down gods or special units to turn the balance towards a losing side to re-instate "balance", which is the key in this game. Then you watch your actions have effects as you hit "end turn". And then you do it again, and again, and again, and again. No variety, no excitement. Just the same strategies again. Place some buildings, end turn. Place special units. End turn. Etc. The game was honesty better on paper than it is in-game.
I give it a 3/10. Now it's not buggy in any way, so that's a pro, but that's all it really has going for it. It's too boring, and games are suppoed to be fun. This doesn't fit the bill, avoid it, save your money.

This is a very unique game, combining automatic turn based combat with godlike with city manager, it is hard to place this in any particular catagory. The game itself is nice, although there are some features that are not so likeable. The game itself feels like a board game, and could easily be played as a board game, which is a great thing if you like board games! (Note, I am the founder of the Tabletop RPG Gamers League, so you could say I like board games!) Anyway, enough said for now, let us proceed to the pros and cons list.
Pros-
Literally A Board! It feels and looks like a board game! Moving tiles around, characters, stat cards, and so forth, it just is a cool concept! Anyway, this isn't a pro for all people, so let us continue.
Audio/Music, the music is great and doesn't get old. The sound effects are so-so, but the sounds definitely fit the game so I am happy with them.
Gameplay, the gameplay is very cool. You are a godlike being who manages different cities, trying to promote both peace and war at the same time. Although you can't have a "Endless" game, the gameplay is doesn't need an "Endless" mode in order to be good. You get to change the entire world if you like, from the tiles to the bandits to the empires themselves, change literally everything with a simple click or two.
Combat, the combat is entirely automatic. The empires will build armies for you. The empires will send their armies to die for you. All you have to do is sit back and watch, and sometimes scold an empire that gets to powerful (By scold, I mean brutally smite off the map).
Cons-
Combat, but combat was also a pro? Well, for some people the fact that you can't interact with the characters/pieces/armies directly is somewhat disappointing. Personally, I like the way that they did this, but to each there own I guess.
Multiplayer, the multiplayer isn't really there yet, it doesn't really advance the gameplay any by having more people playing it. It just complicates things, but even so, that is also part of the fun of it I guess. Personally, I don't like how they did the multiplayer, but oh well.
Conclusion-
I definitely recommend this game. It literally feels like I am playing a board game! It is also very fun to play this game local hotseat, having each person control one nation, nation vs. nation! Although the game wasn't developed for this kind of gameplay, it is definitely fun to do no less. If I had to say a way that they could improve this game, it would be to recreate the multiplayer aspect of it by having a more nation vs. nation set up like I described above. It would be more like a Age of Empires feel and would give the game something unique to get more people to play/buy it.
May your adventures be many and always end in reward!
-Donoknight, Founder of Tabletop RPG Gamers League

I have found god games fall into one of two categories. They are either overextended terrain generators, (Reus, From Dust) or they are basically RTS with magic (Black and White 2, Spore). This game is a refreshing break from that. The premise of the game is something I've never before seen in a strategy game, it puts you in a devils advocate situation. Rather than trying to make the Greeks conquer the Norse or vice versa, you are trying to keep them alive despite their unending war. You control what and where they build, and you have some control over the terrain, but what each archer, horseman or knight does is beyond your control. And it is awesome. It is so different than any other strategy game that exists.
Pros
-- Gameplay is unique, a new type of strategy
-- Beautiful visuals
-- Fantastic Soundtrack
-- Immense Replayability
Cons
-- This game is not for everyone, it is not your Civilization Clone
-- Can get boring and tedious

Was enjoyable for a couple games.  Don't expect this one to hold you several hundred hours, but if you can deal with that, it's a unique premise worth playing around with.  Higher difficulties are actually much easier and more enjoyable as there's more bandits to deal with and units level quickly.  My first game after the tutorial was on the second hardest setting and there were several close moments, but I was never really in danger of outright losing.
My main problem with the game was the interface.  It's very rudimentary.  When you have multiple towns, not being able to see which of your military bases have had their supports destroyed (and are thus aren't producing units) was the most annoying bit.  It doesn't help that destroyed buildings don't say what they were.  Being able to plan out both sides at the same time, and flipping back and forth, would've been nice as it's hard to remember who has what and who needs what.
The scoring system is a bit obnoxious, but does add a nice little twist so you're not just making perfect towns that don't do anything.
Overall, I came away rather impressed with the concept, but in no way craving another game.  Execution isn't horrible or great; things work well enough to get the point across, but not well enough to provide a ton of depth.

You spend half your time in short, narrow corridors that make sniping impossible. This wouldn't be so bad, but your only weapons other than your rifle are a machinegun you barely get ammo for (enemies drop 2 to 8 bullets) and a pistol that fires once a second and does next to no damage.
The sniping segments are almost as bad. Most of the time every enemy in the area magically knows exactly where you are the first shot you fire. Again, this wouldn't be so bad if no for the fact that they can accurately hit you with a machinegun from 1000 meters away. Every bullet you take throws off your aim and drains the breath meter that lets you make precise shots, so having four for five enemies shooting at you makes sniping very fustating. There is very little opportunity to move to a different location, as there is usually one clear spot you are supposed to snipe from. Enemies barely react to anything other than a headshot: you can shoot a running enemy in the leg and he just keeps running.
The only good thing about this game is the kill cam, and even that gets old after the 40th or 50th time you see someone's skull explode.
