The Good:  A unique take on city-building with some clever ideas and a unique setting.  Mixing RPG, business management, Sims-style social interaction management and city sim elements into a totally unique genre all its own.  Building a business empire is surprisingly satisfying, and the open-ended gameplay can keep things interesting in terms of character variety.
The Bad:  Balance is utterly terrible, two professions earn flat-out more money than any other, the other two can barely be self-supporting and will take generations (literally) to build to a comparable level, by that time the unforgiving AI will have left you far behind.  The game presents the appearance of great depth, but it's ultimately a rather shallow experience with most paths being dead-ends compared to the most lucrative.  The amount of micromanagement is severe, and often frustrating given the time-scale needed to acheive significant gains.  Gameplay gets repeitive with numerous game-breaking powerful paths (like spamming bribes until everyone loves you, while selling endless stacks of herring), if you try not to use those broken paths the AI steamrolls you.
The Bottom Line:  A great game marred by bugs and poorly thought out gameplay.
You'd like this if:  You're a fan of city-building with RPG elements, you don't mind micromanagement, You thought the only thing The Sims was missing was a poorly-thought-out business sim and the ability to firebomb your neighbors.

I bought this game because I like visual novels and it had a lot of good reviews praising the story and characters. I am now really confused...because those are the two things which made this a really weak experience for me.
The plot jumps about seemingly at random, there is little apparent structure as characters move back and forth from house to house, dreamworld to reality at the drop of a hat. The characters, of which there are many, are all rather dull and flat. I didn't care about any of them, they just didn't feel like actual people. Characters like Nanami are pretty much just props, a goal for the male protagonist to aim for. The rest of the female characters are basically defined by their love interests, while the males are likewise one-sided. Hisashi has his
, the protagonist has his search for the killer/Nanami, Tetsuya has
. It's like the characters are all designed around one concept, or one role, and haven't been fleshed out beyond that.
The protagonist storms about like a shoddily-written Hamlet, alternating between being generally inept and violent (although one of the bad endings does sort of address this?). Characters talk in circles, with conversations lasting twice as long they need to. Characters talk about their backstories for no apparent reason, with people who arguably should know already know these things - the exposition is always clumsy.
The world is not convincing. No police force? Really...The protagonist doesn't know the names of the two supposedly ruling families? I would have been able to deal with the police force thing if it hadn't only been mentioned when the protagonist came to the point where any normal person would call the police. You can't blame everything on the translation, although that is also clunky and awkward.
My dislike of the writing aside, there were some good plot points and I liked the general darkness of it - though the game frequently veered into melodrama and a childish effort to be 'the most brutal' and 'the most tragic'. There's something very teenage about it all, particularly the approach to violence and love. There is potential, but its buried deep.
The art is very inconsistent. I see a large numbers of artists worked on the game. Individually all their art is good, but together is makes the game look like a patchwork of art, with varying styles and levels of detail. It was particularly jarring to see two sprites of different style on screen at once, for example Reiae and Saki. Some backgrounds are drawn, others a re photographs - one scene apparently takes place in a grocery store, but the background photo looks to be from a shoe store.
The music redeems the game a little. Theres a nice variety, so instead of just one song being used over and over for the important moments the soundtrack is a little more tailored to each moment of the game.
The game is long, so there's a lot of content for your money.

Maps. They are HUGE and the coords are very confusing.
The ability to choose a spawn point, or CREATE one---such as with a nest or a den of some sort acting a respawn after you die. That way it doesn't take packs/herds 30 minutes to regroup after being killed. ITs extremely frustrating, especially for new players that don't know the maps.

The ability to back up rather than turn around, that way we don't fall off a cliff when we get too close by accident.

Add a flying dino into the game---I'd kill to be a pteranadon, even if you never added another dino ever again.

There's one thing I'd like you to know about this game first: it's not made to entertain you, at least not in a way most games that share genre elements and themes with it. This game is about solitude and maybe also about doubts and confusion, at least for me it is.
Knock-Knock won't tell you what to do and why, it just tells you what you can do, like you can walk around, fix lights, unlock doors, "restore" the rooms of your house and hide from those disturbing entities who haunt your house, but it's up to you to figure out what's going on.
While you play the game it plays you. Yet don't think Knock-Knock is something like those art games with no gameplay and "too deep for you" kind of narration. It has interesting, maybe a little repetitive gameplay that allows you to experiment with your playstyle.
Though I have to warn you, you might get a Game Over in the end, it's not a bug, just a weird way to tell you you were trapped in the nightmare for too long and you've lost your chance to save your sanity in the end.
At last but not the least I can't end this review without telling you how much passion and effort was put into creating and fine-tuning the atmosphere through art and sound.
Again, this is a game you'll either love or you'll hate, but if you love it, Knock-Knock might easily end up to be one of the best games of 2013 for you as much as it is for me.

Knock-Knock is a little rumination about what is more dire, demons from within or from the outside? In this game you must figure out all by yourself how to play it to revel in its entirety. There are general rules told imperceptibly but each one of them has sides it takes time and retries to grasp. Knock-Knock is frustrating, hard and irritating at times, but it remains captivatingly horrifying all through the end. Lend it your ears, pay attention and believe in what you see or decide not to — control the outcome with the help of your senses.
With ingenious intended glitches like those from Anodyne, beautifully drawn visual style similar to Don't Starve's and cunning survival horror mechanics which really do improve the genre. Knock-Knock, despite not being the same game it was intended originally, is still a "phenomenon" which you absolutely should observe.

What does it mean to be human? Does it mean the biological organism, or just the mind? Do you, in fact, need a body in order to have an identity? Can the mind exist without the body? If so, at what sacrifice? Perhaps you may ask yourself these questions while playing SOMA. Perhaps not. Either way, you will take something away from playing this game. You may argue it should have been faster paced, it should not have included certain enemies, or it should have given your moral choices more weight in the direction of the plot so that the experience was perfect. But just like your character at the end, you are confronted with the sobering truth that you can't have your cake and eat it. Life is compromise, and moving forward.

Have you known a Grandparent or Aunt/Uncle who's house you've been to so many times you can't count.  When you're forced to visit them you end up playing board games alone in their cluttered back room. You always find yourself bored. Even though the room is cluttered your relative never takes the time to show you anything they have. When you ask they just shrug you off. Then one day, they pass on, and the family jumps in and starts dividing all the stuff they had in their house and you learn they had a lot of cool stuff. Actually there was a lot to learn and explore, but the place was so cluttered, and your relative never explained much of what they collected.
That's the best way I can describe Skyward Collapse. The single tutorial level gives you a limited/basic understanding of what it's trying to accomplish then sets you out into the world to play god. You find yourself with 2 civilizations, with slightly varied dependencies, different unit types with their own pros and cons, a cluttered interface, and you have to play them both at the same time and keep them from killing each other while they attempt to kill each other.
IMO a tutorial that perhaps took a few levels to complete would have helped this game out a lot. There's no hand holding here and usually I don't like that type of design, but in Skyward Collapse it could have been a refreshing boost in understanding the complex systems in place here.
Also, the building icons are cluttered. Yes, they are divided up into categories, but I still found myself lost a lot of the time. The dependencies between buildings aren't very well explained and I kept backtracking to understand what I did wrong. I played the tutorial level about 5 times. There's just not enough clean design or helpful tutorials to get the average player involved.
I'm also, not a fan of playing against myself. Well, balancing against myself really. You have to build civilizations that will ultimately destroy each other, but you need to build them in ways they complement their destructive potentials into an almost deadlock.

That does sound like a great idea, but honestly it's just a bad execution. I really think this game would have benefited from a little TLC on the GUI and a few extra tutorial levels that would walk you through certain aspects one at a time. The way Skyward Collapse is presented you end up feeling like you're playing a board game, alone, in your Grandmothers' clutter back room.

So far I'm having tons of fun, but I see things in the core gameplay that could still be enhanced.
* When you hit a note there's no immediate ping to tell you you got it, so sometimes it feels you're just pressing buttons and stuff is happening. Adding some kind of minimalist sound to when you hit a note properly would enhance the experience plenty.
* While it touts the game as a blend of a rythm game and an rpg, what really bugs me is that you get damaged from enemy attacks but ALSO when you miss a note in your string. So sometimes I'm having to deal with a tough enemy, get distracted and before I know it I'm dead. This so far is the biggest sticking point to me. It makes the game feel less like an rpg/rythm game hybrid and more like a normal rythm game where on top of everything someone punches me every couple of seconds.
Despite those complaints, I'm actually enjoying the game a lot. The soundtrack is varied and enjoyable and the battles can be super challenging (if a bit cheap sometimes, but that's RPGs for you). Give it a try.

I have a soft spot for Quake II - it was the first FPS game I ever played online, way back on our old 56k router. And it was playable at those speeds, too!
Quake II is a classic shooter. There's no hand-holding here - you're plopped in the middle of a war-zone with nothing but your pistol and wits to get you started. Enemies are plentiful and in some instances, tough. And if you don't do some exploration to find extra ammo and armor, you'll find yourself in trouble quickly.
The graphics don't look too amazing when set against 2013 standards, but they certainly deserve to be appreciated, for a game originally released in 1997. Sound is sparse, a bit like what you'll find in games like Doom, but without the constant ambient music.
I enjoy playing this game every now and then for a little nostalgia, but I usually end up playing for longer than I thought I would, just because the simplified, raw experience can be so much fun.

A very original and unique kind of game. No "this is the good guy, this is the bad guy." No "kill all the other guys." Just - "keep both sides alive!" It's a challenge I've never faced in a game before. It's all about balance, a theme which is not often addressed in games. The music feels a bit off - like they just grabbed a few random tracks they liked and threw them in there. The pacing is pretty slow, but there are options to speed it up a bit. Overall, I'm enjoying this one so far, and it was worth getting.

Quake II was always a bit strange for me. I was expecting Shambers; I found cyborgs. Yet, when I consider the co-operative experience of Quake (1) versus Quake II, I always find myself saying that Quake II was a real turning point for id Software - a plot, objectives, and level progression that made sense. I love shooting Vores and Ogres as much as the next guy, but Quake (1) had a decidedly single-player focus.
Missing out on Quake II is missing out the adolescence of 3D graphics accelerators in the PC world. With both software and hardware (OpenGL) renderers, it bridged the gap in the PC space at the time and showed the power of 3D accelerators to me: the atomospere looks significantly more immersive with OpenGL at 60 FPS.

Having just finished the game on hard, I can safely say that for anyone who has any interest in Crystalis or similair action RPGs to give this one a try. It's not perfect but it does satisfy the fun I had playing the old 16 and 8 bit games of this nature. Also you get to play from the bad guy's perspective. Too many times games that take this route either wimp out and either A: make you really a misunderstood good guy or B: make your enemies even worse then you are. EvilQuest does neither, you're just straight up evil. That being said the rest of the writing is a bit off. It seems at times that the game isn't sure whether it's tounge in cheek or deathly serious. You'll have some humourous dialouge in one scene that's way over the top and in the next be talking to someone whose family was murdered and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ It can be off putting to say the least.
Gameplay also has its ups and downs. Everything controls very well and the spells in the game are very satisfying to use but they also bring up one of the other downsides. The spells are extremely overpowered. Seriously just dump your points in intelligence and you can whip through this game even on hard. While this is a downside I can't deny there being a certain perverse glee in wiping out a whole screen of enemies and eating the bosses for lunch half-way through the game.
The one thing that really bothers me though are some of the enemies (mostly the bosses) hitboxes. This ones kind of hard to explain but it's the worst on the first boss a giant knight. I was standing behind him but for some reason his helmet was hitting me and killing me because the game thought I was touching him. This problem occurs in a few other bosses and considering that this wasn't a problem in actual SNES titles it's a bit unforgiveable here. In fact I almost quit right there but I am glad I didn't as the game is much better then its opening dungeon would suggest.
All in all give this one a try. Despite its downfalls it is still one of the better "retro style" games out there in a sea of similair games that are much worse. Cheers, I hope this review was useful.

Medal of Honour is a good game, although it's weighed down by a few major flaws.
Play it. I recommend it. But bare these things in mind:
Firstly, the single player campaign is too short. Now that's always a sideways compliment for a game and still holds here. I've literally just finished the campaign to write this review and as of now I've played only four hours TOTAL. I feel the major contributor to the short duration of the game is that it's so scripted. Really, the whole game might as well just have you on-tracks and have you shoot as it moves you, for a few brief hours. Everything in every mission is planned and pathed to the T, so making a game longer than four hours is likely unfeasable for the developers. What there IS of the campaign is great and feels cut and polished, save for a sudden ending that leaves you wishing there was a more climactic finale. It feels like there could have been one more final mission.
Secondly, the cutscenes are thick and plenty and most of the cool experiences in the game happen when your screen and controls have been wrestled from you. These cutscenes (often simply arguments between higher-ranked military personell) can go on for a long time and completely yank you from the pace of the game. Too many times does the game slow you down with scripted pauses and slow cutscenes where you could EASILY at least have control of the camera with a little shifting here and there, but no, your character's head is too frequently seized by unseen hands and twisted this way and that.
I don't enjoy playing online multiplayer. These problems I have outlined are less likely to be prevalent in MP, which I'm not reviewing, but if you're a single-player gamer like me, these problems will be the lowlights of the game.
Regarding good points, the game is beautiful, well scripted, and tells a neatly anastamosing story of three different characters ploughing through reams of (the same five models of) bad guys. It's fun and feels smooth. I'm always a sniper and stealth shooter at heart when it comes to FPS, and this game feels tailored to that, although there are some great beserker moments when you're handed a huge weapon too.
The scenery changes a little, but set in the snowy mountains of the middle east it's hard to vary that kind of thing. Some of the quad bike driving and gunnery missions are a nice change of pace in the game too. There are a few lovely and heartfelt moments in the plot of the campaign that make you see a little of the TRUE side of what soldiers do 'out there' but I won't spoil those for you here. They're really the best part of the game.
I bought this game as I'd played Medal of Honour: Airborne and loved it. This has the same soul (and suffers some of the same drawbacks such as short campaign.) But it's a worthy successor.
I'd recommend the game for it's well crafted gameplay and story, although the over-scripting has led to a short campaign that's padded with way too many cutscenes and stuffing. I'd wager almost a quarter of the game is cutscenes or seize-your-head and make you watch moments. But for the experience, and especialy if it's on sale, play Medal of Honor.

I bought this game thinking that it was just a mystery-horror VN but it wasn’t what I was expecting as it delves at the mystery-horror of human capability. How some or sometimes even one past experience can be the driving force that dictates our future and makes us blinded by the truth. Sometimes we know the truth, rarely do we accept it, and it is often that we dismiss it for fear of being hurt.
Human emotions are curious things, as two people can have similar experiences but their perception of the world can be starkly different. Revenge can be seen in two different ways.
1.	You’ve taken everything away from me; I have nothing left, what’s left to lose?
2.	An eye for an eye makes everyone blind.
With Notch, I wasn’t expecting to be brought to tears due to one particular character, Rika, her back-story and one other particular part of her story. I won’t go into any detail, as I don’t want to spoil it for people.
This is one of the very few VN’s were I was overcome with so many different emotions, which pleasantly surprised me, as man’s heart can be full of darkness yet a light still burns.
On a side note, I found that the game didn’t auto save, I only realised this after playing 4 hours and when I went to continue there was no save file. The ‘Escape’ button opens the menu for the game that allows you to manually save, also I found that the ‘control’ button was a life saver, it skips the text that I have read, so I can continue with different routes without getting bored of re-reading the same thing.

is one of those unique visual novels you only come across every once in a blue moon. Thought evoking and story rich, this made for a very good read. I completed it in two 8hr sessions (yes, it was that addicting!), and that was only for my first playthrough.
The protagonist, Yuhito Asakawa, and his childhood sweetheart, Nanami Shio, reside in a remote town that has been long forgotten by the rest of the world. We first meet Yuhito and his beloved in a dream realm of horror, already hoping that the two lovebirds will find a way to escape the nightmare unharmed. And if Yuhito thought that was bad enough, his reality was about to get much worse. His once peaceful little town had been painted red by an elusive murderer, where the victims were all young girls. It is then that he decides to embark on this difficult journey to catch the killer and bring them to justice. Along the way, he'll make some interesting friends, struggle with reality and illusions, and grow braver and more determined with each step he takes.
^That's just my little summary - short, sweet, and to the point, without spoiling too much of the story. Seriously, it took me 16hrs to complete one playthrough. ONE! And there are 14 different endings! So trust me, there is SO MUCH MORE to this story than what you'll find in the reviews (unless you're looking for spoilers). Bottom line is, if you're considering this vn, then do yourself a favor and add it to your collection. You won't regret it! :)
***Also, the narration can be pretty gorey at times, so just be aware of that in case that's not your cup o' tea.
If you want to go through all of the endings, press [F] to skip all of the text you've already read. That button will be your new best friend ;)

The Isle. Ah, what can i say about the isle?
The Isle is an extremely early access game, which seems to be pretty obvious, due to it being plastered on the front of it. Playing as a dinosaur is admittedly very fun, and i feel like many people overrate the game due to that fact. So i will be rather harsh on it in my review:
The game has absolutely ZERO content. While i can say that it's fun for a dinosaur lover like myself, as an open world dinosaur game has been one of my largest dreams, (didn't much like the primal carnage jist of things) for a non dinosaur game lover, this game could be severely dissapointing. It has six dinosaur classes. There are a few notable ones that stand out to me.
At the moment, T-rex is the most disturbingly powerful, and can kill pretty much anything. Any more than a pair of t-rexes is just outright unfair. If this game has any hope of being balanced, the nerf hammer will surely strike t-rex.
In the current stage of the game, Gallimimus is decently in the overpowered realm. It has nigh infinite sprint, making walking a passtime, since it can run for pretty much ever. It is an herbivore, which means it can eat plants and drink water, making it able to sustain itself without putting itself in harms way. With the ability to outrun ANY ingame creature, and the ability to sustain itself without ever coming into contact with a predator, it is very easy to play. Its only downside is that it has the least health of anything in the game, but that doesn't matter when nothing can catch you.
Shantungosaurus falls into the realm of underpower, in my opinion. A few classes, T-rex and Carnotaurus (I will speak of carnotaurus later) can easily dispatch a single Shantungosaurus without much of a difficulty, however, the latter of the two might have a challenge if they aren't experienced. It is a large herbivore that looks similar to an Iguanodon. As of right now, it has zero defence from a T-rex, as it is slower and less physically capable of dealing with one than vice versa. The only way to defend itself is a herd, but seeing as T-rex is often a more popular dinosaur, (Which ironically usually leads to there being more carnivores than herbivores) It will often be outnumbered anyway.
Carnotaurus, for one, falls into the balanced realm, in my opinion. It is a capable fighter, yet cannot deal with herds of herbivores, even if it has a pack itself. (Unless the herbivores are extremely outnumbered) This, i feel, is how all carnivores should be, just in different segments of the food chain. It can kill the herbivore classes if they are alone, and, even a lone T-rex if the Carnotaurus is sufficiently skilled.
Austroraptor may fall into neutral or overpowered realms after it receives its pounce back, but as of the current state, you'd be better off playing as a puddle of water. Before, it required its pounce to do pretty much any amount of damage to anything other than other Raptors and Gallimimus. Now, with its pounce currently in the process of being fixed, i cannot see anyone sane playing it and expecting to have a fair chance. For now, this class is SEVERELY underpowered, and beyond functionality.
Peurtasaurus falls into the realm of SEVERELY UNDERPOWERED. It can do NO damage, and although it has ALOT of health, it is very SLOW. It is what some people may refer to as Longnecks, (this makes me very angry, as i am a dinonerd) And what more seasoned players refer to as Peurtasaurus, its' proper name. Right now, as it can do no damage, it is a matter of time before you succumb to an angry T-rex. I hear it is getting fixed, and as little as less than 24 hours after this review goes up, however. Perhaps when it is fixed again, it may be a balanced class.
The Isle is probably wonderful upon first inspection, but it quickly becomes BORING, TEDIOUS, and a CHORE, if you find yourself in the wrong server at the wrong time, just trying to have fun. The game could be much better. but, it is surprisingly sufficient for EARLY ALPHA ACCESS. Don't buy it if you're not a dino nerd. Yet.

Playing Driftmoon is a bit like reading an old, quality children's story, back when they weren't just written for children.  The graphics are simple, the controls are straightforward, the story is definitely aimed at the younger set and the skills aren't terribly complex.  That said, combat is quick and fun, with just enough variation and challenge to be enjoyable without being overbearing, and there are enough skill choices and options to feel like you're both making progress, and making the lead character your own.
If anything, my biggest complaint is that there isn't quite enough game to fully explore the possibilities of crafting, gear and harder enemies that might have come into play with a larger game or a longer story.  Not that the story provided is too short -- it's exactly the right size.  And even if it was too short, there's a modding tool, so there may be community offerings soon too.
Graphics 2/5, Gameplay 3/5, Story 3/5, Overall 4/5.  The whole is definitely greater than the sum of its parts.  Worth playing.

I love this game.

Driftmoon - Very interesting ARPG.
If you like an ARPG that there is no need to rush, and "it is" worth looking around to find all those little hidden things in each area, then Driftmoon is for you. I have not had such fun in an RPG game for sometime. But I must say for a two person team Driftmoon is excellent fun indeed. Some of the NPC's are rather unique and have some interesting story interaction, querky comments, and the oddest of vendors you find here and there.
I have had a great time already playing through Driftmoon, and some fun looking around trying to find everything I can on each and every area. I recommend reading al the comments from the NPC's (As I know a lot of us skip through the conversations quickly in most rpg's) read the books and notes you find, they give you a lot of clues to your quests, and lore of monsters around the world.
The quests though not brain taxing to work out, fit into the gameworld well, make you think just enough so not to get yourself flustered about how to complete the quests and I have had a good chuckle or two reading some of the dialogue from the npc's that assist and also attack you.
Skill system is rudamentary, but works really well, you also have a stats section for Strength, Constitution, Intel, Dexterity and Agility. A talent system with passive and activated skills to use on your travels. A basic crafting system to make potions, arrows etc - which is made from found bits and pieces around the world and from creatures.
It also comes with a mod toolset - not looked into much yet, but does seem to be interesting. There is already some mods out and I am sure many more to come.
For the price on Steam, Driftmoon is a great addition to anyone who enjoys RPG games.
Well done to the Two person Dev Team to bring a great little title out to the RPG gaming community.

I was given my copy of the game for free and have been helping playtest The Metronomicon for several months. That being said, I will be giving my full and honest opinion of the game.
==The Concept==
The Metronomicon is the fusion of rhythm style Rock Band and Guitar Hero style lane gameplay with a fully fleshed out RPG with unique and voiced characters, skills, equipment, and detailed storyline.
==Gameplay==
The Metronomicon immediately throws you a curveball going with four lanes of notes instead of just one. Each lane corresponds to one of your four party members. To cast various abilities set by the player, notes must be played on rhythm with the music in order to charge up and cast their abilities. Think of Chrono Trigger style active combat except instead of just waiting for a bar to fill up, you play musical notes to charge up your abilities.
Each song plays out with monsters coming at you. Defeating them earns you currency you can use to unlock songs as well as a chance at equipment drops. Each stage also comes with a mini-boss that can be defeated for a special type of currency to further enhance your party members.
As you defeat enemies and stages your party members will level up (just like an RPG!) giving them access to new skills and making them stronger. As you continue your adventure through the various lands, you’ll be gearing up, refining your character loadouts, and farming up loot drops just like an RPG but to some dope♥♥♥♥♥music! Normally I’m not a particular fan of the straight up Rock Band/Guitar Hero gameplay, but the RPG framework tying everything together struck the perfect chord with me. (GET IT?! That’s a music joke!)
==Music==
With the included original songs composed for the game, the Metronomicon offers 50 tracks, some with and some without lyrics. The soundtrack is amazing. Every song was hand choreographed and feels great to play on all the difficulty settings. I personally play on Easy and Medium difficulty, with Hard being a little out of my league. For those rhythm game fanatics out there, I think Hard will definitely prove a decent challenge.
==Controls==
The game can be played with a controller, mouse and keyboard, and even a dance pad, or quite frankly, just about any device that can be bound to keys! I play with a mouse and keyboard and have had no issues. The controls can be completely customized, so find a setup that works and is comfortable for you.
==Conclusion==
As I stated above, I received the game for free and have been playtesting it. Take everything here with a grain of salt of course. This review has probably sounded like a big ad for the game, but honestly, any negatives I found I had with it while playtesting were changed or addressed during development. I love this game. I wouldn’t have already put 30+ hours into it already if I didn’t love it. I know I’ll be playing it all over again now that the game is being released.
I can definitely recommend this title to anyone who enjoys this genre of gaming.

Rhythm players really need to give this a hard look, because the game not only combines two genres rather well, it feels rather fresh in the Rhythm genre in particular. It's the game design and how it uniquely emphasizes the strategy element that really shines here: every decisions that the developers made seems to have been well thought out. The chaos of trying not only to juggle the 4 different characters and their spells, but doing that while keeping yourself alive and noticing elemental weaknesses and the such, it all really works. While it's more leinant in the rhythm genre then others, it works due to the RPG elements. And the soundtrack for the most part gives a good variety of songs that are of a reasonable quality, despite there being a few duds in there. Granted, there is a rock/pop focus, but every now and again you'll get a surprise of a 8 bit tune. In the end, The Metronomicon not only feels a lot different from a lot of the rhythm games on the market, it ends up being addictive and something that you won't want to put down. A definite day one purchase for rhythm gamers out there, and a great gateway game to the genre for those who have always wondered if they'd enjoy it.

Story - you have to visit several different kingdoms to cure people cursed by a witch.  The interesting side effect of this story is that each kingdom is totally tailored to the type of person you are curing.  For example, one person is a painter, and all the puzzles and HOP's involve paintings and sculptures.  In another kingdom, you are curing a scientist, and all the puzzles and HOP's involve machinery and lab equipment.  I thought this was kind of neat, as it added a lot of variety to the game.
Graphics - Decent, with a lot of little interesting animations to add to the atmosphere.
HOPs - Good variety with list based ones, find x amount of one type of thing, and the put objects back into the HOP type.  One HOP that I particularly enjoyed was a circuit board where parts had been ripped out or damaged.  You had a list of parts and tools that you had to use to repair it.
Puzzles - Like the other "Echoes of the Past" game on Steam, this game really shines in the puzzle and mini-game department.  It's packed with them, with tremendous variety and originality.  Most of them were even different than the previous "Echoes of the Past".  I love it when developers really put the effort into fun, original puzzles and mini-games, instead of just putting different graphics on the same old puzzles.
Features - unlike it's predecessor, this "Echoes of the Past" does have a map, with instant travel and indications of stuff to do.  There is a hint system, strategy guide, bonus chapter, and more puzzles and mini-games in the "Extras" section.
Length - About 6 hours on Advanced setting with no guide/hints.  Another 1 1/2 hours for the bonus chapter.  So quite lengthy as HOG's go.
Overall, an excellent HOG, and highly recommended.

Quake II is a long and rewarding journey through a Strogg installation where you must shoot your way to dismantle many key components to disable the Strogg attack force. Featuring a really long campaign and a wide arsenal of weapons, items and many enemies, this game brings back the Quake experience in its essence, this time more brutally and with a re-imagination of the Strogg anatomy. Part of the Quake Collection, which every FPS fan should have in their accounts.

Skyward Collapse is a turn based god/strategy game. The goal of the game is to balance two opposing factions by supplying them with resources and buildings. You must cause enough chaos between the two factions to get your score high enough to pass through three rounds until you reach the end of the game to achieve a victory.
Skyward Collapse features one of the best tutorials I've seen in awhile. The game can be overwhelming at first, but the tutorial does a great job of holding your hand through your first game. The tutorial will teach you the basics of the game while giving you the freedom to play around and experiment as you see fit. You won't know 100% of everything after your first play-through, but you should understand the basic concepts and be ready to play a better game on your 2nd time around.
Skyward Collapse features very basic animation and graphics, it's best to think of it like a board game. Units move around the game like pieces on a board, and when they fight, they just bump into each other until one falls off the board.
I would say if you are interested by this review at all, you should go ahead and pick the game up. It is only five bucks, and even if you end up hating it, you've only wasted a few dollars. If you do not like turn based strategy, or if a lack of graphics or animation is a big turn off, stay clear of this one.

Probably one of the more strict-definition "God" games out there, in that you're the kind of deity who a) exists and b) does what he can for his people but c) can't order them to do jack♥♥♥♥♥♥because Free Will.
That said? This is a fantastic concept and I actually love it. You manage a pair of nations (and I believe a third with the recent DLC?) turn by turn, with equal moves apiece, reshaping the world and controlling the resources of each side. Afterwards, every living player from those factions makes their moves, and you hope you've done enough to keep them both safe (from roaming bandits, one another, and horrible curses known as Woes). The game's not so easily solved, though, due to the random factors that'll shake things up. Tiles appear after every turn to fill in gaps in the floating world you manage, and again, bandits/Woes.
I don't know how long I'll stick with this after finishing a few games? But it's totally a fantastic title and the recent overhaul patch makes me wonder if more tweaks like that might hook me further. I would love for this to be the birth of a new strategy niche.

I was lucky enough to get this game for free the day before Sniper Elite III came out. While the game rewards you for droppin' Nazis without detection, the number of enemies present in a given level usually only makes that possible in close quarters when you can use your silenced pistol, and that's not too sniper-y, eh? The player goes through a tutorial that gives the impression of carefully scouting a location, setting up all manners of nasty tricks to stop them bad guys, then taking a shot in the perfect position and moving so that you're a step ahead once detected. Thing is, it only plays out like that until you shoot your rifle and, oh look! More Nazis coming from around the block! Better stay in the same position and snipe a wave or two, maybe lay down a trip mine behind me in case they sneak up while I'm trying to fend off a dozen or so coming up the road. Not to say this isn't fun, it's just that the meat of the gameplay isn't nearly as calculated as it was set up to be, and I would have liked it better that way. The shooting is a lot of fun; the x-ray bullet cam is great, the "breathing system"  I guess you could call it is great (try running up to the top of a building, trying to get a shot on an enemy who's getting away in a car, only to find you're out of breath and the scope is moving all over the place. Adrenaline!) though these both tend to get old, again due to the sheer number of enemies that require bullets to the skull and/or groin.
All of this raises a question: is it possible to make a carefully calculated sniper game when it's still the player vs. the world, huge environments and armies pitted against you like every other military shooter? Sniper Elite V2 is nearly there, and it's compelling enough to make you want to finish the game. Will I now buy Sniper Elite III as Steam's promotion intended? Maybe, I'm curious to see whether the creators have improved upon the formula. Would I buy V2 for $30? Probably not, but then again, why would you buy any two year old game on Steam for $30? It'll go on sale eventually...

is a Chinese Visual Novel that tells the tales of broken forms, iron wills and unbearable truths. Through my many experiences with either emotional, philosophical or psychological narrations in visual novels, I've rarely felt thoroughly shaken until this one little tale of loss and misunderstanding...
The narration opens up to a silent night as heavy rain washes the outline of a forest clean. A lone traveler moves within the darkness and attends his uncanny business, away from the spectators' eyes... By the arrival of the next scene, narration switches to first person, as we find ourselves in a rather dark and alien mansion. We stroll in the endless corridors in hopes of finding an exit, yet what we encounter would be beyond our most gruesome nightmares... Nightmares? "Was this... a nightmare?" Yuhito thinks as he wakes up, shaking in his bed. "So real..."
Our hero is Yuhito Asakawa who lives in a rather secluded little village in a forlorn little island, alongside his family and his friend/childhood crush Nanami Shio. For reasons unbeknownst to us, the village is somewhat forsaken and no one seems to even remember the names of the two governing families nowadays. There is an air of unnatural peace weaved with shadows of memories long gone. The eerie peace this little village harbors is about to be disrupted by a quite malicious occurrence, and Yuhito's silent, blank reality is about to be filled with both wonders and horrors as he dashes out on a rather hopeless quest.
most surely does not deliver your common expectancy from a visual novel. The story and character dynamics are rather brutal, gory and disturbing with detailed narrations most of the time with thematic implications of abuse, torture, abandonment, suicide and countless other traumas. Thus, if you are to pick this one on a drive, you should know what you are getting yourself into. Be ready for a cold hand reaching for your heart and a lump in your throat as you discover many happenstances of the past, the present and the future.
My sole complaint is that the translation is quite direct during the idle conversations between characters, failing to present nuances and context, - especially during Yuhito and Nanami's early conversation - which usually ends up being either out of place or straight boring. But when it comes to environment descriptions or the telling of ongoing actions, the narration gets elevated to a completely new level of immersion. If you'd clench your teeth and see through the first two chapters of the game, you'll be glad that you went through with this one.
The visuals - especially backgrounds - are wondrous alongside character animations. The soundtrack is quite good and underlines the mood of the narration any given time. Characters themselves are vivid and interesting thanks to brilliant storyline and tragic character backgrounds, even without any voice acting. If I were to be completely honest, the character development of the main hero, Yuhito stays subpar compared to other main characters of the story. He is somewhat of a one track minded simpleton, nothing remotely interesting. You keep playing to learn the story of other characters and admire the quite interesting yet creepy setting though.
is a treat for the suckers of gore, drama and psychosis with 14 different endings, marvelous character dynamics and a story revelation that you sincerely wouldn't guess on your own. Fetch it alongside a box of tissues and possibly a pack of cigarettes. You are welcome!

Absolutely underrated and unrivaled is how I would best summarize this series. This is particularly true with "Renaissance" as the latest and most comprehensive addition.
Ambitious at the outset, what The Guild II Renassiance successfully accomplishes (with minor flaws) is a faithful recreation of medieval life and its jarring transition to early capitalism. Everything falls under the purview of this simulation -- politics, economics, family, and what I view as its most compelling aspect -- murder, intrigue, and the subsequent games one might play with a court system as an extension of the earlier mentioned politics.
It's a sociopath's kind of simulator. "The Guild II" has always, from my perspective, marketed itself on the player's ability to place the daughters of your character's enemies into prostitution, engineer methods of spreading plague to your rivals, and of course, its ability to rouse the jolly spirit of arson in everyone.
Here is something that happened in one of my playthroughs. An AI owner of the town's hospital would not leave the building so that I could murder them and buy the deed to the place. My character had a high charisma and was able to fabricate a claim that the owner of the hospital had committed a serious crime and went to the court with said claim. From the AI's reluctance to leave the hospital, they failed to appear for the court summons and were deemed a persona non grata.
The AI still did not leave the hospital at this point, so I firebombed the facility. As the building was engulfed in flames, the AI owner immediately stormed out of the place and was quickly lynched in the streets by the townsfolk. I got my hospital and without murder.

Chip is an interesting puzzle game. The concept is solid, and the artwork and usability is spot-on, but the only thing that puts me off about it is how abruptly it ends.
Don't get me wrong - there are enough levels to justify buying the game. My playtime for this game reflects playing through and completing levels, as well as achievements, if you want to gauge how long you'll probably play this.
There is a lot of room for expansion and additions - all the framework is there to build this game up. Unfortunately for the game and the players, the final bonus levels are where the puzzles get very interesting, which would allow for some pretty cool combinations. If it didn't abruptly end. Despite a lack of strong story or narrative (there is a basic story, but it's not an important theme), the game felt like it ended on a cliffhanger.
This is one of the few games in my library that deserved more attention from Steam users than it received, and would be a great addition to your library if you like puzzles.

The Guild 2 Renaissance is, well, quite the different game and it's hard to pin down. Imagine if you
will a cocktail, three parts The Sims, two parts Crusader Kings and a dash of any German made
simulator game. Shake well and you've got yourself The Guild 2.
Now I think it's best to point out that I have not played most of the game modes available. I have
played the dynasty mode which is kind of just the games free roam mode where there’s no quests or
objectives apart from keeping your family/dynasty alive much like Crusader Kings.
So the first thing you do is pick a map, this entails what villages, towns and cities you'll have in your
world and the environment. I pick the "Sheriff of Nottingham" map since it was smaller, had a village
and a town to work on and well...you know...Robin hood n'♥♥♥♥♥♥
Then I picked my family shield, which also dictates the colour of your dynasties’ clothing, so naturally
I went for bright orange to show my power or some such and then went on to make the founder of
my dynasty, one Benn Grey. Good old Benn, was a rogue one of the four classes in the game and the
more...violent and backhanded of the classes making his money and way in the world collecting a
toll from passing traders dotting the road since personally I found earning money the more legal way
was pretty dam tough and will take a lot of learning on the players part. As for most jobs you'll have
to buy/make ingredients then make whatever your business makes, from bread to bracelets made
out of bones stolen from a graveyard and sell these items in different markets and counting houses
or otherwise risk lowering the buying price of your goods till you can barely make any profit
anymore. Whereas being a rogue all I had to do was kidnap, murder or force people to pay a toll.
Hey it's a dirty job....but I'd rather do it.
So with that in mind, I set forth to make old Benn Grey the most feared gangster of the 1400's. I built
my own personal merc castle and started forcing people to pay a toll just for walking through the
market place, which everyone hated me for so when looking for a wife to pop out a baby and keep
my family line strong, nobody wanted to marry me. So I did the smart thing and brought my own
wife, good old Linette who totally didn't mind me buying her off her family. She was a Craftswoman
so with my extra money I bought her a little forge to make weapons for my mercs so I would be
unstoppable! She also did pop out a brat so all was looking up for Benn.
So the next stop would of course be for Benn to get political power. Which in my humble view is the
best part of the game. Bribing people, flirting and killing your way to the top feels so dam good and
it's tough but not too tough so you feel like you have to plan and slither your way to be mayor. With
Benn being a rogue I wanted him to be the village mayor because it granted him the ability to
embezzle public funds and not be arrested for any crime he committed, and so sure I was that I
would get the office I murdered the captain of the guard in the market in front of everyone and shot
the mayor in a duel after kissing her in a pub and then calling her a ♥♥♥♥♥ after she slapped me. After
this I thought I was unstoppable, until I lost my campaign to be mayor when the victor, a woman
from a rival dynasty won by having her name pulled out of a hat since everyone who could vote had
been killed by me. Then poor Benn was put on trial for killing the mayor and captain of the guard in
public and since he didn't have the immunity he craved, was sentenced to death. After screaming
"OH YOU'RE NEXT!" at the judge he was taken out side and had his head lopped off right where he
killed the captain. A somewhat fitting end when you think about it.
Finally poor Linette tried to avenge her husband by getting the Mayor’s office and killing the judge
but failed over and over losing all her money in bribes selling the castle and her forge and then
getting a cold and dying since she never had the coin for medicine.
Overall if you enjoy roleplaying and have a stronger imagination this game is great. Oh the stories
you can spin about your dynasty. You'll laugh, you'll cry, you'll kill your way to the top before dying
from a sprained ankle and leave a two year old boy an orphan. Although you'll just as easily get
muddled in the economics of the game and crash the market for grain.
Personally speaking the role-play value is a 7/10, but is more like a 8/10 if you put the effort to
understand the economics.
I hope to see you all soon buying wives and killing mayors in this gem of a game.

The concept of this game is good but the execution is rather poor.  I enjoy the idea of this game and I am entertained enough to stick around awhile and try to play it despite its flaws, but there's no question that it deserves the low metacritic score it has.  The game has some major shortcomings that should have been resolved at release and I cannot recommend it due to those shortcomings.  I'll list a few of them:
If you slow down the gameplay it also slows down your user interface for instance.  There's no excuse for that.  Telling your wagons where to go should be responsive whether you are paused or playing in fast forward, but because of the way the wagon command ui is tied to the world movement ticks entering commands for them at low speeds is slow and annoying.
The pause feature is fairly buggy.  It stops time but some of the people are still moving around in slow motion the whole time you are "paused".   This is probably because the wagons and such would be completely unresponsive if they were actually completely paused due to their response to commands being tied to their movement.
Sometimes my character becomes unresponsive and it wont respond to any commands anymore.  I end up having to save and reload the game just to get it to work again.  I'm sure this is also related to the buggy pause feature.
Pathfinding is sometimes buggy and people will get stuck at one spot on the map and just turn in a circle repeatedly.  This is fairly rare but has happened to both my characters and the AI characters in my game.  One time I saw 20 AI stuck at one spot with my wagon and I had to save and reload the game to get everybody moving again.
I still can't figure out if you are actually supposed to eat in the game.  The only time I fed two of my characters a biscuit both of them contracted tooth rot which I couldn't even treat because there was no hospital in my game.  When I run a shop I place items for sale in it that other people can buy, but when I go into the npcs shops they never seem to have anything for sale so I have to buy everything at the market.  This works, but it breaks the immersion of the game.  The tutorial has no coverage at of food or equipment or artifacts at all.  Note that there's only a tutorial currently if you download the 4.20 beta.  The base version of the game has no tutorial at all.
The user interface for analyzing the profitability of your business ventures is poor.  You can't tell how much each individual business is earning or losing.  You just get some totals that encompass all your business and house expense into an end of month total.  You have no easy way to tell how much you are earning or losing on individual products in a business.
I tried to participate in politics.  The political board listed the requirement as Citizen for almost all of the positions and it did not specify a level requirement, but when I bought my way up to Citizen and tried to apply for one it told me I wasn't high enough.  Either there's a hidden level requirement too or the requirement page for politics doesn't list the actual rank requirements.
Anyway, you've been warned.  If you have too much time on your hands like me and you want to play a mediocre game that only costs a few bucks on sale, then go for it, but you should not pay more than a few dollars for this game.  You can get some entertainment out of it if you are willing to deal with its faults.

*You are a Dinosaur!

Cons:

There are no time limits or pressure to perform, it's just a matter of working out the solution and implementing it.

If you're looking for a real challenge, something to make you think hard and plan and revise and strategise, then this isn't the game for you, but if you're looking for something simple and beatiful to poke at while you relax then this is probably worth checking out.

Have you ever wanted to play Pick-up-sticks in a minimalist 2D enviroment?  Well now's your chance.
Hook is a deceptively simple puzzle game where the object is to clear the field of all sticks.  The sticks don't lay over or under each other but pass through and interfere with each other.  Because of this the order in which you remove the sticks is vitally important.  One mistake and you have to restart the level though the last 10-15 levels allow 3 mistakes.
The game starts off simple, the sticks don't even overlap, but after a while they interlace and have bumps that must be accounted for.  They also introduce switches to control the flow once you hit the go button or one of the go buttons and even "wireless jump" elements to further complicate matters.  The higher levels often contain 10+ sticks, 10+ switches, multiple paths and multiple wireless jump elements.
Herein lies the weakness in the game.  While it will probably only take you an hour to finish the game, the first 40 of 50 levels feel like tutorials to introduce all the mechanics and once you get to the high level problems, the stars of the show, it's over all too quick.  More of the complex problems would be ideal or some sort of steamworks integration.
All in all it's still a great little puzzler for the price and well worth a play.

This is a strange one.
With that being said, it was an experience that I cannot recall have gotten out of any other game before.
It was an interesting mix between horror, survival, psychological terror, mystery and not knowing just what the heck is going on.
The replay-value is very high for me in this one, since (and this one actually DOES stay true to the concept) your house and the rooms in it never looks the same (unless you are awake/ outside of the nightmare-world), which makes it a challenge trying to get used to your surroundings that simply refuse to stand still.
One would think that it's as simple as just turning on the lights in your home, in which the so called "guests" cannot have physical form, but then again, the "Visitor" sure does like to break your fresh lightbulbs and close and lock doors in your path.
Hiding behind an object in an attempt to escape a guest still is not a very safe card to draw, since it's actually realistic enough to make it a "either they find you, or not" scenario.
My advice is:
Follow the rules
Don't be brave, but also don't be a coward
Don't get comfortable
Try to focus
Do not linger
Do not slow down
You cannot trap them, only yourself
Turn on the lights, but keep to the dark
Flee whenever you can, but never try to escape
And lastly, don't look to the skies
The visitor wants in
Don't let it.

This is one of those games that you wished had a rating system rather than a thumbs up or down.
To jump right into it:
1. Is the game worth 40 dollars? No. You get three maps, about 7 or so counselors, 6 different Jasons. Is this game worth 29.99? Yeah. But not 40.
2. Is the game fun? Yes. It's some of the best fun I've had in a very long time. It's not the BEST game i've played in a long time, but it is definetely the most fun. This probably has to do a lot with me being an avid fan of the Friday the 13th franchise. Ever since I was a little girl, I loved this IP. If I never seen any of the movies, I would probably not have liked it as much.
3. Is Jason OP? Sure he is. But he is suppose to be. In the movies, the guy doesn't die. A shotgun blast in the movies will only stun him. The guy is utterly immortal..even when you blow him into meat chunks. In the movies, no matter how fast you run, he always catches up. They incorporated this into the game pretty well with a VHS "tear."
4. Graphics. Def above average and pretty damn good for an Indie developer. The shadowing is on point and the atmosphere is pretty good.
5. Music. They nailed it. They incorporated the original musical score into the movie (including the ki ki ki, ma, ma, ma..Kill, kill kill, mom, mom, mom)
6. Customizations: the clothing customizations are not that great. Just the same clothes but different colors. But the true customizations come with the perks you can earn and randomly roll to get. The perks for counselors is better survivability perks and for Jason, it's different movie classic murders he performs.
Bugs and glitches:
I won't lie, there are a lot. The most predominate ones are plaguing the PS4 and Xbox 1 players where a great deal cannot even log in. Remember the fiasco with Diablo 3? Yup, it's here as of the date of this writing. PC players don't have much of an issue but there is a bug plaguing all:
Cannot incorporate those perks you get. You just sit there while it tries to update your perks in the game and it doesn't happen.  The worse out of all of this is the DEVS are utterly silent about this and refuses to even acknowledge them. They will respond to positive praises on Twitter but will often ignore the bug issues. They should learn the lesson of No Man's Sky developer team and be more vocal about these things.
Honestly, since there are more positives than negatives right now I am giving it a thumbs up for now. However, if you don't have a lot of money at the moment, this isn't a game for you. It's just too expensive for the issues it has.
How to make it worth 40 dollars?
1. Add more maps. Three maps just seems like an insult. Yeah, the maps are limited to the movies but you can get creative.
2. Patch the bugs. For 40 bucks a game and thousands have purchased this game already this is not an excuse.
3. Add more skins for Jason. They are missing a few from the movies.
4. Add the ability to change key bindings.
5. Add the ability to activate mic via chatting and not having to press t

Skyward Collapse is a strange little game. And to be honest, far from little. It is a turn based strategy game in a mythical setting, where ancient greek and norse fight a never ending war. A war that threatens creation itself. You are the Creator in charge of this world and it is your duty to ensure that this war never reaches that point of doom, while at the same time keeping creation "interesting".
Each turn you have a build face for each of the two factions, allowing you to place buildings, summon mythical creatures such as minotaurs, create mountains or even nudge the gods to do your bidding. Death and destruction increases your score but too much of it and a faction runs the danger of getting wiped out and you would lose the game. And as if the constant warmongering of the two sides wasn't enough, bandits raid everyone equally and calamities (like floods, draughts, serial killers or tartarus spitting the dead back into the land of the living) will spicen things up.
This game is well worth checking out for everyone who enjoys turn based strategy and would like to try something different. And as an added bonus, the devs are extremly communicative on their forum.

A rather unique game that plays like a 4X strategy mixed with shades of Populous. You play the role of a Creator who is tasked with bringing balance to the world populated by two factions, the Norse and the Greeks. As Creator, you have the ability to shape the world as you see fit by adding lakes, fields, etc, to an ever changing landscape, and to help the two factions prosper to greatness.
When military buildings are built, they create units, and these men will move on their own to the other faction to destroy them. Your ultimate goal as the Creator is to make sure these two sides don't destroy the other completely, and no, you can't win simply by never giving the factions military based buildings, for bandits will randomly spawn in the world, and they will start attacking the cities if you don't have a military force.
However, balance isn't one sided. In order to create balance in the first place, you must also encourage war and destruction so you have to let them duke it out and destroy some buildings or two while you watch from above and see how things go. However, if one side starts dominating the other, you must step in and bring in the balance. Does the Norse have too many infantry and are now laying waste to the world? Drop a Minotaur at their feet and watch them get themselves wasted by a bad♥♥♥♥♥bull. You could also drop some mountains and/or lakes in their path to halt their progress.
Did I say minotaur? Each faction has their own mythological monsters that you can plop anywhere on the field (as long as you have the necessary resources) that can tip the balance if things are going to pot. Each monster has their own set of skills, and be careful when you use them because that monster might start going out of control and you'd have a new set of problems to deal with.
In addition to monsters, there's also Gods that appear after a while with their own set of skills, along with various items that can do things like letting both sides be able to fly, or killing all human units on the map to get some breathing room.  There's also various Woes that pop up after a set amount of turns that can really cause havoc, such as a total map change or dropping bandits near the cities.
As mentioned before, Skyward Collapse is an unique twist on the strategy genre, and it's much harder than it sounds to balance the playing field so that you must let each side cause enough havoc to get the scores, yet also having to keep them in check to prevent total destruction and a game over. Easier difficulties aren't so bad, but harder difficulties will really test your ability.
Skyward Collapse resembles a board game, which I'm sure is what the devs strived for. The graphics are nicely detailed, especially the various units and mythlogical creatures. There isn't much animation to speak of, but that's not much of a negative considering the whole board game look, and the fact it's not very important for the genre. When you start having over forty units moving on their own, the last thing you'd want would be to have them all animated. The music, which I think is just one track, is great.
Everytime you win a game, you unlock a new building to give the game more depth/options, athough if you are the impatient type, there is a cheat you can use that gives them all at the start.
There's also co-op multiplayer for up to 8 players although I haven't tried it.

It was the first online multiplayer game that I played, it was the first time I used the handle “KoreRat”, and the first time I downloaded extra content for a game.  Quake 2 was a lot of firsts for me, so I’d be lying if I said I’m not a bit partial to it.
To start, there are mods for Q2 that bump up the graphics to look more in the area of Quake 3 Arena, along with many other additions.
The game starts; you are part of a massive invasion force attacking the Strogg home planet, Stroggos. After getting hit by one of your comrades, you find yourself heading in a different direction.  But luck is with you, when an unknown gun opens up on your unit and you are the only solider left in the force. Crash landing in a base outpost, you are quickly given orders to rendezvous with other squads.
Playing through Q2 again for the first time in a few years was a very reminiscent experience for me.  I found that I still remember where all the secrets were, and all the spots where the Strogg’s jump out at as you pass.  Along with remembering all the times I had played online deathmatch and capture the flag.  A lot of good memories with this game, and perhaps that is why I score Q2 so high.  It’s not just a great game on its own but, for me at least, it brings about a lot of memories of late night gaming.  This is one of the foundation games that really brought about online multiplayer to what it is today.  Without Quake, Doom, Quake 2, and Unreal the entire gaming landscape would be different.
Two mission packs were made for Quake 2, The Reckoning and Ground Zero.  I played these next.  They both add some new weapons and enemies.  They both have a similar story to the main game, wherein you get separated from your squad on entry, they die, and it’s up to you.  Between the two I prefer Ground Zero more.  The Reckoning feels too rushed and almost tries to hard to be as good.  It also reuses The Makron for the final fight.  Ground Zero on the other hand switches it up on you a bit, with a new final boss, The Black Widow, and having you go in disguise for a short while.
Over all, I would say that even after fifteen plus years Quake 2 still holds it’s own with many games out today.  If your looking for a great frag fest or a taste of where modern games started, you definitely want to check out Quake 2.

I really liked EvilQuest.
This game isn't a timeless classic, and it won't win any prestigious awards. It IS, however, a fun action RPG that offers a decent challenge with a surprising amount of flexibility in play style. It's everything you would expect from an intentionally retro-style game. The graphics and music bring up those good old nostalgic feelings, but EvilQuest stands apart from similar games because of its dedication to its story. While most gamers may be tempted to overlook the story for its simplicity, I found it to be wholly satisfying.
Without spoiling too much, I'll say that EvilQuest's story trashes the Good VS Evil in favor of an Evil VS All approach, and it works really well. I found myself caring about what happens next and who the protagonist would encounter. Think about that. These days, it takes a dash of something special in a game to make you actually care about what happens to the people in it, and EvilQuest has that spice.
If you want a quick game with a moderate challenge and a rewarding story, you'd do well to grab EvilQuest. Don't sleep on this one.

Well what can I say about this game?
The community is totally...and I mean TOTALLY...splitted between a "HEY THIS IS AN AWESOME GAME!" and a "WHAT A CRAP!"
Let's say that this game is not bad as they say but is not even ultra awesome; the scenario is good, the graphic and the effects are good, the sounds are good and even the concept is really good.
Yes it had a lot of bugs, like the huge frame drop (neither me or my friend had this issue while we were playing so I guess that the developer are not so "crappy" as other says) or the "I find soo much stuff that I can live really easy in this game so is not a survival at all" (actually earlier we had to STRUGGLE to find stuff to survive and even to STRUGGLE to find a safezone...is that enough "survival"?) or even the graphic (yes is quite good and with some good effects but there are still some little glitches here and there with some textures).
Yes it still even have the "freeze" at the startup yes (just wait for the servers to load and then it will goes like a rocket).
Alone it can be an agony because you will LITERALLY thrown in a world that you don't know with a not so clear tutorial (actually if you have the patience to read everything is clear enough) and finding yourself alone in the middle of NOWHERE with creepy sounds and the night incoming can be REALLY frustrating but with a friend of two this game become so engaging (I was really impressed about this) that even if I've started like "this is a bad situation I want to log off to not die" I've fastly turned to "hey let's go ahead a bit more" because I even found it challenging!
Yes even having one life can be a pain, and if you die you die and you lose everything...but, how many lifes you have in your life? One...so...again...is this enough survival as a simulator?
This game is not bad as a lot of people says (sorry Dayz's fanboys to not agree with you.......) and it has indeed a lot of potential, it is fun, it is challenging and it is engaging in an impressive way after a while (2 hours passed in a snap of fingers).
Better to try it with a friend or two (or at least make one friend fast in the game....beware because there are good people...but even people that will not think twice to kill you at the first occasion to get your stuff).
From the beta the game improved a lot and it is still in developement so I can only suppose that it will be better patch after patch even thanks to your feedback and not to your whining...and for the price it is now (summer sales), for me it was and it is an istant buy

So... Medal of Honor... Infamous for it's "racism" and overall mediocre presentation.
I'll just tell it how it is.
The gunplay feels good only if you score headshots. Otherwise the sound design and the feel of the gun leaves much to desire.
The story starts off really weak and continues on the same level for the most part. The last hour of the game though is really great and emotional. And I think that's the reason why a few of these people reviewing here claim that the story is amazing. Some complain that the story is too short (4-6 hours, depending on your skill) and to them I'll say "What are you talking about?" This is perfect length. It shows an operation and you get enough. Anything longer would feel just like filler and it'd get boring.
The multiplayer is dead. Don't buy it for this. I had the chance to play it when it was still a body that was twitching and in all honesty, you're not missing out on much.
The graphics even now look beautiful. The soldiers that are currently deployed still say that the game looks like the world actually does and I have to admit, that's pretty impressive then.
The main issue that I have with this game is the FOV. I tried changing it but to no avail. It's a constant 60 FOV or so and it's pretty disgusting because of it.
The options menu is mediocre, but it still offers a few options in terms of windowed mode, resolution and some graphics changes.
It runs fine as well.
Overall

In videogames, there are good translations, bad translations, and horrible translations. Good translations capture the soul of the story as well as the raw meaning of the words; horrible translations at least stand a chance of being funny or charming for their onvious badness. Bad translations capture the meaning, and only that -- all the depth, all the charm, and every single drop of subtext get sacrificed on the altar of "makes sense gramatically, that's good enough."
Notch - The Innocent LunA is an object lesson in why even if you get the words in the right order and they're all spelt correctly, It doesn't mean you have a good translation. I could discuss the plot, but the plot doesn't matter because it's extremely hard to care about what happens to the characters. It's extremely hard to care about the characters because they don't have a single shred of personality between them, and the reason they have no personality is because every single line of the VN is written in the baldest, most simplistic style that still passes for English.
"Well," one might say, "even if we can't rely on the style of the text to make our characters likeable, what about their actions?" Well, the main character spends a good portion of the story being a condescending, sexist jerk without even realising it; then bad things start to happen, which prompts him to intentionally be a condescending, sexist jerk. The initial female lead is less of a character and more of an object/motivation. Random characters pop in and out of the story to do a little murdering; most remained unnamed and uninteresting for many acts.
Actually, I take back what I said about not talking about the plot. Even accepting that the poor translation might be stealing a lot of the thunder, the plot feels very shaky. The story is very dedicated to trying to be mysterious and not explaining anything for as long as possible; the problem is that it keeps doing for this so long that you don't care by the time things start to be revealed. A lot of the backbone of the work rests on the supernatural, and imho, this is what suffers most from the artificial mystery. Oftentimes, the story will explain its most recent plot twist with some kind of supernatural occurence, without explaining anything further; it feels contrived, like a bad fanfic.
What is there other than the poor translation? The artwork is honestly fairly mediocre. The special effects that the game occasionally uses are a nice touch visually, but there's not really any striking beauty here. It's anime characters against forgettable backgrounds. While there's certainly nothing wrong with an anime artstyle, it's definitely no better than any other VN with anime artstyle out there, and worse than a few I could name. The soundtrack suits the mood most of the time, but there aren't really any standout pieces that I would want to listen to outside of the scenes they appear in.
In summary: this game's main problem is that the "visual" element of its visual novel structure is nowhere near good enough to compensate for the sub-par novel part. In a genre that relies so much on the written element of the work, there is no reason any English-speaking consumer should accept a translation like this. Maybe, in its original language, this is a powerful and thrilling story; in this language, it isn't. Buy only if you want to support more Japanese visual novels making their way to the steam platform, and even then, I'd recommend looking for alternative studios with better translations so you can encourage quality at the same time.

They all seem to be based around the cliche kind, gentle, girl-next-door/victim variety and never seem to do anything except cry and wait to be rescued (there's the one exception of course, but just one).  I'm not a feminist, but really...some variety wouldn't hurt here.
The story itself isn't a bad one, in fact with better writing and more consistent characters it would make a good visual novel.  I'm rather surprised this has gotten so many positive reviews.  The key to writing dialogue, as a writer, is that after you write out a conversation read it out with a friend.  Does it sound like a conversation two people would actually have?  Do the characters sound like people?  If not, time for a rewrite.
Edit:  Well, I made it as far as chapter 8 and near the end ot the chapter I'm throwing in the towel.  I've never read such drivel in my entire life.  The way the case is solved and the 'clues' presented are such utter nonsense I can't stand to go on.  This is not how detective work works, even in reality.  They basically just threw a bunch of totally circumstancial evidence together and claimed it was obvious.  I'm done.

The basic idea goes something like this. Buttons are connected to rods by wires; push the button and the rod will be reeled in. If there's nothing in the way, the rod will disappear; if it gets snagged, you'll have to try again. If you can visualize that concept, you know pretty much all there is to know about Hook.
Of course, it wouldn't be a puzzle game without a few speed bumps scattered about - as you progress through the game's 50 levels (which shouldn't take you much more than an hour to complete) you'll encounter, among other things, rods with inconvenient curved segments, or pieces that overlap and must be cleared in a certain order. The strategy is the same every time, i.e. "which piece is safe to clear, and how do I connect it to a button without screwing anything else up", but I must admit I found the process more entertaining than I expected, and felt satisfied as I finished up.
There isn't much more to the presentation than there is to the game itself, as should be obvious, but for a single dollar I really can't complain - they might not stick around for very long or make any headines while they're here, but small, well-executed projects like this deserve some love too, and I do hope this one gets it.
