This is one of those games that you wished had a rating system rather than a thumbs up or down.
To jump right into it:
1. Is the game worth 40 dollars? No. You get three maps, about 7 or so counselors, 6 different Jasons. Is this game worth 29.99? Yeah. But not 40.
2. Is the game fun? Yes. It's some of the best fun I've had in a very long time. It's not the BEST game i've played in a long time, but it is definetely the most fun. This probably has to do a lot with me being an avid fan of the Friday the 13th franchise. Ever since I was a little girl, I loved this IP. If I never seen any of the movies, I would probably not have liked it as much.
3. Is Jason OP? Sure he is. But he is suppose to be. In the movies, the guy doesn't die. A shotgun blast in the movies will only stun him. The guy is utterly immortal..even when you blow him into meat chunks. In the movies, no matter how fast you run, he always catches up. They incorporated this into the game pretty well with a VHS "tear."
4. Graphics. Def above average and pretty damn good for an Indie developer. The shadowing is on point and the atmosphere is pretty good.
5. Music. They nailed it. They incorporated the original musical score into the movie (including the ki ki ki, ma, ma, ma..Kill, kill kill, mom, mom, mom)
6. Customizations: the clothing customizations are not that great. Just the same clothes but different colors. But the true customizations come with the perks you can earn and randomly roll to get. The perks for counselors is better survivability perks and for Jason, it's different movie classic murders he performs.
Bugs and glitches:
I won't lie, there are a lot. The most predominate ones are plaguing the PS4 and Xbox 1 players where a great deal cannot even log in. Remember the fiasco with Diablo 3? Yup, it's here as of the date of this writing. PC players don't have much of an issue but there is a bug plaguing all:
Cannot incorporate those perks you get. You just sit there while it tries to update your perks in the game and it doesn't happen.  The worse out of all of this is the DEVS are utterly silent about this and refuses to even acknowledge them. They will respond to positive praises on Twitter but will often ignore the bug issues. They should learn the lesson of No Man's Sky developer team and be more vocal about these things.
Honestly, since there are more positives than negatives right now I am giving it a thumbs up for now. However, if you don't have a lot of money at the moment, this isn't a game for you. It's just too expensive for the issues it has.
How to make it worth 40 dollars?
1. Add more maps. Three maps just seems like an insult. Yeah, the maps are limited to the movies but you can get creative.
2. Patch the bugs. For 40 bucks a game and thousands have purchased this game already this is not an excuse.
3. Add more skins for Jason. They are missing a few from the movies.
4. Add the ability to change key bindings.
5. Add the ability to activate mic via chatting and not having to press t

SOMA is a survival horror game. It's main selling point is its story. You solve small puzzles to advance the narrative of the story. Most of the puzzles are fairly easy to solve, so if you're looking for a true challenge, look elsewhere. If you don't enjoy the story, you will not enjoy this game.
Those are the basics of what this game is, now let's talk a little bit about the story...
You play as Simon Jarett. Simon is a 20-something living in Toronto in 2015. He has some sort of unspecified degenerative brain illness. It is hinted that it is terminal. His doctor suggests an experimental new treatment. Simon goes to his doctor to get his brain scan. He sits in the chair, the scan begins, lights flash, and he wakes up in 2104, at the bottom of the ocean in an underwater facility where some sort of disaster has occurred. How he got there and what he must do to escape is what this game is about.
While SOMA does contain its share of jump scares, this game's true horror is in the unsettling narrative. This is something Frictional Games does well. And it's ending will stick with you. SOMA's ending is unexpected and horrifying.
Overall, if you like survival horror, if you liked Amnesia: The Dark Descent, you'll like this game. I recommend checking it out.

Quake II definitely lacks the freshness and excitement of its predecessor. Rather than sticking with the peculiarly medieval-ish look of Quake, Quake II attempts to switch things up...by going back to the space marine idiom. With less-satisfying weapons/combat than Quake, and a VERY slow start (the first 5 or 6 maps are a generic slog to get through), Quake II is unquestionably an inferior sequel. HOWEVER, in the interest of seeing it through, I soldiered on (SO NOBLE), and eventually found myself enjoying the latter half of the game. The maps get more varied and interesting (or else my senses gradually dulled to the point where I found them to be), and it finishes much stronger than it started. Not quite a full-on recommendation, I know, but if it's on the cheap, pick it up -- if for no other reason than to experience the first (of many?) flawed id Software shooter.

EvilQuest is an action adventure RPG in a retro style. It comes off as something like a late NES or early SNES/Genesis title... if that perspective helps. You are a very powerful, evil dude that gets betrayed by his army and locked up. However, you escape captivity and go on a quest to regain your mighty power and ultimately seek to destroy God himself. Sounds pretty cool, right?
You basically go around overworlds seeking towns and dungeons. You can do some generally mean things along the way, but you're focus is to find four elemental things and then go to the final area once the barrier is broken. It's some standard, by the books stuff. But it works. Along the way, you fight through monsters and bosses in a Zelda-esque fashion. Defeating them will net you gold, which can be used to purchase equipment to make yourself stronger and items to recover from loss of health, loss of magic, or status ailments. As you progress, you'll find stronger weapons and different spells to help you tackle your foes. Also gained from defeated enemies are experience points. Getting enough of these will allow you to level up. Upon gaining a level, you have the option to distribute a number of points into whichever stats you see fit. This can be fun for building a specific way for different playthroughs. Want to beef up your magic skills? Maybe you want to deal mighty blows with your weapons. Or perhaps you just want to be a well rounded warrior. It's nice for some customization and replay value, yet not too complicated as to overwhelm the player. I also would like to point out that I thought the music was alright, but I do enjoy the art style quite a bit. Guess I'm a softy for that kind of thing.
However, every game has its faults, as does EvilQuest. I can't complain too much with the main character being bad, as it is not often done still and keeps things a bit interesting. I guess I just wish they had maybe gone a little further with that idea. Maybe that's just me. My biggest complain comes from some expectations that were built up a bit and never capitalized on. Near the start of the game you get the charge ability, letting you shoot a projectile from your weapon at no cost to magic. You then use this to hit a switch through a wall and open a gate. A little while later is a switch puzzle, where some need to be up and some need to be down. Ithought this would mean there would be cool puzzle elements throughout the game like in Zelda games. However, there weren't much more like that to be found. I guess I was hoping it'd break up some of the grinding and killing, but I guess I didn't need to grind so that part was my own fault. My most minor and rather meaningless complaint is that, in order to get all the achievements, you have to play the game twice. Yet there seems to be only one achievement that absolutely forces you to do it. The one based on difficulty. If you play on normal, you have to beat it again on hard. Also, if you play it on easy, you'll get no achievement, which doesn't make much sense. But it's all in the achievements so it's really not even an issue with the game itself. Hardly worth mentioning but... I did. So... sorry.
It's a cool retro-inspired action adventure RPG. If you like Zelda games and the RPG leveling stuff, give it a look. The game is only two bucks normally, and even less when it goes on sale. It's very much worth the price. This could possibly have passed for a ten dollar game, five at the least. But the fact that it's only two bucks makes it hard to pass up. Sure, it could use some more stuff in it, but the things included are good, especially for that asking price. So go ahead and get your copy. Forget the hesitation and go for it.

If I were to compare this game to others, I'd say it's a combination of 'The Sims Medieval' and 'Stronghold' which results into a wonderfully complex strategic medieval life simulator. You can choose to begin as a humble farmer, a dashing rogue, a dedicated craftsman or a studious scholar. And that's just your day job! You can become involved in politics if you so choose and possibly, with enough effort invested, becoming a member of the ruling class.
All of the above, and more... if you have the patience and determination to learn how the game actually works. There is a tutorial provided, but it's unfortunately lacking in content. Weather it deliberately leaves out so much so we can discover fun little actions ourselves, I don't know, but you will spend a good hour learning how to actually play the game even after playing through the tutorial.
I'd like to have had more character customization. Unlike 'The Sims Medieval' your individual avatar is quite limited in appearance. I can understand this considering your initial character is going to be among the first to die; leaving you with his offspring and offspring of their own to continue building your empire.
When it comes to your dynasty, as it grows in size and scope, it becomes a micromanaging nightmare. There is an AI option for your businesses, but I find it to be less than satisfactory; which results in me having to run each and every establishment I own. It rapidly gets obnoxiously tedious.
There are still quite a few bugs present but none of them, in my experience, seem to be game breaking. They are, at worst, an annoyance.
Overall there are a few things I would have like to have been different (character customization for one), but for the price this game is an absolute steal.

A fun little game where YOU ARE THE BAD GUY!
Graphics:
The graphics are colorful, but simple looking.  All look handdrawn in a paint program, but the detail is good.  All of the sprites, special attacks and certain backgrounds are well animated.  But the bright colors do get hard on the eys after a while.
Sound:
The sound is decent, but the music kinda bland and reused in some parts.  Not really memorable.
Control:
The controls were decent enough and I had no problems with it.
Gameplay:
Despite it's look, the gameplay is good.  You get MANY different attacks to use, from charging your wapon for a LoZ-style ranged attack to screen-wide magic attacks.  You can also set certain  items for a quick slot of easy use during heated battles.  Also, most battles are a challenge without being cheap.  Never do you feel the need to grind to beat the boss because if you just kill the enemies you see on the way, you will be fine.  But money will be an issue when you want (and need) certain spells and armor.  The Cure spells are a MUST!  But most of the important attack spells are given to you.  The story of this game is, despite it's premise, very hilarious and the writing had me smiling.

I honestly thought it was great. In the recent market of moddern warfare shooters, companies never get the balls to make a game about the actual modern wars. We've seen plenty of fake wars in the Battlefield and CoD series, straying from the real conflicts of WW2 that made those games successful. EA took the original concept of Medal of Honor, following valliant soldiers through the real life conflicts that have shaped our world, and brought it to the 21st century. Accompanied by music from Ramin Djawadi who's work I'm sure everyone is familiar with from Game of Thrones, this game truly takes a leap out of the standard Call of Fields that we've all become so used to. How EA managed to let a gem like this slip though the cracks without ruining it on the way out, I'll never know, but it truly is the unsung hero of modern day shooters. I'm not one to recommend FPS games like this, but I absolutely recommend this one if you care at all about the single player in FPS games. It's not just a Call of Duty clone.

I don’t consider myself a particularly smart person. Which is obviously why I greatly enjoy puzzle games, because they fill me with a sense of intelligence after overcoming certain particularly difficult puzzles. It sort of gives me the feeling that I’m smarter than whoever came up with these challenges in the first place. And I know that this is a very inaccurate representation of people who make puzzle games, because I realize that coming up with these difficult brainteasers in the first place requires an intellect far greater than mine in the first place.
One of my favorite ways to interact with puzzles is if they require spatial awareness. The goal of each level in
is to untangle the mess of connections you see before you. But since it’s a plain 2D affair, it’s more reminiscent of electrical circuit diagrams than anything else. And it also works quite the same way. You have the equivalent of logic gates available to you in order to steer the “electricity” from your button to the appropriate elements. And since all the elements are interlocked in some way, shape or form, you have to keep track which piece has to be removed next. One wrong move, one incorrect decision means that you’ll be trying to remove more than just that one hook you had it out for and send you frantically going over all of your connections again.
Don’t be fooled by the deceptively simple design of the title, it does have quite a few hard puzzles to solve. Unfortunately, to get to them, you’ll be treated to around 30 to 40 levels of mostly very simple puzzles and tutorials that you’ll breeze through without much stopping you. But the final 10 levels – and yes, the game contains a total of 50 levels – can test your patience quite a bit and require a lot of preparatory work, before you even touch one single logic gate.
It’s also unfortunate that the game is completely devoid of an options menu. There isn’t much to complain about the performance that would require an extensive selection of settings, but basic features like resolution and sound options would’ve been much appreciated.
If the price were any higher than what the developers are currently asking for – which, for the record, is $1 – I’d probably have more qualms over recommending this short little title, but as it stands, you could spend that amount on a lot of worse entertainment that doesn’t tickle your brain to the extent
does. So yeah, I’m willing to give this short little game a recommendation, because it’s flawlessly executed, elegant and simple in design, visually and aurally pleasing and doesn’t require a big investment for the privilege. The only real downside is that I would’ve liked some more levels. But in the end, isn’t that really a compliment if you want more of the same out of a title?

SOMA is very similar to Alien Isolation, except it's everything that game should've been. I like Alien Isolation, but this game does it right. There’s a great story to uncover, no weapons, some puzzles, and a few monsters that you have to avoid. Some people think the game didn't need monsters, but that would've made the it much shorter and less entertaining. The monster encounters are perfectly sprinkled into the game and were always very intense. They don't constantly hound you and you don't have to hide in lockers or anything.
I really enjoyed this game as the world felt real and lived-in. While the story doesn't have any major twists it does have many harsh, thought provoking events. You even have to make some tough choices. These choices have no real effect on the game, but maybe on your psyche.
I’m impressed that they resisted adding weapons and repetitive shooting. I’m also impressed the Steam community has embraced this game so well. This is a good sign for video games in general.
If I had one minor quibble, it would be that the game allows you to pick up many objects in the game for no reason. There are times you do need to pick up stuff and it’s made very obvious, but  It would’ve been nice if there was stuff we could’ve collected or something. I also ran into a glitch late in the game with the Omnitool, but luckily the game keeps many saves for you to return to. It seems to be a known issue that they should really patch. Long story short, after picking up your Omnitool, always wait a few seconds before interacting with something else.

I haven't read many visual novels, so my review may be a bit off. I've read Narcissus (An extremely good read), as well as Love at First Sight (A good but short read), and I have to say Notch falls a bit short in quality, but makes up for it by pure quantity and length. This is, in my opinion, a slightly longer read than I'm used to, and the writing is... mediocre. The story is decent with some twists and turns you may not expect. Anyway, time to make a easy list of pros and cons to look at:
Pros:
-A ton a dialogue for those who can't get enough of hearing what the characters have to say about anything
-Blood and gore for those into the horror genre
-Multiple endings meaning you have to be (very) careful about the choices you make for the protagonist
-A lengthy read to keep you occupied for the long weekends, or whenever you're bored xD
Cons:
-Somewhat repetative dialogue. I find that sometimes the characters talk a bit too much, especially during situations where something important is about to happen. This is just my oppinion though.
-Dialogue is rather simple, and the narrator is absent most of the time. I would prefer more descriptive writing, but this is just my preference.
-Difficult to get a good ending. You may end up near the end of the of the story but finding yourself reaching a "bad ending" because of a decision you made very early on, forcing you to start over from the beginning multiple times. If you have the patience to do this, then it's not so bad, but I found it fustrating and had to look up a guide to finally find a proper ending.
Overall 7/10. I still recommend this. I would have enjoyed this more if I didn't have to restart multiple times to find a good ending. Luckily I found out that holding down ctrl speeds up the process ;)

I played my fair share of translated visual novels, and rarely touch indie visual novels, and my verdict is that this was a pretty nice read-through. It had what you would get in any mystery/horror novel. The scary deaths, creepy descriptions, artwork in-detail of important scenes, and high quality music.
but... I wouldn't recommend this to anyone I know.
The protagonist, and (most of) the character interactions in the story were horribly written (from myself as a reader's perspective). The protagonist makes way too many stupid decisions to the point of trainwreck. Some of the characters had their moments, but too few to point out. Most of the time, the interactions felt too 'robotic'. That was the feeling I got when I was reading through the course of the characters development as the story goes on. The backstories for many of these characters were well done, and I was touched. Music is really the highlight of this visual novel, but that is where my compliments end. If it were only the soundtrack, I would recommend purchasing; but you would need to read the visual novel to understand the feelings and emotions of each track... so my stance is neutral towards the soundtrack being on sale.
Normally, voice-acting in visual novels can compensate for a lot of things, especially the amount of emotion required to be portrayed during the course of the story; but since indie visual novels don't normally have the funds for voice-acting, I never held any hopes since the beginning. Of course, there are few exceptions like Katawa Shoujo, which also didn't have voice-acting but was beautifully written, drawn, composed, and laid out. It seems Notch isn't one of those few exceptions.
Enjoyment: 6/10
Characters: 4/10
Soundtrack: 8.5/10
Personal visual novel  score: 5.6/10

TL;DR Summary: SOMA is an excellent game that deserves to be experienced by anyone with even a passing interest in psychological horror or existential philosophy.
It's hard to say a lot about this game without spoiling it; the less you know about its themes going in, the more that the game actually gets to unfold them to you at its own pace, the better the experience will be. That said, the game strikes a fine balance between different kinds of horror: fear of the monster around the corner, fear of what unknown things might be lurking in the darkness, and fear of a more existential nature. At the same time, the mood is not quite so thoroughly oppressive as it was in, say, Amnesia; there are moments of lightness, even humor, amidst the bleak backdrop.
The game features no combat, instead emphasizing a mix of atmosphere, stealth, and puzzles. The various elements are balanced so that you're frequently moving between them, making for overall excellent pacing that gives you time to breathe in between the tensest moments. The "monster encounters" were generally tense enough for me that they achieved their goals: I dreaded encountering one, and was always glad to get past it, and I don't mean that as a criticism. At the same time, there could have been a little more variety to them, and some more variety to the set pieces wherein you encounter them. More dynamic interaction with the environment would have been welcome--for instance, creating cover on the fly, hiding in lockers, or more actively manipulating the monsters to navigate past them. Maybe next time.
The game looks excellent, and I was able to run it at maximum graphical settings on Borderless Windowed mode at 1920x1200 without any slowdown. Sound design is top-notch, too, with solid voice acting. I experienced no crashes and only one major bug throughout my 10-hour playthrough: in one section of the game, a staircase did not correctly load even though it appeared to be there, preventing me from progressing until I saved and restarted the game. No progress lost and only a couple minutes to fix.
The game features no collectibles, no resource management, and no scavenging. There are scattered notes and letters and terminals that you can seek out and access for further insight into the story--and I strongly recommend that you do--but the game's pacing is otherwise very tight and never gets bogged down in demanding that you scour every corner in order to maybe find some bullets hidden under a chair. In some respects, yes, this game is an interactive novel--but it's an excellent one, immersive and interesting and powerful. If you can look past the fact that you're not going to be hunting for gewgaws or wielding a weapon, SOMA is an excellent experience that will leave you thinking.

EvilQuest is a satisfying revival of action-adventure RPGs of the 8- and 16-bit. This game reminded me most of Crystalis on the NES, though it also has some similarities to Lagoon on the SNES. The map designs are similar as are some mechanics (jump boots.) Early on, the combat is fairly easy, though you may fail if you attack recklessly. Positioning and timing are most important for success, but, unlike the earlier action-adventure RPGs, enemies appear to have predictable cooldowns on their projectiles and abilities, making it far less likely you'll get surprised.
The controls are responsive, however you can perform only one action at a time like in the older games previously mentioned. The one thing that sets it apart is that you can move and turn your character while attacking, allowing you to control quarter- or half-circle sweeps with your weapon; otherwise, every attack is a forward jab. Opponents can do this also, which can catch you off-guard when flanking a foe.
While formulaic, it's a tried-and-true recipe. I recommend this to anyone who enjoys the genre and art style.

For the price point of 20 dollars- I'd say this game is just about what you pay for. If it was another cent more it would be getting a no instead of a yes recommendation. ... actually- an edit here. After typing through this and realizing just how very much I did not enjoy this game, I cannot give it a recommendation at this price point. If it's on sale for 10 dollars, sure pick it up. Otherwise I'd suggest passing on it.
Aside from the several game-breaking bugs I encountered while playing through the campaign, setting me back ~30 minutes or forcing me to make the conscious choice to restart the level completely due to an inability to stop crouching, jump, or run... the gameplay as a whole was rather unenjoyable. It felt almost like an indie game... a B-movie among video games I suppose. There were parts where it was damn near impossible to find what you were supposed to shoot at, there was a section where you had to use "hellfire missiles" but it did not tell you how, leaving me stuck at that section until I finally looked through all the control bindings to find them on some crazily arbitrary key when they could have simply used right mouse button... The enemy AI wasn't even lacking. It was nonexistent. All the enemies shared the same ~8 models/textures, and the same type of enemy would always run into the same exact position wave after wave until you got your air support to blow it all to hell for you. This is essentially 90% of the game. The other 10% is the game forcing you to stealth through some areas even though being the super soldier any FPS game innately makes you, you could just plow through easily.
The actual sounds of gunfire were pretty good, but the MUSIC... god. You know how all games have their OSTs- and then at that one point of the game where everything gets real or goes wrong, you have the really feelsy ones that make the scene feel epic? And how EVERY game does it? Well it might seem like a broken record, but there's a reason things are like that. Because it's a winning formula- it works. Unfortunately the people making Medal of Honor decided to try to fix what was not broken. EVERY single track felt like it was trying to be that "epic scene" to make the game feel 100x more exciting than it actually was. When all the music tries to compete for sounding amazing, nothing feels special.
The story. Full of holes, nearly nonexistent... without spoiling anything too much, when big scenes happen I just don't CARE. You don't get any backstories. You don't get any personality building. It's just you're there, you do stuff, and the game ends pretty damn abruptly. There's also a very strange "ending after the ending" that made no sense whatsoever. I have no clue if it was hinting towards the next game or what, but it was extremely out of  place and even further undermined the "big scene" of the ending.
The design was also sub par. As I said all the enemies seemed to share the same few models and textures. The environment all felt the same and the map design was poorly laid out for progression- I constantly also ran into invisible bumps that made me stub my toe and unable to move somewhere I clearly should be able to.
Overall if I had to score this- I'd give it a 4/10. At least the credits give you a link to donate to a good cause...? Maybe this game was supposed to be promotional for that? If it was- it shouldn't have been. It'd be much more effective if a GOOD game were to be used for that end.
EDIT: One last edit. There might be ONE thing this game "did right". If I had to take a guess- this might be what war actually feels like (to some extent). Everything feels confusing. There's nothing pointing you in the right direction. It's chaos all around you. Everything looks and feels the same. Unfortunately that just doesn't make for a fun video game for the masses that have been raised on the modern FPS games we have now. I feel like it's possible to get the same "realistic" (again this is an assumption of maybe their goal with the game) experience while still keeping it fun and interesting. I never did mention- the guns feel horridly inaccurate. I've shot guns; they're not pinpoint like in other games, but they're not THIS bad either.

Tried very hard to play through this game. There's quite a bit of frustration to be had in just trying to figure out some things that the tutorial never mentioned.
!@#^$(#$(* things:
-The AI handling your business isn't that great at all.
-The interface you have to use for everything is a bit painful.
-It is an older game and the graphics are dated.
-Annoying management problems start popping up when you own more than 8 businesses.
-There's even more frustration to be had in figuring out how exactly combat works. There's big delays and many times either your friendly AI or enemy AI glitch out and sometimes don't fight. Sometimes you have a higher skill over another in just about every category that matters for combat (including armor), but just can't seem to land a hit while they are dropping you without effort.
-You setup a cart to have an automated supply route for business, but they lose the route the second you click on them to do something else that is needed. There's no way to save the route and re-apply it as needed. Extremely annoying when you have a cluster of businesses that rely on 2-3 carts taking the load with multiple stops for each from a central location.
-Some other minor annoying bugs such as: AI walking around in circles with eachother, Serfs stop escorting a family member or other without telling you they need further action, Employees can't heal up consistently, No notifications for when an employee is killed and another needs to be hired, A plethora of other annoying things that should be easier to automate or set and forget.
-Duels (more on that in a sec)
Good things:
-For being an older game, the graphics were tolerable.
-I really liked the fact that you could create a huge family if you wanted and run the whole city.
-You can bribe people giving you problems.
-You can wipe out a whole family tree that opposes you.
-Money is pretty easy to make once you know how the economy works.
-Feuds are fun to end.
-There's a good sense of growth early on in the game from both character and the game itself giving you more options.
-You can duel others to the death if they insult you or you insult them.
I got really frustrated with having to go back and forth between every single business, every popup, every cart, every employee, and every family member just to make sure they were still doing the job that I had set them out to do in the first place. After playing for so long, I found myself still having to look at everything in a detailed way to see if I had missed anything that wasn't clearly explained by "right clicking" on it for information.
This was the last straw: My character was accused of a crime he didn't commit. I insulted the accuser. The accuser wants to duel. I duel knowing that I am 3 levels above them in every category with a pair of dueling gloves for added bonus and armor all over. I missed every single one of my shots on the target. My accuser lands every single shot on me about 3 -4 times in a row doing over 100+ damage each hit. Alt f4.
It really did seem like it was going to be a great game at first. I just couldn't get over the buggy gameplay, bad mechanics in some areas, lack of automation options that actually worked, other inconsistent aspects, and the lack of clarity what was going on. The learning curve reminded me a bit like the X3 series of space games that lacked explanation and clarity, but turned out to be pretty fun. So, I gave this game a shot in the same way. Nope :/
I may give this another go. It does have it's good points about it and keeps you hooked in. It's a bit masochistic after thinking about it...

In short, it's a good game for it's price. But it's just too easy.
Story:
Not great, it's just the same as a hero saving the world - In reverse! It's about a villain destroying the world. It's predictable, but it's not bad.
Graphics and Music:
Aren't great either. The graphics represent all they should, but I feel like it's too plain. The designs are good, though, the bosses look awesome. The music is your usual MIDI medieval track. Nothing too shiny.
Gameplay:
Super simple. I've finished the game in the Hard difficulty in the exact registered play time that I have. In the boss battle, I've only died once, and that was in his first form, just because of a little fumble...
There aren't many secrets, and that is a bad thing for me. Just make sure you explore everything and you'll get all the equipment and spells. I've only used the heal spell through the entire game, also.
Game Entertainment:
The hours that I put into this game didn't feel empty. It's a fun game, but sometimes you feel like an area could have been shorter. But the final boss battle is going to counterbalance any bad things in the game - It's great.
Overall:
I rate it 9/10. It's not like you can ask more for this price! Just needs more secrets, filling some empty areas, a better looking grass, and it would have been perfect!

What an absolute masterpiece.
BeamNG is a game that uses soft-body physics, which emulates the way real cars crumple and deform in the event of a crash. Lots of cars to choose from, and a multitude of objects to use to crash in millions of different ways on tons of different maps.
The only issues? Mods. The only mods that work are the ones that are simply ♥♥♥♥♥♥ modded versions of the standard cars in the game that you get by default. Want a real world car? I've tried 3 different methods, and none of them worked.
The game runs amazing, and it looks awesome too. But the menus within the game take an hour to navigate through because they are buggy and are very laggy.
This game heavily pushes mods as its largest feature, but it fails to deliver because there is no workshop and hardly any mods work, and all mods offered by the community are boring or "outdated." It's the lack of this that makes the game a little boring and even frustrating at times.
Other than that, the game is absolutely incredible. All of the many worlds you can choose to drive around in are enourmous, and take hours to fully explore. This makes the game fun, replayable, and its a damn good game if you just want to hop in a vehicle and explore a vast and expansive world.
Overall, the experience is incredible and I love every minute of it. Even when you crash, it's utterly satisfying to watch as it is as realistic as it gets in driving games of this generation. Like smashing things? Like driving around? Like realism? Then get yourself this game, because it delivers all three in a perfect package.

Notch - The Innocent LunA: Eclipsed SinnerS is the first Angels Blue novel published on Steam, and a fairly solid entry at that.  Despite being clearly inspired by Higurashi When They Cry, the intriguing story, imaginative ideas and gorgeous artwork make up for a somewhat shaky translation.
The story opens with Yuhito Asakawa trapped in a dream-like world filled with death and horror.  He discovers his childhood sweetheart amidst the mayhem and attempts to escape together, only to end up lost and alone before he awakens from what was only a nightmare.  He soon realizes that the nightmare may not have ended as young, mutilated girls begin appearing throughout town.  Determined to catch the murderer, his pursuit will lead him on a nightmarish journey that will change his understanding of the peaceful world he's always known.
What started off as a fairly generic slasher tale ends up a lot more complex and involved than I was expecting.  Everything experienced early on is turned on its head as details and explanations emerge.  Plenty of clues are there, but without knowledge of the inner workings of this world it's hard to guess at the ultimate outcome.   This isn't a bad thing; far too often I figure out these stories well before they've ended.  But too many curveballs lead to a sense of incredulity when improbable plot developments seem to come out of nowhere, not to mention the liberal use of
to conveniently move the narrative forward when the story has written itself into a corner.
That said, there are plenty of interesting ideas explored here, and the horror elements are visceral and terrifying.  Many of the bad endings have the protagonist in creatively horrific situations that will make your skin crawl.  The mythos is also imaginatively conceived and leaves the door open for more stories in this interesting universe.  My biggest disappointment, however, are in a few intriguing story elements that were hinted at but never returned to.  In some ways, these ideas were more interesting to me than the overall narrative.  Ending the game without exploring them left me feeling  shortchanged, like I was missing an important story point that explained away some of the plot holes that were never addressed (
).
Things start off slow, however.  There's enough horror and mystery to hook you early on, but the plot takes its time to draw you in.  It often feels like Yuhito is wandering between random, unrelated events with little clue on how to piece them all together.  It wasn't until Chapter 6 (out of 11) when a back story begins to materialize that I became fully engrossed.  And let me tell you, once some of those revelations hit, you won't be able to pull yourself away.  But the challenge is getting to that point.  I blame part of the slow burn on a shaky translation that fails to engage the reader with more descriptive writing.
For the most part, the dialogue and narration is acceptable: everything is clearly understandable without any glaring grammatical errors.  However, I feel the translation likely followed the literal meaning of the original language too closely as the style can be stilted and plain.  While the graphic depictions of gore and violence were extremely vivid and creative, the bland dialogue often left me bored in between these instances of deliciously gory detail.  There were also many points where characters repeated themselves over and over.  Perhaps this was done to emphasize the emotional impact of certain scenes, but I suspect it may have been the result of linguistic nuances lost in translation.  Cutting out some of these lines would have smoothed out the narrative flow and reduced a lot of the melodrama.  Writing tone was also a little too casual in some areas with wording that was far too light for the themes present.  Utilizing words with heavier connotations corrects much of this, especially in darker scenes where conveying the severity of the situation is contingent upon them.
Story and writing aside, the artwork is phenomenal.  Character sprites are beautifully detailed and creative, all appearing as if they came right out an official Japanese visual novel.  Event CGs are equally as gorgeous with emotive imagery that greatly enhance the scenes they take place in.  My favorites have a slight impressionistic edge to them which helps convey fear, despair and pain much more effectively than words alone.  The backgrounds range from unremarkable interior buildings to truly breathtaking outdoor views and abstract images that build the chilling atmosphere spectacularly.
The novel is quite long.  As a slow reader, it took me 10 hours to finish my first play through plus an additional 10  searching for all 14 endings.  And you'll want to get them all as there are important details hidden within each that shine a light on several enigmas earlier in the game.  Depending on your level of determination, you could spend upwards of 25 hours unlocking every ending and achievement, which is impressive for a novel with a $10 price tag.
Despite any misgivings I had with the translation, Notch's intriguing mystery, creative horror, and imaginative ideas were enough for me to overlook deficiencies in its writing, which is saying a lot as I consider writing to be the most important element in visual novels.  Would the game have been much more enjoyable if the translation were better?  Absolutely!  But if you can get past the problems, you'll find plenty to entertain you.
Bottom Line: Recommended for visual novel fans who enjoy creative horror storytelling with high production value to back it up.

At first I thought this might be an interesting and unique take on Space Invaders. However, I was quick to learn it is nothing more than Space Invaders with a different name and here is why:
Pros:
♦ Easy Achievements (For Achievement Hunters)
♦ Two language modes Russian or English (This is good to have for people who speak either language. It's nothing spectaculare as it's only two language choices, but I always find it positive when Devs try to include multiple languages)
Cons:
♦ Expensive ($1 for a free poorly made version of Space Invaders)
♦ Space Invaders with nothing unique (This is annoying as the Devs have just basically taken the basic Space Invader concept, put a price on it and resold)
♦ Controls can't be remapped (This doesn't need keyboard controls changed for my personal likings, but some may want to)
♦ No Steam Trading Cards (Game released in 2017 with Achievements but no cards? What is this?)
♦ Sound is generic one track (Seems like sound is one track on repeat which isn't too bad, but needs variety)
♦ Only 10 Levels (Needs more variety in levels and needs way more levels)
♦ Survival Mode is buggy (Enemy character models overlap each other, showing how poorly made the game is)
♦ Survival Mode has no highscores (It needs highscores to make you want to even play it more than once)
♦ Repetitive with no reason to play it more than once (Once you beat the 10 levels, gotten all the achievements (Which is handed to you in under ten minutes for beating all 10 levels) and have tried Survival Mode once, there is nothing to make you want to open the game ever again)
Overall, the game is a bare bones version of Space Invaders with only 10 levels, no variety and lots of bugs. Therefore, as you can play a better version of Space Invaders (Better than this game) for free legally online by doing a quick google search... as this game costs $1 to play this on Steam, I can not recommend it to anyone.

I've reached the second chapter of this game and have played for 3 hours at the time of this review. There's a summary at the very bottom if you don't wanna read the whole thing.
I bought this because the several reviews promised an engaging, interesting storyline complimented by a colourful cast. I was warned the English was shaky, with translation awkwardness riddling the script. But I can manage the occasional awkward English, so long as the story was strong and the characters interesting.
And guess what? They aren't.
The story is good initially, I'll admit. It immediately kicks off and you're pulled into the world. Directly after the prologue comes the scenes introducing us to the main character, a frightening dream-sequence that raises hundreds of questions.
But then the actual game starts, and you're staggered by how throuoghly moronic the protagonist is. The plot couldn't advance if he wasn't such an idiot. Also, he's not likeable at all - he's openly sexist and talks to his childhood friend, Nanami Shio, like she's 10 years old. He refuses to explain anything to her because he doesn't want to upset her, completely ignoring the fact that by withholding important information, he was setting her up for a tramatic experience. He doesn't talk, think or react like a real human being.
Spoiler: after finding a mutilated body, he's briefly afraid, but calms down and begins to think of it as a crime scene. Suddenly, he's not disturbed, or even vaguely upset, by the violently murdered human being lying in front of him - just embarrassed that he freaked out. I thought, maybe, he was emotionally withdrawing, as people sometimes do when confronted with something so horrible, but nope! He's fine, guys. / End Spoiler
He makes the whole experience less believeable and frustrating.
Nanami Shio is the only other character I've met thus far (aside from a girl in a maid outfit, but she appeared very briefly before vanishing). The protag talks to her like she's 10 - and she sort of acts like it, too. She's obsessed with plants and flowers, is constantly expressing worry over the protag, and easily cries. This in itself isn't bad - there are women like Nanami, and there's nothing wrong with them. There's nothing wrong with an emotional, naive female character. The problem is that she isn't treated respectfully by the protag, who is constantly reminding the audience how lovely she is, even after a tramatic dream where he saw dead people, and Nanami covered in blood. Literally, that's the first thing he thinks after waking from a dream where Nanami is pertified and bloody - she's so lovely. He treats her like a child who can't handle bad news, infantilizing her in the same breath he uses to scold himself for sexualising her.
It doesn't help the translation is utterly terrible. They translated the Japanese so literally, the characters sound like robots. When I say that, I don't mean to imply the Japanese language lacks emotion, but what flows properly in Japanese sounds awkward, jerky and needlessly repetitive in English because of how different the languages are. Characters often repeat themselves like they're trying to up the word count on an essay. It's annoying to read.
The game's saving grace is its art - although the characters are very "anime", which I'm fine with, but might disturb some people - and its animations, which thus far are all good. Its music is average, setting the mood but adding nothing in my opinion.
I'd recommend not buying this - unless the translation is redone so it's flows and the characters stop sounding robotic. I think the reason the protag feels so stupid and heartless, and  the reason that Nanami sounds like a woman-child, is because of the bad translations.
tl;dr: While the story is good, the game suffers from idiot characters and terrible translations that are awkward and jerky. The main character is a sexist moron who doesn't act like a human being with emotions. Don't bother with it.

There’s a great story to uncover, no weapons, some puzzles, and a few monsters that you have to avoid. Some people think the game didn't need monsters, but that would've made the it much shorter and less entertaining. The monster encounters are perfectly sprinkled into the game and were always very intense. They don't constantly hound you and you don't have to hide in lockers or anything.
I really enjoyed this game as the world felt real and lived-in. While the story doesn't have any major twists it does have many harsh, thought provoking events. You even have to make some tough choices. These choices have no real effect on the game, but maybe on your psyche.
I’m impressed that they resisted adding weapons and repetitive shooting. I’m also impressed the Steam community has embraced this game so well. This is a good sign for video games in general.
If I had one minor quibble, it would be that the game allows you to pick up many objects in the game for no reason. There are times you do need to pick up stuff and it’s made very obvious, but  It would’ve been nice if there was stuff we could’ve collected or something. I also ran into a glitch late in the game with the Omnitool, but luckily the game keeps many saves for you to return to. It seems to be a known issue that they should really patch. Long story short, after picking up your Omnitool, always wait a few seconds before interacting with something else.

This is a really good visual novel, so good that I found myself replaying over and over to see different endings and actually ended up putting together a guide for the first time ever.  Definitely worth it if you like VNs, in my opinion.
However, bear in mind that this is not a happy, frilly, frolicking-in-the-sunshine-with-a-unicorn sort of story.  It is substantially dark, and that is reflected in many of the endings.  There is graphically violent subject matter, which didn't bother me in the slightest, but if you don't like a lot of gore you might be put off a little bit.
There is minimal fanservice if that's something that impacts your VN purchases.  For this story, it wouldn't have fit well with the story and I appreciate it wasn't forced in; it's something that has its place and doesn't bother me at all, but I'm glad the writers opted to keep it to a minimum for this story.
The language, like many VNs, is a little stilted and clunky in places which is likely a simple translation issue; some concepts and lines simply don't translate well from one language to another.  It didn't take away from the story at all.
The artwork, music, and sound are all nicely done.
All in all, a good choice if you like a dark, bloody story, and with fourteen unique endings, there's a decent lot of replayability.

I hadn't played a Visual Novel in quite some time, it wasn't until recently I had my interest piqued as of late. While browsing for one, I stumbled upon ACE Academy, and I had a flow of nostalgia. Though it is a Visual Novel I've yet to play/experience, I was fortunate enough to experience the demo of it years ago when it still went by the name Kendo Crush (I believe). I had loved every moment of that demo, so I thought I'd take a gamble with this one.
I passed on buying ACE Academy for this game, because I prefer the fantasy setting over Sci-Fi. I cannot say that I was really disappointed by it. So I'll start with my most prevelant and really only gripe about the VN in it's current and possible future state. In the description it boasts "an intricate relationship system", while there is only currently one romacable option. Although the developers explain the method to their madness, I can't help but just believe it makes the game as a whole more linear and gives it less replayability. Besides a few glitches here and there like characters missing irises in their eyes, making them look "off" to put it lightly; or their bodies missing entirely with only their mouths visible and moving and their eyes blinking. This VN in my eyes doesn't have many other faults that are worth really noting since this VN is still in it's early access stage.
The characters given in this story are what really get the gears going. I enjoy the cast of characters and their varied but kind of expectable tropes, but I can let that slide. The VN throws in references here and there, which I found pretty well done with what was given. There are some moments that I generally found myself laughing to myself at. And I like this live 2D Modeling, it makes the characters feel more lively rather than having stale images change stances every now and again. Voice acting is done moderately well, save for a few extra characters/side characters whose images we don't get to see. Artistic direction gets a thumbs up from me as everything really looks nice, and so do the characters and locations especially.
The Kendo Crush demo I played years ago, I believed at the time was one of the best VN's I had played at that point, for it only being a demo. After playing it I craved more, I needed it. To my surprise, I feel the same way after experiencing this one now. Fortunately all I can do is wait for when the developers release a new update for this ongoing work. For what it's worth, I can definitely recommend this. Support this team because this is honestly a VN cut from higher cloth.

TL;DR Summary: SOMA is an excellent game that deserves to be experienced by anyone with even a passing interest in psychological horror or existential philosophy.
It's hard to say a lot about this game without spoiling it; the less you know about its themes going in, the more that the game actually gets to unfold them to you at its own pace, the better the experience will be. That said, the game strikes a fine balance between different kinds of horror: fear of the monster around the corner, fear of what unknown things might be lurking in the darkness, and fear of a more existential nature. At the same time, the mood is not quite so thoroughly oppressive as it was in, say, Amnesia; there are moments of lightness, even humor, amidst the bleak backdrop.
The game features no combat, instead emphasizing a mix of atmosphere, stealth, and puzzles. The various elements are balanced so that you're frequently moving between them, making for overall excellent pacing that gives you time to breathe in between the tensest moments. The "monster encounters" were generally tense enough for me that they achieved their goals: I dreaded encountering one, and was always glad to get past it, and I don't mean that as a criticism. At the same time, there could have been a little more variety to them, and some more variety to the set pieces wherein you encounter them. More dynamic interaction with the environment would have been welcome--for instance, creating cover on the fly, hiding in lockers, or more actively manipulating the monsters to navigate past them. Maybe next time.
The game looks excellent, and I was able to run it at maximum graphical settings on Borderless Windowed mode at 1920x1200 without any slowdown. Sound design is top-notch, too, with solid voice acting. I experienced no crashes and only one major bug throughout my 10-hour playthrough: in one section of the game, a staircase did not correctly load even though it appeared to be there, preventing me from progressing until I saved and restarted the game. No progress lost and only a couple minutes to fix.
The game features no collectibles, no resource management, and no scavenging. There are scattered notes and letters and terminals that you can seek out and access for further insight into the story--and I strongly recommend that you do--but the game's pacing is otherwise very tight and never gets bogged down in demanding that you scour every corner in order to maybe find some bullets hidden under a chair. In some respects, yes, this game is an interactive novel--but it's an excellent one, immersive and interesting and powerful. If you can look past the fact that you're not going to be hunting for gewgaws or wielding a weapon, SOMA is an excellent experience that will leave you thinking.

Maze: Subject 360 has a warning of psychological intense thriller. I was kinda disappointed because I was really expecting something way more scary or with real fear but I suppose that I've expected too much for a casual adventure game. Yet, the psychological side is present and well, Maze: Subject 360 isn't really set for anyone, I understand better the warning: the game isn't really "safe" for children, with the darkness and the twisted beginning of the game.
And the disappointment is also due to the twist after the first part of the game, which ended too soon for me. But well, similar sequences are happening after but you're just missing then the real beat you had first. However, the story is well written.
The gameplay is quite the standard here: use items, find objects, solve puzzles, etc.. The driven by choice mentionned in the description isn't really present, which is a shame. It would have been great to have more of that. However, the rest of the game is quite easy and I must say that I really enjoyed to find how to get past traps. Hidden objects scenes are easy too, which isn't a bad thing in the end (I've finished Mystery Cases Files: Hunstville and it reminded me how it was in the early era of hidden objects games: challenging but sometimes too much).
The graphics are great: it's really fitting to the ambiance of the game, like the soundtrack.
Anyway, Maze: Subject 360 is really a good game, though the description can set higher expectations - it would have been really a true new experience if you could have more choices, more paths. But hey, it's a casual adventure game and it's probably a choice not to get further. Go ahead, the game is worthy of your pennies.

First of all, I had to think long and hard about whether to give this an overall thumbs-up or thumbs-down.  I finally concluded that since I put in the time to not only finish it but get all achievements, and for all its faults it was only made by two guys it seems so it's somewhat forgivable, that it had *just slimly* earned a thumbs-up.  That being said...
WHAT THIS GAME IS:
An action-RPG straight from the NES era, very specifically based heavily on Crystalis to the point at which it's basically a poor man's copycat of that game in every way.  I would suggest skipping this and going to play Crystalis if you like the basic gameplay but want to waste as little time as possible, but if you love Crystalis and want more just like that you might as well give this game a try.  When all's said and done, the gameplay itself is actually quite fun with some fairly well-designed boss battles.
WHAT THIS GAME IS NOT:
Deep in any way, shape or form.  The artwork is laughable, the music is horrendous (some of the worst I've ever heard in any game, indie or not; do your ears a favor and turn it down on the main options screen before you even start your game) and the story is nonexistant.  Oh, sure, it has the barest-bones skeleton of what could have been a unique story, taking the role of a villain rather than a hero on a quest to destroy the world rather than save it, but the entire thing is presented in such a paltry manner it would be considered mind-numbingly boring and predictable even by 80s video game writing standards.  And if you're looking for some kind of character depth or heel-face turn or the actions of your character to mean anything beyond basic evil instincts, look elsewhere.  This game's all about being utterly and remorselessly evil, your character starts out as a more twisted take on a Saturday morning cartoon villain and only gets more evil from there.
Aside from the fact that I feel the art, music and writing are all inadequate even for an indie game made by two dudes, the attempts at humor fall short and there's a bit much killing and implied♥♥♥♥♥♥for a game that's meant to be a throwback to the simple, charming early era of Japanese RPGs.  Again, it teeters ever-so-closely to the edge of getting a thumbs-down; however, that basic element of gameplay is fun enough, especially for an action-RPG junkie like me, that it's the game's saving grace.
There are myriad ways in which this could have been done better, even with such a small team and null-budget; the most fitting comparison I can think of is Breath of Death VII, which is a similar type of NES RPG throwback that had a bit more competence put in the art, MUCH more care and attention put into the music, and writing that doesn't nearly mar the experience with the mentality of a 14-year-old boy who draws dudes getting disemboweled in his spare time; in fact, the follow-up to BoD, Cthulhu Saves the World, displays a much less clashingly unpleasant idea of a villain bent on world-destruction being the hero; it's played up in a much more over-the-top and cartoonish way that fits this style of game much more than the weirdly grisly and depressing 'evil guy' outlook deployed here.  But I'm getting off-track.
Basically, its quality is sub-bargain-bin in almost every way, it's as deep as a dried-up puddle and it's quite short at that (over half my 'gameplay time' here is leaving the game on AFK, and that's with going through it twice for all achievements) but the basic elements of gameplay are so fun in a simple and straightforward kind of way that if you're into this kind of thing you'll probably find it worth the asking price, ideally if it's on sale.  The main point to take from this review is "these guys can and should do better next time, but they're on the right track".

THE BASEMENT is a minimalist Canadian independent horror film. The vast majority of the film takes place in the titular basement, in which five teenagers take refuge after they are attacked by a person unknown, for reasons unknown. The emphasis is on a character driven narrative and psychological horror.
At the start of the film the viewer is presented with very little information about what is going on: who these people are, how they know each other, how they came to be attacked, or where exactly they are, other than in a nondescript basement. The basement itself is almost exclusively shown from a handful of angles, giving the viewer a very limited idea of the size, shape, and contents of the room. This leaves the viewer to piece together the details slowly based on scraps of information revealed as the film goes on, but also from context and inference.
From here, a relatively small portion of the film is dedicated to the teenagers trying to escape. Instead the focus is on the relationships between the characters, and their deteriorating mental states as the situation goes from bad to worse.
While the horror is primarily psychological in nature, that is not to say there is not violence and blood, both of which are present in copious amounts. Also, I want to watch this movie again just to count how many times an F-bomb gets dropped. There is a massive amount of profanity in this film, so if that type of thing offends you, I would stay away.
The acting is solid and for the most part, quite believable. While trying to avoid spoilers, there are several fight scenes, which are both choreographed nicely as well as visceral and brutal. There are not a lot of special effects to speak of, but I was impressed by the attention to detail in character's injuries. Music is used sparsely, but does a good job of creating tension when it is used. While I feel the cinematography is done well overall, I do also feel like we see the room and the characters from the same few angles an awful lot, and would have appreciated some more variety. The film's pacing is a bit slow near the middle, where not a lot is happening.
I recommend this to fans of the horror genre, though not necessarily those who prefer the slasher style of horror. If you enjoy a slower paced, more pensive story and don't mind not having everything explained to you outright, I think you should definitely check this film out.

I just bought this game today and I've had a ton of fun playing it so far.
The gameplay so far is admittedly very simple. You walk around, press E to eat/drink, press F to roar, and left click to attack. There's just something about the fact that you're walking around, eating and roaring as a DINOSAUR. The animations are beautiful and smooth, which definitely makes the experience more enjoyable. There's no real goal, other than to explore, meet people, maybe attack some things, maybe run away from things.
There are problems with the game, of course. It's early access, and that's accepted. As a raptor, sometimes you get stuck in the "pounce" position and you're sliding around on your tail with your little claws up in the air as you grin as everyone you pass. The puertasaurus definitely has some work that's needed, but from what I know it's just a placeholder, and honestly I spent most of my time playing as a puerta. They move achingly slow, they cannot deal damage, and they get caught on trees they could realistically step right over. However, when you're walking a quarter mile an hour with three rexes, a carno, two raptors, and a galli circled around you like your own private carnivore army, it's pretty fun just to walk around and enjoy the scenery. Just remember not to go into the trees, because you'll get a face full of foliage.
The other dinosaurs are also fun, though carnivores seem to be the most powerful at the moment. It's hard to make dinos realistic while also balancing, because herbivores travel in herds and carnivores are usually on their own. However, instead you end up with packs of 6 rexes against 2 gallis and there's not much you can do about it. There are some balancing issues; rexes are probably the most powerful, rivaled by the raptor solely because of their pouncing ability. Raptors can pounce and latch onto larger dinosaurs, and there's no way to get them off once they're on. There should be a way to shake them off, or make it more difficult for the raptor to stay attached. Herbivores could definitely use a buff; if they have no defenses, they need to be faster than rexes. Otherwise, they need defenses.
Other things I'm hoping for is perhaps a minimap, a health bar, a hunger bar, and of course flying dinosaurs. I would also love some underwater dinos but I realize that's a whole new environment with a whole new set of coding rules and that could be a far way off. I'm really excited to see where this game goes, as it's a lot of fun to play even as it is now.

I've been playing games for over 25 years now and I can safely state that this new interpretation of MoH is the worst FPS I have ever experienced.
- Story and dialogue consist of either a) military gibberish that is probably supposed to sound cool and badass but comes off as nothing but incomprehensible and boring or b) cringeworthy and corny exchanges of either patriotic or SUPERRRRRR TOUGH lines. My favorite? Early on you rescue an Afghan, but your men aren't sure if they can trust him:
Grunt A: For all we know he set us up a trap. We can't trust this guy!
Grunt B: You're right. Hurr durr.
Tariq (the Afghan): I have a daughter, I want her to live in freedom.
All grunts together: Oh, ok, now we trust you. You're cool.
- Your playing field is EXTREMELY limited despite many areas appearing to be open. So you're just blocked by measly small boulders and the likes. Some you can hop over, some you can't. Have fun finding out which are which.
- Despite the pipe-shaped levels it is sometimes way too easy to miss the exact spot you need to step on in order to trigger the next event.
- Occasionally these triggers are even bugged, forcing you to reload from a checkpoint. Once, for example, my men told me to secure a hut...in a village full of huts that basically all look the same. So I approach each and every one multiple times to no avail. After I (on purpose) blew myself up with a grenade suddenly my men didn't just stop, but pushed on.
- Moments that are supposed to stand out are even worse than the general gameplay. Directing missiles and whatnot from far away for minutes is pure valium; sniping is tedious and the game obviously acknowledges it by pushing you towards your targets if you can't find them within the low resolution, all-lookalike mountainsides; and that part where you and your men take cover inside a hut, fending off dozens of Taliban that reduce your cover to little more than a few bricks would even be too ridiculous for a Bugs Bunny cartoon.
- mission objectives just kind of pop up all the time and are marked as completed all out of a sudden. You never feel like you're actually accomplishing anything, instead merely pushing forward and letting the game do the rest. And if you ever do get lost because of the game's bugginess, the mission objectives don't give off any useful information as to what to do exactly.
- Press F to get pulled up a small ledge by your buddy? What for? It doesn't add ANYTHING to the gameplay and it feels completely out of place when your men can take the same ledge on their own easily. It's just supposed to show off some sort of comradery. Woo, these guys are so cool...
- which leads to another downer: None of the soldiers you meet is charismatic or memorable. They either come off as complete♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that don't give a damn about the values they are supposed to be fighting for but merely loving the fight itself, or they are so forgettable, you won't even remember their names for a minute.
- Combat simply doesn't feel good. Weapons don't pack a punch and often you're left wondering if you hit a guy and whether he's just hurt or dead.
- Not a single moment in the game sticks out.
- a mere 4 hours long
- even the ending sucks. The moment I realized the game was about to end was when, ironically, one of your men says "This is not how it ends.". The rescue mission right at the end of the campaign is probably meant to be some big highlight. Some huge event the whole tension is building up to. Only, it doesn't work that way at all. It just felt like I was in the middle of the game, not like I was nearing the end. Rarely have I seen such an anticlimactic ending, which is made even worse with a stupidly blunt cutscene wrapping things up. Supposedly, teh mountainside is void of enemys (they even outright tell you so), but still we see them bombed to smithereens. Why? Maybe because the director said he'd need some more explosions. And what about the brief segment showing a busy street in peaceful Afghanistan? I haven't got a clue. Maybe worst of all is the Linkin Park song playing afterwards. I like Linkin park, that's not the problem. My issue is that it seems highly out of place. It feels like the song went right over the guy's head who was responsible for licensing songs.
How about some other slapstick moments the campaign despite being so short is loaded with?
- Airplanes delivering airstrikes magically fly straight through mountains popping back into sight at the other end.
- You are supposed to mark a bunker but it won't work? Oh, silly you, what the game really meant for you to do is to mark some nondescript boulder a few metres away from the bunker. Don't worry, the airplanes are still going to hit the bunker, not the boulder.
- Your highly specialized teammate opens up a door to a dark tunnel? I'm sure he'll do it carefully, taking cover and using flashlights or thermovision. Oh, too bad, he just stands in the entrance - upright - and shouts "oh, it's so dark in there" only to get shot.
Bottom line: Horrible game that is in no way realistic, but tries its best to convey such an image and thus sacrifices gameplay. So in the end it gets neither right.
At least the so-called Tier 1 mode is a nice idea. Here, you replay the SP missions, aiming for fast times, earning medals in the process. If only the gameplay mechanics would make for a better foundation.

Evil Quest isn't terrible. But that's really all there is to say. It's playable if you like top-down action RPGs. The combat isn't inspired, and the hitboxes take some getting used to (it's bigger than it looks on your sprite). Attacking is a bit tedious, and magic, especially early on, consumes so much of your meter and takes so long to recharge that you'll find yourself using the first spell, Ice 1, through most of the game, just because it's cheaper to cast. Heal 3 makes the game trivially easy. Once you get that (you can get it just before the ice dungeon), you can almost instantly heal up from any attacks, and unless you get overwhelmed by a rapid assault, nothing will kill you. The final boss can be defeated by standing still and spamming projectiles and healing, even in the hardest difficulty. Hard difficulty is barely that. The only difference is that enemies have tons more health and do a little more damage, meaning fights take longer and you have to heal more often.
The characters are one-note and repetative. Your main character has only one mood, angry, and he will resort to murder for virtually every situation. Even some potential allies wind up being killed for essentially no reason. The main character's motivation is nothing more complex than "destroy the world". So yes, in that it features a quest of an evil character, this is an evil quest. However, that is all it is. The other NPCs come in two types: "I will kill you, you monster!" and "Please don't murder me, Mr. Bad Guy!". You will always kill the first type, and usually kill the second type. That's it. There is nothing more interesting to the plot.

I probably have hundred of hours in this game, on steam and when i owned it before in a different medium. At least half the bugs people complain about are not bugs, it is people not being interested in figuring out how the game is played. Are there bugs? Yes, but as a rule it is not all that hard to play around them, and i have successfully played around them for years.
To my astonished suprise though, this game is suddenly being updated. I mean who updates a game 5 years later?! These guys are doing just that. And not tiny updates, we are talking full on bug bashing. Sure it looks like they are taking some fixs from the community mods and implementing them into the game, but they give credit for it and why shouldn't they? I am honestly sick and tired of unofficial patches fixing all the things a company is too lazy to do themselves. Especially when most of the work is done for you. Thank you Guild II devs, you are geniuses.
This game is massively complicated, with so many different game mechanics you will have to completely relearn it when you change classes. Sometimes these varying mechanics can be so complicated and different you will find yourself scouring the internet to find answers on how and what to do. A bad thing? Maybe. Even after hundreds of hours there are still things i can not figure out, and its honestly irksome. Large portions of witches and wizards and alchemists are a mystery to me, and i have yet to find anything online to explain how they work. So i am assumign this lack of information means others are as stymied as i am. If anyone knows how summoning circles and transmutation works, please for the love of god explain it to me!
If you like the idea of being able to mod your game, you will enjoy this game. It has mods, lots of mods. It is beginning to seem though the intergration of some of the better mods means you wont have to go through the trouble of downloading them, and some are making their way into the game itself thanks to a rebirth by the devolpers.
If you ever loved the concept of the sims, or better yet breathed heavy over medieval sims, and yet felt insulted how easy the game was, you will be in heaven with Guild II renaissance. I wish there were more ways to decorate houses and businesses, but buying upgrades and having them appear is still rather satisfying. Equiping and arming you player characters is fun enough, though i would like a more immersive system and choice of clothes.
What I think game is missing:
- Interactions with NPCS that aren't 100% game plot driven. You can talk to NPCS to bribe them. Or woo them. Or threaten them. But you never really get to interact with this big world for just fun reasons. Give me a "Hey bill, whats up bro" option please.
- More stuff to make at your job. Does it need it really? No. But it would be nice if they grew the massive economy more to be epically huge and new options to build more things at your shops and crafthalls. I suppose having so much just makes me greedy for more. And in all honesty it is unlikley super difficult for the devs to give us more.  Therefore since the bug squash has begun, maybe soon enough we will get treated to more a content addition. After all there are lots of unofficial mods out there with some neat things, maybe some will be made official.
- Bug fixes. but these are coming. Some of my biggest long standing gripes are wiped away with the new patches at the end of 2014. I love you devolpers. Seriously i do!
In the end is this game a buy? ARE YOU KIDDING?! you can find it on sale sometimes for $2.50 and even if its not on sale, $10 is a steal! If you like sims and but think you have more to offer a game then choosing a Sim's bathing suit pattern, this may be the game for you.

This game is a very fun and addicting roguelike.  And it's an actual turn-based roguelike - not a roguelikelike, or rogulelite, or whatever the currently preferred term is for games of other genre which borrow roguelike procedural generation and permadeath.
Lord of the Dark Castle is definitely of a smaller scale than many of it's roguelike peers such as Tales of Maj'Eyal or Dungeons of Dredmor - there are currently only 7 levels (with 3 more to come), only 6 inventory slots (not counting active equipment), and no choice of class/race during character creation.  In fact, the character creation consists of choosing the difficulty level, the character's name (optional), the character's appearance, and purchasing some gear in the starting shop.  The money you have depends on the chosen difficulty level, and any unlocked in-game achievements - more on this last part later.
After exiting the starting store, you find yourself in a forest level.  You see a gold sack, sprint towards to pick it up, and get hit for 20% of your health by a trap.  Reeling, you bump into a goblin bandit, who quickly steals that expensive spear you bought in the store, and takes off another 30% of your HP, while you manage to fisticuff him to death.  He drops a little gold for your trouble, but your spear is nowhere to be found.  Which really makes no difference, because the next beastie you encounter is a spider, which proceeds to web and poison you from a distance.  As you struggle to free yourself from the webbing, you watch your HP get lower and lower.  Thankfully, a bear stops by to put you out of your misery.  And this is on the MEDIUM difficulty setting.
So yeah, this game is HARD :)
Then you create a new character, and maybe think a bit more about your starting equipment choices.  Perhaps settle for a simple club and minimal armor, and use the extra money to buy the Detect Traps skill and a Cure Poison potion.   Then manage to defeat a few of the weaker looking enemies, and on level-up select the Sneak skill as your first reward - which will play well with the low "Detection Modifier" granted by your lack of armor.   Level up more and find out what more skills do, how they impact the game.  Encounter new monsters, and discover their strengths and weaknesses.  Find *GREAT LOOT*, and try to keep it from being stolen and destroyed.  Agonize over what to keep in your meager 6 inventory slots, and what to sell in a shop (or better yet convert to gold directly with the Alchemy skill.) Die over and over, but learn more about the game in the process!
Once you have a basic handle on things, check the Achievements on the main menu (hopefully to be integrated with Steam at some point.)  Until unlocked, all you'll see is the achievement name, a "hint" about the unlock requirements, and the gold reward you get for unlocking it.  This reward is the starting gold bonus, which means the ability to exit the starting shop more prepared for the dangers!
So yes, this game is very fun, though it does feel unfairly difficult at times - but all the more rewarding when you do manage to overcome it!  It *is* still in Early Access as I write this, and there are bugs of varying severity, but the dev is very active in the community hub discussion topics, and receptive to bug reports and suggestions.  At the $5 asking price, I'd say this is a very good value for any roguelike lover.
