Adventurezator is an adventure creator for point and click adventures.  Still in its early stages at the time of this review, It shows a lot of promise, and the style and ease of use are pretty good, allowing a complete amateur to create professional looking levels in a 3d world with little knowledge and experience of adventure games.
The way the npc's and the puzzles are 'Emergent' is the main goal to this.  You just add various elements, set a few simple parameters, and let the npc's act accordingly. Set them a few objects to interact with, set up a few friends and enemies, and things to say and just let them go.  You don't have to worry too much about pathing or complex dialogue trees (at the moment, though I imagine this may change later)
The cutscene creator is of necessity a bit more complex than the other editing tools, but it looks like it won't be too hard to make a nice looking  cutscence to add an interesting story for the campaign. All it requires apart from some experimenting  is a bit of artistic skills or use of others work, which makes the ability to use the workshop to use others content a boon to this type of game.
The problem at the moment, apart from the inevitable bugs during development is the simplicity of the puzzles available and lack of ability to customise objects. Only had the game for a short while, but looking at the current state of the game it seems the developer has concentrated on getting the look and the basic mechanics in place first, so while it looks good, and is easy to use, the content and ways to interact are a little limited if you want to dive in and create devious puzzles, and truly create your own world.  The current playable levels are also rather limited, as another reviewer put it, they are more to give you examples on which to to base your own work.
Time will tell of course. The developer has to balance ease of use with the complexity and flexibility of the tools available. As more content gets added we will be able to see just how powerful this game creator will be. I can say that even at this early stage, its fun to mess around with and create a little world, and I look forward to seeing what else I can do in the future.
The humour and style of the game is great, and I think it can be a  very interesting and involving way to tell your own story. I would recommend this to anyone who would like to express their creativity and make an adventure game, but do not want to have to mess around with the more complex tools available elsewhere.

Unlike some other Dinosaur games I have backed, some which I eventually got to play, this game actually shows progress of its development. BUT...
-EDIT 2nd JULY 2017-
I have been playing the Early Access game for a while now, and while many of the issues I encountered in my last edit (27th April 2017) are still present I have just been encountering more and more with the community, and now within the game itself.
"Carebears" and "Kill-on-sighters" run rampant in the mainstream servers, ruining not only the immersion experience, but also the "progression" system should you happen to be on a server that uses it.
Here, stuff for you.
PROS
+ You play as a Dinosaur, and can choose Herbivore or Carnivore with many different skins for each species, providing variety in player looks. The other good thing about it is you don't have to pay for the skins, or camp for loot crates to get them.
+ Basic Survival mechanics present and functional, with a Progression system featuring multiple "ages" for some species, plus a Growth system. Servers can make the growth/progression stuff optional, so you may actually find a Sandbox server which lets you pick a dino without any hassle earning it.
+ Playing Human -will- be optional, no being forced into it!
+ Maps huge, diverse in biomes (Minus cold/alpine/arctic) and the graphics are pretty, but the LOD of some trees looks bad.
+Herbivores diet is well balanced and progression feels natural, but Carnivores are not so fortunate.
+Support for scavengers! And future support for fishers!
+It runs fine on a laptop, just keep your graphics at medium or less.
CONS
- Besides No Man's Sky, this game makes me feel completely alone; the map is huge, and in servers of up to 100 people I am lucky to see a single person.
- There is no AI implemented yet, and unless you turn cannibal you are doomed to starve as a carnivore, because Herbivores progress so well that by the time you find another player you are seriously outmatched and cannot hunt them.
- It takes up to TWO HOURS to reach Tier 2 of the predator tree, this is not acceptable for people who play games with minimal free time.
- Do NOT expect "natural behaviour". Human beings control these Dinosaurs, so you might see two carnivore species hunting another one instead of attacking each other. This at present is just another PvP game where people kill on sight, it might change but with how I see things I seriously doubt it.
- The community is borderline toxic, made from remnants of Primal Carnage's and PvP bandwagon hoppers. If you want to play the game properly without the headaches, wait until AI comes out and  play on your own server, or join a realism server that requires group membership.
Trust NOONE, not even members of your own species, and especially people who aren't your friends on Steam; everyone is out to screw each other over in this games current state and it feels more like Battle Royal for Dinosaurs than anything else.
Game is showing signs of significant improvement and stability, so I would recommend it...just don't expect to like the playerbase much or be liked by the devs.

It's December 22, 2014 and a patch just got released for this 4.5 year old game. Whomever these guys are that bought this license are serious about cleaning it up, but the thing is it was already a great title to begin with. Yeah there were some translation problems, and ai issues, and general problems like that, but it wasn't terrible.
Anyways, this game is just great. You play some male or female person set in old timey overseas land (you get to choose the map to play on), and try to stary a dynasty. You find a spouse, make some kids, and play through the generations. Jobs include stuff from politics, farming, to robbing people. You can make buildings like inns, pubs, churches, and so on or eleminate competing dynasties and take over their buildings through violence or cash. You can select your own stats on the dude or chick you're creating and level up skills through actions, so some rpg elements exist.
You got some trading elements in here as well. Own a mine? Send a caravan of ore to the neighboring village to sell, or import the stuff to make your own jewelry factory. Or make armor and weapons and attack villagers with your bandits. You got a lot of options here on what to do as far as playstyle is concerned. It's a sandbox, but you can't just plop buildings down everywhere. Still there's a lot of options to be found and fun to be had by picking this up and giving it a shot. It can be a little daunting to get into, but I ended up having a lot of fun with this and The Guild II. Well mainly vanilla Guild II, but this is just that with more stuff, so if you can decide which version to get, this is the one to grab.

Early Access First Impressions
An emergent adventure game about making emergent adventure games?
It makes one wonder if it might just be trying to reach a bit too much. After all, maybe it’s either just a game creation tool, or just a point n click adventure. Could it possible be both, and actually good at both?
Well now, in simple terms; Yes.
The game is spit into its two main components, Adventurezator, which is a rather detailed system for creating your own point n click adventure games. By detailed, I mean just that. Everything from unique characters, cut scenes, and levels can be created so far. With the option later to tie them all together in a campaign creator.
It’s simple to use, and rather intuitive, as shown in my first impressions video. Among it’s rather plentiful objects, and creation settings, it also allows the user to import images, sounds, music, and more. Featuring a rather detailed little NLE editor for creating your cut scenes and will access to any folder on your system to import needed files.
If you’ve ever played the Sims, or a similar game; you can easily create a level, building or forrest with rather amazing cartoony detail. A rather pleasant system indeed, and if they continue to add more it will only get better.
This brings us to When Pigs Fly; the point and click adventure game what according to the developers was made entirely using Adventurezator. After playing around in it,  can certainly see this as being true.
You only have the option of a ‘Quickie’ though, 4 pre-completed levels to play. The Arena is a mess in my opinion. Without so much as a even a single que or popup telling me what’s going on I was quickly mangled by a rather large bear. There were no instructions on how to fight, much less what to actually even do.
Frustratingly I left to explore the When Pigs Fly chapters that are the point and click.
They’re actually rather good, although once again there aren’t any instructions on how to play. There are some objective in the top left corner however.
Sadly shortly after starting I was left confused and frustrated once again. Unable to complete a prime objective, or simply talking to a Zookwinkle. Now matter how many times I clicked, wandered about or interacted with the little gnome, I was unable to engage him in dialogue. Frustratingly I felt like just giving up and writing off the game entirely.
Good thing I didn’t, as I chose instead to play the other two Quickies, and oh my are they good. The lack of gameplay instructions did mate it tough, and I did fail a few times. Yet in the end I completed both, and found I had actually enjoyed the experience. The puzzles weren’t so much as complex and difficult to solve, as much as the gameplay and mechanics needed some polish. Easily forgiven, as the game is still in the Alpha changes at the time of writing this.
You really need to explore and hover your mouse cursor over every little nook, cranny and object to make sure you don’t miss anything.
I was also rather delighted at the fact that instead of simply evading the three bears to steal their food; I could wield an axe and murder all of them. Including the little bear cub that though I was his nanny. Such sadistic freedom made me chuckle, as I stood axe in hand over the bodies of these bears. Blood slowly pooling at my feet. Bacon might be their favourite food; but on this day the bacon made them pay.  All in all Adventurezator: When Pigs Fly has some amazing potential, and despite some gameplay issues all relating to their point and click the rest is rather wonderful. The toolset is perfect for people that want to create their own adventures, and once the game is completed sharing these with the community will easily expand the game and keep the community happy and engaged.
Pigasus Games have given people the tools with which to create their own unique stories, whether these are feats of heroism, or madness incarnate. This is certainly worth trying, and keeping an eye on for both the tool set, and their adventure game.

"The difficulty crops up here, because it is difficult to explain past this point. True to its marketing, Circles relies on a what could be considered subconscious suggestion to to train the player’s mind to find the solution to its puzzles. When I first started playing, I didn’t notice the training my brain was going through for several puzzles, until I started taking more note of the seemingly basic music. What I thought was just meant to be inoffensive background noise to keep engagement, I realized that the music actually had a drum beat that would respond to my movements. Different beats and sounds will enter the musical pattern based on whether or not I was closing in on the solution.
The music isn’t the only suggestive tool used. To keep things engaging, Circles utilizes some color theory tricks. While many puzzles will have very complimentary colors that are easy on the eyes, other puzzle sets use contrasting colors. Now, color theory itself isn’t anything sound, I can personally vouch that many puzzles felt mentally satisfying to complete, not just because of the challenge, but to clear the conflicting colors from the screen. The colors are never offensive to the eyes, thankfully, again, the effect is mental. These color arrangements almost double down on the satisfaction of finishing of the puzzle."

Really enjoying it so far. Best recommendation I can make is to keep track of people who are fun to play with since it makes all the difference in the world with this game. The communication and potential for role play and comedy is one of the game's greatest features.
For example, I play with my wife and we were both being chased by a killer who had taken on the persona of a murderous Hodor. All our pleas and bargaining as we ran for our lives were met with a solemn, occassionally confused, "HODOR!"
Some people are talking about Jason being overpowered, but I think that is early day salt more than actual reality. Once you know the mechanics, Jason is pretty easy to avoid as you can negate his sense ability completely with high enough composure. I have seen some melee oriented players do well at stunning him reliably as well when working with a group. More than likely, as perks begin to roll out, Jason will need a bit of buffing, but right now the balance feels pretty good.
Games can drag a bit if you die early and someone is trying to be sneaky, but this goes back to that orginal point. Having good company to chat and cheer with makes spectating fun or at least helps pass the time. I respect why some people don't like that 20 minute turn timer, but anything else feels like it would make the problem worse as people would be more likely to try to run out the clock than hit objectives.
Oh, and the price is an obvious point of contention. I won't lie, it almost kept me away, but despite what looks like a small amount of content on paper, I don't feel like it is going to stale out on me any time soon.

Now, I know I'm going to get a lot of flak for this. But the Peer to Peer is actually a blessing in disguise. This game is a FIGHTING game at it's core. No matter how people want to think of it, it's still a fighting game which requires fast reaction times. Peer to peer is used WIDELY in almost all fighting games due to it being faster. Being able to connect directly with other players and no middle man (servers). Allows for much faster, and smoother gameplay. Sure, it may have to resync every once in a while, but those moments don't ever last for more than 5 seconds and is barely negative to your gameplay.
Imagine if we did have dedicated servers, okay cool. Now think if someone joined a server because they couldn't find a game in their region and their ping was TERRIBLE. We would have constant teleportation around the map, gimmicky reactions, and unfluid combat. Sure we get the occasional teleporting guy (hasn't happened to me). Though these moments come far and few in For Honor.
Now people claim P2P allows for lag switching and ddoss attacks.
This has been happening for as long as gaming has been around. People used to do this all the time, especially on PC. Theres nothing we could really do to completely stop that, and the occsaions this happens is quite RARE. We need to stop acting like Ubisoft broke 5 years of no ddoss attacks, or lagswitches because they didn't. It's always been around no matter if a game had dedicated, or p2p networks. It's going to be around with future games for a long time. Let's stop acting like this takes away from whats great in the game.
For me personally, and this is complete honesty,
-Gear Stats which affect revenge in 4v4 modes. (Revenge is a great feature, but gear stats allow some people to abuse and survive for a lot longer than they should by increasing the rate at which they get revenge)
-Passive gameplay, as you get higher, players become more defensive and slow paced in duel modes which the game generally favors. I think they need to make stamina drain if they are constantly blocking hits to allow a more even play style.
-Party disbanding when everyone leaves the lobby
-Voice chat being automatically disabled (A lot of people don't even know voice chat exist!)
-Faction war only matters on the last few turns, I think Faction war needs a rework on the round systems.
-No community manager as of now (Someone that is very social on sites like twitter, reddit, steam forums, etc and respond to all the questions).
-Matchmaking (Currently if you level a hero up high, and then switch to a new hero, you'll still be matched with high levels)
-People refusing to "Get Gud" as some of the community doesn't believe they should lose or get better at timing certain things. *Cough* guardbreak.
-Possible Hackers, though this happens in every game on PC, and Ubisoft has already spoke about protecting the community and keeping it hack free.
For Honor is a game with great, and interactive gameplay. I see myself playing this for a very long time and applaud Ubisoft for redeeming themselves with games such as For Honor, and Rainbow Six Siege. The multiplayer offers a great experience, that is barely hindered by things that people make such a big deal about. The issues such as p2p and ddossing is widely blown over and this game was worth every penny in my opinion. The singleplayer is a decent experience, but nothing groundbreaking. If you are getting the game just for singleplayer I would not reccomend it. The fun is in amazing multiplayer experience.
Trust me when I say, the issues about P2P and such that you see on the steam reviews are completely blown over.
9,200 reviews at the time I wrote this.
About 3,500 roughly wrote negative reviews on steam reviews. The game has about 60,000 people playing daily and probably have sold MUCH more than that. So 3,500 making negative reviews is extremely small if you look at the numbers
More people are obligated to write a negative review than a positive.
So yes, the problem is virtually non existent. Though there are always those few unlucky ones who get issues. The issues most likely come from their end and their internet provider. Or their NAT type being closed/blocked by programs such as antivirus.

Just finished Episode 3 about 5 minutes before I started writing this. As of right now, I can safely say this Visual Novel has been the best I've played so far. I've played PixelFade's other VN, ACE Academy (which I highly recommend checking out), and most of the problems I had with that have been improved with this game. After seeing how PixelFade takes criticism and the love they seem to have for their work, I WILL be purchasing and trying out their future releases. The sheer level of improvement is amazing.
Here is my breakdown:
PROS:
- Hundreds of Choices: Most of the choices in this game are just how the main character reacts to a scene, which alters how the other characters react to the scene, or may slightly alter the path of events later on (like choosing to get drunk with Zack or staying sober (I'm also assuming this one, because I haven't exactly tried the alternative. Drunk Zack is too great)). Needless to say, it gives both the main character depth and keeps it interesting.
- Voice Acting: I'm a massive fan of the English Voice Acting. Whilst some words are mispronounced, it's generally high quality, with only one or two character's voices really stand out as out of place. Definitely massive props to both Leanna and Zack's voice actors, as both do fantastic performances in Episode 3 especially.
- Animated Sprites: Something I haven't seen before is moving sprites. Characters move around, blink and their mouth is in perfect sync with the words they are saying. It's truly amazing to see such an amazing step in quality here.
- High Quality CG's: The actual artwork is just incredible. Miles better than ACE Academy, and the only thing I can fault it on is a lack of it. But when it does pop up, it's fantastic.
- Decent Story: Whilst I have seen this type of plot done before, it's still nice to see it done in a different style. It's interesting enough to keep your attention, and build a nice connection with the main character and those around him.
- Believable Characters: Every character has a personality, with a level of depth to them. I've thoroughly enjoyed interacting with them during the course of the game.
- Comedic: I like to have a good laugh, and some of these scenes are just amazing.
CONS:
- Early Access: First point is kind of a given, but at the stage of writing this review, the game is unfinished. It kind of kills immersion to see the "early access - minigame not yet available" message pop up when combat is meant to initiate. And the end of Episode 3 leaves me wanting more. Once it's done though, this wont be a problem (obviously).
- Lack of Sprites: I understand animating and drawing sprites is difficult, but not seeing who I am meant to be talking to is immersion breaking. Only the lead characters actually have sprites, so be warned.
- Limited Routes: I'm going entirely off the Steam Description here, but it looks like Leanna is the only romance route at this point. I hope this changes in the future, as it adds so much more to the game if you can take another heroine route.
-Scores-
Story: 6
Characters: 9
Art: 10
Music: 5
Enjoyment: 10
Overall: 8/10
tl;dr, buy this game if you are happy with it being not yet finished, and want a fantasy based VN

The "It's $2!!" excuse doesn't work if the game would only be considered mediocre at best if it was free....
The first thing you notice right off the bat is the music. They are MIDIs. Oh wait, sorry.
So you can't even use something like TiMIDIty++ or BassMidi to make them sound at least somewhat decent.
The next issue is the main character. The whole gimmick of the game is "play the villain". By villian, it means "horrible psychopathic murderer". Seriously, there is no depth to the character at all. No tragic backstory, just "let's destroy the world because why not". There is no motivation for playing as him. You don't root for the guy at all. He literally kills people for no reason.
The graphics are nothing special. Just your usual "retro 8-bit" fare. What you see is what you get.
The controls are horribly inconsistant, especially in the menus. Sometimes escape exits the menu, sometimes it doesn't. You press 'e' to open your equipment, but can't press 'e' again to close it. The in-game controls are also slightly unresponsive. It does mess you up slightly, but it isn't god awfully unplayable. Also, the best part about the controls is that you can see an enlarged view of the map by pressing 'm'. Except, you can't pause the game with the map up at the same time, making it almost useless.
The biggest flaw by far is the linearity of the game. There are no sidequests (I don't count achievements because they don't give you anything special in-game). There are also no real "transitions" to the different areas. You just wander around and beat dungeon after dungeon. This is probably why the game takes only around 2 or so hours to beat. There is next to zero real backtracking (which would be good if the game wasn't horrifically short). The only other real thing to go do is to get some hidden treasures (which really aren't that hidden).
The last thing of note is the uselessness of 90% of your items. Your charge shots can hit switches from far away. How many switches do you need to hit?
The charge shot itself is also useless 90% of the time as well because you have to charge while standing still. The damage output isn't great either. The only real use is when you have to because the enemy is far away and you're waiting for your MP to regenerate. You later get the ability to jump. How many times do you need to jump?
You later get running shoes, except you have to hold down alt of all things to use them. The uselessness expands to the towns as well. There are inns, but I have no idea what they do because I've never once needed to use one. The only thing you need from towns are potions. The armor you can get there you can usually get a few minutes of play later from a chest. Spells are next to useless to buy. You get most of them in game, and the ones you don't are obsolete or never really used. The major exception are the cure spells.
Avoid forever

It might be a strange thing to say after 12 hours on record, but I don't really like graphic horror. It grosses me out. Which makes it all the more amazing that Amnesia: The Dark Descent grew on me the longer I played, mostly because there's so much about this game they actually did right.. It's an atmospheric survival adventure that tells a complex narrative as you stumble around a very dark place, literally and figuratively. So much could have gone wrong about this formula, but didn't.
The pacing feels just right. They ease you in, feeding you just enough mysteries to keep you interested before you get to the fast-paced survival and cerebral puzzle parts. Puzzles aren't of the impossibly hard variety, which is because they're nicely logical. Everything about your enivronment works and reacts very intuitively, it all feels natural, which means this game actually rewards observation and logical thinking in every step you take. The narrative is told by flashbacks and written notes you uncover along your way, which isn't nearly as wooden and obstrusive as it sounds. The dose feels just right. It's also one of the few games where bad visibility actually provides creepy mood rather than plain annoyance.
I would have appreciated a bit less of the gory and disturbing stuff, as the creepy atmosphere alone really stands its ground. But add good writing, good pacing and convenient mechanics, and what you have here is a rather competently executed game. If you have even a passing interest in adventure or survival games and don't mind the gross stuff, you probably want this.

This game sets off some primitive part of my brain that gives me some sort of morbid curiosity and interest in car crashes. Evolutionarily, it makes no sense; I should be scared of them. You know, winning a Darwin Award is not a prize one would like. Yet, dashcam compilations, Burnout Revenge's Crash mode, and BeamNG.drive are SO DAMN INTERESTING AND FUN. What sets this game apart is its soft body collision physics engine. Which is just a long way of saying that the car physics in this game is really realistic. Let's compare this to Grand Theft Auto where a non-branded Honda Civic can withstand several highway speed crashes much like a M1 Abrams. Sure you lost a door or two and completely destroyed its resale value, but the only thing that matters is that it still runs at a reasonable speed. If you run your car into a wall at highway speeds in this game you'll be assaulted by a hail of windshield bits while you're screaming in agony because your car's A pillar is now embedded into your skull. Hell, if you run into a mildly large rock at a speed suitable for a busy school zone, you'll probably majorly mess up your radiator. This game is just a toy box for me to watch realistic car crashes without the guilt, knowing that no virtual people were hurt in my vehicle destruction. While, sure this game is still in Early Access, it is still worth the money. Surely it's leagues better than some stupid low effort asset-bought Unity game that plagues the Steam store now-a-days.

Recommend. Well worth the price. Great minimalist puzzle game!
It's just you and your mouse out there! (Please don't try to play this game on a track pad). Literally all you do is move your mouse. You don't even use mouse buttons... JUST movements. And with that, Circles is a fairly original and clever puzzle game. On each level, NOTHING happens until you move your mouse. The levels are all based on how you're moving. Which direction are you moving your mouse? How fast or slow? How close to another object is your object? These are the types of factors you'll have to consider when completing a puzzle.
Artistically, the simplistic style works perfectly. It reminds me a lot of the feel of Anti-Chamber, including the visuals, the music, and even the cleverness and simplicity of the puzzles.
It's not a long game by any means. As a completioninst, I completed the game in about an hour, and one-hundred-percented it in about 3 hours. For its price, I definitely feel like it was worth it.
Also, don't think of this as one of those twitch dexterity mouse games. The puzzles MOSTLY rely on thinking them through, although some levels do require a little bit of dexterity.
I definitely felt like there was some very professional level design behind each of the puzzles. Recommend to any puzzle game lover.

Circles is not a terrible game, but it is deceiving, even after having played the demo.
Circles presents itself as a 90+ levels puzzle game. However, it is not a puzzle game. There is no thinking required to complete any level. Circles is simply a series of mouse-controlled dexterity mini-games, where you will have to move your mouse in the proper way (speed, angle, etc...) to complete a level. These 90 levels are also extremely simple, and even without paying attention I blasted through the game in less than an hour - for a 8€ game, that's pretty terrible value. There are four additional modes that make you replay through the same levels with an added gimmick for difficulty (like rotating levels), which could kick playtime to 3h or so, if you really want to replay the same levels 5 times.
On the other hand, there is definitely some interesting elements in Circles. For one, the entire game UI is based on circles. There are no words, no menus, and not a single shape on screen that is not a circle. Everything the game needs to convey, it tells via circles, colours and sound cues. While the design in itself is intriguing enough, what actually makes this weird choice compelling is that it is up to you to understand what the game expects of you. That would make for great puzzles, if...Circles ever resisted you, but it doesn't. It is too simple for this to become an enticing challenge.
The other aspects of the game are pretty weak too. The minimalistic visuals (colors + circles) actually manage to be eye-seering in a few levels, due to downright idiotic color choices (yeah bright yellow on bright red, this ought to work, right?). The sound is nothing you haven't heard in a million puzzle games before: jazzy/electronic atmospheres, with sound cues based on your mouse movements.
While it is not bad and has some interesting elements, I cannot reasonsably recommend anyone to use 8€ on this game when there are many superior puzzlers on Steam for half the price. Cool concept, but Circles is really just that: a concept.
Pros:
- Really nifty UI
- Unique mechanic in trying to figure out what the game expects of you
Cons:
- Extremely short (under an hour, 3 tops if you replay the same levels with modes 5 times)
- Barely any thinking, more dexterity than puzzle
- Dirt easy
- Some terrible color palette choices which hurt the eye
- Beside the UI, you've seen it all before
- Expensive

The short version:
The best game ever.
Complex story set in the extended Star Wars Universe in all shades of muddy gray - there is no truly good or truly evil.
D&D 3ed based game mechanics - slow paced combat with a lot of staring at an RNG doing its thing.
All dialogue matter - you need to do a lot of reading and a lot of thinking for yourself.
Party, Inventory, Stat and Skill mangement aplenty and a dab of Crafting.
One of the all time most (in)famous buggy releases due to the publisher rushing the game, so remember to add TSLRCM from the Workshop - you are not modding your game, you are completing it.
The long version:
Star Wars Knights of The Old Republic II The Sith Lords, or KoTOR2 among friends, is one of the absolute finest examples of quality game writing. Even though the game was originally released in 2005, the story is still the deepest, most intelligent and thought provoking I have come across. Here you'll find no clear cut good or evil, everyone has an agenda or an angle, and you'll at times feel like your actions have no impact on the game world whatsoever. It is a muddy, all gray zone, emotionally hard story without much silver lining to ease your feelings when you finish the game.
Even today, after countless play-throughs on my 4-disc version and on Steam, I still find new angles to ponder, lines of dialogue with a deeper or larger implication and general amazing writing topped off with quality voice acting.
Be warned though, the game does not play like a modern game. This is a slow burning RPG from the days when that term meant more than "choose the order you want to upgrade your skills". The game is dialogue heavy, and while you can skip through it, I'd advise against it on the first few play-throughs. There is no colour coded hints to guide your choices, you need to think for yourself.
The combat is based on D&D 3ed rules and is RNG heavy. You'll spend a good third of the game staring at your screen waiting for the RNG to declare you the winner of a bout. If you sought out KoTOR2 for the combat rather than the story, please back away now.
The D&D rules bring stat and skill (and power) mangement topped off with inventory mangement and a light weigh crafting system to the show, and you need to be on top of it all to get the most of the game.
KoTOR2 is also famous/infamous for being a exceedingly buggy game, and all the blame lies with the publisher. The game was rushed and large parts of the game was left out of the final release. The developers released bits and bobs of what was cut, online a few years later, and the modders took over. Several groups tried to make a complete-the-game-mod, and the most succesfull is avaible in the Steam Workshop: TSLRCM from DeadlyStream.
Fast forward to 2015 and out of nowhere, KoTOR2 gets an official update with widescreen and high Hz support and Steam Workshop for easy access to mods.
The game is now as close to click-and-run as a +10 years old game can be. But the game has not been fixed as such.
You can press "PLAY" straight out of the "box", but be warned, you'll crash quickly. Rather than subject yourself to that, quickly enter the Steam Workshop and subscribe to your localization of TSLRCM. If you are a "no mods"-gamer, think of it as completing the game rather than modding it. Be aware that TSLRCM does not eliminate all crashes, but take it from me, if you crash less than 5 times over the circa 40 hours of game time, you are doing fantastic.
So if you like a great story with plenty of choices, get the game now.

SOMA was totally worth the wait.  Never before has exploring the depths of the ocean been so surreal and horrifying. Andrew Ryan can suck it!! This is the real Rapture...and it's absolutely terrifying! (Bioshock, I should apologize for that remark - I still love you xoxo)
The sound design fills you with an overwhelming sense of dread, constantly making you question if you really did just hear something...or perhaps it was just your imagination. This game oozes personality and also oozes....a lot!! Seriously, there's ooze aplenty in this game.  The slippery, dripping sounds; your character creeping through darkened vents and hallways w/ labored breaths; flickering lights and the remains of crew that you discover along the way; the monstrous abominations and wildlife you'll encounter while in the station and outside it (don't even get me started on the Abyss...my sleep will be troubled for many years thanks to that place); all this makes for one truly unforgettable experience.
The protagonist, Simon, is just an average joe w/ a head injury and thought he was going in for a revolutionary new scan of sorts that would increase his life expectany. Little did he know that it would work, though not in anyway he would have thought...he wakes up nearly 100 yrs later and that's when both the mystery and horror of the situation he finds himself in begins.  Now, armed with an Omnitool (why do I feel like all sci-fi games set in space or underwater always have one of these devices handy?) and the aid of Catherine, he'll unravel the shocking truth of the situation he has awoken to on the Pathos-II station.
I can go on more about the plot but then I'd have to reveal dark/deep secrets that would ruin the experience for those that have yet to play this.
If you've ever wanted to explore the murky depths of the ocean while digging away at the complexity of the human psyche, then look no further.  You've found the means of accomplishing both tasks at the same time - enjoy the ride!!

What a mess this game is, a total mess. I don't understand how a AAA developer like Ubisoft can get away with releasing such a busted and broken product. While the game isn't a complete utter and utter failure it is a disappointment nonetheless. Well, let's start:
I won't sit here and repeat what so many other people have said about this game's awful servers, but I will touch on it. P2P networking is completely unacceptable for a competitive, twitch based combat game like this. Imagine playing LoL and the other guy teleporting/rubberbanding all over the place, then you blast him with an ult for half his health which he magically regenerates a second after becaues of lag. Yeah, that's For Honor.
That's providing you can even get into a match because the servers are so trash that everyone has a strict NAT no matter what they do. I disabled my computer and router firewall completely, I even plugged straight into the modem and bypassed the router - none of it works. Ubisoft will try to tell you that it is your fault, but it is their netcode and the P2P host causing the issue.
Everyone plays broken and cheese classes. Prepare to get shove locked to death into a corner and thrown off cliffs because of unblockable/undodgable grapples that 1/2 the classes in the game can do. People abuse ledge and environmental kills extensively. Don't waste your time in any team-based game modes because everyone rolls in deathballs and 4v1 ganks someone. Revenge mode is absolutely useless and does nothing to prevent this. All players involved are rewarded full renown for 4v1ing someone so it only encourages this sort of behavior.
Couple this with the
netcode, and you will take hits you clearly blocked or parried. If I had a nickel for every time I got hit by an attack I clearly avoided I could buy a better game.
I also have to mention here that the game already has hackers and people making lag switches (which is possible thanks to the p2p network).
A slow grind that promotes the spending of real cash to progress. All the while Ubisoft is trying to shove a Season Pass down your throat. People will try to tell you that the game isn't pay2win, but they are full of it. You can buy the best gear in the game for money and give your character an edge over other people, that's p2w in my book. "But, skill triumphs!" - Yeah, it does. However, what happens when 2 equally skilled individuals cross blades and one has a gear score of 20 and the other has a score of 100? Exactly what you think will happen.
Don't bother with this game unless you are using a controller because the KB&M are completely unresponsive and janky. So many times I have moved my mouse up only to have it jitter around between left, right and up causing me to take a hit. I tried messing with various mouse controls and sensitivity options in-game and it doesn't help. The game was designed for a controller. Simple as that.
I have to be fair and list some good things...
Overall there is more wrong with this game than there is right. While the game looks nice and has some cool features it is plagued by janky controls and a flawed combat system. I strongly advise looking elsewhere until some of these issues are resolved, or wait for a sale. There is some good things here, but not enough to justify the $60 price tag and a very forceful Ubisoft trying to get more money out of you.

For Honor seems to be getting alot of hate for its P2P and connectivity issues. I will be putting what most of the negative reviews have to say at the start, in an effort to reduce eye strain.
For Honor has microtransactions. For Honor has P2P. For Honor, for some people, has connectivity issues.
There ya go. All the negative reviews summed up in 3 little sentences,
Lets get onto why I recommend this game, starting with the counter arguments for the 3 sentences.
For Honor's Microtransactions come in the form of "steel" the games currency, which can be readily acquired by grinding matches. This is not a case as in some other games where real money gives you real money points to buy things oyu can only buy for, yes, real money. This is not pay to win, as the things that you can buy with steel are either completely cosmetic, or, you have to play a single character, all the way to reputation 3 (read as prestige 3, if your familiar with COD) and only then can you get the "best" gear. Gear which only affect gameplay in the 4v4 game modes.
TLDR: Microtransactions only pay for gear that actually means something, if you earn it to begin with. there is no pay to win.
For Honor Uses a new type of P2P in which every "user" in a match is host. you can think of traditional P2P as one person has the crown, and everyone bows and offers their internet connection, if youve played Payday, youve heard of "host privledges." For Honor's P2P essentially makes everyone have a crown, and forces each player to connect with eachother. it then picks the "median" between all players, and that is what you experience. What this means for you is that if you have a good connection, you should be fine. if you dont, you will be miserable, and make every other person miserable.
TLDR: P2P isnt an issue for most of the playerbase, but, if you arent in direct control of your internet connection IE a college campus, or a "locked" company issued router. you may have problems.
For Honors "infamous" connection errors... This goes back to the P2P issue, but it seems as though some people are having issues with it even though their NAT type is open, have all the appropriate ports opened etc. I have not had any of these issues, nor have any of my friends. Unfortunately the "works on my machine" mentality works here.

I got this on sale for less than a dollar and it was well worth it. The game has a little charm to it by having an average script. The dialogue is meant to be read is an evil monotonous fashion (or well at leas that's how I did it) and it doesn't take itself seriously at all which is pretty good. You take on the role of a bad guy named Galvis a knight who was abandoned by his troops and thrown into prison to rot. You manage to break free, learn your first spell that'll aid you on your quest to become an all powerful being of pure evil and destruction and then you set out to find your equipment. It's a linear story but in case you get stuck or need a hint, luckily Galvis tracks his progress in his personal journal you can look up any time you feel confused or stuck. You set off on a relatively short journey to seek revenge against those who have betrayed you and to cause chaos and destruction to anyone who may have the misfortune to cross your path, including "God" himself.
All in all I can't entirely recommend this game to everyone, only the experienced RPG players who know what to expect from a low budget game. It doesn't have all those fancy bells and whistles like most games do but you do have the benefit of the old school graphics, the 8-bit sounds, some familiar gameplay (Crystalis comes to mind for likeness but not total likeness). All in all for a game that cost me under a dollar, I enjoyed it for what it is.
So if you're looking for a low budget RPG that doesn't take itself seriously and borrows a lot of elements from older style ARPG/Rogue-like games made back in the NES/SNES days, then this might be for you. At $1.99 it's still worth it for the 15 or so hours you'll get out of it on the hardest mode (requires a bit of grinding because enemies have a ton of HP and do quite a bit of bump damage).
-Keys are awkward and some can be swapped but doesn't help much.
-Dialogue either is deliberately "bad" or just bad, either way it suits whatever they are trying to pass off as an evil personality.
-The combat is a bit awkward due to the keys being awkward and it feels like there is some sound effects missing during fights too.

For it's time this game was a nerve-wracking, unique, horror thriller.
Now it is a goofy, first-person, hide-behind-stuff simulator.
One of my biggest beefs with this game, is it fueled an entire genre of horror games where violence against you is uncontrollable and tolerated by simply running into a dark corner instead of providing the player with clever, intuitive or fun ways of defending yourself.
These games always play like this:
- Vague voiceovers while you wake up in a daze of some sort
- See blurry, creepy figure while passing out
- Wake up, wander aimlessly
- Learn some gameplay feature that the developer created
- Force Gameplay feature down player's throat
- Find locked door
- Run around looking for way to open it
- Find bits of plot devices scrawled on conveniently placed journals and letters
- Get key to unlock door
- Scary sequence
- Realize there's no way to hurt the bad guy or defend yourself
- Hide
- Die
- Restart
- Run
- Find locked door
- Repeat until..
- Forced to use gameplay feature to "win" the game
- Story ends
And so begins the genre of horror, hide-behind-stuff simulators.

Overall, Amnesia is a competent, influential horror game. It's got atmosphere and 'distributed' tension instead of jump-scares, and the creepy mood is built on by the (in my opinion, boring) story.
From the high praise, I honestly expected more. There is little in ambient variety, and lots of backtracking through samey stone corridors and creaky wooden floors, occasionally broken by a sewer or two. Some physics puzzles are a bit frustrating, and the enemy AI is mediocre. Sanity management can get old.
That said, it succeeded in what it set out to do - the castle is creepy, there are a number of memorable moments, and there is the potential to immerse the player. Play it alone to achieve that best.

This game sets off some primitive part of my brain that gives me some sort of morbid curiosity and interest in car crashes. Evolutionarily, it makes no sense; I should be scared of them. You know, winning a Darwin Award is not a prize one would like. Yet, dashcam compilations, Burnout Revenge's Crash mode, and BeamNG.drive are SO DAMN INTERESTING AND FUN. What sets this game apart is its soft body collision physics engine. Which is just a long way of saying that the car physics in this game is really realistic. Let's compare this to Grand Theft Auto where a non-branded Honda Civic can withstand several highway speed crashes much like a M1 Abrams. Sure you lost a door or two and completely destroyed its resale value, but the only thing that matters is that it still runs at a reasonable speed. If you run your car into a wall at highway speeds in this game you'll be assaulted by a hail of windshield bits while you're screaming in agony because your car's A pillar is now embedded into your skull. Hell, if you run into a mildly large rock at a speed suitable for a busy school zone, you'll probably majorly mess up your radiator. This game is just a toy box for me to watch realistic car crashes without the guilt, knowing that no virtual people were hurt in my vehicle destruction. While, sure this game is still in Early Access, it is still worth the money. Surely it's leagues better than some stupid low effort asset-bought Unity game that plagues the Steam store now-a-days.

So you come for a review of the isle? Well hold on to your butts.
The isle will probably be a good game in 2020, but right now it’s an unbalance walking with dinosaurs role playing sim. And with a community that is less fun to talk to but just as fun to abuse as the gmod community... its cancer and i feel bad for the devs.
As of right now the game has two game modes: Survival and sandbox.
Survival is broken, its progression system is completely time based. This means that once you have spent 4hs on becoming a sexual tyrannosaurs and get ganged up on and killed all that time is completely wasted. There nothing else to do in survival apart from eating and not getting killed. AI bots are not yet implemented as they were removed at an early stage for being broken.
So playing as a carnivore is really boring as you'll have to look for the small amount of players playing as vegans, or fight other players as carnivores. And the herbivore's progression system is broken. (Probably fixed now)
Sandbox is what it is; you join a server and play as whatever dino with no progression system. It can get a bit boring even on community servers with their custom rules, and players who kos (kill on sight) is very common because of being bored. This is because there is nothing to kill apart from players as the bots are gone.
Truthfully I enjoy the game for what it is and the devs are adding more dinos and patches. But once the humans and PVE bots are added that’s where this sim will become a game, with base building and weapons to wreck scrubs with. Also you won’t have to worry about some bs progression system. Fun will return to lands of Mordor... I mean the isle.
Also this game will definitely need a single player/coop survival mode and privet matches that save your progression as relying on community servers is a very bad idea because they are completely unreliable.
I give this a positive as I’m being nice and supportive but in reality it’s a no for me. Only get this game when it’s on sale, if friends are willing to play it with you, or when the humans are added.

Chip is basically a puzzle game. Basically you are a robot, who get's 'botnapped' and is stuck in a cell. Now you need to charge yourself up in order to escape. The graphics are 2D, similiar to "Scribblenauts Unlimited", and colourfully appealing. Gameplay resolves around solving puzzles (ie charging up the robot) by manipulating barriers, objects, electrical charges and time. There are plenty of levels (each unlocked after completing the previous one), with each one throwing different obstacles in your face. After each level, you earn score based on the number of moves  you made and the time it took you to complete the puzzle. You also earn coins which are used to by customisations for your robot.The music is cheerful and suits puzzle solving fine.
If you want a light-hearted puzzle game this is the game for you.

Gameplay:
Okay, so the gameplay here is what you expect. You pick a dinosaur from a list of six dinosaurs (currently), and it plops you in the world with a ghostly UI of a food and water meter. You drink and eat simply by pressing "E" on the respective source. Now, here's where it starts to differ from other games out there; It literally plays out like a dinosaur version of DayZ and it's awesome. I can't even begin to express the look on my face when I saw another Rex and we just bellowed at each other until we got close enough to see each other's names. After doing so we formed a makeshift pack and roamed around the island, hunting and stalking our prey. Eventually we came across a herd of Gallimimus and quickly dispatched them as they did not see us coming. The fact we were these massive animals, and we efficiently hunted and killed an animal much smaller and faster than us, is simply amazing. Okay, so the gameplay of the Austroraptor is also something short of a miracle. This is the first time in a video game that I have seen actual human players be able to efficiently stalk and kill a Rex by jumping onto it's body and actually latching on. The raptors in this game can jump, press right click and left click, and they will bite and latch onto the target and do a slow damage over time. Impressive.
Content:
As of right now, there are currently six animals to play from but a handful of skins for each, even glowing bioilluminescent ones! There is a very simple and shallow eating and drinking system, but the coolest part is by far the herbivores eating plants and the plants disappearing. Love that. Crouching and stalking as a Rex, as read about above, is amazingly fun. Currently if I were to rate this game based on content, it would get a solid 5/10. But since it's EA and I have faith in Dondi, I'm not going to waste anyone's time with a number system for this category.
Community:
Not much I can write here as of right now, but it is definitely a milestone when you can see a random dinosaur in the distance and become packmates or herdmates with it just by roaring and biting the air. So far so good, keep up the good work people.
Playability:
Optimization needs work, but it's miles ahead of what the demo was. I hope to see it increase over time but something tells me with the roadmap planned that it will remain the same strictly because of how much they are going to ADD to the game. Overall the game plays perfectly fine and the dinosaurs are a blast to control!
Problems:
Okay, this list is short and sweet CURRENTLY. My only 'problems' are such;
-Take damage from packmates
-Server browser sometimes doesn't show a loading screen when a server is being logged onto
-Names above dinosaurs are too big
-Push to talk is not in yet, so everyone's microphone is live all the time
-The stomping is too loud, compared to the walking sound
-Sometimes the server I am on crashes for no reason
-Being able to glitch into a dinosaur as another dinosaur bothers me, haha
-Definitely need a way to 'smell' herbivores, otherwise starvation is an actual concern
-Quetzacoatylus isn't playable yet.
Overall, I say this game is worth the asking price.

As a fan of Amnesia: The Dark Descent (and somewhat disappointed fan of Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs), I have been anticipating SOMA since its first teaser for the PS4. As everyone knows, SOMA is a game in the horror genre. However, it is far more appropriate to be specific with SOMA: it's a psychological horror sci-fi. The game introduces ideas that seem a bit reaching (in terms of scientific plausibility), but like all good science fiction, there is a purpose to the not-so plausible science.
SOMA constantly has the player asking "Who am I?" as they explore dimly-lit corridors teeming with biological monstrosities. This may seem like a strange compliment, but that's what makes SOMA so amazing. The monsters do get the heart pounding, but they aren't what makes SOMA such a horrifying experience. The philosophical questions we're left with are far scarier than any monster.
Right from the start, SOMA shows us that the human brain is going to be the star of the show. The main character, Simon, had a recent brain injury. And when he "teleports" to PATHOS-2, he discovers that artificial intelligence may not be so different from the human brain. With these things in mind, Frictional Games very cleverly presents ideas that not only progress the game's story, but also leave the player pondering moral and philosophical questions regarding consciousness and identity.
Though the story is very good, I should mention that the game does not stand up as mechanically as it should. I have found numerous glitches (none that are game breaking, just distracting), the gameplay can become a bit tedious (shocking; another medium of transportation suddenly stopped working and I must now fix it/travel on foot in the ocean), and some of the visuals detract from the game (for such a realistic looking game, the sight of animated characters and cartoonish computer screens is very distracting).
However, despite some graphical and gameplay flaws, SOMA is a must have. Fans of both horror and sci-fi will not be disappointed. If you are new to either genre, however, I would recommend waiting for a price drop or sale. $30 can be a bit much for people who are just looking for a new game.
One last thing: The ending of this game is what I consider true terror. For those who are losing interest in the story as they play it: KEEP GOING. The ending of this game is possibly one of the best (and most horrifying) endings to a horror video game I have ever experienced. It will haunt your thoughts for days.
PROS:
- Good graphics
- Interesting world and story to explore
- Terrifying mechanically and with regard to the story
CONS:
- Some art direction misteps
- Fairly unrealistic characters and dialogue
OVERALL: A very strong 7/10. A must-buy for fans of horror. Otherwise, wait for a sale.

single-player and multi-player modes are literally two different games with different graphics and gameplay.
The single-player part is kind of generic, but still may be fun. Every level offers something different: breaking through enemies' lines with your squadmates, perfroming a stealthy mission, playing as a helicopter gunner, operating an anti-materiel rifle, etc. Voice acting is very good. Guns feel realistic and are nice to use. The graphics are dated, but still good for a 2010 game. In my book, the biggest flaws in
are its modest length (about 5h) and its difficulty, or rather its absence: even on the hardest difficulty level enemies lack aggression and are not so dangerous; your character can survive more hits than you'd expect. Beating a level without dying once is not a hard task, especially if you're an experienced gamer. Overall, the single-player mode is decent, but feels more like an interactive war movie.
I haven't played the multiplayer mode a lot, however I can confirm people are still playing it and there are active servers. Gameplay-wise it's similar to Battlefield: Bad Company 2 or Battlefield 3 (as it was made by DICE, creators of Battlefield), but with smaller maps, faster gameplay, no vehicles and a few CoD-like killstreaks.

Frictional is at the top of their game with this masterpiece. Continuing their tradition of innovating the horror genre that began with the seminal Penumbra and Amnesia titles, games that have inspired so many since, with Soma they have achieved nothing less than inventing a new genre for gaming: Existential Horror.

Soma has all the hallmarks of great horror; atmosphere aplenty, immersive sound, suspense and tension, shocks and scares. They had already achieved mastery over these elements in games that so many have borrowed from. But Soma introduces another element, something deeper and more truly horrifying than almost anything imaginable. It delves into the human psyche and threatens it's very core needs. It identifies the fundaments of who and what we are, then takes them away. This can potentially cause an existential crisis in the contemplative mind. What other vehicle of media can claim that? Perhaps some movies and great works of fiction touch upon it, but the closest I've ever been to such a feeling is upon waking from a nightmare.
Get it. Play it. Feel it. It's ok if you need to call your Mommy afterwards.

is a good game. It's not a great game. It's not a pretty game. It's not a complex game. It's not a deep or elaborate game. It's not a highly-polished game. It's
not a big budget game. All the shine and frippery normally associated with a professional product is pretty-much absent here. But the core gameplay is
.
Like most things from ultra-low-budget publisher Ensenasoft, the menu structure is bare-bones.  Four clickable obects take you to one of four identical submenus, each featuring 21 puzzles, imaginatively titled 1-21.  Word lists are thematic, but the puzzle is always the same: a word search taking place on a rotatable cube, where the words can bend around edges from one side to another.  Words appear in up, down, forward and backwards orientations, but never diagonally.  This adds a novel twist to an otherwise tired genre.  It's easy to overlook a four-letter word when two letters are on one face, and two on the next.
For those who need to quantify their success, each word find adds points to your level score based on how soon after the previous word you found it, and you are awarded 1-3 stars at the end of the level based on your total.  Since I've never had anything but three stars, I presume that the star system is quite generous.
Sound and graphics are adequate, and not much more, but that's all a puzzle game really needs.  The similarity of the puzzles makes the game tedious if you do too many in one sitting.  But if you do only one or two puzzles at a time, this is fun and novel.  For a bargain-bin priced title, that's good enough.

A top-down 2D Action-RPG.  The main draw of the game is how over-the-top the protagonist is.  It's not uncommon for you to learn spells and get equipment by threatening some NPC and then after getting said upgrade, to kill them.  The entire game is played out in this tongue-in-cheek manner and I found it amusing enough, though some will no doubt find it to be a bit try hard.
The artstyle is crude and bland at times and dungeons are a bit long and boring to traverse, but the dungeons have save points so replaying long stretches of them shouldn't be much of a factor.  Puzzles are rare and quite simple when they show up.
The best aspect of Evil Quest gameplay-wise is how easy it is to become a walking flamethrower.  Magic regenerates over time, so if you level-up and make it a point to pump intelligence, by the halfway point of the game you can constantly spam spells as you walk around and it trivializes most enemies.  I don't find this a downpoint since combat is rather simplistic and mowing down enemies with various spells is fun enough.
The game is pretty short, you probably won't end up with more than a half-dozen hours at most on a playthrough, though that's about right and it ended just as I was tiring of it a bit.  I had fun with this and the price point puts you in position of not having much to lose by taking a chance on it.

This game does have tutorials - which I played again and again - in order to get my head around how it works. Feeling brave, I then attempted my first skirmish... and lasted minutes before having my company taken over ! Luckily there IS the option to play without any competitors and I have used THAT, starting at the easiest level and upgrading eventually to Guru - but all without a competitor, with the only issue being the choosing of the various industries and in what order to place them. Playing in this way allows you to learn and experiment - time is the issue here as if you get your choices wrong, you will take hours and hours to drag yourself out of debt.
This is not a RTS game in the normal sense - you do have skill upgrades and resource management, but the upgrades are to improve resource gathering rather than to upgrade fighting skills. You have limited plots of land each time you upgrade your company and these plots are as much a resource as the actual iron, carbon, water etc.
The skill is in the initial positioning of the company base and then careful choice of which resource to gather on each very limited plot of land. Get it right and do it quickly enough and you take over the enemy company - get it wrong and face immediate retirement !
If you want a change from the standard games in the RTS genre, give this one a try - but learn as much as you can on your own first BEFORE attempting a battle with an opponent...

Something new and really original on Steam among bunch of Indie trash!
There are a big amount of advantages:
Minuses:

Story: The story follows Daniel, a fellow from London who awakes in Brennenburg Castle with amnesia. The game tells the story primarily through audio flashbacks Daniel has while exploring the castle. These flashbacks along with notes you can find inform you of your past. Through these notes your past self directs you to the inner sanctum where you must kill a man named Alexander. Past Daniel also mentions a shadow that follows you relentlessly and cannot be stopped. Amnesia’s primary story and message is found in these flashbacks and journals, here you’ll learn why Daniel has no memories, why you wanted to kill Alexander, and what the shadow is. A major theme of Amnesia is morality and it is primarily studied through Daniel’s actions before he lost his memory. Without spoiling the major plot points, the game does a great job of putting the player into a state of mind and position where they can weigh the moral decisions made by their player character Daniel and not feel a great dissonance. That is important as the moral dilemmas Daniel faced are another whole terrifying aspect of Amnesia. This being said, the story and past events add to the suffocating and tension-filled atmosphere. The story and atmosphere prop each other, each benefitting from the others consistent delivery. The story of Amnesia is not brilliant or revolutionary but it does plague the character with the dark realities of his past, in turn adding to what is truly exceptional about Amnesia, its atmosphere.
Atmosphere: The setting of Amnesia is Brennenburg Castle, a dark, crumbling castle somewhere in Prussia. This setting is a truly perfect fit for the gameplay and story. The castles interior is eerie, wet, falling into ruin, and mysterious. The interior design of the castle is pretty standard stuff for the most part, with your archives, cellars and such. Although standard, the aesthetics and sounds combined with just enough mystery and dark influences make the game very original in execution, especially for a video game. Nearly the entire game takes place inside the castle, as you dive into its bowels. Only for a moment do you step outside. This moment was pretty cool too. For me it provided some real context and sense of where I was in the world, even if I only saw a vast dark forest. Something about seeing what surrounded the castle added another layer to the isolation and overbearing darkness of the atmosphere. All this darkness and weightiness of the atmosphere becomes suffocating and nearly a deterrent to continuing the game. Luckily, there are skillfully placed hub areas that provide a much needed contrast to the claustrophobic, monster inhabited areas. These hub areas take a weight off your chest by providing just enough light and calming sounds. That leads me to the sound design, which truly amplifies the feelings of suffocation, claustrophobia, and ultimately terror. The sound effects pick and gnaw at you, with sounds of rats, insects, and the unknown. Meanwhile the soundtrack provides a deep, trembling groan that is ever-present. Sounds like grinding or cavernous echoes ebb in and out seamlessly. That is the greatness of this sound design, it is seamlessly bound to the atmosphere and gameplay. This effectively immerses the player entirely in the game world. Aside from the main menu, there is no remarkable track that you’ll recall afterwards. You’ll only be left with the feelings that sounds and visuals provided you.
Gameplay: The gameplay of Amnesia is fairly simple but deep in its applications. The way you’re able to interact with objects physically is satisfying and intuitive. This is primarily implemented in three scenarios: searching for items, solving puzzles, and hiding from/blocking monsters. While moving through the game, the physics engine really connects you to the game. I see this as a huge benefit in a game where you’re banking on becoming immersed. Using environmental objects to solve puzzles makes the puzzles see less contrived and more natural for the situation. Using wardrobes and stacking barrels to hide for monsters really throws you into the world, giving you a fantastic physical sense of the game. This mechanic adds serious depth to gameplay that isn’t up in your face. The moments when you come across a monster for the first few times, the game leaves you feeling helpless and overwhelmed in terror. It takes you a second to think of what you can do. Then you realize you must push on, so hiding and running often are a temporary solution. In all, the monsters and their encounters are well designed and used sparingly as to not reveal too much.
Your inventory stores a few essential items along with puzzle items. You’re also able to craft here, although crafting is not a big component of the game. This interface also houses your sanity status. Sanity in Amnesia is a crucial mechanic that pits the player against a rock and a hard place. The idea is that you lose sanity in the dark but while you in the light you’re easily seen by monsters. It’s a mechanic the whole game rests on to keep the player on their toes. An aspect that ties into sanity is solving puzzles. Puzzles will boost your sanity when solved and holy crap is this an effective way to encourage the push on! The satisfaction from completing puzzles is really felt by the player, as a wave of relief rushes over you. Overall, I must say I love the gameplay here. It takes a step back to let the atmosphere do its work, while bolstering the players’ connection to the game world.
Overall: Since the release of Amnesia, its formula has been reused several times with some games reaching larger audiences. I’d recommend this game to anyone who wants a first-person horror experience. If you’re someone who has played any of Amnesia’s contemporaries and influenced works and enjoyed it, this game is well worth your time. From the outside looking in the game may look outdated or silly/cliché. Amnesia will prove these notions wrong as I have not come across a game more terrifying and immersive. This game is an example that graphical fidelity is not all important if you have excellent game and world design.

Motte Island is a low-fi horror game, with a top-down perspective. Your objective is to go into Motte Island to save your sister from the townsfolk, and uncover whatever secrets they were hiding.
You'll probably be able to finish the game in 3 or 4 hours, and while there are different endings, it does not warrant a replay, since the endings are merely decided by the final section of the game. There are collectible photos spread around, though, each providing a cutscene for you to learn more about the island.

As I said, this is a very
game, especially regarding its artstyle. The goodside is that low-fi actually works great with horror games! While everything is low-res, dark and full of blurry fog, it sets a nice atmosphere, and lets your mind piece in what's missing.
However, it's not a pretty game at all, on the contrary, it's quite ugly. Lone Survivor or even Home, were low-fi, but still weren't as ugly and Motte Island is. But overall, I think it sets the tone, and achieves its purpose!
Animation is very limited as well, which is more noticeable in the cutscenes, but it's not a big deal in the whole scheme of things.
The
in general was pretty good, actually! Everything worked towards the same atmosphere, and there was also a more oppressive track whenever you were engaged in battle. Unfortunately, the track was always the same, which got tiresome at times.
There were also a couple of jump-scares thrown in, but were quite repetitive, losing its effect.
The enemies didn't sound very scary, but all of the other ambience sounds were good.
It's not perfect, but taking its scope into account, I think it comes out as a positive, and helps the game!
So far so good! Now comes my reasoning for not recommending this game.
I see what it's trying to do, but similarly to Eleusis, the
at all. It has a
, but lacks purpose and place to use that atmosphere in.
Most of the time, you'll be traveling around the island (which is essentially just a small village), collecting random items. And, very much like Eleusis, they force you to go back and forth several times while you could easily collect several items at once. (These also blend in with the ground, at times, making them very hard to see... this, of course, increases frustration when you're just constantly walking around, not sure what you're looking for)
While you have (supposedly) 3 guns in the game, I only found one, and even that was necessary to the story and not through exploration. What I did find, was a bunch of ammo that I didn't get to use... And some enemies also carried guns that you couldn't pick up, for some unknown reason. Missed chance.
This means that I've only used melee weapons for the whole game. Think of it as Hotline Miami. But instead of the very fast in-and-out, twitch gameplay, each enemy requires several hits to die (you have
attacks, but the heavy are mostly for stealth), so you'll just hit them and backing off repeatedly. A more reliable way of doing it, is using stealth. You can approach enemies from behind, and kill them in 1 hit.
... or you can just run away from them. Why would you do it? Because they respawn. Yes, every time you enter/exit an area, the enemies respawn. This really does defeat the tension. There's a lot of pointless fighting, and not much fear. While I did kill them at first, I eventually just started running away since fighting was pointless and laborious. While there is a decent number of weapons, they all play similarly, so it's not exactly a positive.
So yeah. The atmosphere is completely wasted on shores and backtracking, as well as too much "safe" combat.
Aside from this main gameplay, there also 2 other sections: a side-scroller, and a cover-based fps.
In the first, you "drive" a car, while obstacles come down from the top of the screen. This was the most disorienting experience I've had with gaming in a loooong time. Everything happened too fast, with the obstacles sending you flying to the sides... Jesus... I'm not even sure it was possible to fail. I was hitting almost everything (it was unpleasant) but eventually go through with it.
Then, there's the fps sections. One functions as a mini horde mode, and the other as a Boss fight. You can shoot, and you can be in cover, reloading. It wasn't very good either. The hit detections, specially, was not very tight. And there were always enemies spawning in the limits of the screen. In the last boss fight it was especially bad...
These two sections are extremely forced and have no place in the game, to be honest. I understand "variety", but come one!...
One last aspect I want to mention, is the story/writing. It's... bad. And I'm not talking about the number of grammatical errors (quite a lot), but the actual story and characters. The plot is completely senseless. For example, the villagers act like a bunch of maniacs, but suddenly, they're not the bad guys because everything goes to s***. It makes no sense how they're portrayed. It's a very artificial way of making you dislike them. And that would be fine, if they didn't change their minds halfway through. By then, how could I side with the villagers?
My actions from that point onwards made no sense, which threw the story out the window. The dialogue is also pretty cheesy, but hey...
I'm sounding really negative here. To be completely honest, I did enjoy the game during the first 2 hours. It was cool, the atmosphere immersed me more than I was expecting, and everything was well, while I was exploring the village. Unfortunately, it then started just going in circles, and then introduced very rushed mechanics, ruining the overall experience.
I can see what it was trying to do, and it's unfortunate that it simply didn't get there quite yet. But it has a couple of good aspects about it, so I'll look forward to their next game. Hopefuly, they'll learn from mistakes and make much more competent experiences!

INTRO
After spending many more hours in this game, I'm rewriting the review from scratch.
-- Immediately After Buying --
The biggest frustration starting out was the awkward and confusing UI.  It really can break the game if you want to start playing quickly and nothing works as expected at the most basic level such as trying to click to get someone's profile info.  Long-clicking was apparently a thing at some time.
If you can get past that, and if you can overcome the economics which are not easy, the replay value that follows is significant and gameplay is very deep.
-- After Playing A Significant Amount --
The biggest frustration after playing for a while, is to discover this is beautiful game.  "Why didn't I play this more earlier!"  But, of course, you couldn't play it more because of the beginner's frustrations.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
MAIN
There are many strategies to explore and always throttled by a complex economy.  It might be too complex -- the "people" running around have their own interests and whatever parts of the economy that are artificial, those are kept to a minimum.  It feels very realisitic - but as impressive as it is to watch, it doesn't always make for fun gameplay.  Instead it can be somewhat grueling.
First of all, courting and eventually falling in love and marrying someone and having children or adopting to raise them and send them to school is a great mini-game that integrates seamlessly into the gameplay.  It's probably the first thing to try out (even though your children won't get a decent education because you'll be too poor to pay for their schooling).
But eventually vast amounts of money start to pour in, and looking at the higher teirs of buildings is intruiging (and overwhelming).  This is where the richness of the game starts to shine.  It's also where you want to think in terms of how to prevent enemies from doing nasty things.
The game itself is completely open-ended.  You can commit all the crimes you want, or spy on enemies to gather evidence to take them to court with.  The depth of realism is where this game shines.  I just watched a courtroom drama where my character took an enemy to court over small offenses like burglary and assault.  She was sentenced to death unanamously by the jury, and they executed her in the street immediately after the court hearing!
All the issues with the UI are forgotten eventually - but it's too bad it gets so badly in the way of getting started.
I will probably hold off on The Guild III until I see evidence that is very well polished.  In the meantime, TG2 offers a very entertaining and thoughtful experience.
