This game claims to be an RPG... it isn't. What it is is a management sim and it ain't a very deep one at that. For something that's supposed to be about you living the medieval life there's not an awful lot of you livin' a life and probably a bit too much of you micro-managing your businesses and your employees. It is possible to set the AI to manage the buisnesses you build but you're very unlikely to make a sustanible profit doing that.
The political system seems interesting at first but once you've climbed to the top it doesn't feel very fulfilling, and it doesn't add anything to the game to make you want to continue playing longer.
The family system could've been interesting if it wasn't for the fact that it requires almost no effort what-so-ever. The most complicated thing you'll do is court your mate, but all that consists of is using four or five actions in the right order to increase your prospective spouse's affection, but each of these actions have a linked cool down with the rest so you have to wait a good few hours of ingame time (you can speed up the clock thankfully) before you can perform the next compliment. Children you send to school with a push of a button and there's no need to keep either parent at home to look after them either.
Combat does exist in this game as does criminal actions but it's all rather pointless, you'll be far more successful running a lawful business than you ever would a criminal one and using actions like threats or murder are far too risky and made pointless by the fact that you can just bribe anyone and everyone into liking you.
I find it hard to decide whether or not to recommend this game. Yes i've been critical but as a management game it's not bad and i've certainly played worse. It does carry an interesting premise, if not a particularly well implimented one. What it comes down to with me is, tho, the fact that it claims to be an RPG and a medieval life simulator and it's just not.
A word of advice if you still wish to pick this game up go for the Renaissance stand-alone expansion since it has everything that both the main game and the Pirates expansion offers.

It's not a complete game yet, but I recommend it.  The game has evolved since I bought into it's Early Access; so it is not abandonware.
The soft-body damage sim system is bloody fantastic and deep.  Not completely realistic, but fantastic.  I'm sure you've seen YouTube videos of BeamNG.drive crashe motages and cars tumbling down mountains getting all smashed up.  The only thing missing is the ability for cars to explode.  They never do.  All they do is sometimes catch fire if you rupture the fuel tank.
While this is not yet finished, there is a very large selection of activities (scenarios) you can do.  Checkpoint races, jumping, stunts, destruction missions and other ways to take advantage of the game's unique and extensive soft-body vehicle engine.  There is plenty to do here; it's just not a complete game yet.  The game is also highly moddable so you can create your own scenarios and even 3D props and tracks if you know your way around a 3D modeling program.
The game's configuration and control options are DEEP.  It works spectacularly with the Steam Controller once you can figure out how to configure it all.  Steering with the track pad feels great.  The only thing better would be a real steering wheel controller.  Some day!
The game's graphics are not state of the art, but they are very crisp.  Let's say crisp but a bit dry.  It would benefit from some ambient occlusion, physically based rendering or other cutting-edge graphic engine elements.  If the game had the graphics engine of Rocket League or Mad Max it would be a very impressive thing indeed.  But what is here is very servicable.  The frame rate is silky smooth on my GTX960.  On the other hand the amount of trees and other foliage around the road is impressive.
Now for the negatives.  The game has a beginnings of a campaign.  Appropriately named "Rocky Start."  The actual gameplay is fun.  It has the beginnings of an open-world map with activities you can choose with rewards.  Great stuff.  But the presentation...  It is disjointed.  They chose to use cartoonish, 2D flash-type animations to lead into each part of the campaign.  The art is flatly drawn cartoons.  The people...  I'm sorry.  They look like they tapped someone from DeviantArt.  Crudely drawn cartoons.  The animation looks very low-budget.  This directly contrasts with the actual game world where everything is dimensional, lush, detailed and obviously lovingly crafted.  The 2D art really brings the game down a peg.  And there is other 2D art within another part of the game that is far superior.  They should sack the new artist and use the first one.  Yeah it had the limitations of being 2D but it has style and looks much more professional..  Ugh.. Sorry.. as an artist it's just a pet peeve of mine.  If you aren't going to do it right, don't do it at all.

BeamNG.drive is a driving game/tech demo hybrid with an impressive amount of detail and surprisingly addicting. Having started as a proof-of-concept in the CryEngine by the former developers of Rigs of Rods - another very similar, more rudimentary game focusing on trucks and heavy vehicles, it has since switched to the Torque3D engine to handle the physics.
There's no storyline or career as of yet. Updates have added a selection of campaigns to complete, such as a driver's license test and wrecking stuff up.
It's a pretty game, for sure, but don't go nuts with the dynamic car reflections if you treasure your framerate. Rather odd post-processing artifacts, or that might be me just not knowing how to work with them. Crashes look a little bland without particles or extra bits flying out.
The sound effect library is slowly expanding - as of now, we have a decent selection of car sounds, depending on engines. Inline 4, V6, American V8, Italian V8, even Inline 6! Environmental sounds aren't too neglected either, even if they tend to be repetitive still. No music as of yet.
The selling point lies in the revolutionary soft body physics. At the expense of requiring an ever more powerful CPU to simulate multiple cars interacting with each other, you get what is possibly the most accurate car deformation,
While it remains prone to clipping, gripping and other odd issues, 99% of the time it is consistent and logical.
An ever expanding list of official cars cover more or less any stereotype conceivable, and if you can think of more, there's mods to remedy that too. You can drive a 4-wheel steering sedan, a pickup truck for your hillbilly rock climbing purposes, a surprisingly fun and nimble hatchback, a dangerously difficult 70's supercar, and many,
more. All of them, of course, have varying tolerances to crashes from whichever direction, but also a healthy collection of parts to choose from. Slap a stage 4 supercharger kit on your muscle car and rocket to terrifying speeds - and send your engine temperature shooting, your wheels screeching due to no grip, and your hapless car careening into walls.
It is such a robust and well built engine that it can simulate airplanes and helicopters, lift and drag, and all sorts of intricate stages of mechanical failures like blown engine gaskets, fried piston rings, bent connecting rods, broken driveshafts, snapped axles, faded brakes, so on and so forth. This is a respectable driving simulator in all the right ways!
Mods further increase the game's variety, with aforementioned planes, helicopters, and varying flavours of land vehicles and configurations. Simple to install and remove (usually).
Updates are somewhat slow to deliver, but when they land, you should expect a couple more cars, a lot more car variation, and several new, possibly experimental systems to improve the simulation aspects of the game. I dare say the devs have picked up significant momentum as of late, and they're eeking ever closer to proper LAN, or even online multiplayer. Until then, we have replays and AI control to bring our destruction derby and "Slightly more sensible Crash Junction" dreams to life.
It is totally worth the money if you're a car/physics nut. It surely is deep in its mechanics, but the current content is a bit too thinly spread to easily warrant a purchase for anyone else; patience is a more wise idea when tackling Early Access titles, even better developed ones such as this.

Thanks to the pause button (spacekey), this is an RTS game that fans of turn-based games (such as myself) can enjoy.  After 80+ hours, I'm still exploring and learning what the game has to offer.
Some times you will get plopped down on a "high resource" location only to discover that while there may be many resource spots, they are mostly the same thing.  For example, 50+ iron spots and 3 water spots.  The game provides various ways to work around challenges such as this, and that is part of what makes it fun.  The factions in the game are distinct and one can utilize a variety of playing styles to succeed.  Figuring out what is the best base type to utilize in a given situation is nuanced, but this makes a big difference to the outcome, and one strategy won't work in all situations.
In other words, you have to think to win and there is a lot to learn.  Key ingredients to a good game.

[Mild Spoilers Ahead]
for the longest time Pixel Fade's Ace Academy has been my bar for Visual Novels. So I was highly anticipating their follow up and now that I have it, so far, it shows a lot of promise! It's art style is great as last time, the added animations are highly impressive (though my crap computer doesn't always run them very well, which leads to some amusing results in which hair and... other areas, just move on their own rapidly. Though I'm not blaming the game for that.) And it's story, though reminiscent to other fantasy stories out there, does stand it's own in presentation, humor, and it's cast of characters.
Every new original character really stands apart from their previous project, which I can appreciate. Everyone is so different an interesting and learning about them so far has been good fun. I'm going to leave it at this, Crystalline IS a great project, you SHOULD check it out and give these guys all of your support. From here on out I'm going to talk about some cons I had, so if all your wanting is a quick opinion: CRYSTALLINE IS GREAT, BUY IT.
But with as high of expectations I had I do have some concerns. This is more or less just to bring them to light to the production team, tops. There's on ne major and one just a minor technical nitpick. Let's start Major:
I have noticed that so far it doesn't really feel like all your "relationships" are very open. I have only played through it once and it's still early in the game life so it's hard to tell, but it feels like there's only one real choice so far: Leanna. I'm really intereted in getting to know both Kara and Amelia but it just feels they're more often than not... left out? Especially as any interest in Amelia you can show feels frowned upon (so far) and Kara shows very clear interest in Zack, which isn't a bad thing. They did the same thing with Mayu and Shou in Ace Academy, but here's the difference; it gave you proper alone time to feel you had a chance and you could make a difference in that sense. So far I feel alone time has been all but deminished, save for with Leanna, so it feels like Kara and Amelia are barely options. However this is only up to episode two and things didn't get interesting in that regard in Ace Academy until episode three. I could also easily be missing something? It was stated the system is more intricate this time, maybe I'm just not noticing it and picking things that only lead to Leanna stuff. If so, someone please let me know and I'll strike this whole note from the review as it's my only real problem as I was expecting an assortment of options here, as far as relationships go, but feel like I've only got one. If I'm right though and people are noticing this slant towards Leanna (which I will admit it's mostly a slant because you're around her the longest, to be fair) I do hope the Pixel Fade team can take note and maybe work on that a bit.
My only other issue is totally my own, not everyone is going to agree with me, but I do feel I have fair argument in my favor. That being: I don't understand why there's no volume for the voice acting? Don't get me wrong, the teams got a stellar cast and they do great work but when I personally play a Visual Novel I prefer them as Visual... Novels. I like reading them and having my own voices in my head, it's just a preference. This may seem like a whiny note, I know, and I wouldn't have even included it otherwise but... Ace Academy had this option? Right off the bat it had this option, in fact. So you'd think for your "next gen" game that simple seeming of an option would be available from the get-go? So yeah this is just a minor thing, and if it never gets added, oh well, it's not a deal breaker. But I would like to at least have the option to enjoy the story my way, when I was allowed to do so in an older project by the same developers.
I know it feels I had more negative things to say than positive, but trust me it's not because I don't like what I see. It's just that with these developers I've experienced the most of what they can do, their previous entry being in my opinion the best VN of all time, I was just mildly disappointed that some things felt more stripped down than built up. So I hope they manage to read this and take what I've said into consideration; making all relationship options feel a bit more obviously viable and the option to have no voice acting if we so choose. In their defense though; it IS early in the game's life, they have plenty of time to iron these things out, all this was just hopefully to bring some very, very, very mnior issues to light. Crystalline is still a wonderful experience and any minor grievance I had is sheerly out of bias for the team's previous work. I look forward to Episode Three, and beyond.

While still in the early access stage and with only two episodes out I must say I'm quite enjoying my time with Crystalline and look forward to the finished product and its various current missing features. Mini games which will be added?
Having once played and spent many nights of my youth huddled around a table running a D&D campaign I'm reminded of this while playing Crystalline and some animes like Record of Lodoss War or Slayers or even a few J rpgs.
The story is fun, and the culture and characters are interesting and fairly well rounded. The art style is beautiful and the presentation is top notch. This is a visual novel with one romance path at present. The game itself is simple and has very nice english voice acting.
The relationships do feel rather organic and seem to flow naturally, I was pleasantly surprised. However, I find the odd ocassion, which also seems to be the case with other games, even Mass Effect, Dragon Age, and Deus Ex to some degree,
where the choices you make do not always come across as you are expecting them to. To some extent this can be frustrating as there's very little explaination as to how your character might respond, and I admit sometimes I felt some of the choices I could make came right out of left field. For example, you might be presented with three dialogue choices to choose from, and the description of what your character might do or how they might respond can be quite silly or out right vague in one or two cases. However, in most cases it gives you a pretty good idea,but not always.
The game has a very enjoyable atmosphere  and I have thankfully not encountered any technical issues.The animations have had no slow down and I've yet to encounter any bugs.
I would highly recommend this game to anyone who's wanting a well presented, intereresting, and rather light hearted comedic take on the fantasy rpg visual novel. It has wonderful presentation values, an interesting cast of characters, and an enjoyable story. It's a fun game you can pick up for a few hours and come back to. I'm looking forward to the full release.

Also, for those who don't do well with the Frictional Games type of monsters, there is a mod in the workshop which allows the faint-hearted to play through the game without the enemies ever attacking you.
As for the plot, it explores various topics, some of which have already been treated in other games, and it's also the first videogame that I've seen represent an ASI in a way so close to what's actually possible .
It is truly a fantastic game which I'm pretty certain I'll play from beginning to end again.

SOMA is one of the best games of 2015, if not the best.  Often classified as a walking simulator, it has so much more to it than that.  It has characters to interact with.  It has puzzles to solve.  It has exploration.  It may not be true horror to some, but Frictional Games has come a long way from the somewhat lackluster Amnesia.  SOMA is better in every way.  While I didn't find it particularly scary, I would call it creepy good Sci-Fi.  The voice acting and dialogue are a bit unpolished occasionally, but that does not detract from the overal atmosphere and chilling story.  Besides the puzles, the gameplay might not be much more than a 3-D Pac-Man, but there is nothing wrong with that.  It is the perfect way to experience the unnerving plot of SOMA.  It is not an action game, and people outside the walking simulator lovers might find it a bit slow, but it is worth it in the end.  It is a far better interactive movie than Until Dawn or Heavy Rain could ever hope to be.  Anybody who likes thoughtful Sci-Fi novels or movies should give it a try.

Amnesia is a solid Lovecraftian experience. It places you into an environment you have little control over, gives you a protagonist who has little ability to fight, and almost everything can hurt or kill you. You struggle to find light sources so you don't go into a panic attack in the darkness, you hide in wardrobes from monsters, you avoid organic sludge that can kill you just by touching you, and you hunt down scraps of journals to piece together what caused you to come to this point and how you can save yourself. It's very atmospheric, and gives a different experience from a lot of video games that would resort to combat to spice things up. Dark Descent is really more of a first person point & click adventure game.
Where it suffers is in the variety department. The beginning of the game is fantastic and genuinely terrifying. The puzzles can be quite good, and the environments and graphics are pretty immersive and detailed. About halfway through, though, the game kind of stops developing and becomes a series of puzzles. Even the threat of darkness isn't really an issue because you've found enough lantern oil and tinderboxes to manage it, so one major element of terror is gone. Where I think the game missed a major opportunity is in being able to interact with the monsters in ways other than running and hiding. If there were some way to trick them, or dispatch them with elements of the environment, it would have added another level of puzzle thinking to the game and given it some more variety. I would also have liked a little more exploration of the events and deeds in Daniel's past to show why he was driven to madness, because it feels a little underdeveloped.
Overall, this is a good game, and I think that if you play it in a few sittings, rather than spacing it out over weeks the experience will be more enjoyable and powerful.

BeamNG.drive is a driving game/tech demo hybrid with an impressive amount of detail and surprisingly addicting. Having started as a proof-of-concept in the CryEngine by the former developers of Rigs of Rods - another very similar, more rudimentary game focusing on trucks and heavy vehicles, it has since switched to the Torque3D engine to handle the physics.
There's no storyline or career as of yet. Updates have added a selection of campaigns to complete, such as a driver's license test and wrecking stuff up.
It's a pretty game, for sure, but don't go nuts with the dynamic car reflections if you treasure your framerate. Rather odd post-processing artifacts, or that might be me just not knowing how to work with them. Crashes look a little bland without particles or extra bits flying out.
The sound effect library is slowly expanding - as of now, we have a decent selection of car sounds, depending on engines. Inline 4, V6, American V8, Italian V8, even Inline 6! Environmental sounds aren't too neglected either, even if they tend to be repetitive still. No music as of yet.
The selling point lies in the revolutionary soft body physics. At the expense of requiring an ever more powerful CPU to simulate multiple cars interacting with each other, you get what is possibly the most accurate car deformation,
While it remains prone to clipping, gripping and other odd issues, 99% of the time it is consistent and logical.
An ever expanding list of official cars cover more or less any stereotype conceivable, and if you can think of more, there's mods to remedy that too. You can drive a 4-wheel steering sedan, a pickup truck for your hillbilly rock climbing purposes, a surprisingly fun and nimble hatchback, a dangerously difficult 70's supercar, and many,
more. All of them, of course, have varying tolerances to crashes from whichever direction, but also a healthy collection of parts to choose from. Slap a stage 4 supercharger kit on your muscle car and rocket to terrifying speeds - and send your engine temperature shooting, your wheels screeching due to no grip, and your hapless car careening into walls.
It is such a robust and well built engine that it can simulate airplanes and helicopters, lift and drag, and all sorts of intricate stages of mechanical failures like blown engine gaskets, fried piston rings, bent connecting rods, broken driveshafts, snapped axles, faded brakes, so on and so forth. This is a respectable driving simulator in all the right ways!
Mods further increase the game's variety, with aforementioned planes, helicopters, and varying flavours of land vehicles and configurations. Simple to install and remove (usually).
Updates are somewhat slow to deliver, but when they land, you should expect a couple more cars, a lot more car variation, and several new, possibly experimental systems to improve the simulation aspects of the game. I dare say the devs have picked up significant momentum as of late, and they're eeking ever closer to proper LAN, or even online multiplayer. Until then, we have replays and AI control to bring our destruction derby and "Slightly more sensible Crash Junction" dreams to life.
It is totally worth the money if you're a car/physics nut. It surely is deep in its mechanics, but the current content is a bit too thinly spread to easily warrant a purchase for anyone else; patience is a more wise idea when tackling Early Access titles, even better developed ones such as this.

The Chosen RPG is a short RPG maker game, that honestly has had bits and pieces of every RPG maker game I have ever played and reviewed. The question is if the bits and pieces are the right ones and if it is put together in a nice game.
The story starts off with a lot of backstory and lore to get you into the story. The stereotypical, there is a legend that needs to be fulfilled, they tried to diffrentiate with making the characters as if they are straight from an anime. What also makes it a complete stereotype is that the character does not acknowlegde him being part of the legend until almost the very end. The story would be less linear if there was multiple enemies trying to stop you in your 'quest'. Well quest is not the right way to say this, since the game is another find along as you go RPG. I remember playing this game for a little and coming back after a few days and completely forgetting what the objective was without any way to figure out, without spoiling the game by checking a playthrough, how to continue it. The story turned out to be pretty decent but right as I was getting into it, it ended. After this they gave the classic, "to be continued...", hinting towards a sequel.
The battle sequences have the classic background, enemies and fighting style. Added along to this is pretty nice music and battle animatuons from both sides which is a pretty nice but small feature that you don't see much from RPG maker games. The things they kept from the RPG maker package is that the enemies have no healthbar, which is a nice feature but not mandatory, also the effects like balance, poison, blind, paralyse, sleep and many more. The combat would be way better if they payed more attention to the balancing in general. For story purposes you start off with the 3rd best sword in the game, which in the end 'evolves' into the best sword in the game, which makes you start off with a giant advantage. The difficulty is on point in the beginning, the back to back challenges made it very intense to play, afterwards once you got better items it turned out to be way too easy. For the people who enjoy grinding, you will get satisfied. Aside from one boss which you can battle over and over, seems like a bug honestly, you have a training hall where you can battle different tiers of monsters to your liking. The training hall also has an unique boss that gives you second best sword in the game once you beat it. Honestly that boss was harder than the final battle which is pretty sad.
Concluding a verdict for this game with a yes or no rating is a challenging thing to do. It keeps showing itself in a good spotlight but gets pulled down again by the things missing in this game. They hinted pretty hard at a potential sequel but I see a lot of space for improvement. The story could have been in one game but they have many opportunities to go into with the sequel. If you are a fan of RPG's, take a quick look at this before you instantly buy this. If you don't like the anime theme or need a challenge you should look towards other games.

is a generic old-school role-playing game made with RPG Maker. Gameplay-wise, it ticks all the boxes but there's nothing to this game that'll blow you away. Add to that a very clichéd story and a strange choice of avatars (the scantily-clad girls), and we're left with nothing but a slightly above-average RPG Maker game.
You've noticed the 'nudity' tag and maybe also the screenshots showing scantily-clad girls, so let's talk about the nudity for a moment: there is none. There's just the portraits of the three girls you'll recruit as party members, which shows them in underwear. But beyond that, there's no nudity or even any innuendo in this game. Not one bit.
The decision to portray the three girls in their underwear
to show those portraits as three of the six screenshots on the Steam Store page is most likely the worst decision I've ever seen in game development. It's a very, very bad call because people add the 'nudity' label to the game, even though that's inaccurate, with the following consequences:
- people who're looking for nudity won't find it in this game so they won't be happy;
- people who're not looking for nudity may stay away from the game after glancing at it and seeing the screenshots and/or the 'nudity' label;
- because of the 'nudity' label, Steam always displays a warning
you open
page related to the game (store page, guides, discussions, achievements page, …), which gets very annoying.
The story is one big cliché: an adolescent has a dream about his missing father and is dubbed the 'chosen one' to fulfil a prophecy that tells him to gather some sacred artifacts in order to defeat an evil warrior who's at the service of an even more evil warrior. The game tries to shake things up by adding a twist to the story at the end, but the player most likely saw it coming a mile away
.
To make matters worse, the paper-thin story ends with 'To be continued…' after defeating the final boss. So if you want to see the conclusion to the story, you'll need to buy
. Lame.
The writing is okay in that we usually get to read a lot worse English in these RPG Maker games, but nevertheless the wording is sometimes strange e.g. 'Potion was found' and 'Wanna beer?'.
The gameplay is typical RPG Maker. You walk around towns, enter houses and stores, leave the town and explore the surroundings where random combat may be initiated at any time. You control a party, in this case a group of four, and equip them with increasingly better gear. By defeating opponents in tactical turn-based combat, the party members gain levels, increasing their stats (hit points, magic points, attack and defense) and allowing them to learn new skills and spells.
The level design is decent. You'll find yourself in towns, forests, deserts, castles and dungeons - classic stuff, really. The game world seems open at first, but you'll soon learn that you always need to complete the next part of the main quest at location A to be able to enter location B, where the next part of the main quest will take place. So the game is actually very linear.
The combat is made interesting by adding a mix of skills and spells. Skills use TP that are gained during combat. Spells use classic MP. It takes a few levels before the party gains access to interesting skills and spells, making the first part of the game very repetitive combat-wise. Also, you'll soon find out which are the most useful skills and spells, and likewise discover that most of the other skills and spells are actually completely useless.
Overall,
is a bit too easy, so I'm sure a lot of people would have preferred to see an option to set the game to a higher difficulty mode. The good thing about the low difficulty is that
requires little or no level grinding, unlike a lot of other RPG Maker games.
During combat you sometimes get status effects that persist after the combat has ended, but there's no way to check what these status effects are exactly.
Your party gains levels but the game doesn't mention how much stats they gain. You do get a notice if they gain a skill or spell, though, which is the most useful information.
The graphics are classic RPG Maker graphics. But the problem with
is that Windowed Mode is too small, whereas Full Screen Mode has wide black bars to the left and right of the screen, and it renders the graphics way too blurry, as graphics get blown up too much to fill the screen. So an option for an in-between size would have been very welcome.
One further gripe is that your party members are tiny. During combat, they're literally five times smaller than any human opponent, even though your party does not consist of toddlers or dwarves. It just looks ridiculous.
's music is fine except for the annoying 1990s dance music in the starting town. To make matters worse, a bit later on, when that town is under attack, the music changes to a groovy jazz tune. Both are completely out of place. But okay, the rest of the music is fine and combat music is even reminiscent of classic old-school JRPGs, so it's just unfortunate that the problem with the music lies in the very first area of the game.

Yet another RPG Maker game we have on Steam, but is this the one that will redeem all the wannabe-SNES JRPG copycats we’ve been swarmed by lately?
The Chosen is…
+ Experimental with somewhat inherently busted skill system, but in the good way: every RPG Maker games suffers from it in some way, since the easily exploitative and spammy skill system offers the player to become too imbalanced after only a few gained levels. The Chosen remedies this by including separate skill bar that keep filling as the combat goes on, especially when the player takes a massive damage. You can use skills that cost next to nothing on the skill bar to produce basic but sufficiently powerful combat abilities, or you can wait for the higher tier skills that cost more for battle changers.
+ Playful with skills: basic ones are satisfying to use and powerful. Our main hero has a useful power attack that deals a double damage, while one of his companions has the Tackle that has a chance to prevent the enemies’ next attack, and is one of the most useful skills in the game.
- Very short: you can finish this game in 4-6 hours easily, and the replayability is next to zero due to serious lack of content.
- Unambitious, way too much generic: The Chosen is a painfully “by the numbers” JRPG game, there are literary no interesting quests except “fetch me this” and “get that bloke!” generic quests. Level design is poor and simplistic, battles are boring and grindy, there are no interesting characters, whether they are main heroes, few and rare NPCs that you meet, not to mention the main villain.
- A bit too much asset-flipping: too much of generic assets, not enough of original artwork. RPG Maker is a powerful JRPG maker that comes with a sizeable library of audio and visual assets, but that does not mean you should use them in the product you’re selling, because this feels cheap, lazy and effortless. Except the skimpy design of the main heroes and a handful of NPCs, along with one or two enemies, everything else is an asset flip. Putting as much effort in your product as you can with your artwork always pays off since people who play notice this, and respect the developers who’ve put a proper effort in making as best game they can. So after designing story and screenplay, this should be you next priority.
- Narratively poor: Since the game mechanics in RPG Maker games are inherently simplistic and anarchic by the nature of the game engine they’re based on, story should be your number one priority. An interesting and involving story can and will remedy the many flaws a game can have with most of the players. Sadly, the story in The Chosen is childish, full of plot holes and unsatisfying. Characters that populate this world have even worse treatment since they are walking and spewing trope generators, utterly boring and one-dimensional, without proper inner goals that lead them, and every sentence they say sounds something a child would say. And this is the biggest flaw of The Chosen one, since the game already offers so little.
I cannot recommend The Chosen even by the extremely cheap price it’s selling almost every week, since it feels like content-poor, incomplete and a lazily made product that barely got the care it needed. With absolute power comes absolute responsibility, and just because you have a powerful game engine you can use, doesn’t mean you should create a sub-par game you wouldn’t want to play and charge people money for it. I only hope that developers will grow mature soon and respect the power of making games more.

Graphics 5/5
Crystalline is an amazing visual novel with graphics that are absolutely out of this world. In most visual novels you get still frames and occasionally mouth movements and eye blinks as extra features. In Crystalline, you get tilting heads, swaying hair, and complete shifts in their body moments that almost creates an illusion that these characters are in fact breathing entities. In this regards, I have to say, it's pretty cool. The creators have gone that extra mile, so to speak.
Story 2 to 5/5
Let me explain the rating I give towards the story. Since the story is NOT complete I have to give it a rating of 2. In respect to the time and effort of what is available at this moment, I have to say the story is really good and deserves a 5 in my expectations towards its final product. Every character is well developed with depths to their characters. There are also many dialogue choices and options which ensures active participation of readers who partake in this visual novel. I like choices. I like having many choices. There are alot of visual novels that do not deliver as many choices as I have seen so far in Crystalline.
Mini-Games Pending/5
There are a lot of hints of mini-games being developed in Crystalline, but at the moment are not available in its early access. I am very excited to see what they are and as far as I can tell there are already at least the possibility of 5 if not more once it is completed.
Humor 4/5
So far, there is a lot of humor in the story including moments that makes subtle references towards X-men and Breaking Bad. If you are familiar with those shows, you probably will get a kick out of seeing those jokes.
Final Thoughts
As long as the producers finish the story as I believe they will there is no better bang for your buck than by jumping the gun and getting early access. The time and effort that went into the novel so far tells me it is probably going to jump in price by the time it is finished and depending on the final price, justified. There is simply too many details and polishing that has gone into the novel so far to suggest otherwise.
Visual novel lovers will not want to miss out.

So Crystalline...
Let's split this review up into three parts: Story, Characters and the World (read this in Dio Brandos Voice)
Story:
Well the story... let's see, how should i say this it is basic. Young Protagonist finds himself in a fantasy world and tries to find a way home while fighting the powers of darkness along the way! So yeah like i said it's basic and does it's job. It gives the characters a goal to work for thus driving the plot forward.So to sum this up quickly the story is no masterpeace but it works. I don't wanna spend much words here so to sum it up,
Grade: E
Characters:
Our cast of main characters consist of 4 People Leanna, Zack, Amelia and Kara. And sadly and as of this point they are all pretty basic, they are all likable in their own way but none of them stands really out. They are all good characters but it's nothing you haven't seen before in one way or another. They are not copy and paste characters i want to clarify that but i always thought "hmm somewhere i've seen this before" as of this moment they don't really set themselves apart from other characters in fictional media ecpecially when it comes to anime. They all lack, how do i put this the right way uniqueness. What they need is to shine to have their moments, they need to set themselves apart from the rest of the world. Again right now they are fine but they need to be more than just another edgy teen, just another mage with awkward behavior, just another sexy thief and just another waifu.
Grade: C
So now that thats over i wanna move the subject over to the villains. The villians are, in my opinion the most boring part in this entire story right now. They are just another evil cult tainted by the powers of darkness. Wich again is sad because this entire setting offers much more when it comes to villians that just your evil cult of darkness, or your evil wizard or your evil king. These are all things that work as an antagonistic force because they create a conflict but that conflict sure is boring (again in my opinion). It's a simple black and white conflict they want to rule the world of course thats bad and of course our heros fights against this. But it isn't really an intresting conflict. A good conflict is created by having at least two sides with understandable motives who "fight" each other (doesn't has to be a literal fight). Now maybe PixelFade can still pull this off and give their villains a good and maybe even a sympathetic motivation. I sure hope so because as of this point in time: Grade F
Oh and theres another thing i personally want to point out. It is about certain cameos.
Warining Spoiler:
The World:
Well to be honest there isn't much to say about the world it's a medieval fantasy world wich is powerd by crystals. Again it's the same thing with the characters you've seen this somewhere before even if you can't put your finger on it. However theres an easy way to improve this, the lore. It's as simple as that just exploit the lore a bit more, give us some history about this world. Something that is not absolutely necessary for the plot but something to show how this world works why do people behave this way and not in another way? As of this point: Grade: D
Alright so... do i recommend this game? Hell Yes i do! Of course it has it's weaknesses just like any story (just look at a song of ice and fire, the books are in the works for years and even they aren't perfect, though pretty damn colose)
Like i said earlier even if the cast isn't as great as it could be in my opinion we're only at episode two so theres a lot place for improvment. This can still be a shinig example of a western visual novel and i hope it does.
But even if the story would continue this way and there wouldn't be much improvments this VN still gives you a good time.
It has a likeable cast, a lot of funny moments and is overall completly fine.
So my total overall verdict for crystalline as of episode two: Grade: C-

I art is very amatuerish but do not let that fool you this game is about gameplay. The game does seem very derivative and it seems to get really repetitive the thing that saves it the most is the fact that you are the villian instead of the hero which turns the old school action RPG on its head. Our "hero" is on a mission to conquer and pillage and burn everything good. A very strong start, especially when compared to their previous title ACE Academy. The overall production values and voice acting are considerably improved, though the new Live 2D sprite system does cause some significant slowdowns on my system from time to time, something I don't usually experience with visual novels.
Having said that, this only leaves me wanting more. There are a number of scenes, particularly battle scenes or events such as festivals and the like, that do not have unique CGs dedicated to them, and this does take away from the experience a bit. I understand that there are minigames planned to mitigate this somewhat, but even then, immersion is key to realize all the scenes to their full potential. If this aspect of the VN is not adequately improved, Crystalline will remain distinctly inferior to most quality Japanese visual novels out there in the market.
Early Access pricing can vary by region, and while I got it at a pretty affordable and reasonable deal, I don't know how it will affect everyone else's financial situation. If you're considering purchasing it, make sure you're completely comfortable with doing so and not feeling strapped for cash. However, setting that aside, I definitely think this VN shows a lot of potential, and I dearly hope the developers can fully realize it.

Still one of the best-written RPG's ever made (and possibly the best-written Star Wars game ever made), and the mechanics are solid, if a little unbalanced in places. (If you've ever played D&D 3.5, you know over half of the mechanics already.) For a game with a binary morality system, there are many discussions and scenarios throughout the game about the more subjective natures of morality.
I highly recommend playing this with the Restored Content Mod (RCM), which repairs some of the content that Obsidian couldn't quite finish in time for the game's rushed release.
With the mod, my only criticism of the game is that the game doesn't open up and let you explore until easily 1/4th of the way in, so you will have to survive a while through two extended tutorial levels. (That being said, even those levels are pretty good; just not great.)
Even without the mod, if you like an intricate story with fleshed-out characters and the Star Wars universe seen through different eyes, I can't reccommend this enough.

I recommend this game, mainly because of the price. If not for that, it wouldn't be worth owning. EvilQuest, is not the kind of game that is fresh, or new. Many of the retro styled games at least try to advance on old ideas; whereas this one is a blatant copy of one of my favorite titles, Crystalis. The charging of your weapon, to the layout of the overworld. There is however a refreshing feeling I have, when playing it. It may be a copy, but it is done quite well. Sure, one could argue, that the sprite design is poor, and cheesily bad. But then again look at LJN; they were charging full game price, and most of their games were hardly playable. One area 'EvilQuest' tries to advance, is the story. Now, back in the old times of NES, and SNES, we were always forced to play as the 'Hero'. This was the way things were; and it worked, damn well, at that. This was the golden age; the stories were good, the gameplay was majorly addicting, and the sprites were done so well, that we could literally see them pop off the screen. Evilquest does some of these things right. But I digress. The story is one area where they advanced, as we get to play as the villian, for once. You start out as a reknowned antagonist named, Galvis. He is all sorts of evil badassery. We are only told this through the title, game trailer, and some of the dialogue. Thus, it is the weakest point in the game. When all you are killing is monsters in the overworld; how can you call your game, EvilQuest? Seriously, this is my only real annoyance. 6/10 Great price, somewhat good title.

EvilQuest is a fun Action RPG in a 16 bit SNES style, similar to games like Zelda.  Story wise the big difference is this time rather than trying to stop the generic EVIL bad guy bent on world domination you play as the EVIL bad guy bent on world domination.  The story is fine and the EVIL twist makes it all feel fresh even though its about as simple as a RPG story gets.
The gameplay consists of attacking enemies with swords and such, holding down the attack button for a projectile attack, and some different magic attacks that you can find while exploring, or buy if you save up enough gold.  There are plenty of armor pieces to find to make you stronger, and accessories that make you more powerful in various ways, even a cape that makes you invisible.
The graphics look good for a 16 bit style, some of the enemies are merely reskined as you progress in the game, but others like dragons and ghost make for a nice visual treat as you make your way thru the game.  The levels are all based on elements like fire and water and look and play nice enough with just enough exploration to give the game some meat.  My only complaint is enemies respawn after you slightly move away from an area, so you can't clear a level per say, the enemies are always respawning.  This dose give you plenty of opportunity to gain exp points and level up, but as the game wares on it all gets a bit repetitive, but at about 5 hrs for a diligent explorer EvilQuest isn’t long enough for this to become a problem.
Overall EvilQuest is a very fun ARPG that lets you experience the generic RPG story of those 90ies RPG's from the eyes of the bad guy and plays like a dream.  For the cost of less than a gallon of gas (in the US at least) this game is an absolute steel and should be played by anyone who likes Zelda like ARPG's or wants to be EVIL.

Cons:
- P2P connections make a lot of problems in multiplayer.
- No dedicated servers.
- Microtransactions . . . All weaponry can be purchased via ingame money but the amounts that you earned from match is a joke.
- Your connections restrict into 3 different NAT type (open, moderate, strict) that make finding matches and host/join group become so much harder that it's supposed to be.
- Lack of customize matches for multiplayer mode, so far there are only three main mode (deathmatch, duel-brawl, dominion). Which is weird considering the game provide a custom match section that have a complete customization
- No Battle Royale mode . . . what a totaly miss opportunity from the devs considering this is an all out war type of game.
- No matches Browser, all match will be hosted by random player that could have bad internet.
- No customizable feature in the matchmaking.
- No multiple Loadout for your heroes equipments (untill reputation 1). So you've to manually changes everything before the match to suit certain condition. also this feature isn't available between round so you can't adapt the play style that could tackle your enemy/enemies.
- lack of emotes, so far you've got only 2 "free" emotes.

A game about economics and posturing where you and your "friends" are engaged in corporate warfare. Using a mixture of honest business acumen to build supply chains and underhanded tactics to prevent your rivals from doing the same, you fight for the right to create a resource monopoly on foreign worlds. Matches rarely last longer than about 20 minutes with relatively-even competitors, and a large part of gameplay is keeping your secrets to yourself. This typically results in tense stand-offs punctuated by thirty or so seconds of the closest thing the business world has to "action", seeing aggressive buyouts and crucial usage of the black market to suddenly swing things around.
If you like strategy but hate managing armies, definitely give this a shot, because it's focused more on "the big picture" and less on how fast you can click (for the most part).

This small card game has more in it than meets the eye.
But let´s start from the beginning.
TCG is a card game where you put your cards (units, spells and traps) on the field and let them fight against other cards automatically. The battle system is decent enough. Not too complicated, nor too simple. All cards have their strengths, weaknesses, abilities and speed that you have to consider when putting them on the table to fight.
That´s basically all there is in the game. It doesn´t really have a story, apart from the few lines you get to read when starting and the tutorial, which explains the basics of gameplay. At least they did a good job in this. Easy to understand and beginners won´t have any problems with getting started.
The game splits into two areas.
-Campaign mode is an area where you train against non-player-cards, complete numerous goals and conditions and earn some gold and other stuff to make your cards better or earn more cards. The goal part is actually challenging. You can spend hours trying to figure the right combination of cards needed to fulfill the different tasks. Sometimes you won´t be able at all, because you will get the cards needed in a later stage of the campaign. Which isn´t a problem. You can skip them and return to the unfinished ones later.
-Then there are numerous modes for player versus player. I found it unfair at first, but after over 30 hours of gameplay I have to revise that. I just didn´t know how to built a proper and working deck. But the practice on campaign mode teaches you step by step the working combinations and you will find yourself soon with a deck capable of putting up some fight and earning you victories against human players. No real money so far needed and I still have fun watching my team win.
Truth be told, I find the campaign mode more fascinating and motivating, but I´d still go as far as recommend this game. I find it interesting that most players who rated it bad didn´t really spent any time with the game. Once you give it a chance and look deeper into the upgrade system, transforming cards and collecting them, you´ll find it quite worthwhile.

While this is still in Early Access with only two chapters, I felt I should give a slightly long review on what was given so far for those reading and for the devs to get feedback, to have a fair assessment of the VN so far.
No major spoilers here, but anything outside of the general synopsis I put in spoiler tags.
- Art Style: Pretty good. The backgrounds in each location are nicely presented, and add to the tone for each part of the story. The character art is phenomenal, not to mention all the characters constantly do something when they're shown, ranging between facial expressions to other characters to simply breathing, which does add a lot to the interactions as the story progresses. The only complaints I would have now is some repeated use of a single background despite the story changing to different rooms, and an example would be
, where it still uses the hallway background despite being in another room. Another minor issue is the backgrounds feel too static for the scenes they were trying to portray at some points in the story. The character animations do help though.
- Story/World Building: To be honest, it is not an original premise: MC lives in the real world, MC magically gets teleported to another parallel world, MC tries to find his way back using the
through magic. Of course, you can always boil down stories to only its major plot points, but so far it isn't as in-depth with its world as I thought it would be. Of course, this is only the second chapter, so we'll see how it goes. Additionally, there are points where there could be more player choice for conversations as the dialogue would just keep rolling, and I wish there could be more side events happening later, like the card game. Yet despite these flaws, it remains interesting: the conflicts so far have been moderately interesting, and moments such as
were bits of world building that I enjoyed: they showed this world existed outside just of our little group, and that there is history here. I do hope there are more conflicts coming up in the future, though; again, only the second chapter as of reviewing this so I don't expect all the plotlines to start immediately.
- Characters: Probably the highlight of this VN so far. The interactions between all of the major characters feel natural, and quite a few times I was laughing at some of the comments between them, especially some of the conversation choices. They have lives that they wouldn't mention as soon as you meet them. I hope that these characters only get more interesting, and overall I never felt disappointed.
- Sound/Voice Acting: Nothing really to say for the voice acting besides great. The voices always seemed to match the scene and what the character felt, and it was believable. Music wise though, it didn't feel bad or phenomenal, but so far nothing memorable.
Despite only containing two chapters so far as of writing this review and its occasional flaw, this VN has been entertaining and I'm definitely looking forward to the upcoming chapters. For the flaws it does have, this is still in Early Access so I give the developers the benefit of the doubt for now. For those just glancing through the reviews, it is worth keeping an eye on at the least.

This is a really hard game to review. I was torn on whether to say Yea or Nay to it. Ultimately, I decided to not recommend it—even if it is pretty neat.
Puzzle games are my thing, for sure. Simplistic and minimal? That counts for double. For what this game is, the vibe is absolutely perfect, starting right from the title screen/first level. I have to give props to the game trailer, too. Leaving it to the player to discover what the game is about is very compelling.
However, sometimes you have things are too simplistic and too minimal. I'm afraid Hook falls into this category. I completed all 50 levels of the game in 50 minutes. That's all there is. There is nothing for me to go back to. (I wish there was.)
Things don't get satisfactorily difficult until the last 10 levels. To me, the first 30ish levels felt like an expanded tutorial. They built up new concepts nicely, but in the end there are very few levels where you are really challenged on them. In fact, there is one mechanic that is introduced then abandoned after just 2 levels, never to be seen again. Why put it in if you don't have a real test for it later in the game?
I read the reviews for this game beforehandand I knew that I was going to get what amounts to a disposable, one-time use product. You buy it, you use it, you're done with it. I'm satisfied with what I got, but that doesn't mean I'd recommend it to everyone.
Hook is a neat game, but it's not a good value. There are many other games, on Steam or on smartphones, that also cost less than a dollar, but they will have much more content and are probably worth your time more than this one is worth your money.

I've never played a game with an atmosphere as well-crafted as this.  If there is such a thing as video game as art, then the immersion in a particular circumstance that this experience evokes is my new paragon.  It is believable and horrifying and gorgeous.
Unfortunately, in the context of
, this magnificent artisitic accomplishment has to be contrasted against its gameplay.  There is a story, a good but fairly run-of-the-mill science-fiction plot that you are woven into as the protagonist.  It is not particularly believable but not ridiculous, either.  The narrative captures a few interesting points about the nature of being and even surfaces some of these points in the form of (inconsequential) decisions.  Those moments are thought-provoking but nothing you probably haven't thought about before.
As many others have noted, the inclusion of the "monsters" is just silly.  Once you are briefly scared (really startled) in each encounter, dealing with them is just an annoyance.  I appreciate that there is not much pointless violence, but this approach isn't the answer either.
You might consider playing the game with the "wuss mode" mod so that you can enjoy the game's story and atmosphere in some places rather than wasting it dealing with these things.  Doubly so since you are unlikely to play the game again; therefore in some places, you will not get to explore at all because you are busy dodging these things.
In addition, there are no significant puzzles to speak of.  Anything that qualifies is trivial or amounts to "which other thing in this room do I need to click on?"
In sum, this is a game to buy because it is a magnificent, immersive experience in a brilliantly crafted world.  Not because of the story or the gameplay, but because of how it will make you
to be in this place for 10 hours or so.  If this had been coupled with something non-linear to really engage with, it would be one of the great games of all time.  Still, I give it my strongest recommendation.

As much as I would love to, I really can't recommend this game. I loved "Amnesia" by Frictional Games. In fact, it still remains one of the best horror experiences I've ever had the priviledge of playing. However, SOMA just doesn't cut it, as it does away with nearly everything that made "Amnesia" such a wonderful experience.
For starters, inventory management has now been eliminated. Sure you still
an inventory. However, it isn't really used for anything throughout the game, as your character will pretty much always just automatically use an item as soon as you are standing in the correct location. There are also no health-related pickups (i.e. no Laudanum) as in the previous game. Instead, if you want to heal your character you just need to find a healing point and use that. Not that you'd need to, normally, as the gameplay really varies very little depending on whether you're beat up or not. If anything, you just walk a bit slower, and that's about it. This detracts from the urgency of the gameplay that was so prevalent in "Amnesia", in which careful resource management was the crucial key to survival.
Another aspect that detracts from the overall experience are the monster encounters. In SOMA, you usually get another chance if a monster catches you (as long as you are at decent health, see above). So, basically, the monster beats you up, leaves you lying there and then just leaves. Compare this to Amnesia, in which encounters were always fatal. Sure, you could try again an infinite amount of times if you were killed, just as you can in SOMA, but this "catch and release" mechanic still manages to detract from the overall urgency and terror of monster encounters as compared to those in Amnesia, as you still
you'll survive the encounter if you are at decent health. On this note, it is also important to point out that the "hiding" functions of the previous game, in which you could take cover in lockers or closets and the like, have now been stripped as well. You can stand behind something and crouch, but that's generally it. This further reduces the experience.
Yet another thing that makes the game less scary is the abscence of the sanity mechanic, one of Amnesia's most innovative features. Using a gameplay mechanic where you can't even look at upsetting things, much less at monsters, because it drives you insane, was incredibly well thought out and greatly enhanced the terror of the unknown you experienced as a player. This mechanic is now completely absent. In SOMA, you can look at monsters until you die from boredom, with no real negative aspects other than some visual distortion of the in-game graphics. There are at least a couple of monsters that will begin to chase after you if you actively look at them too long, but otherwise staring them down usually has no ill effects. The removal of the sanity function is, in my opinion, the greatest drawback gameplay-wise as compared to earlier Frictional titles, as the gameplay just doesn't feel as urgent or scary anymore. Keeping this function intact would have greatly improved on the overall experience.
All these things aside, however, SOMA:s real selling point is its supposed philosophical content. If you haven't played the game yet, I'm not going to give away too much of what the plot details, but it again left me feeling sorely disappointed. The  philosophical issues of the game mainly deal with the concept of identity, mental and physical, and whether a person is still the same person if his consciousness is no longer contained in his own body, or in any biological body at all, or even uploaded to and duplicated across several storage mediums all at once. However, the game really does not go into any in-depth discussion concerning any of these issues; instead usually preferring to introduce questions to the player and then just "leave them" there without ever arriving at any real conclusions.
This should be contrasted with the "Bioshock" series by former Irrational Games, in which philosophical issues were not only introduced to the player but also expounded upon in detail by the creators throughout the gameplay, often resulting in the player arriving at critical conclusions simply through his or her own journey through the game. SOMA does away with all this by just essentially asking the player
and then throwing its arms up and going
This leaves you feeling as if you're playing a Bioshock designed by a philosophy freshman, who may not even have paid all that much attention to class.
Speaking of which; the philosophical points introduced by the game aren't even all that interesting to begin with, as most of them have already long been a staple of science fiction literature (in which they have been given considerably greater and more in-depth treatment than in this game). For instance, the question of whether or not a person is still a "person" if s/he is "just a bunch of ROM" is adressed in Gibson's 1984 novel "Neuromancer", in which it is discussed by the deaceased character McCoy "The Dixie Flatline" Pauley and the novel's protagonist, Case. Even though no real answer is ever arrived at between these two characters either, you still leave the novel feeling infinitely more satisfied than when you've finished playing this game. My advice would therefore be to purchase Gibson's novel rather than the game, as it'll probably award you with a more satisfying sci-fi experience (and be a lot cheaper, too).
In summary, SOMA simply is not all that good a game, gameplay-wise or other. I left the game feeling dissatisfied, and since the game literally has no replay value at all (none of the choices you make in-game seem to impact the ending at all); odds are pretty good this is how you may end up feeling, as well. The graphics looked very nice, however, so I guess that was a strong point of the experience. Except that the nice graphics didn't make for a good game, just for nice graphics.

SOMA... where to begin.
I've been meaning to review this game (and some other games) for quite some time now, but the pressures of doing my Research Masters have made this to be quite the impossible task. I like to put some thought into my reviews and a game like SOMA deserved some more time for me to... gather my thoughts.
And for good reason. I was merely a few minutes into the game and I could tell I was going to at the very leasy enjoy the experience of SOMA, it looked intelligent, seemed to be touching on neuroscientific ideas very early on. What I didn't anticipate was just how much I would enjoy this game.
I'll cut to the chase and proclaim SOMA with little doubt (though there is some; Life is Strange was stellar too), my GOTY. I'm usually hesitant to say things like this nowadays as I enjoy different games for different reasons, and it's not usually fair to do like for like comparisons of games like, say, Invisible Inc. and Life is Strange.
SOMA is intensely thought provoking, philosophical and damn well terrifying. Not the scariest horror game I've played, but it's pretty damn high up. I'd say Alien: Isolation holds that crown, but SOMA is well executed horror. It builds up the feeling of horror through atmospheric tension, small changes in your environment, sounds. No reliance of cheap jump jump scares to generate horror. Smartly done, draws you in, retains immersion. Almost a perfect recipe, in my opinion, for horror.
Something that really stood out for me was the atmosphere - the ambience. SOMA is set deep under the Atlantic Ocean (would you kindly?) in a decaying scientific research facility. There is great scope to utilise darkness, and the sounds of the ocean to really help immerse you in the story. SOMA does all this and more. What I love is in the decaying, abandoned corridors of rooms and ships, you can catch glimpses of the facility and the world around you, through audio logs, televisions, ship recordings. It's essentially stuff that's just THERE, but it adds so much to the experience.
The dialogue that goes on is great. Another strong point. The discussions that go on between you and Catherine are intensely thought provoking. SOMA explore themes regarding life, death, sentience, consciousness, morality, and the very idea of self. And SOMA does it in such an organic way - it's an integral part of the game and it's story and it all comes together, in my own opinion, almost perfectly. As a budding neuroscientist, these ideas especially spoke to me and I was drawn in.
The gameplay is nothing too complex. There's no combat, much like predecessor Amnesia: The Dark Descent, there's no fighting - only hiding and clever navigation. So use the darkness as cover, hide when you can, don't make noise. All good stuff. The design of the various beings you meet is especially intriguing, particularly as a research interest of mine is organic-inorganic interfaces. From an artistic point if view, I felt these ideas were highly imaginative and pretty original. I feel these artistic choices were key components of the horror aspect of the game.
Also furthering the strong points of horror and game design was that, much like Alien: Isolation, it doesn't hold your hand. There aren't way markers - you gotta figure out your way round yourself, by finding maps or deducing from instructions - even if it's pitch black and some unholy beast is stalking you.
Graphically, SOMA is pretty good. In terms of technical ultra realism, It's not amazing, but at the very least, it's certainly a good looking game. What I would expect from an Indie studio that doesn't have millions to throw at the most advanced graphical engine. I've touched on this already, but the artistic design is very good. I'm a sucker for futuristic/sci fi stuff so I may well be biased. For the most part, many things actually don't look too futuristic or far out, in terms of your environment - it's almost familiar - but when you start meeting other... say, inhabitants, these ideas of sci-fi/futurism become more apparent.
All of these things tie together to make the storytelling of SOMA one of the best I've come across. The characters, the dialogue, the themes, the overall story, the environment. I don't have enough praise for SOMA. It's not a perfect game, of course - there was the odd graphical glitch and on occasion the AI would react weirdly and I wished the game was a little longer, but all in all it's so damn good.

One of the scariest games of all time. As someone who values a good survival horror game, Amnesia: The Dark Descent is one of the greatest. The game has no combat function and forces you to flee from your enemies within a dark castle located somewhere in the woods of Prussia. You play as Daniel, a man who has no memory of who he is, but who has left a note to himself describing the terrifying shadow which follows you along with your main mission, which is to kill a man named Alexander.
The game play mechanics are fantastic. If you are in a dark area for too long, you will start to lose your sanity and hallucinate. You are able to remedy this by using tinder boxes to light candles and torches along the way. If, however, you look directly at the monster who constantly pursues you, you lose a great deal of sanity almost immediately. The lack of combat leaves you feeling vulnerable and scared as you turn each corner of the castle, dreading what may be around the turn. Instead of fighting, you are forced to run and hide from your assailant, which I found refreshing, although there have been many titles to repeat this after this game was released.
Overall, this game is great. If you are a fan of horror games, you won't want to miss this one.

This game is heavily about capitalism, so don't read too much into the space setting other than simplification of the kinds of resources you're dealing with. Much like a properly played match of Monopoly, you see your impending defeat coming long before it happens and you have little in your power to stop it. And much like Monopoly, when someone plays it right basically no one has fun playing it anymore except the person winning. The same can be said of Offworld Trading Company.
The game is polished and functionally works fine, but the black market isn't really fair and ruins gameplay. Playing against the AI, you can try your best to disable them but they perfectly know how to ruin your match and put you horribly in debt. You're encouraged to build buildings close together, but there are abilities that will disable multiple buildings if they're connected. Build your power collectors all together and in one swoop you can go from surplus with profit to heavily in the red. Since the abilities last for a long amount of time, one can easily put you on the slippery slope of defeat.
Of course you can play with the AI on one of the lowest difficulty settings and it's laughably easy to beat. The AI at those levels doesn't even build required resources it needs, so your difficulty ranges from beating a sloth to the finish line to doing a marathon race against a car on foot. I like the ideas presented here, but the combination of too easy/too hard AI difficulties combined with ridiculous abilities leaves me to not recommend this game.

After seeing all the negative reviews for this game and deciding to give it a try anyway, I'm genuinely surprised at how much fun I've had with it.
The somewhat awkwardly-titled Epic Cards Battle is a CCG (card collection game) where you build a small (up to 6 card) hand of cards from your collection to do battle against your opponent. Without going into too much detail, each card can be one of three types; Creature, Spell or Triggered. Your creatures battle your opponent's creatures directly, and also serve as your life-blood - ie. you win by eliminating all your oponents creature cards. Spell cards provide a wide variety of effects such as buffs, debuffs or direct damage-dealing, while Triggered cards are similar in effect to spell cards, but will only activate under specific circumstances. The actual battles themselves are completely non-interactive, but don't be fooled; in campaign mode at least, selecting the right cards for each challenge increasingly involves strategy and careful forethought - something which caught me by surprise having played a few CCGs on mobile which are largely devoid of any real gameplay.
During the 18.5 hours total I've spent playing this game at the time of writing this review, I've completely ignored the cash-shop and PvP elements, instead focusing on campaign mode, daily rewards, and shop items that can be bought with in-game earnings. This is honestly enough. All up, there's probably a good 10-15 solid hours worth of gameplay to be had from campaign mode before you'll hit a difficulty wall, and will have a hard time progressing further without a more fleshed out collection. From there, you'll find yourself logging in for short sessions, mostly to recieve daily rewards, doing a spot of enchanting/combining, and playing maybe a round or two here and there; things I've still found to be satisfying in their own way.
For the type of game this is, I've found the quality of art on the cards to be a little diasppointing - not bad, but not that great either. Even the 4-5 star cash-shop cards are largely so-so (devs, if you are reading this, commission high-caliber fantasy/ecchi artists to do art on the cards you're expecting people to pay for - they'll sell a lot better).
Having said that though, I'd definitely recommend campaign mode to any strategy/card/table-top game fans. I can't speak for the competitive side of it, but there is a lot of fun to be had from the free elements alone.
-------------------
UPDATE: Turns out the number of daily rewards is finite. Now that I've claimed them all, it doesn't really feel like there's anything worth logging in for without paying money - which given the quality vs price-point of the paid content, I'm just not enticed to do. Bit of a disappointing end, but I'd still recommend the game.

If you are considering this title accept that it is only one part (the bigger part) of a two part project. When you buy "Chosen" you will want to buy "Chosen 2" at the same time. Together these two games form a single narrative. This narrative is a short (less than 10 hours) simple Ameri-JRPG. It doesn't do anything fancy and it doesn't try to.
It is my suspicion that this game was a passion project and a training exercise for the developer. Part 1 "feels" a bit under polished. The combat is a little too easy. The protagonist travels with three female companions all of whom choose to travel in lingerie. This feels very amateurish, but also in its way feels very Japanese. The author consistently uses, "your" when they should be using "you're" … it's little things that make this game feel like a fledgling project.
Part 2 takes noteworthy strides forward. The companion characters wear real clothes. The interface gets some polish. The combat is more balanced. It was early in Part 2 that I experienced my first total party death and game over screen. I suddenly became aware that I was going to have to pay more attention. The game isn't overly difficult, or even difficult. It just wasn't a "cake-walk" any more. That was better.
But combat isn't really what this game (or other similar RPG-Maker games) is about. It's about a love for a dying genre of JRPG, and the stories that only these games can tell. It's the reason the we buy games like this. And, as yet another entry in the slog of RPG-Maker amateurware, Chosen doesn't do anything new. But, it doesn't do anything particularly wrong either. The story is well paced and sometimes interesting. You won't spend too much time trying to figure out where you need to go, or what you need to do. Everything is intuitive and the experience is smooth.
I am going to keep my eyes on this developer because they have good instincts for this kind of game and how it should play. Because the best thing about Chosen and Chosen 2 is that I enjoyed playing them. These games are fun, and at the end of the day, isn't that what matters most?
