SOMA delivers great atmosphere and immersiveness in a story that depicts the collapse of an underwater facility after an "event". We'll leave it at that to avoid spoilers; the less said about the plot, the better, as it's worth the ride.
If you're after a linear story and streamlined game experience that does a good job immersing you in the world they created, and don't mind a one-and-done game experience telling a very speicifc story, I'd certainly recommend this.
However, gameplay-wise, the game can best be summarized as a "crouching / waiting simulator", as you move from room to room or area to area and almost universally simply crouch and wait to avoid the enemies.
While the enemies are interesting at first because they're new to you, they devolve into an overused "walking potato" which is not fun to get around (slow, random) and cheats in its movement in order to create drama and tension, which in turn creates more waiting. Distractions and any interactions with the environmental props to bait and lure enemies simply doesn't work, meaning you don't have any options but to crouch... and wait.
There's no inventory mechanics to speak of. You use items automatically when necessary and only when they're the solution to something. There's a few puzzles along the way that are fun for how long they last, but generally you're back to crouching and waiting when an enemy is around. The moments of pure exploration are really more fun than the encounter sections.
If you enjoy heavily directed narrative experiences and are more in this for the story (and it's a good one) then this is worth your time. However, if you're looking for a GAME experience that has more interesting enemy mechanics and interactions, seriously play Alien : Isolation instead.

Disclaimer: I may be bias towards this because it's the first true horror game I've ever played.
This is the most immersed I've ever felt in a video game, partially because when the graphics are pushed to the maximum you can so easily forget you're running a piece of computer software, but also because the game is very consistent in how it follows its rules. Let me just quickly run though some of the things that made me more immersed in this game than almost any other. Soma:
- never takes control away from the player, except for when in the physical reality of the game we ourselves would loose control.
- never breaks or steals the camera/controls to present a different point of view.
- never influences your choices in and out of the plot and never indicates whether what you did was right.
There are one or two moments where you're immersion will be broken and at those point you'll be angry enough to rip a puppy's inn two because you were that invested only to have something technically silly happened.
If I had to criticises any bigger features of the game, it would be that you do not feel like you are the player character, Simon. Simon will almost never talk about the monsters or the horrifying challenges he faces and the fact he just starts talking with NPCs about their situation can make the player feel alienated if you hold a different belief. Also you're tag along NPC sidekick never references the monsters, recognises the mental break down you might be having behind your controller or tries to motivate you to keep moving forward. So it can feel like two separate plots, one with “Simon-Simon and sidekick” and the other “You-Simon vs the WAU”. More over, Simon has a personality: you hear him think and talk so it can feel like you have a companion in your body who just happens to steal control of your mouth from time to time.
Soma lacks replay value but I do not see this as a fault and here's why: Soma was an experience I look up to along side games like “Spec Ops the Line” and “Journey”, games that I think are excellent experiences that are pushing the gaming medium forward, games I think would have the movie equivalent of “Schindlers List” in that they are utterly fantastic but not the sort of thing you come back to every night to worship, this is where the replay value comes in. I love and respect this game but it will be a month or two before I go through it again.
Soma offers everything I ask for in video games: Solid Mechanics and a Brilliant Story that will leave you to reflect on your experience long after the game is over. Even if you've never played a horror game before you should pick this up, while you may be petrified for the first 5 hours, by the mid point you'll find it isn't actually that scary and will be ready to go through it again. I couldn't have picked a better game to introduce me to horror. Again I am bias towards this game because horror is a completely new experience for me, so I might have over sold it for horror veterans, but you will not be able to deny that this is still an exceptional game. The tone and missions shift and vary so it never gets dull, and the story is as deep as Pathos II (lol).
Conclusion:
Now that I've finished SOMA it will be a while before I am ready to play it again, but I look forward to the time when I am. Horror veterans and new comers to the horror genre alike: Buy it as soon as you have 10 to 15 hours to spare, it's worth every penny.

1) There should be a better way to find players' statistics, in this version there's no way to get a leaderboard where one can easily toggle between sorting players based on specific statistics without having to return to the career leaderboards screen, which takes some time to load. A nice example of what this could look like can be found on the
statistics page. This is my biggest issue with the game.
2) I think it'd be really cool if the game automatically selected certain pivotal or particulalry impressive moments from games when they were simulated and kept these moments in their own page. For example, walk-off home runs in the postseason or especially amazing catches would be really cool to see when they happened in simulation.
3) I also think it'd be cool if there was a page that kept track of players' use of performance-enhancing drugs. I believe that the simulation already hands out suspensions to certain players if they are caught with PEDs but it'd be nice to see all of these infractions in one place, maybe along with the statistics of those who are caught, to determine the effect of their use on certain records. You know, like real life.
I think those are all of my issues, but besides these things I really love this game and am 100% glad that I purchased it.

In the era where space battle is basically a wet-naval battle in space, I have loss hope that someone would make a space battle game based upon real physics. I was wrong.
Children of a Dead Earth is the most scientifically accurate space combat simulator ever create, bar none. It's about time someone made hard-scifi space combat game. Physicist and thermodynamic experts deserved to be entertained as well, after all. :D
By "most scientifically accurate", I mean that this "game" doesn't calculate orbital trajectory with Patched Conic Approximation (which is simple to learn but inaccurate), it goes full NASA and use an N-Body Simulator, which mean CoaDE can handles hyperbolic orbits and Lagrange points, unlike most other games.
If you read developers logs, you'll see that Mr. Mankowski's attention to detail is astonishing.
This also mean that orbital mechanics can be pretty frustrating, even for KSP veteran, and involve a lot of trial-and-error. Fortunedly, some aspect (such as interception) have computer assistant. You don't have to have a perfect interception, just bring your trajectory close to the target's trajectory, and let computer handle the rest.
For me, I don't regret buying this game.
Pro :
- Realism.
- Relatively easy and simple control, despite it using N-Body Simulator.
- Heat radiator....Finally, someone remember the laws of Thermodynamic.
- Good worldbuilding. Each factions have their own story. It's one of a few game that factions did not follow "Good VS Evil" cliche, but rather realistic political conflict.
- Come with clear tutorial. Really helpful for a game this complicate.
- Combat is fun to watch, and also scientifically realistic, a nice message to all those who said "Realism will ruin the epicness of space combat"
- All weapon system follow laws of physics, which mean laser isn't god, missile cost delta-V, and kinetic weapon still rulez in term of efficiency.
- A Sandbox mode where you can do anything.
- Soundtrack is nice, it's relaxing enough not to distract you from the game (and force you to turn off the music), and exciting enough not to feel boring (and force you to turn off the music).
- Oh, and they're no sound in space...HELL YEAH!
- And did I mentioned that, after you've unlocked ships and module design, you can design EVERYTHING, the engine, the nuclear reactor, guns,
it. You can even make a gun that shoot nukes!
- Speaking of which, you have nukes! It's really satisfying seeing 120 nuclear warheads tore enemy ships apart. I don't think I have to mention how realistic nuclear detonation is.
Cons :
- As I've mentioned, N-body simulators can be frustrating, and usually result in trial-and-error.
- Most aspect in combat are controlled by computer. You don't get to manually command a spacecraft. Then again, can you actually hit a target as small as a coke can at 20 kilometers away?
- Can be confusing if you have limited knowledge in nuclear physics, orbital mechanics, electromagnetics, etc.
- Learning curve is pretty tought.
- Certain features in certain missions can cause significant slowdown. Applying N-body simulators to several groups of ships and missiles at one time is pretty demanding task for computer, especially if both you and your enemy love to spam waves after waves of missile at each others.
- No multiplayer as of this moment (6/4/2017)

===
===
I have played this game using the Restored Content Mod, which you can find in the Workshop section. The mod doesn't modify the game in any way, but instead restores content that for many reasons has not been included in the original release by the Developers. I recommend this mod to enjoy a more complete experience, this game deserves it.
===
GRAPHICS - 8.5 / 10
Considering this game is from 2005, graphics and art style are totally above average. Everything is very well made and polished, and if you crank up the resolution to maybe even 4K with some graphics driver tinkering, you will be amazed by the results this game still gives out.
SOUND - 9.0 / 10
All the effects are very similar or the same of the Star Wars movies, also the soundtrack and the spoken voice of the alien species you encounter, it is all faithful to the original series. Very high quality in this part, really helps with immersion during gameplay.
GAMEPLAY - 10 / 10
A master-crafted roleplaying experience. Deep combat system, meaningful and astonishingly articulated dialogue trees, myriads of interactions with NPCs and choices to be made. Tons of things to do, varied gameplay that never gets tedious or repetitive, but instead always proposes new things to the player and keeps him/her involved. Exceptional.
CHALLENGE - 8.0 / 10
On maximum difficulty, this game will give even to a seasoned role-playing enthusiast a good challenge. With endless party build possibilities and very varied enemies, you will never have to be too sure of your party's strenght, because around the corner there is always a greater challenge.
===
- Exceptional role-playing experience. As i said before, dialoges are stunningly articulate and will vary in major ways based upon your choices, alignment and several other factors. Choices you make will drastically change what happens to you, the world and your companions, granting top level replayability.
- Exceptional combat system, i mean really, really good. Advanced saving mechanics, opposite attribute test mechanics, tons of different Roll types, all made exquisitely well and in real-time with dynamic pause system.
- Absurd quantity of loot variety. There are literally 30-40 weapons per category, so that amount for melee weapons, blasters, rifles, modules, and so on. You will always find new stuff.
- Quality crafting system. You will be able to craft upgrades, hacking devices, weapons from scratch, armor plates, and much more stuff with a crafting system influenced by attributes and skills, that will unlock new stuff progressively as your skill in a certain field rises. And there are many fields of expertise.
- Meaningful and well-done Karma system, your choices will not only modify your alignment and your relationship with your companions, but also will influence combat, as you tend more towards the Dark or Light sideof the Force, or maybe neither of those, you will be granted unique abilities, bonuses and also maluses based on your actions.
- Deep companions backstory, personality, variety, optional missions to gain their trust, aligments. all this flawlessly done. Nothing is what it seems as your companions may lie, may change during your jurney, based not only upon your choices but also bu the itneractions between them. Exquisite.
- Tons upon tons of quests, if we count the bonus ones, the hidden ones, the secondary ones and the main quest, well let me tell you, there is a lot to do. Really a lot.
- You will feel how the force changes your character. I mean, no spoilers obviously, if you choose the Dark Side you will be a very powerful Sith and then do more damage and be more powerful in battle... but what have you sacrificed to get that power? Instead if you stand in the middle ground and be Neutral or Light side maybe you won't have the raw power the Dark Side grants its disciples, but will have to resort to different means, maybe unaccessible to the Sith ways, to solve problems.
- The story, main story i mean, is quite good. Varied, many possibilities, you won't expect what's coming, mystery, drama, all there. Not absurdly exceptional, but it does the job and maybe something more. Above average for sure.
===
- Alright, in late, late game, Force Power built character, so a character that solely relies on Force Powers, is quite overpowered even at highest difficulty. If you are not careful you will die, i dont' mean steamrolling anything in your path, but some powers and some item combinations can make you and your party pretty powerful. Then again, you are supposed to be like that by being a master of the Force so it could be intended as part of the lore, but still for balance reasons i had to put this in the bad category. Not major flaw and no big deal.
- Sometimes you will be forced to use certain character against your own will, this is quite bad because the game will not ever tell you, and you can find yourself with a completely unequipped character because you have all the good stuff on the main ones. This can lead to MAJOR frustration in some missions, and leads to the player having to reload a previous game, equip the guy good and then go with it. You can always give good stuff to all your companions, sure, but it will cost you!
- There is a certain mission, involving a factory and that is all i will say, that is absurdly difficult and unbalanced. Now i am all for challenge, but this particular mission WILL force you to use only one party member, and you will not be able to leave the area until mission complete, against very powerful enemies in huge quantities. Very unbalanced honestly, but is possible. Will make you very angry believe me.
- There is a bug that happens in the first stages of the game at random. It causes your character to freeze after a fight, so you have to save, reload and then will be fixed. This is random and if it happens you stick with it for a good part of the first 2 areas of the game, but then it just disappears.

I both ENJOYED and HATED this game. The story mode is easy to complete, but its philosophical observations are both sophomoric and (to a potential audience of millennials who consider themselves [prematurely] jaded) quite hurtful and/or resonant, depending on that audience's level of inebriation when encountering said remarks.
The puzzles in Story Mode are fun, but easy to solve. The puzzles in Void Mode (which is unlocked after completion of the default difficulty) are fractionally, not geometrically, more difficult. The trouble comes when convenient checkpoints are removed! In order to circumvent this conceit, I was forced to leave the game paused while I did things like work, sleep, and attend birthday parties. So, I guess the checkpoints aren't gone, they're just removed to another layer of abstraction. (This is why my play time on this game is so high: not because I sat brooding over puzzles and trying experiments, but because I left it on hiatus while I slept!)
Yes, a few of the puzzles enraged me… but it wasn't because they were especially devious; rather, it was because they depended on pinpoint accuracy and a twitchy level of timing that I find hard to replicate from my younger days. If there's one thing I hate most about ANY game, it's being made to do a thing OVER AND OVER again even when I know the proper solution.
(This is a sidebar: it seems like the puzzle designers rolled dice or drew lots to find out which one of them would make the puzzle for a particular screen. Some were created by Satan, others were made by neophytes or interns, with no regard for easier puzzles coming [or teaching you a needed skill] before the ones that drove you to madness. Some screens that took me hours to complete—either for difficulty's sake, or because I didn't have the requisite hand-eye coordination—were followed by three or four screens of puzzles so easy my niece could complete them.)
Overall, the game is quick and simple—if you don't care about the harder puzzles or achievements. If you stick around for Void Mode, be prepared to walk away for a few minutes (or hours) on tough puzzles.

Medal of Honor (2010) actually wasn't as bad as the reviews for it were. I remember the largest criticism being in the choice to be able to play as the Taliban in the multiplayer. I didn't play the multiplayer, so that hasn't hindered my review of this game.
In this reboot of the classic WWII series, the game is set in Afghanistan in very late 2001 and March 2002; being loosely based on Operation Anaconda, more specifically, the Battle of Shah-i-Kot and Battle of Takur Ghar. Takur Ghar is a mountain in the Shah-i-Kot Valley in Southeast Afghanistan where, at the time, Taliban and Chechan forces had dug themselves in with well over 500 forces encamped throughout the region.
The game's plot revolves around a number of soldiers from the Navy SEALs and various regiments from the US Army, such as the US Rangers and the Aviation Regiment. While a number of the characters don't actually meet, they help each other out at certain points during the game, like at one point, the Rangers are pinned down and the Aviation forces swing in to help them out. Then you take over as the Aviation team to sweep the area. The story is rather simple, sweep the area of enemy forces and, at times, the Navy SEALs are actually gathering intelligence, scouting forces ahead for the Army. Not an amazing story, but the amount of research the team put forward when it came to the accuracy of how many casualties were actually lost on the US side during the battles and the specific locations and tracking the troops movement from real life to fiction was neat. Basically, I applaud the effort with the research even if the story is dry.
Technical side, the games graphics are nice, but the AI on your side can get stuck at points and you might have to reload to a prior checkpoint, or worse, restart the whole level, that happened once. Some of the shadows bug out, but it wasn't that noticeable. Sound design is nice. Orchestra score is good, my only complaint that actually annoyed me was the soundtrack with like, Linkin Park. I hate Linkin Park. Seriously.
My only other serious complaint is that at some points of the game, apparently every muslim is an enemy and end up being killed by the US Army. Sure enough, in the game, everone you encounter is an enemy except from the first mission where you drive through a town and see some people, like the guy herding his goats across the street. It was a pretty big village and maybe I half expected to see a woman or child out in the streets, but there weren't any, so it became apparent that everyone you'd encountered at that point would become your enemy, which was very much the case. There wasn't any perspective as to who the civilians were or could be. And even the Northern Alliance, the Afghan army that the US had allied with, barely make an appearance. Instead, they're friendly fired upon by an angry guy in Langley. That was just like a WTF moment. I know some of that happened in real life, but it seemed a bit overkill here.
Still, a few minor complaints from an overall good FPS.

Overall, I highly recommend this game if you like RTS games.

If you're a fan of the franchise or any slasher flick, this game really nails the mood and tone of Friday the 13th ! The graphics, the settings, locations, the score and atmosphere is there. You can see that the devs love the movies and made every effort to finally deliver to the fans a game that is a great tribute to it !
PLUS you get to play Jason and slaughter all those terrified counselors !!
Sure there are some bugs to be fixed as the game has just been launched, but I did not find any that were game-breaking and played a few hours since the launching. This a small and dedicated team and I am sure that they are doing their best to fix all those issues as fast as possible.
Regarding the gameplay :
- As Jason: Your goal is obviously to kill every counselor (or as many as possible) before they manage to escape the summer camp. Since you're the overpowered monster slasher simpleton that we all know and love, you have several skills (other than your main weapon and bare hands) with cooldowns to help you achieve this massacre : You can sense the fear of the counselors to locate them while they're trying to run away or hide. You can teleport on the map as every damned slasher killer seems to do in this movie genre and you can stalk players to slay them by surprise, throw knives, setup traps... Of course, you can grab them by the neck, lift them and use context kills (burn them in the fire hearth, stick them to trees, throw them by the window, smash heir head with a door...etc) plus choose between several special fatalities like crushing their heads, their eyes, decapitate, choke, breaking spine...etc. Awesomeness. But despite all this, you will sometimes have a hard time hunting and killing all your preys.
- As counselor: You have to escape the camp and to do that you can fix cars or boats and drive away, call the cops and run to them when they get there. To escape Jason, you can find and use various weapons (baseball bat, machete, shotgun, small knife to stab Jason and be freed from his grip...). You can hide under beds, inside closets, block doors, set traps... It can be very challenging to survive, as it should be !
Each counselor and each Jason version provides differents pros and cons. As you get XP, you can unlock characters, perks (counselors), kills (jason).
As I said, try it, especially if you're a fan of Friday the 13th and the man behind the mask !

and is the second best Survival Horror game I have ever played.
To me it contains the best story of all videogames I know of.
The heart of this game (as stated) is it's fantastic story which I absolutely love. The core of it and the way in which it is told are fascinating. I recommend playing this game at least once just for the story. To me it was absolutely worth its money and if you are into deep psychological stories this game is a MUST HAVE.
Puzzle mechanics are very fun to solve and feel reasonable and fitting for this games universe.
There are some parts that make no sense or are ultimately pointless and felt like plot holes but as a whole it was very enjoyable if you can forgive some minor futile mistakes.
The reason this game does not score a 10/10 and therefore beeing the best Survival Horror game (to me) is due to it's very lazy gameplay mechanics. Compared to "Amnesia: The Dark Descent" (a game also made by Frictional Games) it was a very big step back considering gameplay. Discovering areas is without reward and hiding mechanics are basically pointless for the first 4 hours. The entire stealth mechanic consists of you crouching behind boxes in dark areas. The "pick something up and throw it somewhere to create distraction" idea is not working at all and therefore pointless and misguiding. Hiding in lockers or boxes (which would seem reasonable) is not implemented at all (unlike in Amnesia) so it comes down to just hiding in the dark behind stuff. That's not much and the stealth sections are a little boring due to that lack of options.
Sound design + music + voice acting are fantastic and to me easily one of the very best you can find in any videogame.
Graphics are good, nothing extremely special but they look fine and capture the dark atmosphere of this game.
Your first playthrough will take you roughly from 6 to 10 hours so it falls a little short in my opinion.

The issue is that the puzzles are poorly written.
Look, I enjoy difficult puzzles, I enjoy brain teasers and struggling to come up with answers. There is, however, a difference between that and puzzles that explain themselves so poorly that either you immediately get them because they're obvious or can't get them at all because they make no sense. One run (on episode 1) I blasted through the whole thing with no problem. Another run I couldn't get past the first room because the riddles were horribly constructed.
The issue with puzzle games is they're held hostage to the logic of the people who write the riddles, and the devs here, although having good ambition, are simply not good at making riddles. In the first room there are a dozen or so 4-letter puzzles that are randomly selected. Some are very easy, some make no sense at all. If you get the simple ones, you'll feel clever and think this game is great. If you get the bad ones, you'll be stuck forever and not progress.
I like spooky games with more than just key hunting and jump scares. What the devs here need to understand is just because they spent every day for months looking at these puzzles doesn't mean they'll make even the faintest of sense to someone coming in new. Cannot recommend. Far too headache inducing.

Nether had one job: to make a survival game that wasn't as bad as The WarZ, both in terms of gameplay and business practices. Sounds easy, all one had to do was not release a game long before it was finished and stay out of stuff such as microtransactions to unlock exclusive content for a paid game. Unfortunately, Nether failed in both aspects, and in my two minutes of actually playing the game (the rest were trying to get the game to run in the first place), I regret spending $3 USD for this garbage.
Nether had a lot of promise, a load of ideas that sounded like a solid plan, such as quest moments to really get players to aggro to one area and make things more exciting, and enemies apart from zombies. But none of these ideas come to light, thanks to being greeted by microtransactions from the get-go, cosmetic or otherwise, game breaking bugs like being stuck in a spectator mode which isn't even part of the game, the random moments where you're not capable of swimming despite it supposedly being possible (and roughly 50% of the game world is covered in deep water with no bridges), and moments where characters spontaneously die.
I have no idea what game the official reviews were playing, but if it was Nether, then I'm going to hazard a guess and assume they were paid for those results. Heck, one review even opens up how great Phosphor Games is.
Nether has one thing going for it, and that's much nicer visuals than either DayZ or The WarZ, but that's as far as it goes. All in all, the game is basically a spiritual sequel to The WarZ, and it's made readily apparent from the moment you launch the game. Save your three bucks and buy yourself something better, like cheap coffee.

I HAVE completed all rooms available at the current time, so if this is read after the 30th, some things I say here may not be true or may not apply.
- - -
This is a very well put together game, the story is intriguing, the graphics are beautiful, and there are very few glitches and bugs that I have run into so far.
First up, the puzzles. The puzzles in this game are very challenging, and are well put together, some of them, however, admittedly do need some work. *cough * the bunker *cough * They are not too easy to figure out, and not too challenging that they are unsolvable within the time frame. One thing I would say is a complaint of mine are the ranges of difficulties in the puzzles, as in, one room you enter may have a super difficult puzzle, while the next one is a breeze, so I would suggest somehow structuring them from easies to hardest when running through.
Next, the story. The story of this game can be put together through notes that your grandfather leaves you, and in one case, a tape recording, but it does require some reading, so be prepared for that rather than cut scenes or other methods of delivery. The story itself is interesting, but not too complicated, and not too bland.
Next up, the Music. There is not much to say about the music in this game, the music they use fits the game very well, but I wouldn't call it anything special. (sorry)
And Finally, the bugs/glitches. As I said earlier, I have been playing this game with my buddy, and we have come across a few bugs in this mode. The ones we did come across were not game breaking, however. I wouldn't exactly call this one a bug, but more of an unintended feature, we found that you can prop surf if you can find the right props, like the chairs in the main entryway of the mansion.  A REAL bug we found is that you can duplicate items by picking them up simultaneously, not game breaking, but annoying when you accidentally click an item at the same time and then have to carry it around for the rest of your play through. There was also an instance (I'm not sure how this happened) where we were able to open a door that lad locked behind us, and when we walked through it, we fell out of the map, but it does teleport you back into the Map once you fall far enough, so good on the devs, I guess.
Overall this is a very fun game, it is well put together, and though it does have some bugs, I very much look forward to playing the next two acts. Thanks for reading :).

In SOMA you play as Simon who wakes up in a strange facility with no idea how he got there. So we have an amnesiac protagonist. Strange place turns out to be an underwater facility. You follow audio logs and radio chatter. There are big monsters around. The beginning is so Bioshock that it makes Bioshock itself feel like a fresh take. It borrows a lot from other sources aswell.
This feeling of familiarity keeps SOMA from being actually that scary. It's like you don't know what is going to happen but you can kind of guess. For example you see an unusually long hallway and you don't know for sure but somehow you feel that "At some point something is going to chase me through this". Then when it actually happens it doesn't feel so terrifying.
Make no mistake SOMA is really atmospheric and at times it makes you jump but i would not call it that frightening. There are monsters around and you have no means to fight them but avoiding them takes suprisingly little of the playing time. Most is spent just walking around, looking, listening and examining objects. The world is built with much care and love: There are so many storage rooms with so many little items littered around. Lot of papers that can be read but have little to no relevance. Photos to look at. Pathos II really looks like a lived in place. It's rare to see such a well made setting.
The familiarity and just walking around was just perfect for me. It made it easier to keep going. It made me want to see what was behind the next door. It made me want to continue the story. A game does not need shooting and action to be exellent and SOMA understands this well. The plot does get interesting and unfamiliar after a while and it does have some deep thoughts in it, but what mostly kept me motivated was the main characters. At times i did feel that the plot would have played differently had the main character been able to do some simple things that everyone should be able to, but i'm not going to spoil what. Even with that said, i very much enjoyed my time. First playthrough took about 8½ hours. Last session was about 4 hours which just says that i really did not want to stop playing.
SOMA is a gorgeous looking game. Just wonderful in every aspect. It is quite heavy on the blurring, depth of field, chromatic abberration, static and all sorts of effects to obstruct the view which might be a bit too much for some players. Personally i loved the look and it was not that taxing on the system. Sound desing is also great and music is lovely.
I did notice some techical issues. Loading times are bit on the long end of the spectrum even with the game installed on SSD. Even after the loading screen is gone, the game hitches for a while before it suddenly turns smooth. In a slow paced game this is not an issue. It also crashed two times with different error messages. Both times suddenly with no heads up. The game autosaves often so it was also not a big deal.
SOMA is not perfect. It has a bit too many familiar elements and some technical stuff but it's still great. Recommended!

Pros:
- Amazingly in depth simulation, from N-body orbital mechanics.
- Incredible time designing a module and then testing to see if it does what you want it to do in your overarching battle doctrine.
- Realistic environment leads to knowledge which may, in fact, be applicable to the real world. I advise militaries, should they be engaged in space combat, to attempt the reverse orbital direction and slam into the enemy retrograde maneuver (burn out to increase your apogee until you get an eliptical orbit, then at apogee reverse direction for minimal delta-v expense and let your spacecraft fall down in a retrograde orbit right at the enemy's, and release missiles, if both combatants are in orbit).
- AI vs AI simulations allow for quick and easy testing of the effectiveness of various designs.
- New game, much potential to improve and expand.
- Destroying things with the power of SCIENCE! Well, admittedly, mostly tinkering, but SCIENCE!
- High moddability.
Cons:
-Controls can be clunky and can be strongly improved.
-Module/Ship no-delete relations are also clunky and can be strongly improved.
-Missile targetting in the strategic map is very clunky and desperately needs a fire and forget lock on mode.
-Multiple physics errors - none absolutely crippling, but all in need of fixing. Errors include:
1. Obscene rail/coilgun efficiencies in excess of 100%. Not actually crippling the integrity of the simulation because: Despite this, they are still second-rate weapons compared to the glory that is missilespam and laser lase.
2. Laser damage model is unrealistic and makes lasers considerably weaker than they should be. Not a massive issue because: Despite this, lasers are still an incredibly dominant weapon.
3. I am not sure, but I believe the resistojet thrust power exceeding input power should not be possible, since that too implies more energy out than in. Also, being able to pump gigawatts through 10cm MPDs seems a bit fishy.
4. Pocket implosion nukes are a tad suspect, but we do have incredibly small suitcase nukes IRL so maybe not.
-Campaign is an excuse to have people fighting in space. If you actually care about having a very in depth storyline, or worse yet, if you care about being a heroic good guy, wait a year or two and then get community campaign mods. Personally, I find the story interesting and immersive, but some will strongly dislike it.
-Targetting and AI can be improved. Maybe let the players build their own AI and targetting rules?
Requests - All of these are if possible:
- Lock on and forget strategic targetting please. Not just for missiles - allowing capship fleets to do that to enemy capship fleets would be nice too.
-QSwitching/Pulsing for lasers, along with less arbitrary laser ranges.
-Solar system-wide open sandbox world map. Something like KSP's system wide map.
-4x style cycling between units/fleets which do not have any orders or whose orders have been interrupted beyond the AI's ability to fix, along with a "needs commanding" box. Mostly if the second item is implemented, allowing for grand strategy on a solar system scale to happen.
-User-programmable AI. Call it battle/fleet doctrine.
-Player-programmable targetting rules for guns.
-Calculation slowdown without framerate slowdown, sorta like Eve's slow down server in gigantic battle system, so to make for a better lag experience and to allow for nice video recordings.
-Built in video replay system. The calculations are already done - save the results and allow a replay to replay the battle in a smoother fashion, if at all possible.

I *love* so-called "walking simulators". I like story-driven, artsy, pretentious games because I think they're interesting. Dear Esther, Gone Home, and Kentucky Route Zero are among my favorite games, so when I heard about 4PM I had high hopes. Unfortunately, 4PM just doesn't deliver. I play story-driven games to be told a good *story*, and 4PM's is just... bad. It stars an incredibly unlikeable, unrelatable (at least for me) protagonist. The whole 20-minute experience exists to deliver the twist at the end, which ends up not being particularly exciting. There are a few parts where you can make choices, but they end up not mattering at all. If you choose wrong you essentially get a game over and can start again at the decision. The whole story is cliche.
I wasn't sure whether the negativity around this game was just people hating on walking simulators (user reviews for Gone Home are bad too, but I loved that game) - but no, even if you like artsy story-driven games, this game really is just that bad. Don't buy it.

The short version: 7.5/10. A worthy successor to the first KotOR, but could be better. Cons first: Influence system is a tug-of-war; lightsabers aren't future-proof, necessitates constant upgrades; and clarity of objective is murky at points. Pros: Lightsabers more modular, game responds even more deeply to how you play, and how you played KotOR 1.
Long version:
I'm not done with this game yet. Not by a long shot. I play offline, which doesn't allow Steam to really count the actual amount of time I've spent on it, so I'll go ahead and say I've spent at least 24-36 hours on one playthrough so far, and that was mostly getting off the first couple of scenarios, which you're basically railroaded into/through. Sometimes your objectives and how to achieve them is a little opaque, so it took me a while to even get through the first act. Plus, now that I'm given a choice, I'm not really doing things in the optimal order.
Took a long time to get my lightsaber. Once I did, though, hoooo boy, I was stoked -- oh, I need what skills to build something to actually make my 'saber effective? Aw, phooey. Good thing I'm speccing Sentinel. I have ALL THE SKILLS! Bring it -- wait, huh, you can't future-proof your 'saber, either? Geeeeez, this deal's getting worse all the time! At least you're close-to-literally drowning in the parts to make the upgrades. I do like the added modular elements to the lightsaber customisation, though. Since inventory space is basically unlimited, you can hoard ALL THE LIGHTSABER PARTS.
The influence system makes me want to drink until I can't feel my mouse. You will not be best pals with everyone in any one playthrough like you could in the last game, unless you cheat. That's just how it is. Wanna play light-side? Oh look, this guy likes it, but your other buddy ain't happy with you. Stand with a rebellion? Now Thing 1 hates your face and you've gained brownie points with Thing 2.
Like KotOR 1, there's an optimal character build for this game, but I'm playing (nominally, anyhow) for fun. This will make my inevitable fight with the final boss probably very difficult to impossible. Still, though, I'm a Star Wars fan to the bone, and I do enjoy the chance to paddle about again in the Old Republic setting (it's one of my faves, dating back to the Tales of the Jedi comics half my lifetime ago).

Great mechanics and strategy, ruined by terrible AI, cumbersome control, and campaign of Darkness Induced Audience Apathy.
Short review:

Control is cumbersome and fairly inaccurate
Missile AI is terrible. It's probably better to just ignore missiles at all.

Campaign should really be rated R18 or something
Longer:
I am not deep into this game yet but I like the feel and the novel strategies involved in space battles. I hope there is better AI for missiles so they don't just run out of dV in the face of the enemy. Come on, it's a nuke! Running out of dV straight into the enemy doesn't stop it from exploding and doing at least some damage!
Then the campaign. More tutorial is better, but that is not my main point here. I feel like being foced to identify with the Nazi. Yes, I think RFP is that terrible. I expected a twist in plot when I saw the Captain R(something) in a pop up tells me not to fight for the RFP. Repeat, I really expected a twist of plot, maybe discovering a dark plan of the RFP, and rebel against this overly agressive faction, or some event like that.
I haven't finished the campaign yet, but I watched Youtube playthrough of it, mainly to check out the suspicious plot. I first wished for a twist, then... I wished that at least other factions are equally evil. Then, I wished that at least it's just like a war to claim land and resources(people do this today, right?).
And then the ending tells me the High Command is going to nuke everyone to the bedrock.
Now I think "screw the campaign, I am going to download a save and skip it, and start designing my own ship".
It is very offensive and outrageous to actually go through a campaign like this. Moreover, ship design and module design are locked unless I actually play the campaign. The developers may be real physicists, but I would say terrible writers. A good plot really lets a game shine, a dumb plot is fine when there is amazing game mechanics, but a bad plot destroys a lot of experience.
In final words: I would probably not play this game unless there is a sequel to the campaign which reverses the current situation.

I am doing now Retaking Ceres mission now and I am disappointed. So much potential wasted because of  clunky controls!
What is good: realistic space combat. For that experience I bought that game.
What is bad: as I’ve said: those controls!
Manipulating those velocity sliders I feel like a monkey. Finding passable trajectory is almost a matter of luck.
In my opinion more information about orbits is needed. Trying to match enemy orbital inclination by eye and by moving this damn blue slider is hard. Flyby and Intercept icons are inaccurate and force me to spend too much delta-V at the last moment.
Ship management is frustrating. Especially tedious are missiles and drones: click the launch button, press Back to return to main map, choose your fleet again, again chose appropriate ship, click the launch button, rinse and repeat several times. And then I press something by mistake and must repeat whole scenario from beginning.
Save Game is feature I miss the most here. If I had known that there is no Save Game in the Campaign I would not have bought it.
Better tutorial would also be useful.
Short version: I am having a lot of fun but it is mixed with strong frustration. Improve those controls and I will wholeheartedly recommend it.

Trials of the Blood Dragon has a lot in common with its infamous E3 presentation; a great, bold, different idea on paper that turned out terrible in execution.
I came into this game expecting very polished level design as seen in the previous Trials games. Trials HD and Trials Evolution both had a great difficulty curve, tons of customization, and different bikes for you to choose from. This game offers none of that. You are set in a 27 mission single player experience. No different bikes. No customization. No user created content. No multiplayer. For the same price point as Trials Evolution, this game is an absolute joke when it comes to content. I was able to complete the *entirety* of the game in under 2 hours.
Plot:
The idea of an actual intertwined story that links the missions together, rather than levels being discrete and separated from one another is a great idea. I don't know if I really needed a story within a Trials campaign, but the idea is great. However the execution on this story was awful. The plot is neither funny nor interesting like that of Far Cry: Blood Dragon. The two main characters have very stilted dialogue and poor voice acting.
Mechanics:
There are three new mechanics added to this game over previous entries in the Trials series. Enemies and weapons, a grappling hook, and... on foot platforming.
The ability to use an smg on your bike is by far the best mechanic added. In order to complete races as quickly as possible, the smg allows you clear a path by shooting enemies, or by shooting switches in order to open doors. This provides a more flexible level design, and seems like a very smooth addition. The grappling hook functions in the same way as the gun, but you use it to reach certain vertical areas. I feel like this addition to the game was not as well executed as the machine gun's, as it removes any and all challenging platforming sections that were available in previous games.
Finally... on foot sections. God... What do I even say. This was an absolute mistake to add to the game. Clunky, slow, repetitive platforming that is not satisfying and NOT what I would want out of either a Trials game or a Far Cry game. One weapon. One enemy type. Not enjoyable in the slightest.
Final Verdict:
In theory, a cross between Far Cry Blood Dragon and the Trials series sounds like a wonderous time. Gun toting, action packed biking. Instead, we get an incredibly short, repetitive, unchallenging, and not too fun game that's mediocre at best.

Nihilumbra is, as others have quite rightly pointed out, a masterpiece.  Although I only just bought the game on Steam, I've already played the iOS version, and it's one of the few games on iOS that I actually respect.  It was for this reason that I wanted to play it on PC, and from what I've played it's the same wonderful game I remember.  In fact, it's one of my favourite games of all time.  Very rarely does a game have a story that stirs the sort of emotions in me that Nihilumbra does.  While playing, Nihilumbra distinguishes itself from many other games by making one truly care about the protagonist Born, a being born from The Void.  A voice narrates Born's journey and his thoughts, making the player feel a connection to Born.  Over the course of the game, Born learns about the world and uses its power over colours to change it, all the while fleeing from The Void.  For my part I was invested every step of the way.
In short, Nihilumbra is a unique and moving experience that you need to play at least once before you're taken by The Void.

I wish I could have played this great game earlier... but of course, Stardock insists on not giving demos, and they always overprice their games, along with milking customers for years and years before any semblance of a finished product is available.  And I'm not even sure they'll ever finish any of their current games.  They just may keep adding on to them for perpetuity.  But for whatever reason, when this game became available for 50% off, I decided it was worth a try.
I only have started to play, but I'm not disappointed so far.  Having played Sid Meier's Railroads, this game has similar elements, but is more cut-throat (maybe too brutal for me while learning, so I'm going to try disabling the black market).  People have complained about the overabundance of options - and that is true, but it just shows that this is a gamer's game, with geeks blathering on and on incessantly about the nuances of so many strategic elements.  It's fine with me!  I would rather a game was never fully comprehensible, than that it was too simple.
There is a huge amount of guesswork in this game in that you try to predict which resources will become scarce and which ones will be overproduced, and building up for harvesting the former while just buying out the latter when needed.
The games seem to play relatively quickly - maybe under 3 hours or so.
Is the game worth the full price?  Only if you are a die-hard economic sim fan, or money is no object.  I feel satisfied paying 50% off - I got something close to a "finished-level" game, and the price was about average.  I bought the "Gold" bundle that came with the Jupiter and other DLCs.  I'm not sure I'll ever find time to play all the expansions, but they are nice to have available.
The learning curve is much higher than the simple appearance implies.  There are some very complex interelationships to build up, and timing vulnerabilities those relationships hinge on.  You can't see what stockpiles your opponents might have up their sleeve, waiting for the opportune moment to buy you out.

The game is written in the Unity3D engine, which means the graphics tend to lag a little.  Some people have complained about this, but for an economic sim, I could not care less if I lose some frames now and then.  This is not a shooter - it's more like a clicker.  Frame rate doesn't affect gameplay hardly at all, and I haven't noticed any issues yet with a minimal level laptop, so I think it's a nonissue.  Still if you're very picky you might want to consider that.
In-game voice acting is good.  Prose tone is semi-humorous (some references to slave-driving in the real world that hits a bit too close to home to be "haha" funny).  The core humor of Offworld is watching helplessly as your company slowly melts down!  The artwork is light-hearted, cartoony and trace amounts of psycho: B+ - for an eco-sim the artwork adds good flavor.  The marketting video voice acting doesn't match the lightness of the cartoony artwork - it's a bit nonsequetor.
I have not found ANY part of this game (in the current state) that feels like they are still holding some major component back for a future DLC.  Of all the turn-offs of Stardock, that has been my biggest gripe, and it's a welcome change not to feel like I paid for a feature-lacking-but-already-planned-for-future-customer-milking-DLC version of the game.  However, if I'd bought it when it first came out - that would certainly have been the case, so I think I timed it okay.  The only risk I can think of here is if they create some new version that becomes a defacto standard, the mod community will split up.
The modding for this game looks delicious!  I'm not sure though whether a full re-skin is possible.

You wake up inside the Brennenburg castle, unable to remember anything other than your name, and that you must kill Alexander of Brennenburg. This "man" has done unspeakably horrible things to innocents. It is this hatred and lust for revenge that will drive you, Daniel, to descend into the darketst pits of Alexander´s castle and eventually, your own mind.
Alexander´s "pets" roam the halls of Brennenburg and are up to kill you at any instance. You cannot fight back. Your only chance of survival is to run and hide. There is also the mysterious Shadow hunting you down, a supernatural being that wants an object you posses...
Amnesia is my favourite horror game of all time, and one of my favourite games of all time. You have probably heard of this masterpiece, especially if you used YouTube at the start of the 2010´s. I remember watching the walkthroughs and custom stories from many great YouTubers, such as PewDiePie, Markiplier, Lakko. I fell in love with the game, and this Winter Sale I decided to finally buy it for my own.
I have not played that many horror games in my life, but holy♥♥♥♥♥♥is this scary. The astmosphere is crushing. As mentioned before, you cannot fight back the monsters. You can only flee and/or hide. When you hear that grunt and the terrifying music start, you KNOW that your life is in danger. This game gave me possibly the most powerful experience a game has ever: I entered
The Insanity system makes the game all around more terrifying: enemies can´t find you as EASILY in the dark, but if you stay in the darkness too long, you will start to lose sanity and the enemies will easily find you. Lightsources, especially the lantern, help you retain sanity, but you don´t need to be smart to realise that THEY can see light.
So, this game will make you crawl through numerous horrifying sights, sounds and feels. It is a constant terror that you might hear the monstrous growl of a Gatherer and be forced to make decisions in a split second. It is a game that will keep you at the edge of your seat through the whole play. And if you do manage to finish the main story, you can download custom stories made by the community to face even more terror.
10/10, most terrifying game ever made, and it´s legacy is continuing even till today.

I will give the developer credit where it is due; 4PM’s store page bills itself as a mature and unique, albeit short narrative promising an emotional ride on the subjects of alcoholism and suicide. Along with the trailer and screenshots, (that admittedly look pretty good), and a low, low price point, it seems a promising option among the rest of the junk that regularly pops up on steam. And that is where I must give the developer his due; he’s made a really good sell. And that’s the best I can say, because the game itself is a laughable experience, and for literally every wrong reason there could be.
First, the entire game is put through a ridiculously prominent fuzz filter, one that is evidently absent from the store’s trailer and screenshots, likely to better entice you into wasting your money. The filter itself is used to try and mask the horrid graphics underneath, but it doesn’t succeed. It loads slowly for no apparent reason, breaking up the many short mid-scene jumps with even longer loading freezes. Worse, the actual animations of the cast, particularly their faces, makes any attempt at creating an emotional resonance with the player fail miserably. Instead, the poor acting and bug eyed reactions will likely give
the same reaction as I had: loudly laughing your head off at the sheer stupidity at every attempt at “drama”.
And what little attempt at a story there is, happens almost entirely at the end. “The big reveal” that occurs near the end of every good drama is shoehorned in with only a couple minutes of♥♥♥♥♥♥poor dialogue, with virtually no real exposition or story prior. The absolute pretentiousness of it all is positively palpable throughout.
Despite how utterly trash this game is, I recommend it to a specific brand of person. Anyone who enjoyed the previous King to the Pretentious Kingdom,
, is in for a real treat. Where I found DD to be comparably boring, 4PM offers several moments of gut wrenching hilarity, particularly during mid-game, where gears shift from pretentious slop to
. The entire thing lasts little more than around 25 minutes, and most of that time will be occupied wondering if something is ever going to happen. When something finally does, the credits come not 2 minutes later, and you’ll be left wondering how a single developer could create such an experience, let alone reach his keyboard, with his head so far up his own log cutter.

First of all - I want to thank the dev team for their incredible dedication and open communication with customers. They could have been like No Man's Sky or ME:A, or hell, even Dead by Daylight with their poop and botting. These companies all jumped ship soon after launch. Instead, Gun Media have been very open to questions and help for the many months their game has been in the public light. They did a TESTING beta, not a marketing beta (like so many companies do.. *cough* For Honor), to work on making the game as fun and stable for us as possible.
All that said, I have really loved the game, both in beta and now. Like several other streamers, I played the game a day early,  and it ran well. There were less people playing, so quickplay and the servers were fine. The big problem now that it is actually out is that SO many people are so hyped for the game that the servers can't handle (and neither even could a big company like Microsoft, as seen by the Xbox store crapping out on launch). To my knowledge, they are upgrading the servers and adapting as fast as possible to the incredible amount of people that are trying to get on. Our love was too girthy. :P
From someone who has got games in, I love it and would recommend the game, if you like survival type games. It is more detailed, has more items, and requires more out of you than a game like DbD. I had an incredible time with it in the beta, and have loved it now (quickplay problems aside). Wait though for a day or two so you don't experience server frustration, and if you have it, just be patient with them. They've worked harder on fixing everything than any dev team I've seen.
TLDR: LOVE the gameplay, just be patient for a day or two to work out release-day server problems.

After being lured in by the letters TCG, I enjoyed it for a while, but there are too many glaring faults with it that I feel the game is too far beyond being fixable.
First, I'll talk about the TCG part of what is wrong with this game.  For those who do not know, TCG stands for Trading Card Game.  The cards are untradable and the game part is pick and pray.  There is no true strategy in the game, it's mostly choose six cards and hope for the best.  The campaign feels more like a puzzle game, trying to figure out the best way to win, then 2 more objectives where you have to win under certain conditions, most of them being "shoot yourself in the foot" types like "This monster powers up when damaged, use 3 weak AoE characters to power him up, then survive for 40 seconds before you win."  Sounds easy, right?  But you have NO control in these battles, which is another issue.  If you could control your own team, you could hold back and then once 40 seconds was up, unleash all hell.  But as I said before, it's Pick and Pray.  You choose your team, then you watch as they fail monstrously.  In a normal match of trying to win, this sort of works... sort of... but in trying to devise a team build which can do some monumental task against all odds, you need some VERY specific cards.  So most of the objectives are undoable until you get 1-3 of these very specific cards to do it with.
The next issue I want to cover in depth is this pick and pray gameplay.  In the campaign, you can see your opponents deck and pick a team accordingly, but multiplayer you don't have such a luxury.  You have to design your team and then hope your opponent doesn't have some deck breaking card.  For example, you go with a team who focuses on magic damage, but then your opponent has cards that disable and/or destroy spell cards.  GG, you lose and not only do you see that instantly, but you have to watch and wait as you are crushed inevitably.  Any TCG I've played, there is a small amount of luck to it, but usually you can come up with more than one combination of cards or tactics, so even if your ace in the hole is destroyed, you can usually have some back up plan.  No such luck with this one, it's all or nothing because 2 strategies with 3 cards each just weakens your "deck" that much more instead of adding to it's diversity.  The real "strategy" of this game isn't trying to figure out a good tactic, it's how do you defeat said tactic.  Or just spend money to get 5 star cards which are usually pretty powerful.
Speaking of power, there is also a card "levelling" system, but for the cost of the levels and the bonuses they get, it seems pretty pointless unless you actually go from level 1 to level 50.  In most cases, a stat only goes up one point or so, which is a pretty small drop in the ocean.  In the long run, it's actually rather pointless as I saw no discernable difference in my battles with the few cards I upgraded.  The only point an upgrade had a statistical advantage was in a battle where I needed one card to tank an enemy with Threat targeting, so I gave one level to the tank card so it was one point stronger than the other.  That was the ONLY advantage I saw with levelling in the 20 hours I've played.
Now that my little rant about the problems with the game are out, I will share what I did enjoy from the game.  Mostly the fact that every card had a purpose.  Unlike most of the major TCG's who just make "filler" cards such as Uraby from Yugioh, every card in this game had some use to it and could be properly implemented into a deck.  And there are some good combinations and strategies you can go with, but the gameplay itself is so limiting that it makes them all pretty pointless.
I feel this game COULD be good if a few features were implemented, changed, or removed, such as Trading, more player control over battles (like after the CD completes, then you choose when to trigger the card), actual decks where you draw and play cards from (or a hand where you can hold 6 other cards, then withdraw a triggerable card and summon a new card which then has to charge it's CD as the "cost"), either better card levelling bonuses or scrap the levelling system completely (perhaps just do a branching skill tree for some cards, some that boost a stat or add an alternative ability at the cost of some strength?), making ALL RARITY CARDS available to players and find some other cash shop bonuses that would be worth going for, like new avatar images, or reskinned cards with a different Limited Edition image.  If people enjoy the game enough, they'll willingly spend money on trivial stuff like that.  Many games already do this, Loadout, Awesomenauts, Dream of Mirror Online, etc.
Also, couldn't hurt to add some bonus to the levels that makes it feel like you are accomplishing something with every level, add stats in for the player themselves that could affect things such as getting magnified bonuses (and penalties) for putting points into a faction loyalty for those who like a specific faction, or a luck stat that increases your rewards from farming, etc.  Then reskill books as a cash shop item, plus it would make the XP gains from VIP more worth spending money for.
I also won't get into too much detail about the drama I saw with the dev in the forums, but your attitude also needs a change.  You need to be the professional, even if others aren't.  I appreciated the fact that you palled around and were there to help many players with their problems, but you gotta change your attitude about accepting criticism.  Sometimes it's good, sometimes it's just straight up hurtful, but you gotta understand that some people out there will hate on your game.  Just accept it, either change what they attacked you for or stick to your guns, but don't single out or attack specific people for a bad review or comment, that will only lose you support, not gain it.
In the end, I want to see this game succeed, so I won't really abandon it.  If the devs truly want to improve the game, then I hope they will bounce around a few ideas with the community and see what sticks.  Some of mine might be good, or they might be bad, I know a lot of them are undoable due to hardware limitations of phones and such, but the game as it stands right now is far from being something PC users would expect to enjoy.  Perhaps instead of trying to do just a cross platform phone game, you might even just focus on a new, standalone, virtual TCG project that has everything and specifically cater it to the PC market.

Ultima Online, Shadowbane, Mount and Blade, and A Tale In The Desert had a baby, and this is it!
I bought for this mainly MMO access starting Nov 17th, 2017, and to use GM commands for testing builds/mechanics before hand.  (PM if you need a guild) ;)  Now for the review:
If you started playing MMO's when WoW came out, or post-WoW, there is a high chance you can't handle games like this.  No instant gratification, no hand holding, doing anything alone takes forever, doesn't have that tripple A polish, and it's a sandbox... meaning no quests and such.  You and the other players make up the content.
If you loved old school MMO's, pre-WoW, like Ultima Online, this may end up being the game you were looking for all these years. It's still glitchy, but it's getting there.
You really want to be part of a guild if you want to enjoy this game.  Everything takes a lot of time to do.  You do get faster at things when your skill gets higher... but multiple people working on the same goals/tasks makes the game more enjoyable.
Things are pretty indepth... for example:
Shadows from buildings effect crops that get hit by them,  the weather effects crops as well.  There are 66 herbalist ingredients, and their properties are unique to your character.   What does one thing for you, does something else for another player... meaning you have to discover  it on your own.  You can't just google their effects... but you can trade ones less valuable to you, to a player who finds them valuable to him.
Combat is similar to Mount and Blade but, atm, not nearly as polished yet.
You can terraform... even dig mines into the side of a hill.
Hopefully these dev's come out with a couple big patches, and this game could be one of the greats.

Offworld Trading Company is an (excellent!) boardgame in disguise.  Unfortunately, it's easy to mistake this for something that it's not.  It's not a relaxed city builder, it's not a realistic economic simulation, and it's definitely not a traditional RTS.  Instead, it plays like a euro-style boardgame on steroids. There's plenty of jostling possible via building placement, the black market, and commodity price manipulation, but it's still about building a stronger and more flexible money-making machine than your opponents.  Theme is more present than most eurogames, but the mechanics are clearly tuned for gameplay rather than realism.  My boardgaming buddies and I all gave Offworld Trading Company a pass when it originally came out, but after taking a closer look we're come around and are having a blast playing this in multiplayer.  Just know what you're getting into when you buy this game.

The singleplayer is linear, the gunplay is almost a run-and-gun despite having lean mechanics. There are quite a few breaks where the game gives you a minigame where you mark targets for a gunship to fire upon.
Gunplay:
Walking bloom is not very high and so the run-and-gun playstyle is a possibility. The game also lets you play safer with leaning if you'd prefer that instead. The ammo is infinite if you use the guns you start with on each mission, as you can just ask your teammate for a full set of ammo and you'll get it quickly. Recoil is almost nonexistent and bloom is mostly negligible for most weapons, especially if you can control your firing. Because of this, spraying-and-praying is also a possible play style. If you pick up an enemy weapon, you'll have to get your own ammo from other enemy guns.
Difficulty:
This game is pretty easy, even on the hardest difficulty. Because of the difficulty and the easy gunplay, I found myself dying simply because I was running and gunning like I was playing DOOM or Shadow Warrior; in other words, I got bored and found myself running far ahead of my team in more open areas to clear a room quickly. You can move and clear so quickly that you may find youself shooting enemies that haven't even settled down to shoot at you yet, or enemies that are still looking at your teammates while you kill him from behind. In short, it's pretty easy if you don't play like an idiot.
Graphics:
Very meh. Nothing particularly nasty, nothing noteworthy. There are enemy spawn-points in the game where enemeis come out of when you are fighting in the open. Some of these rooms do not render light by intention and are almost completely dark, which is inconsistent.
Conclusion:
The gunplay is nothing special and quite boring, and the difficulty is too low. Even though I spent less than a dollar on it (through a Humble Bundle) I would personally not buy this game, even on sale. There are some that would be entertained by it, though.

If you manage to get this game for very low price, it's worth trying out.
Well-optimised, not too hardware-demanding, runs on max settings without any hiccups, with good graphics.
The singleplayer is good:
I like the Afghanistan and military atmosphere. Audio is very good, graphics are beautiful and sharp. Character animations are somewhat good.
The story is short, characters are noticable but rather character-less (bearded guy with a cap).
There's no customisation, no ranks and no collectibles, in singleplayer. The cover system is working great.
But as said, it's good - I installed this game because I felt like playing a shooter, taking place in Afghanistan (or
something with lot of sand) and I got just what I needed.
The singleplayer deserves a 7/10 rank, not bad. Good atmosphere and fun combat.
The multiplayer is extremly mediocre. Very few players still play, but you find one-two full servers every now-and-then.
While singleplayer is running on beautiful and polished Unreal Engine, the multiplayer is powered by a watered-down Frostbite engine. They removed cover mechanics, character animations suck, detection of hits is pretty damn bad, maps are too small and most of killing is ruthless spawntrapping. Movement is extremly sloppy and bulky, there are problems with delay (even if your ping is low).
At least, I didn't encounter any blatant cheating, at least something.
The unlock system is decent. Also weapon customisation. There are three classes, each one has unique equipment for both faction (Taliban and US).
Rarely, you get a good match with the right type of players, in that case the multiplayer is great. But as said - very rarely.
Multiplayer deserves the ranking of around 5/10, not sure.
It mainly suffers from the engine, removal of features (comparing to singleplayer) and strange map and encounter design.

I was kind of surprised to see this pop up on steam, I honestly thought it was one of those ♥♥♥♥♥♥ rip-offs that slide in through greenlight. Turns out this is all legit and once you actually start playing the game that becomes pretty obvious. The production values for the levels are way ahead of any of the previous Trials games. With most of them featuring at least one flashy set piece.
Of course the downside of that is that you end up paying more attention to the background and crash a hell of alot. In fact one of the biggest problems with the game is the fact that it mixes so many playstyles in together. In a single level you can go from driving a Tank to a motor bike to a Jetpack. Which is cool but does mean that you are not likely to get anything approaching a good time the first time through a lot of levels as you wrestle with the widely different handling of each mode.
One of the other downsides to the more polished and flashy levels is the length of the game. Even with a bunch of deaths I still beat the game in about two hours. Obviously I will go back and try to ace the levels which should double the time but compared to the length of Trials Fusion this is depressingly short.
Along with that the game never reaches the challenge of Fusion. You never really have to be that precise with your controls and it's only in the last level that you start to face more advanced challenges.
Having said all of that there is still a bunch of stuff I have yet to do in the game outside of the story missions. There are five secret keys to find each with a clue to where it is along with rewards for acing levels.
For £11.99GBP I think it is a tight little package. If you go in expecting something on the scale of Fusion then you are going to be disappointed but by the same token there are no levels in dull static warehouses to grind through. I like Fusion but it was pretty padded in some areas and this game doesn’t do that. Choosing to cut out all of the fat to give you pure spectacle.
