I like the fact that someone is trying to make a game that is science based and not just eye candy. I wouldnt call the game "early access", it is 100% playable and I found zero bugs in the few hours I have played, BUT the game is still a little rough around the edges.
Here are a few thoughts (based on only a few hours play and only on the first few missions) :
- Nothing like KSP. You can build your own ships and adjust orbits, but that is where the similarities end. I do not want anyone to read this review thinking that this is KSP with nukes and lasers. [EDIT: This is more like the old game Harpoon or Command: Modern Air Naval Operations] This game is about battlefield decisions. Having played KSP first, I found lining up orbits and intersecting kinda easy (at least in the first few missions), but each mission is decided in a battle at a single intersecption or fly-by. You have either are entering a battle that uses your strengths or not. You dont have have the resources to try another orbit or "attack" again because you wont have the delta-v or undamaged systems to even bother trying another pass.
- Since each mission is determined by a single encounter, things go bad in battle fast. This is fine, but the battles seem to play in real time only, no pausing and no time scaling. This makes the game hard to control and it is hard to try new things (and it is hard to see what is really going on). More importantly, IT IS HARD TO ENJOY BATTLES. Given the short nature of battles I think the graphics are fine, but the battles happen sooooo fast the player does not get a chance to look around. You cant say to yourself, "I wonder what kind of damage happens if I concentrate all of my railguns on their engine", because as the battle starts if you are just staring at the enemy ship, watching the light show, so many other decsions have to be made. How are my drones doing, how are my missles doing, should I launch more, how much damage am I taking, should I change the angle of my ship, how is my weapon range, is the enemy closing or moving away, how much ammo do I have left. Having two ships to baby sit makes it even harder to watch the damage to the enemy ship. All of this kills the enjoyment factor when the battles only play in real time. Maybe a battle replay would help too.
- Above I mentioned that "the battles seem to play in real time only" because I am not really sure what all of the keys do. Other reviewers have mentioned this. There doesnt seem to be a list anywhere of the keyboard layout. I even did the old "run your hands across the keyboard randomly" just to figure out some of the keys. This is the year 2016, come on.
- There is no quick save, or at least I cant find one (maybe it is hiding with the keyboard layout). Once you start a mission look at the orbits, make some burns, line up a perfect interscept, start battle, BAM ! Forgot to turn my ship to broadsides. START THE MISSION OVER FROM THE BEGININNG. Now the player has to rework the orbits and the timings, make the burns, interscept, start battle. Draw, no one won first pass. Neither side has fuel to try another pass. START THE MISSION OVER FROM THE BEGINNING. As the missions get harder, this is more of a pain. This makes it very hard if not impossible to try new things. Trying new things means starting the whole mission over. After a successful, hard mission, you dont feel like starting over just for the sake of trying something new, you just move on to the next mission.
- I wish it had a campaign more like KSP's career mode, where money and what you accomplish really matter. You are just dropped into these crafted situations that dont really matter in the long run. There is no "long run", but I knew that going into this game, it is just wishful thinking. The author of this game does such a good job of thinking things through, maybe a grand strategy version of this game would be bleak. The strategy game probably revolve around fuel transports, fuel producion and depots. I think it would quickly end up like the BattleTech universe where the first few wars whipe out so much so fast, all of the warring sides would come together and agree not to attack some targets (jumpship yards in BattleTech)(and they agree not to ues weapons of mass destruction).
This post is getting too long, I will come back later and edit after I have played more.
Summary - interesting, science based space battle sim, not like KSP, graphics are fine (easily improved in future), needs a quick save, need to be able to change the rate of time in battles, UI could use some polish, needs a sandbox campaign of some sort.  Even though I gave it a negative review I think of this game as "early access" with improvements yet to come ... ( and I dont mind supporting games like these)
P.S. Edit begins here -  After playing a few more hours , I have more thoughts : the more I stare at the orbits screen, the more I shake my head. I am currently on the "Homecoming" mission and it seems like a waste of time to make the player worry about complicated orbits and picking up some general (the mission is to return your ship to Mars, from a far away asteroid).
I hate to even mention KSP, but I think KSP makes figuring out orbits so much easier. In comparison, KSP shows you how fast you are going and your orbital altitude, and CoaDE primarily uses your delta-V and an orbital picture. So in KSP you are staring at numbers and in CoaDE you are staring at an orbital picture.
In CoaDE you adjust your orbit to the target, the intersect icon appears, you click 'intersect', BAM!, warning not enough delta-V remaining (or there is a warning that the mission's time limit is up). You say to yourself, "Ok, my orbit path is wrong, I can't do that. Hmm what is really wrong with my orbit ?" Because CoaDE doesnt use numbers (or any other hard information about your orbits) you dont know EXACTLY what to do adjust to make a perfect intercept. The only thing you have to work with is the orbital picture showing your path.
Long story short, this leads to a lot of trial and error adjustments, pretty much making random adjustments (or series of adjustments).  You slowly learn how to make better paths, but the game does not teach you why that path is better. I looked for help on YouTube and found a playthrough of the mission I was having trouble with, and that guy was just making random adjustments, all the while talking to himself sort of saying 'ok I know what I need to do, how do I get the game to do it'. To make matters worse (or "easier") you can base your path on the orbit of your target. This displays your orbital path as a curly q line, which can make it easier to intersect an orbit, but it makes it harder to understand the consequences of your actions (your actions dont matter as long as the curly q line ends up where you want).
P.P.S. Edit #2 - I feel my review has a few too many negative points so I wanted to add a few positive moments that have hapened in the game. I have played up to the 13th mission Vesta Overkill, but I have switched over to playing in sandbow mode, creating ships and modules (you can unlock the design aspect early if you find the right menu in the game). Most of my weapons revolve around nuclear bombs.
There is something satisfying about designing and detonating a 3.25gt (3250 megaton) nuclear missle in the middle of an enemy fleet. I have also designed a cannon firing 4.4kt nuclear bombs that are about the size of Coke bottle (10cm x 40cm), at about 10 rounds a second. It seems like nuclear bombs will dominate the future too. I have spent most of my design efforts trying to guard against nuclear bombs, by upgrading stock ships so the AI has a chance.

Ah, behold the genre that never existed. There are two games of this genre: OTC and MULE. MULE is like, 20 years old and while good, this one is better. This is a real-time strategy game where you control a corporation on Mars, but unlike Starcraft, your goal is to extract resources for money and buy your competitors hostile-takeover-style rather than kill them. To do this, you're going to want to manipulate market prices ruthlessly, causing shortages of what you produce and surpluses of what you buy. There are a whole lot of ways to do this, from obeying supply and demand, to sabotaging power plants and key buildings to disrupt the production of a resource and cause a price surge / achieve a monopoly, to outright hacking the markets and resorting to orbital liftoffs that are pricy buy use a different market, to a wide range of tactics that are predatory and designed to weaken everyone else's earnings.
There are a ton of tactical ways to ruthlessly manipulate the market, and even in multiplayer, the game rewards fast reaction to changing strategic circumstances over fixed build orders. Basically, if you enjoy the idea of experiencing capitalism at its nastiest and most ruthless, or you just like damn fine strategy games, or entire unique genres, this is a great pick. Oh yeah, solid procedurally-generated single player campaigns too.
I don't usually mention sound tracks, but this one's is great and is timed to in-game progress that really feeds a feeling of intensity to every fast-paced match. Its intensity fits the tone of the game, and the music actually changes as base levels and in-game progress increase, building from brooding but relentless marches to symphonic, percussion-heavy crescendos of full-blown planetary exploitation. The music is a constant reminder that love it or hate it, the Martian capitalist machine is relentless and insatiable. The sheer tone of the game is accidental social commentary that can be appreciated, no matter your political leanings.
The game deserves "Overwhelmingly Positive" reviews IMHO in that it does what it aims to do amazingly well. That said, this game is NOT for everybody. Not everyone likes number-crunchy market manipulation at coke-addled-quant realtime paces. You need to be the kind of person who enjoys the mathematical/strategic exercise here to enjoy this kind of game. Not every game is for everybody; so when you're deciding whether to buy it, don't think of it as a traditional RTS.

Sherlock Holmes is one of the most well known detectives. So many movies, TV shows and games are based on the adventures of Sherlock Holmes and his trusted companion Dr. Watson. But will Sherlock Holmes: The Awakened will be a game Sherlock Holmes fans Want to play ?
Sherlock Holmes: The Awakened is a bit of a departure from the more kid friendly games and what I mean by that is that the previous Sherlock Holmes games were pretty tame compared to this or even the later games in the series.
Story wise this is an interesting title. Sherlock Holmes has to solve a supernatural case which involves the legendary Cthulhu created by H.P. Lovecraft. Some illegal immigrants go missing and soon wind up dead in crime scenes that look like ritualistic sacrifices and it's up to you to solve the mystery.
As I stated before this is a departure from the more teen friendly games. This game has this unsettling mood. The atmosphere in every location feels great even though the graphics don't look that good.
Locations range from Asylums, to swamps in New Orleans and abandoned light houses and you can explore everything at your own pace and there is a lot of stuff to find.
Now originally this game only had the first person mode, but the remastered edition has an added third person point and click mode that helps out in some locations which have bad textures (I'll get to that in a moment)
Graphics look outdated. Some of the items you need to pick up blend in with the environment. Some of the lip syncing is just hilarious when the character models look like dead people. Some of the environments looks empty, but that's only for a second.
Now I want to cover the most important aspect of a Sherlock Holmes game and that's the puzzles. After playing Sherlock Holmes Mystery of the Silver Earring I was put off with the illogical puzzles. This time I was surprised with how smart the puzzles actually were.  Now there was some hard puzzles and some of them are kind of stupid, but mostly really smart and well thought out puzzles.
Voice acting ranges from well done to incredibly horrible. Some of the voice acting is just incredibly funny. When they talk about serious situations all I did was smile at the voice acting.
If you do plan on playing the game I do recommend saving quite frequently and backing up your save file, cause there is a bug where you can lose your save file. Apart from that there's not many other bugs.
The game took me 8 hours to finish and apart from the one run of the game you will do, there's not much replay value as nothing really changes.
In the end I have to say I loved my time with Sherlock Holmes: The Awakened and I might say it's the best Sherlock Holmes game I've played to date. The interesting story and puzzles are great in this game, because I felt they were the biggest flaw in The Mystery of the Silver Earring. If you like Adventure games, Sherlock Holmes and you like the work of H.P. Lovecraft you will love this game.
Final Rating:
8/10 - Worth to consider buying it.

Brilliant game, so far probably my favourite in the series. It's really well designed, the puzzles are good and the story gets very interesting and sinister. It looks very nice too, I actually had the urge to take screenshots often, because I liked the sceneries. A great thing about this Remastered version is also that you can switch between classical point-and-click style and a first-person perspective. You can play either way, depending what you like more or, like me, keep switching back and forth between them to look at everything from a different perspective.
What some people might not like is the presence of some supernatural elements in a game about a detective known for logical thinking and solving regular human crime cases rather than dealing with cults. As I managed to find out these supernatural elements are related to the works of H. P. Lovecraft, but probably very loosely. I don't know for sure, since I'm not familiar with his works, but I expect his biggest fans as well as biggest fans of Arthur Conan Doyle might both be disappointed and feeling the game messes up everything about their favourite universe. But I'll tell you something... I really don't mind. It may do some things differently, it may break some established canon, but it's a pretty damn cool and involving story. Don't treat fictional works so seriously, don't say the writer tosses in his grave, don't clench your fists in anger. This is just derivative work and it should be allowed some artistic creativity. Enjoy it for what it is, because it's actually really enjoyable and for me this was an unforgettable experience.

The game itself is not terribly bad, but it is not terribly good either.
It has a good soundtrack, decent tutorials, and factions are varied enough (though the game could use more factions). More resources and buildings would also be nicer.
Nevertheless, nearly every match turns out the exact same. There's always an initial rush to expanding to rarer resources (which can very from map to map). You are forced to do scanning prior to landing your base to find the most optimal spot, but the AI knows the most optimal spots on the map and are set on a random timer before they choose to land their initial base. If on a high resource map, you can wait until they found their initial bases to get additional founding bonuses. Otherwise, if it is a scarce resource map, you're racing against the random clock to get one of the few good starting positions. The scanning, except in multiplayer situations, is thus a needlessly annoying feature in the game. In multiplayer, there's an actual strategic element to it.
Computers will often use "black market" actions liberally against what they perceive as the biggest threat, which will almost certainly always be you. Doubling annoying if you are playing against the scavenger AI, because they get extra black market items. Even if you are not in the top position, or do not control a particularly valuable resource, they'll nearly always choose to mutiny, power surge, or strike your buildings. Sometimes they will spread out these actions to other AI, but when you look at the post-match stats, generally you will be the top target. That can be pretty annoying, particularly when they chain one after another.
If you survive the initial round of black market actions, the AI can be pretty easy to exploit, because they will not bid particularly high on some valuable auctions. They will even sometimes research patents when they do not make any sense (like researching using water instead of energy to power buildings, when energy is trading for $1 and water is trading for $80), even when on high difficulties. They will rarely rush for the "must-have" patents, like teleportation, which will generally leave you an opening to dramatically reduce your maintence and make your goods more liquidable.
Campaign mode is the most enjoyable mode in the game, but, again, every mini-match within the campaign is nearly a repeat of the previous, with minor deviations. The game simply does not have enough variation.
I would not have bought this game at its current price. I received it through Humble, but might be happy if I spent less than $5 on it.

This game is a bit of a departure from typical Holmes, as it mixes in a Lovecraftian element that gives the story an unearthly taste.  I don't have a problem with that, but if you're not really a fan of sort of "out there" paranormal storie, you might not appreciate this game.  However, even if you're not a Lovecraft fan, you might be engaged enough with the story to enjoy this too.
Gameplay is pretty standard pointy-clicky fare.  As in most of these styles of game, the puzzles range from very basic to ridiculously difficult, but thankfully there is an in-game hint system that does help a lot to keep frustration to a minimum.  The only truly difficult part I found was a point when you're in a dark area with a lantern and must find all the clues to progress; the last "piece" was very difficult to locate in the dark.
For mystery/detective fans who also are fans of Agatha Christie, there is a delightful "easter egg" partway through the game.  As a Christie and Doyle fan, I squealed like a wee happy baby.  I won't ruin it here, just keep your eyes and ears open for it. :D
My single real complaint (and it's just a nitpick really) is with the sound; there's a point where there are a lot of people using alert/warning whistles and they were piercingly loud (and over and over and over again, ouch my head).  I didn't even have the sound up that loud but I thought my eardrums were going to rupture.  Just a minor thing to keep in mind; you may want to keep the volume lower or even off when you hit that section.
So go grab the Sherlock Holmes Collection where you can get all six of the games at once and save a good bit of money.  They're definitely worth it for fans of Doyle's Holmes.

If I was to liken Amnesia to a film, it would almost certainly be Texas Chainsaw Massacre.  If you have never watched it then you probably wont know what I'm going on about.  But despite its title, there is virtually no gore in it at all.  No chainsaw massacres, no nothing really.  But one thing it does do, and does well, is it is disturbing without being shocking.  It is a series of well placed shots, well paced story, and inventive camera and sound play.  In short, this is what Amnesia is.  If you turned the sound off you would probably think what the hell the fuss is about.  But the developers really know their genre.  And better than that, they don't really go in for jump scares.  Amnesia is about a sense of building danger and suspense as you discover more about the protagonist you play.  This is well played out through scripted notes and flash backs.  The other game of this kind - Outlast - is very similar.  I would say Amnesia has more character.  Outlast is top dog for jump scares and its graphics are also better.  But I think over all Amnesia is executed better (although they are both good titles IMO).  Along with Alien Isolation, these are without doubt the best 3 survival horror titles in the market today.  I would put this on a par with Alien isolation, and Outlast a close(ish) second.

I picked this game up when it was free from Steam.  To be honest, I had always seen the DLC and whatnot floating around when I logged on but never gave it much thought.  Snipers, DLC for zombies, to me it smelled of call of duty... Lets start with the fact that I was very wrong.
Sniper Elite V2 IS very good.  The game has the basic WW2 setting.  Russians closing in on Berlin, the allies are winning, the Reich is in it's last days etc.  Where this game shines is in the Sniper effects.  Drop into the game you are presented with your main weapon which is (generally) a bolt action rifle.  Scope up and you will find having to adjust for wind and gravity on the distance to your target.  Squeeze the trigger and watch your rifle round fly through the air in slow motion only to Mortal Kombat XRAY an enemy.
At its heart this is where the game shines.  There are pistols and submachineguns to assist you in your romp through Berlin, however I caution people who decide to take on a FPS assault on German positions.  You will find very quickly that you can get blown out of your socks by Nazi's when you face them head on.
To sum it up, got it for free but would have paid for it.  I think that kinda says it all.

I see many reviews smashing the game for Jason being overpowered, login issues, lack of content,etc so let's debunk some of these shall we?
FACT: There was 10 thousand people on when the game released on PC and had no server issues what so ever, then other versions started to go live which overloaded the servers. Since then, illfonic has been working tirelessly to restore connectivity, which they've done partially.
Jason if he finds you, most times you will die. However, those complaining about his shift ability I doubt have played Jason much, you can easily juke this by doing sharp turns as shift requires the Jason player to do a large broad turn. You can also notice jason shifting if you look behind you occasionally.
Login issues are caused by multiple thousands of people trying to play all at once which is slowly getting and better, the fact that they've been responding to questions all day and night on twitter/discord shows they are dedicated.
Lastly, in regards to content this game has 3 maps the size of an average Battlefield conquest map. It has 10 counsellors, 7 jasons (6 playable for normal players, but 7 if you got a savini Jason), 60 kills in the game, everything is motion captured, dedicated servers, tons of customization and unlocks from rolling perks, not to mention singleplayer coming in summer. Does that sound like a lack of content? Certainly doesn't to me.
As someone who has been playing this game since it launched off and on (for sleeping obviously), I enjoy both sides of the game. If a jason gets me I can normally go "oh he caught me because I didn't know he was shifting/not paying attention", normally you can juke this like I've said before. This game is much more casual then what people try to compare it to (dead by daylight) which the only comparison to be made is that it's a killer versus player controlled survivors. I enjoy the game, if you take it seriously you will rage, most games you will die, you will get better. At the end of the day, this game relies heavily on RNG which can also cause your death. Understanding game mechanics such as fear and how composure affects that along with how noise bubbles work for Jason to let him know where you are factors into "Jason is overpowered". Many people do not understand how to hide, regain composure, and are full sprinting around like idiots. Do NOT play it like a running simulator, you will get yourself killed.
My only complaint is that this game should be 25-30 USD instead of 40 as the singleplayer w/bots is not in the game yet. This is a fun game.

Alright. I rarely review games (mostly because I am working on a Master's degree, so, while I have time to play them, busting out a review is a little bit more than I want to give). Nevertheless, this was a great game. I happen to be getting my M.A. in Philosophy, so the themes in this game were right up my alley.
So, first, let's look at the story without spoilers: I think this was really where the game shined. I don't want to get into it, but I really felt like I could relate to Simon. His backstory was tragic, yet he had a very mature outlook (hopeful, not desperate, joking a little about his dire predicament, etc...). I have known people who have been in similar situations regarding their health, and this was believable. 10/10
Second, let's look at the philosophical issues brought up in the game. This was good stuff: are we (our persons, that is) reducible to electro-chemical impulses in the brain? If our brains were scanned, would the "scan" be a person (and would that 'person' be the same person as our person)? The two main characters, Catherine and Simon, sort of take opposing sides regarding this issue. I can tell you that there is no consensus in philosophy regarding this question (though I have an opinion, I won't share it). The next philosophical issue has to do with Artificial Intelligence. Is it possible? Is it truly 'intelligence'?  A third prominent philosophical issue the game brings up has to do with end of life issues. Is it morally acceptable to end someone's life because of its poor quality, including your own (another way to look at this: Is the value of life rooted in its sacredness or its quality?). The really cool thing the game does is NOT OFFER YOU ANSWERS, but simply offer you decisions other people made regarding these issues, and their reasoning behind those decisions. This is philosophy in a video game done right! 10/10
Third, the visual experience is wonderful. I really felt like the graphics were fantastic. I never had any framerate issues or really any issues at all. My only beef with Frictional Games is that they don't animate a player's hands. This really makes for a less immersive gaming experience. 9/10
Fourth, the puzzles were super easy. However, solving any puzzle usually came with lots of backstory and the like, so that was nice. I did get stumped when I had to plug something in once to get the power on a console, but it was mostly because I never looked down at the ground to see the "blinking" hole for the cord (duh!). 7/10
Fifth, how were the characters? I really felt like Simon was well-done. However, I had a lot of trouble finding some of the other characters believable (you meet them largely through recordings and the like strewn throughout the game). I was thinking as I experienced these other characters (including Catherine), "Wow. Um, I think if people were undergoing (the kind of thing this game has people undergoing), most people I know (which, since I am an educated dude, are mostly people with Ph.D.'s or getting them, which is relevant to my review because all the people in this game are "scientists" of some stripe) wouldn't be so chill about their situation. So, I felt the game lacked the kind of desperation that people in their situation would likely experience. 5/10
Finally, was it scary? On this point I guess I will give it a 7/10. I was initially on the edge of my seat but got used to it, then Johan Ross scared the crap out of me, and Robo-girl terrified me (after all, she is super fast, and chased me down this really long freakin' hall to chop off my head!). But knowing what I knew about Simon (what he was), for some reason lowered the fear factor.
So, with that said, I loved this game. It was fantastic. One of my top-ten favorite games ever (AND FOR ONLY $30!).

For lovers of hard science fiction this is pretty much the dream game. Heat radiators, nuclear thermal rockets, lasers, real n-body physics, and orbital mechanics, it’s all here. Star Wars style space battles, you won’t find that here. This is all about matching orbits, flinging missiles at targets hundreds of kilometers away and drilling away at your target’s armor with concentrated laser and rail gun fire. The campaign is challenging enough but the ship and component editor is a whole ‘nother story. Making your own ship components is, to put it lightly, INSANE! The amount of parameters you can modify is mind boggling. Just trying to make a custom laser weapon I have to chose a lasing medium, what material to make the mirrors out of, what are those mirror’s dimensions, what will the freaking coolant pumps be made out of and what fluid will they be pumping and how fast!  I feel like I need several advanced engineering degrees to wrap my head around all this, which is cool, but overwhelming! I like that it gives you these insane custom tinkering options but unless you know what you’re doing it’s best to just stick with the stock parts to build your ships. I really can’t think of any other game out there that takes hard science fiction this seriously. Probably Kerbal Space Program is the closest thing to this but that’s really not a helpful comparison.

I bought this game on sale in a pack of similar old-school RPGs for less than $1. While this game, along with its siblings, aren't old-school as far as time goes, they are in spirit and in style.
To be honest, after beating two out of the 5 purchased, this one is my favorite so far, and well-worth the buy. I'm actually only posting this review since it received so many negative reviews recently, and I think it may be due to lack of perspective on the reviewer's part.
The Chosen RPG, unlock some others of its kind, is a bit more in-depth regarding stats and equipment. Like some more modern RPGs on mobile devices or on portables, you can optimize your equipment quickly for the gamer-on-the-go, and there's more than just the minimum 4 stats that some RPGs have.
The graphics aren't great, but if you're an experienced gamer who grew up with worse, then they're about on-par when considering the RPG Maker engine. Yes, the most detailed of the graphics mostly include scantilly-clad women with erect nipples, take that as a positive (if you're into that) or a negative (like other recent reviewers), but either way the game mechanics are more streamlined than others of its kind available on steam and if this game was made back in the 90s when these types were more popular, it could have been a serious trend-setter.
Really this game is a matter of perspective; if you expect to spend $2 (or less, like me) then you should usually expect a game of slightly lesser caliber, or at least equal to this one's.
Overall, this game has been a positive experience for me, and I've enjoyed it more than similar titles.

This uncle just so happens to be a horrible alcoholic and embarrassment to every party... but also has that really cool classic car collection that you only dream to inherit some day... you know... minus the drunk guy stumble about in it.

I've met life-long friends in this game.
I've learned things about myself in this game- like how I have this crippling phobia of this little thing called "desync"
All-in-all this game is an experience.
Maybe yours will be amazing, maybe it'll be trash.
Maybe you'll play it only a few times every couple of months.
Maybe you'll play it nonstop and then never touch it again.
But I promise you, it will never be the same game each time.
ArmA isn't a game, not a simulator or some test bed.

Before I get into this review, know that they are offering 20 'in game diamonds' for 'informative' reviews.  They don't care if it's good or bad, just so long as you're honest.
That being said, I love this game.  It's not Pay2Win and it's really really fun.  The turorials are pretty good.  They teach you all you need to know.  The campaign is fun, informative, challenging, and rewarding.  You get tons of gold, cards, diamons, and rubies to expand your collection.  Everything can be bought through grinding, and even those who pay money don't have an advantage over people that spend zero money.
The matchmaking system is fair, balanced, and fun.  You can get into quick matches, pro matches, and ladder matches - all of which have gold bets to win from.  Quick matches are where you pick your deck and get matched with someone of similar skill.  Pro matches are somewhat of a 'draft' system where you pick two cards, two more, and two more, while the enemy does the same.
The actual gameplay is weird for americans, or so I assume ( I am american).  You just pick your cards, and enter the battle.  After that the game just plays itself.  At first you might think, "Well how is that fun?" but trust me it is and there's a lot of strategy involved.
Overall this game is fun, challenging, and rewarding.  You should check it out.  It's free man, what do you have to lose?

I gave this game a few hours to wow me, and while the initial areas provide a rather pleasant experience, the difficulty spikes quickly, with enemies multiple levels below mine proving unbeatable very early on. Perhaps if I had equipment of a level equal to my party, I might not have had as much trouble, however, the game didn't see fit to produce any in previous battles. If not dropped through battle, equipment can only otherwise be crafted or bought from the in-game auction house, both of which are, based on what I saw, prohibitively expensive options for new players (this is why most MMOs include actual stores). Because of this, the only ways to advance are to either grind for an unreasonable amount of time (to either hunt for decent gear or vastly outlevel the target), or pay real money to get an advantage. If this business model sounds familiar at all, it's because it's a hallmark of predatory mobile games such as Candy Crush Saga. In light of that, I can't in good conscience recommend this title, much as I enjoyed the core concept and mechanics. If a future update smooths the curve of enemy stats, however, you should at least give it a try if you enjoy strategy RPGs.

So, here's the issue that came with the game at launch.
That's basically abusing the review system by offering direct paid inducements for positive reviews. To add to this, the developers attempted to ban any and all reviews that referenced this event as it happened along with screenshot evidence that confirmed it. Censorship by abuse of the ban system. When the steam mods unflagged the screens it left them with the only route of attacking the users, which they did, in my case, calling me a "Hatred liar", see exhibit B:
This sums up the case against the developer. Now on to the game.
The game masquerades as a skill based game but in reality has a massive set of pay to win mechanics laced into the underbelly (see ruby upgrades for cards), the game plays itself automatically with players setting up their choices before the game begins out of their pool of cards, they pick six, and then launch into battle. Now for the single player campaign, this isn't QUITE so bad, as it basically plays out as a glorified puzzle game, you figure out which set of cards gets you through each fight, and then move onto the next one. So that part works out alright, but in the PVP pool, you basically have to guess based on psychic prediction or...
... you spend money on buying in the most powerful cards (invariably 4 and 5 stars) which means paying out for diamonds. And then upgrade them using rubies (which will cost you more money). In short, unless you've a significant sum of money, you'll not get into the upper levels of the ladder of this game, you might finish the perfunctory campaign (which hasn't been finished off), but as for PvP, your success is strictly defined by either wasting a LOT of time grinding or pumping in vast sums of real, actual money and converting it into funny currency.
All into a game which plays itself.

This follows a long line of puzzle platformers and it really hits the spot. The history of puzzle platformers is a long one and very much is a genre I've always loved. Way back in the 90s there were many. Usually cartoony in form and had stories and plots. Original Prince of PErsia fits this bill but with the Playstation came 3D and very cartoony characters like Crash Bandicoot and Spyro and such. Also in the past shooting has been part of the mix. But the indie wave since about 2010 had taken things back to its 2D sidescrolling roots and added an art to it that was so new and appealingly fresh. The biggest addition to this line was Limbo. A totally beautiful game. A game that was totally the opposite of lots of platform sidescroller shooters from before as it not only featured a helpless protagonist that was relentlessly tortured throughout the game but had an artistic style and statement that just was pure beauty. So goes Nihilumbra. Yes Nihilism. It's not just for Lebowski fans anymore. This is another success in this genre and it really taps into the most fun bits of Portal 2. Remember the goo levels? This game features a lot of things like that. YOu have this character, this blob...this "nothing". That escapes "the void". And he mimics the form of a scarecrow. I LOVE this choice. Your ragdoll man floats and blows along. He doesn't walk. He kind of floats. And his "clothes" are always flopping in the breeze and especially when he lands from jumps. It's so appealing of a character. LIke the best of disney sidekicks. And then you have gruesome bizarre monsters. Think of all the craziest scariest designs from Dr Seuss or Tex Avery. Stuff of nightmares in shape and form because all these things are alive. And there are different ways to avoid and outsmart these creatures. And traverse this world. Okay now....the guy. There is a narrator that comes across like one of those positive self help cassettes. Always telling you your place in this world. Telling you what a failure you are. Telling you how waful your life has been. Telling you you will never win. And then reinvigorating you with his soothing tones what a success you will be, are being, will continue to be. You are special and goshdarnit people like you, Stewart Smalley. I still don't know what to make of this really. The narrator gives you all the instruction for the game. And then visual aids appear in a lot of places to tell you EXACTLY how to solve a puzzle. In fact they don't wait for more than about 2 failures before the game actually tells you how to solve a puzzle. I am not sure if it does that all the time. Maybe just when you are learning a new move? But I see it often. I've conquered the first two worlds thus far. I guess that means levels. And each world seems to offer new types of gameplay and monsters and moves. Very much like Portal 2 did. More moves and thus more puzzles you solve for those moves then puzzles combining those moves and monsters with previous ones to remind you. It does do a bunch of handholding for sure. But I do feel satisfied playing it. It's like relaxing in a hot tub. And when the swirly purple void emcompasses me...and the whole screen. I don't mind. It's beautiful. Well....unless of course well yes I do mind when it is chasing me and I'm trying to plan for moves that haven't come on the screen yet because...the ....screen....is....scrolling....by....so........S....L...O...W...L...Y.... However any frustrating bits so far have been solved with a few tries, trial and error and whatnot. Seeing how you die and then remembering and preparing for that offscreen jump. And it is satisfying changing the ground to grassy bouncy, maybe just a LITTLE less satisfying to shooting goop everywhere with a goopgun. I'm liking it. It's a satisfying PP...and a satisfying experience. I'll let the narrator lull me with his dulcet tones and float away in my scarecrow body. I really love the animation of the characters by the way. And the scenery and weather are just gorgeous. This is also one that goes on sale a lot from it's list price of just 8 dollars so it's a steal when it does. Get it.

First a disclosure, I am mainly leaving this review to the free gems. Normally would not leave a review as in my eye this game is neither good or bad enough to merit one. Honestly the game is a hair further in the bad category so that is why it does not have my recommendation. In the vein of being helpful here is a quick pro/con as I have seen in the game.
Cons:
1) The free packs and random cards are not that good. The packs you purchase with in game gold rarely give you anything good. Mostly get a lot of 1-2 star cards. The packs which claim to give better drops cost a special currency which is really hard to come by in game, but can be bought via cold hard cash.
2) Mission rewards seem a bit lackluster. To get the better rewards for missions you mainly need a specialized set up requiring certain cards. To get the cards you need to do missions... which require a specilaized set up. Depending on rng you can find yourself in an unfun situation of just grinding away. Also, red gems are hard to come by and you need a goodly amount of them to level cards to make them better.
3) Limits on how much you can play and ineffecient energy system. Everytime you complete a mission or do something it drains your energy. You get a certain amount of energy a day, and it can be replenished by leveling up. The starting missions cost very little energy to complete, and you level up quickly. The issue is that you hit the cap of your energy and you never receive a lot of energy you get by leveling. EDIT: It appears the energy replenishes faster than I first assumed. This alleviates most of the issue. I understand it prevents people from exploiting things, but if you bing out and play it can prevent you from doing thing you want to.
4) Basic features are purchaseable via in game gold. Things like being able to view your match after you finish and speeding up the matches are purchaseable.
5) The farming feature to go back and reap rewards from earlier levels is not really worth it. You only get 20 or so gold and expend a significant chunk of energy. No way to get red gems other than completing quests.
6) Hints are really not that useful if you do not have the cards. In the 3-4 cases I have used all I got was 6 sets which all included the same 2-3 cards in different orderings. Also, doing what the hint suggests does not always give you victory, there is still a fair amount of rng at play.
Pros:
1) Game plays itself. Been playing this on one computer while playing skyrim on another. Gives me something to do during loading screens.
2) Card art and music is nice.
3) Solid rock/paper/scissors mechanics.
4) Good solid time waster to play while your doing other things
The game has a good base. And my complaints can be solved if the developers do the following things:
1) First time through the campaign missions costs no energy.
2) Implementation of an energy bank. Something that your spare energy that you get by leveling up goes to so it is not wasted.
3) Better drops in the non-gem packs. At least always give us a 3 star. Have the 1 or 5 random card have much higher odds of giving you but no guaranteed 3 star. While the booster pack randomness stays the same but guarantees you a 3 star.
4) Easier way to get red and blue gems. More repeatable missions to gain them that do not drain your energy so much. Perhaps a mission that when you play it gives you energy. That way you are always able to play if you want.
I hope my feed back helps.

You are the void, created by the void itself, and your purpose is to outrun a ghastly purple entity. You'll be traversing different landscapes along the way, as the title attempts to relay a message that's moving at times, and touches upon the idea of destruction as a means to survive.
Gameplay-wise, the release is fairly simple. It's a standard 2D platformer with a twist, which arrives in the form of colour-based powers. Along your sombre journey, you'll encounter flowers, which provide you with unique abilities. You'll start out slow, frail, and unable to attack enemies, but as you soak up these vibrant skills, you'll find yourself able to bounce off the floor, slide on ice, and much more.
Nihilumbra is not the biggest game, but sometimes great things come in small packages. The puzzles are not especially difficult, but there's a nice plot and some decent presentation here which will push you through to its conclusion. If you're looking for something a little different for your Vita, then make sure that you don't a-void this one.

Received this in Humble Monthly, although it had been on my wishlist for some time.
The first thing you need to know is that this is entirely a niche game.  It is an in depth economy battle that just happens to run in real time with a standard style of rts map.  Imagine if the board game Acquire was genetically spliced with a custom map from Starcraft and then bred with Railroad Tycoon.  This game would be an expected outcome from that particular union.  The learning curve is steep, but the almanac with the game is abudant with useful information.  Speaking as primarilly a single player user, the campaign offers a staggering amount of replayability, and the dlc/expansions appear to offer significantly more.  I am actually somewhat terrified to try multiplayer because of the fact that human players adapt (except apparently for me haha) and my comfort level with the game is not yet high enough (though I have a few rl friends with the game shelved and look forward to some matches).  All in all if you enjoy any style of management/economy game, this deserves a try.

Long learning curve, but other than that a all in all very intresting RTS which ends by buying out your enemies rather than killing them. Offworld reminds of other building RTS games in many ways, resource gathering, building different base buildings and such to grow your economical empire. The maps have limited resources so eventually you'll need to end your opponents. The building parts are like those in Anno 2070, with farms to make food for your "workers", mine iron and produce steel. The game is simply won by buying into your opponents company, or by losing to you opponent by him/ her buying all of your stock. The game is a perfect example of real world economics and how to succeed as a company who competes for the customers. Don't mind my hours. I just started.

The Awakened is a great starting point for players new to the Holmes series. In this installment, the balance between puzzles, dialogue and hunting for clues has been perfected, and the new in-game hint system *usually* has the answers if you're stuck. There's been a pretty good graphical update, and the addition of the first person camera angle has totally removed the previous games' problems of pixel hunting and difficult controls. I personally encountered no technical problems playing on Windows 8.1.
If you're a fan of the classic Sherlock Holmes, Awakened may not be for you. The story has a lot of paranormal elements, which may be a turn off for some players. However, I am typically not a fan of paranormal mysteries and I was still able to enjoy the game. Each location has a totally different atmosphere, so in a way there's something for everyone. The mystery is interesting and intriguing without being convoluted, and at around 8 hours the length feels just right.

After 75 days of playing this, I noticed many patterns that made me realize that I had wasted time and money on a game where the market is broken, and the kickstarters, and repeated prize winners ruined the gameplay. Every four hours a prize goes out to one "random" player that has an approx cash value of $20-100. Just about every other prize goes to one of the five or six "elite players" every single day. These players "randomly" win one a day where as normal players may win once a month, or never depending on their activity. The game is extremely expensive to play and get started in already. Nearly forcing you to spend real money to participate fully in battles, and to upkeep your gear and fighters. You start with nothing, and you will be able to kill nothing worthwhile until you get gear, but guess what? Gear is extremely overpriced because of the wealthy, and gear is hoarded by the wealthy. Only second hand or extremely low durability gear is sold (gear that will break after a few hours of pvp in game). The gameplay itself is fun. But the whole point of the game is investment and grinding. Which is not fun to do when you see the same people sailing past you by winning free things repeatedly of extremely high value. There have been suggested fixes for this made to the developer and it's been ignored.

It's a great baseball sim game, but only recommendable to business and strategy players. One of my favorite features is the historical section keeping records of your team. I would like to see the game have former players and coaches die when they get older. It's odd that a 150 year old man can return and play or coach through commissioner mode (unless anyone has seen it happen other ways).  I would like to see an improved trading dynamic where you could shop a player (say an All Star) and be offered very good prospects or players in return. In addition, the option to pay a certain amount of a player's remaining salary should be available during a trade (think Ricky Nolasco for the Twins). I'm not sure if anyone else has had any trouble with this but I have never been able to develop that guy that hits .300/30HR/100RBI. I've had several guys that could have done it and should do it easily but always fail. My biggest issue with the game is that some star players experience a MASSIVE decline at around 30-32. I made a huge trade for Sonny Gray and got 4 great years out of him but when he hit 31 he was a completely worthless $22m man. If you're expecting something as unforgivingly brutal as the first Sniper Elite, you'll be disappointed. Enemy snipers are no longer hidden death traps that call for careful, 20 minute scouting sessions with just your binoculars and a slow crawl along the ground.
This gives the game some much needed arcade action moments, and thankfully V2 manages to deliver these without compromizing the whole "sniper" deal, as so many other games have. By that I mean that the best course of action is still to find a high place and go prone. However, you are allowed to risk a few trick shots at close range without being punished immediately by a game over.
Even if you wanted something more brutal and sluggish, I think you'll enjoy V2 as a co-op target shooter, I certainly am.

Amnesia is, without any shred of a doubt, the most frightening game ever made. The combination of the audio and visuals give the game an atmosphere that makes practically everything seem scary. Even though you don't see a single enemy for the first section of the game, it STILL somehow manages to put me on edge. Unlike most other horror games, you don't have any weapons to fight back against any enemies, so your only way to not die is to run into the nearest room and pray that the enemy won't follow you. The objectives are never very complicated, but they all require you to make your way to a different location in the castle. This essentially means you are constantly walking through dark hallways scared out of your mind that you are going to encounter a monster. Games and movies don't scare me easily, but I can't even play Amnesia without sometimes needing to look away from the screen because I'm getting too darn scared. Even though I'm playing on a 1366x768 monitor with the volume way down and in the middle of the day, the game still is able to work it's magic. Buy this game when it's on sale, which happens often.  The only thing scarier than this game is people buying steam games full price.

Best game by Frictional Games yet.
You are Simon Jarrett, an ordinary guy stuck in a sci-fi dystopia. Saying more is spoiler territory, and spoilers will hurt the this game more than most, it is a really a story driven game. (Although if you read this review you will probably have seen all trailers and read countless reviews.)
This is not Amnesia the Dark Descent. The horror is less about being afraid of monsters ripping your face off than it is about being in a very disturbing place and situation that makes you think.
The graphics are mostly good, not perfect but sufficient for what they try to do.
The sound design is near perfect. I have probably never played a game with a sound design as good as this one. Everything from the protagonists breathing, footsteps, to shrieking enemies, to the sound of dripping water to the humming sounds of ventilation is suberb. It is worth playing this game just for the sound. Use headphones.
Gameplaywise the game can be seen as lacking maybe if you play this game like it were a game to be optimized. If you play it like a game to immerse yourself in it would be near flawless.
The puzzles could be seen a too simplistic perhaps. I felt that they were tasks that felt realistic given the situation such as activating backup energy to open a door. No moving statues and finding rubys like in resident evils police-station, no arbitrary pulling levers in the right order and no combine items in the inventory stuff.
The inventory management is reduced to a reminder-list of what you carry. There is not sanity meter or resources manage. The health does not regenerate and can be refilled at different stations.
If you study the enemies for too long you will learn their behavior and much tension is lost and you might find them too easy to avoid. On my first playthrough I played the game as if the enemies were really dangerous and it kept the immersion for me.
If you in any way like horror games. Play this game. You should give it a try if you like adventure games as well.

I think it's been stated before, but I'll say it again: This game is not for everybody. There's even some argument that it isn't, first and foremost, a game, but rather a simulation system for realistic space combat. The graphics aren't great, the sound is largely made up of a soundtrack (a decent one, too), and the gameplay is difficult to learn, even harder to master. You'll be spending a while figuring out how to set your drone maneuvers up to get minimal-dV intercepts, how to time your missile launches so a whole horde of them show up on target at once, how to get from this orbit to that orbit without emptying your tanks. It's difficult, and complex, and not intuitive if you've grown up on popular media. (If you've grown up on orbital mechanics and physics handbooks, and/or in space, then it might be really easy, IDK...)
But the fact remains, this is the most realistic space combat sim game to ever exist. It sets a new standard for what you can call 'realism', and if that excites you, then this game is for you. The simulation engine used here is worth the asking price alone - anything better would require a heavy-duty scientific simulation system, and you won't get that for $23!
This game is gritty, crunchy, detailed and hard - just like real world space combat would be. It will challenge you, and teach you. And mastering it will mean that you understand what fighting in space would be on a visceral level given only to very few.

Heroes of Dire is a turn-based game with deep combat system and perfect itemization.
Pro's:
1) Co-op. Up to 4 ppl (they increase that number in upcoming patches) can take part in battle. So you can play with friends. Also co-op battles provide bonus exp and loot, so it's really beneficial.
2) Community. Both players and developers are nice and responsive. If you ask about some location or quest, you most likely will receive direct answer instead of being sent to google.
3) Like i mentioned, itemization is perfect, great potential for min-maxing
4) There's nothing like energy or wait timers, that blocking you from playing the game
5) PvE and PvP are separated = you wont be ganked, or steamrolled by higher/better players unless you seek for it.
6) There's only one currency in game, means there's no pay-to-win only benefits. No vip lvls, premium heroes/items.
Cons:
1) Lack of active actions for your fighters, which hurts tactic depth a bit. There's 6 classes, 3 of em have 1(!) active ability, 2 have 1 passive (they even share it) and poor pallies are only determined by item restrictions )
2) Interface. It's mobile game after all, and as PC player you have to deal with it.
Mixed:
1) Camera. While there's 3 camera modes, i didnt manage to find one that suits me.
2) Instead of daily/weekly login prizes there is per 4 hours free lottery. Prizes are valuable. Let me rephrase it: 100$ of in-game currency valuable! When you win it - you can freely send this point to pro's.
3) Your success in combat based on luck, setup, tactics and gear. In that order. Luck>setup>tactics>gear. That means you can withstand overwhelming forces sometimes. Or die to random minion because of 2 110 rolls (there's -10 to 110 dice used for determining action result)
If you're enjoying turn-based, and, especially if you want to play TB game with friends i strongly recommend to try it, and see if playstyle suits you.

tl:dr version:
- You can get all the cards if you grind, or pay to get them sooner.
- It isn't about actually playing your cards in a match, but rather about selecting the best ones for battle.
Long version:
This is indeed one of those games where you can obtain higher end cards by spending cash, or you can complete daily challenges to earn rewards to gather them up, or try to craft them from lower tier cards to higher. Just like about every other card game out there, even mighty Hearthstone.
One thing that is vastly different about this game, is that you don't actually play the cards in the match. The strategic focus instead is being familair with your cards and selecting the best ones for the task, then the game simulates the results. The cards deal in ranges - such as dealing 100 to 200 damage, so there is some random number generation aspects, that when combined with weaknesses and skills can actually create a pretty diverse approach.
Matchmaking is some of the best. When I started playing Hearthstone, I could find myself getting stomped on in PVP play by someone who had rare cards that were only available in their Solo Adventure expansions. A brutal learning experience. Here, I have no card presently better than 3 stars (it goes up to 5 stars I believe), and in over 25 pvp matches, I've only faced two people who even fielded a 4 star card, and I won 1 and lost 1. That to me is pretty fair for matchmaking.
It also gets props for being pretty intense, as like old school Magic the Gathering, you can actually have matches that wager cards used.
Pros:
- Solid campaign play compared to a lot of the other card games, with three different difficulty levels for the missions and those missions collected in different chapters (at least three chapters, as that's how far I'm at this point)
- In game public, guild, or campaign chat
- Nice artwork
- Good matchmaking
- Pro format is interesting with two cards at a time selection between seeing what your opponent has, adds more strategy as you adjust.
Cons:
- User Interface is a little odd at times in trying to figure out where you're at.
- Somethings are well explained while others aren't,  such as evolving cards
- If you have a run of bad luck, you can see your energy depleted, which apparently ends your ability to play, which is dissappointing. I've not run out of energy during a play session, but I've come close after getting used to the pro matches.

I have a hard time leaving a negative review for this game, as I think it is well done.
However, I have to be honest. I don't think one negative review is going to affect the ultimate outcome of this game, and if it does, so be it.
This is a zero-sum game. That means that there is one definite winner in every match. Everyone one else loses. It is also a highly competitive and fast paced game. They managed to turn the relatively slow machinations of business into something that requires constant attention.
My gripe with this is that it is unrealistic. Business is not a zero-sum game, at best it is a true non-zero-sum game. There is no option for cooperation. Also, the game is entirely about being cutthroat. There are numerous options to use illegal means to negatively affect your other players so that you win a monopoly in the marketplace. This is business at it's worst.
Good business is about innovation and service to the public. Bad business is about incremental or no-improvement and a turfwar over existing services with little to no improvement on current benefit to the public. Yes, these things do go on, to some extent in the real world. But they aren't all that interesting, nor do they present truely profitable industries. The industries wherein drastic profit is generally made have to do with innovation. However, there is one exception to this rule. Profit based on the capacity to invest in business which are innovative and profitable. This is the case of Warren Buffet. That being said he has invested in some existing blue-chip companies which offer little in the way of innovation. Still, his business, or investment firm really, is built on his ability to decide on whether a company is well run or not. This has little to do with sundering your competition.
We were taught that competition is good. This is true if you have a monopoly on power and you want your populace to be willing to compete with our peoples who are ruled by someone/someones with a monopoly of power in their own respective region. This competition does innovate some change. However, it does so inefficiently. Directed Cooperation is by it's very nature more efficient as it does not waste energy/resources to competition and, "warfare."
It is less relevant who owns the power than what that power does, in terms of the happiness of the public. This game is all about who owns the power.
This is a paradigm that we need to do away with. If we maintain this paradigm it is more likely that our species will suffer needlessly into the future.

Sherlock Holmes vs Cthulhu, it shouldn’t work, but it kind of does.
Tracking an evil group of followers across the world is entertaining, and the discovery of a dark plot across the world fits somewhat with the take that Frogwares have on the character and licence.
Unfortunately, the usual Frogwares problems are here en masse -
-The atmosphere is often inconsistent with the theme - instead of a dark, brooding adventure into an ancient cult, you get a trek riddled with bland, insipid dialogue and voice acting, and inappropriate reactions and asides that have no purpose.
-The third person navigation is easier for spotting items, but is reliant on poorly placed transition points, and while moving around in first person is far easier, it literally requires you to be on top of objects before you are able to interact with them.
-The progression can be incredibly frustrating - in most point and clicks, gameplay consists of picking up and examining everything you can, but in Awakened, you actually need to have a reason to look at or pick up an item, or even to use something you already have and know what to use for. Let me tell you a story.
I installed the restored content mod, booted up the game, made a Consular and went into the options to crank up the difficulty to the max before I started. I consider myself pretty good at games built off Bioware systems, and I played KOTOR I on the hardest difficulty without issue.
Fine, all was dandy. Played the game going full sith. Corrupted all my companions, which was a very memorable experience. Downloaded it on my laptop and kept playing from there. The first 35 hours of the game was absolutely amazing, and I was rejoicing in my EEVIL.
However, around the 30 hour point I noticed how easy the game seemed to be getting. Being the stereotypical arrogant gamer, I thought that was down to my epic skills and great build. I got lazy, thought the game was so easy, I only bothered to level up 3 characters, and the others were left in the dirt.
How wrong I was.
See, the first 35 hours or so are epic, but the ending of the game is unfinished. There are a lot of endless rooms with the same trash mobs. The restored content mod is a mixed blessing, because it brings back a lot of extra levels which feel very empty, as the devs only half-finished them and didn't put them in the game. By the 50 hour point, I was getting fed up. Just wanted it to be over.
Then came the HK factory. Oh boy. The goddamn HK factory is one of the half-finished levels put in by the restored content mod. It's in the ending sequence, so you can't back out once you've got there without losing hours of progress. Would usually be fine, but it turns out the HK factory is a solo mission. A solo mission for one of the characters I'd never bought gear for or levelled up. So I was stuck there. With a character with default starting armor, no weapons and no accessories. He has level 3 stuff, against endless level 23 trash mobs of EXACTLY the same enemy.
Let me get this straight, there are at least 100 enemy droids in the HK factory. Every single one of them was capable of oneshotting my character. He did like 10 damage to their health pools of 200+ HP with every shot. Whatever, I thought, I'll turn down the dificulty.
To my horror, when I opened up the options menu, I realised that when I transferred the game over to my laptop the difficulty settings had not transferred. I'd been playing the entire game on easy. This was as easy as it got. Oneshots and 10 damage per shot. It seemed impossible.
At this point, usually I would just laugh at myself and watch a let's play of the game's end. But for some reason I was determined to finish this game. It played me! I would get my revenge at any cost!
So I scraped together all the health potions I had and RAN through the HK factory level. If I got hit more than once, I'd have to start over again. It was absolute agony. I died so many times, as many rooms had 5+ enemies which could jump me at once. So I had to learn, gradually, the exact patterns I could run so that I could avoid taking the damage. It was the most pathetic I've felt playing a game. It took quite a few hours, and I was so close to giving up. But in the end, I did it. I suffered, but I did it. Upped and ran past every single enemy in that large level. And after doing that, I felt more satisfaction that I can ever remember feeling from playing a game - even after defeating Dark Souls bosses or something like that. I was rewarded by the game's real ending sequence (which is awesome).
I felt a warm glow of pride from being able to successfully run away from trash mobs on easy difficulty. 10/10 game is an emotional rollercoaster, would recommend the suffering to anyone.

Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic 2 is a tough nut to crack in terms of a good review.
The game was released too early and so there are still broken missions, to this day. It was also meant to be a build up for a third installment, which never came due to EA's Star Wars: The Old Republic which (and by trying to spoil as little as possible) leaves you with an incredibly bitter after taste when the credits roll after Knights of the Old Republic 2.
And yet, I replay it at least once a year and have done so since its release. Even though this sequal to the classic is a lot lazier in terms of character substance and campaign.
So, what is it that takes us back to this unfinished sequal of, what I think is, one of the best RPG's ever made?
Star Wars: Knights of the Republic 2 goes dark. There is no better way of saying it. While its predecessor let you choose the Dark Side for the sake of sadistic fun, Kotor 2 shows you what the force really is, and how little it means in the end to be a Jedi or a Sith.
I recall a particular moment, very simular to many from the first game, where a beggar comes up to you and ask for money. Choosing the Light Side option as I normally do, my Jedi gave the beggar a few credits and sent him on his merry way. I was given a few Light Side points for my kindness.
Then, a wild Treya appears.
Treya is an enigma, and the very first character you meet in the game. She will keep a close eye on you, be you Light side or Dark and right there, she shows you a vision of the man, and how he walks off to get himself a meal. She tells you that every action has its consiquence, followed by your vision of the man being robbed, and murdered. You gave him the money. You made him a target.
And this is the excellence of Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic 2. It goes further than option one and option two. This game will test you, not only as a player, but as a person. It has its bugs, to the points that it actually needs a MOD to even be playable on some machines, but if you get it running, and if you have the time to put into it, I strongly recomend this game.
To me, this is not only one of the very best RPG's, but one of the very finest storylines ever written.
May the force be with you.

In theory you can consult the game's built in hint system but it reveals more spoilers than help.
This is all a shame as the plot and character scripts are really, really, good. Playing it with a walkthrough close to hand I actually really enjoyed the story and some of the puzzles which didn't require too much hunting in huge 3D locations.
If you happen to be buying a bundle of Sherlock games then 'Testament', 'Silver Earring', or 'vs Arese Lupin' are worth about $10 each on their own so don't be put off by the inclusion of 'Awakened' but I wouldn't buy it alone.

"Holmes: Awakened" is a fairly strange story, because of its themes, and its characters.
At least Becker's in it...
Nevermind. You'll understand when you're older.
The game starts with you trying to solve the disappearance of a man's servant. From here, the game takes off, like
.
For a start, you get use what I like to call
; A standard feature carried in future Holmes games.
Basically, you press Shift and the screen highlights all the interactable elements available in the overworld.
No more scavenging for cloths, dirt and related objects! Just press the button and pick up the stuff.
Thematically, the game has various elements that differentiate it from previous games.
For example,
.
Not only do the characters give off their own vibe of individuality, but the Cthulu themes sure make the game ever so cryptic. Especially at the end. And that man who -- let's just say "chewed more than he could swallow".
So, characters are certainly novel, especially the disciples of The One, with their dillusional dialogue and behaviours (one guy was a cannibal). Other characters, like Lucy's employer, have certain quips and remarks that make them more memorable than others.
Interface is also an improvement, as they've included "teleportation" feature as valid travelling (unless a cutscene is required somewhere), which works by selecting a place on the map, and travelling there instantly. Plus, all dialogue between Holmes and Watson is recorded down, so you can save at a crucial moment, exit and return playing while
. Revolutional! I found this was a major issue back in "Holmes & the Silver Earring", as I'd spend about 10 minutes trying to find out what I was doing last play session.
Also, they've included an in-game guide, so whenever you get stuck
, you got some help nearby.
Very handy for some of the trickier puzzles. The good thing is that you can choose how much of the guide to look at, so if you want a small hint in the right direction, you can get a small peek at the solution process by clicking on the arrow a small number of times.
Watson is also a spooky character, sometimes.

In summary, a great improvement means a greater rating of 8/10.

Amnesia is, without any shred of a doubt, the most frightening game ever made. The combination of the audio and visuals give the game an atmosphere that makes practically everything seem scary. Unlike most other horror games, you don't have any weapons to fight back against any enemies, so your only way to not die is to run into the nearest room and pray that the enemy won't follow you. The objectives are never very complicated, but they all require you to make your way to a different location in the castle. Offworld Trading Company is a great game for anyone looking for challenging RTS that focuses on macromanagement and long-term thinking. There is no combat, only economics and markets! There is a lot of depth in gameplay, which requires a good player to be aware of a lot of variables in order to profit most effectively.
Offworld is a great RTS game that does not require intense focus on micromanagement, so I like to play a round or two if I'm too tired for games that require that kind of focus. Most games I've played are between 15 minutes and an hour long. Each game begins with founding an HQ, and gameplay revolves around generating enough profit to buy out your competitors, which are determined by market prices. These market prices change according to how the players act during the game and other map factors. The resources in the market are interconnected, so the way prices change can get very involved. For example, if food prices are high, you might want to produce food, but to do that you need water, so a competitor could drive the price of water up to lower your profit from food. You might combat this move by producing water yourself, but your opponent could go produce power, which you need to run your pumps and farms. Generally, it is very unprofitable to produce everything, so these relationships in the market make each game different but well-balanced.
There are other details to the game such as the black market (to buy things that slow down competitors), patents, optimization upgrades, market price hacking, and offworld launches. It's important to learn how to use these effectively, because Offworld is not like other RTS where you counter X with Y, which you counter with Z. Every situation in Offworld is different, where it might not even be the best strategy to produce what is most profitable at the moment, but to produce what will be profitable later in the game because no one is producing a resource that will be needed later. Long-term thinking is important for wins.
The AIs should give the player a good challenge through the beginning and middle stages of learning the game. I'm not sure what professional players think about the AIs, however.
Although Offworld is based on economics, don't expect the game mechanics to be exactly like real business. For example, you don't start by owning 100% of your own equity. These mechanics were implemented for balancing, so don't dwell too much on these "inaccuracies."
Offworld is a unique RTS game that deserves a bigger following.

It is a parts-gathering and puzzle-solving type game, ala Myst, but the puzzles are fairly simple and don't detract from the story.  If you're looking for a challenging game to eat up countless hours, this isn't that. Well this was a nice surprise. It is astonishing that a fundamentally complex simulation has been made both usable and fun. Not without some rough edges and a bit of a learning curve but after a few hours the positives are clear:
* Excellently-designed tutorial/progressive campaign that gradually unlocks new techniques at a fair and challenging pace.
* Workable interface for orbital maneuvers, deliberately familiar for KSP vets.
* Surprisingly good windowing interface, and honestly some good music and sound design too.
* Servicable graphics. No frills but good enough!
* Deep, realistic simulation with lots and lots of fascinating source material.
* Well-written, believable future history setting.
* Plausible and thought-out approach to the tactics of real spacewar that springs naturally out of the simulation. One example among many: too few nuclear missles in a flight can be picked off one by one, so you need to send a bunch at once -- but too many at once and they detonate each other before they can all do damage. Stuff like this is just mainline spaceporn and you gotta love that he not only thought this through but designed a game mechanic out of it.
The author's commitment to a realistic hard-science space-fightin' simulator just has to be rewarded. The fact that it's fun to play as well is almost too much. It's a brilliant marriage of simulation and gameplay. Must buy!

Woah, i hadn't heard anything about this until I saw a post on the KSP subreddit earlier today. The concept has definitely been on my "I wish there was a game like this" list though. Although the initial learning curve is perhaps not perfect (it does gradually introduce concepts and it wasn't hard for me to pick up - but if you haven't played KSP or otherwise gotten a feel for the basics of orbital dynamics it could be a bit rough) and the maneuver nodes are not as intuitive as KSP (although there are handy ways to auto calculate stuff like intercepts - just be warned they work best if you're already most of the way there.)
It definitely feels more like a simulator/toy/puzzle than a "game" per se (like, decisions were clearly not made from the perspective of encouraging a fun gameplay loop but rather to fit with what makes sense for the subject.) So I can definitely see it not appealing to everyone - even people who like KSP. But IF you've been interested in the idea of realistic space combat/read hard SF/etc, then it's definitely worth getting it. And if you've played KSP much the orbital mechanics are definitely easy to grasp even though it's using full n-body physics and not patched conics.
It did crash once on me at the end of a mission (but only once in the course of two hours, so i'm not too bothered.)
If you're the kind of person who is interested in this, and you should definitely know if you are, then I can say that i was not disappointed - and i haven't even gotten to the sandboxy bits yet, I'm just working my way through the campaign missions.
