THIS GAME ISN'T FOR EVERYBODY, and it really could have used a few weeks on Early Access to round off the edges.
First and foremost: I'm mostly liking the game so far, and I'll probably change this to a recommendation in the future, but as of the writing of this, the game has only 15 positive reviews and no negative ones, so I'll put an warning here before people think this is something it's not and we get a flood of bad reviews.
Some general points:
Graphics - Rendering realistic space battles isn't an excuse to not at least try to make it pretty. Sorry, but this game really needs a bit love from a 3D artist. I see your normal maps stored in JPG, and if any 3D artist see this they'll try to hang you. This game screams programmer graphics everywhere, and while I'm a programmer myself, this isn't excusable on a $25 title.
Interface - Generally quite well done and useable, but could use some more work on the finer points of orbital maneuvers, like being able to move the execution point of the maneuver to change the timing, and splitting fleets of drones/missiles after launch.
Sound - Pretty good sound effects and music in general, bit repetitive theme on the menu, but it works overall.
Setting - The story and science of the game is the reason you should be getting it, it's pretty well done and a lot of research went into making this game, and it shows.
So far I've played up to the 5th campaign mission, and enjoyed the first 4 quite a bit... On the 5th though, you are introduced to missiles, and they just aren't ready for release yet. The main problem is that the terminal guidance (and really, the guidance in general) can't get the job done and even if the target has had its rocket disabled, the missiles can't get a solid hit on the target ship, and much less anywhere near any priority target you set, which makes you being able to finish the mission totally random.
Overall, if you like Rocketry, has a general sense of how orbital mechanics works and like realistic simulations, this game is for you, but you might want to wait a bit and see if the rough edges are polished down first. If you can't get a rocket built and on orbit in KSP, you're probably better off passing this one.

After
, I thought myself quite accustomed to hard science. I was in for a hypervelocity slug to the face.
is an attempt by Zane Mankowski (alias
) to determine what realistic space combat would look like by creating a number of subsystem models based on real-life publicly available engineering data, and then handing them to a bunch of playtesters. The final version comes with a range of premade systems and ships, of course, but the ability to build everything to your specification is a key selling point. If you know what “q-switched” is, it’s a good start, but you’re still going to run into a whole mass of hard science, as you fine-tune chemical and nuclear rockets, cannons, railguns, coilguns, lasers and even good old shrapnel warheads.
The other key selling point is the hard sci-fi space combat. The game uses N-body simulation of orbital mechanics – thus you’re looking at some counterintuitive maneuvering in order to just get into combat – and is largely set in the asteroid belt and the gas giants’ moons, hence disabling stationkeeping and allowing your trajectory to be perturbed alone can be used to foul up your enemy’s fancy plans. Your maneuvering is limited by Δv budgets. Combat occurs at high relative velocities; contact can be very brief; distances are still quite large – hence the battles are quite hectic.
Beware that this game is likely to ruin all of the soft sci-fi for you, permanently. If you’re a fan of
site, this game is mandatory; if you’re a fan of
, there will be no coming back from the Hard Side.
The game uses a quasi-turn-based system for strategic maneuvering – with steps from one hour to several days that are quite necessary for skipping through uneventful orbiting. Once anything happens, the game snaps to attention. In Inspection Mode – where the most you see is your drones being released – or if a hostile force makes contact with yours the game reverts to real time, and doesn’t let you to take turn-style steps until the fireworks happen.
I dare say the game is not particularly user-friendly, forgoing ease of control and decluttering in favour of giving maximum under-the-hood control. Wanna plate your spacecraft into 10 m of solid gold? Sure, but you’re going to have to skim through 20 lines of physical qualities of gold to conclusively find out why it sucks as armour. You can also use that gold for gun barrels, and virtually anything else; just don’t expect any good results outside,
, coilguns. Wanna take your drones into battle? Be sure to watch their fuel levels, lest they will burn out of it. Ships have all too few control options.

The combat is variative enough, although lack of planetary bases/bombing/defence and AI (which is limited to encounters) hurt the tactical potential of the game a bit. But I'm only ~6 hours into the game so I guess it might change later. The game can be somewhat hard to learn for people unfamiliar with orbital mechanics, despite of having the tutorial. Assuming you understand the basics, the interface is clear/friendly enough.
I can definitely recommend this to any hard sci-fi fans or those who want a military tactical combat game.

First off, this IS a good game... BUT is very harsh with stock actions speeds, durability and certain recipe requerments IF you are playing alone or with a few friends. Second, I AM NOT a programmer and everything I know about scripts is from browsing the forums for info about this game. I believe the developers would have been smart implement a quick and easy menu screen to make it easier to customize the gameplay and game speed but unfortunately they haven't. If you heard it is a CRAB game, you might be right. Crabs move sideways, too :-)
Going far off the beaten turn-based tracks, this game requires some different tactics than the 'normal' games.
The interface is functional, you should check the key bindings to speed things up considerably.
How tough is it? Well, there is a steep learning curve and the AI is quite challenging once you passed the tutorial. This is mostly due to the special attacks from some mobs that are tricky to calculate and keep at bay. Don't think the AI is stupid because it moves his units around aimlessly at the start of a fight. This is only masquerade to make you think it's easy as taking candy from a baby. Believe me, IT IS NOT.
Once you get some special troops yourself, the tactics get quite complicated. Lots of options, lots of possibilities.
Someone compared it to chess, but that's a bit farfetched, since chess has no random factors. But playing chess helps in some situations, since the tactics are related, like setting up blockades and winning by attrition.
Lots of quests to do, big game world, good clan system, friendly developers (often online in the game) and a cool boss who likes to curse the internet establishment. I like this :-)
So, my thumbs up for this F2P game, try it for about 3-4 hours and decide for yourself.
Update: after reaching level 10, it gets very 'grindy' and tedious. The fights are often influenced by (bad) luck, like your healers healing ridiculous HP or your full-blown two-handed sword doing minimal damage. Higher level mobs are blessed with hard-hitting units, often decorated with lots of HP, making fights with all your fighters surviving hard to achieve. Bad thing is your items get damaged when a fighter falls, and repairs can be costly. In addition, some guildies do not understand coop mechanics and solo the fights, so it's basically a single-player game.
The AI is kinda dumb at these levels, mostly relying on superior gear and luck to cause damage.
PVP: the 'cashcow' part is ofc the PVP where you can take on other human players. Problem is there are some long-existing guilds with high-ranked players.
These like to plunder your guild hall and kill your guards, and if you don't have the right gear (purchasable for silver which is purchasable for bucks) and/or the matching transmuted fighters, the fights are, well, lost for you.
The developers are aware of this, but since the buck-spenders are business, don't care too much.
The last update brought guild territories, giving the old guilds an even bigger advantage.
I decided to quit at this point, since progress is really slow and it would take ages (or bucks) to enjoy the PVP part.
Final rating: still thumbs up, but don't play it for the PVP part if you don't wanna invest a little more bucks than expected.

Why have I not done a review for Siege yet?  Oh well, here I go.
So, the actual game itself is, well, amazing.  It is hands down my favorite FPS of all time.....wait.  Scratch that.  It is hands down my favorite VIDEO GAME of all time.  I love this game……okay, got that out of the way.....now I can get into the specifics.
The first and most important thing you must understand about this game before you purchase - It is a team based game.  Are you looking for a run and gun game like COD, or a tactical shooter?  Siege is the latter, a tactical team based shooter, although some choose to treat it as a run and gun (Jager scum!).  You have to be willing to work as a team with other people to succeed at Siege.  No it's not as team based as Squad or Arma, but SOME team coordination is absolutely needed.  At least if you want that sweet elo.
The second most important thing to understand before you purchase - YOU WILL SUCK/THERE IS A LOT TO LEARN.  Yeah, you will suck.  Really, I mean you will hate this game.  You will get rekt for AT LEAST a month before you become DECENT.  This is part of the reason why personally I love this game, it has THE highest skill ceiling I've ever seen in a game.  I have been playing this game since the week it came out (early December 2015) on both console and PC, and there are STILL new tactics and things I am learning.....STILL.  I guarantee you will HATE this game for the first week you play, but you will love it at the same time.  Its difficulty will drive you to get better and better.  You have never played anything like Siege before.  "I've played plenty of tactical shooters, thank you very much" you might say.  Kewl bruh, but you've never played Siege before.  Siege does not abide by the typical FPS/Tactical shooter laws.  It abides by the Laws OF Siege.  Because despite what you may have thought, this game IS NOT an FPS.  This game is NOT a tactical shooter.  This game is Siege.  There is nothing like it.  Sure, you need good aim, but you must do much more to win.  You'll barricade and reinforce certain rooms and walls to slow the attacker's push.  You'll determine what barricades and reinforcements to destroy to push the defenders.  You'll setup flank routes, watch for peeks, drone out rooms, and lay traps in choke points.  You will not simply shoot people.  You will distract, bait, and outsmart people.  And occasionally.........well you'll get team killed by a toxic salt mine BUT HEY IT HAPPENS SOMETIMES.
Unfortunately, Siege has some flaws too.  Well……no it doesn’t.  The GAME itself is perfect, at least to me it is.  But BOY does Ubisoft cause a lot of problems for it.  There’s a really annoying bug that needs to be fixed?  Okay, just wait ten years, we’ll fix it.  Aaaaaand done, bug is fixed.  Now here’s 20 new bugs to accompany this bug fix.  Oh, you all want more/better servers?  Okay, we’ll roll that out in 14 years, but look at IQ’s finger nails now we’ve improved their texture!
Yes, it is sad, but this amazing game has a fair share of bugs and problems.  It runs fine, in fact (I think) it’s one of the best optimized PC ports I’ve ever played, but alas, the bugs.  Hit registration problems will make you scream HOW WAS THAT NOT A HEADSHOT?!?!?  Lack of enough servers will make you wonder why you have to play against Brazilian ping abusers. And for god’s sake, ASH’S HITBOX!
Now I don’t want to exaggerate, with all the technical problems this game has, it is still probably in the best shape it has ever been in.  But still, the game is almost two years old now.  It should be (near) perfect by now, yet it feels like a new release that’s still getting its kinks ironed out.
But with all the frustration these problems bring, there’s a reason why I have a $1,500 gaming PC capable of playing literally anything, but still only play this one single game and nothing else.
So in conclusion, GET IT.  NOW.   (Just please don’t get the startup edition, it’s a rip off)

Ugh...I wanna be nicer to this game, but the last bit of it left such a bad taste in my mouth.  Okay, short version.  Basic mode is pretty fun save for the last ten minutes, when it gets frustrating.  The New game + mode is sadistically hard and not worth my time, or probably yours.  If you can put that aside, buy it on sale, it's pretty cool.
Long version. Nihilumbra is an interesting puzzle platformer that uses colors and properties associated with them to create some interesting situations.  Ice, fire, and electricity, as well as bouncing, play just like you think they will, but they get a bit clever with the color for stickiness.  It's got an interesting aesthetic, very pleasant music, and a decent curve of challenge, except for the last ten minutes where the final levels get stupid annoying and feel poorly designed.  The new game + mode is sadistaclly hard in all the worse ways and is not worth my time.  The narration can feel a bit forced since it's everywhere in the game and it does a lot of telling rather than showing, but it's forgivable.  This game could have been much better, but I've also played much worse.
Give this a look if you want a decent puzzle platformer that uses the mouse controls to create some interesting world affecting situations.  It's pretty short, unless you're a masochist who wants to try Void mode, so get it on sale.  This and Camera Obscura are what I would call almost there indie games.  Good concept, fairly decent story and level design that unfortunately does more telling than showing, needed more polish. They don't stand up with games like Bastion, Stardew Valley, or Jamestown, but these kinds of games are fun for what they are.  They won't blow minds, but are agreeable enough to get through.
I had fun with it, for a bit.  Maybe you will too.

I don't write reviews on Steam often. This game is one of my exceptions. KOTOR II may also be my favorite Star Wars story. The movies are great, so is KOTOR I, and I highly recommend them as well, however KOTOR II is very much the Dostoevsky to their Stephen King, forgive the dorky literary analog. One is entertaining, whereas the other makes you think. KOTOR II is, on the surface, a rather standard RPG. You're railroaded from point A to B through various locales, picking up side quests, and trying to beat the Big Bad. Standard♥♥♥♥♥♥honestly. Where the game excels is in how this is presented. Rather than the standard adventure approach we are so used to, KOTOR II instead takes the chance to tell a dark, ambiguous, and complex tale exploring betrayal, anger, hope, apathy, revenge, the nature of good and evil, the nature of the Force, the complexity of human emotions, relationships, loss, and most importantly, finding out who you are. This is not in the sense we explore in KOTOR I, for those of you who've played it. This is not the tale of an amnesiac, it is the tale of a broken man/woman who has been repeatedly betrayed by everyone, and everything they've trusted. It's the tale of someone trying to find meaning for themselves in a world that has repeatedly stolen meaning from them. Even as you make the choices for your Jedi, man or woman, good or evil, Consular or Sentinel, it all ingeniously boils down to who this character is. You can help define them, but unlike the MC of KOTOR I, the history truly means something more than an interesting twist, or a way to move along plot. It starkly defines all that you do, from beginning to end in ways that require you to question every action you make. This might be one of few games out there, where being the good guy can still make you feel like♥♥♥♥♥♥by the end of the game. As the game so splendidly relates, all that you do has an effect, both seen and unseen, and how neither extreme, light or dark, can be wholly considered right or wrong. Even after all of that I'm nowhere near describing the amazing characters, quest-lines, quotes, philosophical dialogue, and beautiful moody/dark feeling of looming doom, and ambiguity that is summoned by the central plot of this game. Just go out and buy the damn game! It's awesome, and if you're tired of the same old copy and paste characters, and horrendous or uninspired dialogue that saturates most RPG's, look no further. The game is a masterpiece! As a quick side note, get the TSLRCM mod, the base game is good, but sadly Obsidian, as is often the case with them, had a tight deadline, and couldn't make the game as bug free, nor as filled with content as they intended. The mod adds a lot of cut content, including a new planet (It isn't huge, or filled with tons more quests, so don't get too excited.), fixes several game breaking, or quest breaking bugs, and generally just irons out a lot of issues the initial release had.

I started Frogware's Sherlock Holmes series in chronological order of the games. Currently, this is my favorite Sherlock Holmes game. I have always been a fan of H.P. Lovecraft  in addition to Sherlock Holmes. The only way to make it even better is to include H. G. Wells to the mix, but I digress. This game set the standard of how the rest of the Sherlock Holmes Adventure Games are presented and produced. The story walks a fine line between the two worlds of H.P. Lovecraft and Sherlock Holmes and surprisingly the resolution is satisfy for both worlds. The adventure felt like Sherlock Holmes was on the case while the Lovecraftian themes never felt like a gimic. When I finished I sat back and pondered if the Lovecraftian themes were real or not; which is how Lovecraft should make the reader, or in this case the player, feel.
This is also the fist Sherlock Holmes game where I took extensive notes with a pen and paper. I am not saying that the game presents a bad summary of the clues or even that you need to take physical notes, but I found that it was more enjoyable when I did. I never felt, atleast to my memory, that the game was unfair with its puzzles or logic.
Furthermore, refrences will appear from this game to the next game in the series, Sherlock Holmes - Nemisis. So to fulfill that experiance you should probably play this one.
In summary: This game does a fantastic job combining H.P Lovecraft and Sir Arthur Conan Doyle's worlds. This is a rare game which uses Lovecraft correctly, which will please any Lovecraft fans. Buy this game if you are a fan of either litature. I also suggest this game to individuals who would like to try Frogware's Sherlock Holmes Adventure series but are not sure which game to start with. This game is a great Point and Click game with a strong atmosphere. I at this time of writing palyed this game for 9 hours, and after writing this review I want to replay this game from the beginning.

This game, this game....now I understand where the “average rating” scored came from and here's why.
I played the first game and gave it a review; it was a good standard star wars space opera game that had good story, characters and good gameplay. When I bought the sequel I thought it would be epic but no, it felt more on the lines of average. Probably slightly below average but average is what I most felt it.
The story here had potential it really does! It builds up to this sense hype of the reveal. As you start to progress from the story you meet this old Jedi name Kreia and you start having this bond between you and her as apprentice master, you start noticing that the Sith is back (not big surprise honestly) and you must convince the Jedi order to join your side but it will be difficult because of your exile from the Order that you had committed.
It felt so exciting but it began slowly with plot holes that make no sense, like leaving the mining field and suddenly boom! Sith just appear right out of nowhere in the mine facility, those moments you swear you feel you miss watching some cut scenes. Not to mention the ending where it leaves you a cliffhanger and you just ask what happen to this certain event, or why is he important to the certain role that at the end you forgot about him in the first place. All of this doesn’t explain and it acts that kotor 3 will come “for the truth” which honestly doesn’t deserve that excuse for an easy explanation to the minor plot holes (especially of how nice the revelation came to be.) Not only that but certain moments of the game you feel a rush of excitement when combat starts but in moments where you think the “badass” comes, it falls flat. Sometimes those moments are good but sometimes there are weak moments I can’t explain why they didn’t pursue those moments to be epic once, maybe budget or time cuts?
Now don’t get me wrong, there are now many new aliens in kotor 2 and they have improved on the human models to not look the same all the time. No, I am talking about your AI companions, they aren’t that bad is just that first I notice that most of the personality they act comes from the previous characters from kotor 1, I don’t know if is me but I swear Atton is like a copy of Carth, but much annoying, his back story doesn’t even help liking him more. As for the rest of the characters I don’t find them as much of a connection as to my old crew, for one thing the new “trust” system looks good at first but then certain dialogues tend to repeat themselves if not few, so there is not much of open conversation unless I’m missing something? The worst thing about your companions is that half of them are useless on their purpose to "follow you", Mira and especially G0-T0 is the worst offenders because their existence is absolute pointless, they could just be easily set aside as quest favors or temporarily companions, those characters I stumble upon almost at the end of the game, which by the time I go for the final mission I forgot I can select this character she/he decide to tag along.
There are few new characters I sort of fond of like Visa a blind Sith who seeks the truth of your adventure and Kreia, an interesting wise old (yet selfish she seems within her reason) Jedi who wants to lead the protagonist to the right path, at least in her view. The technician and finally the always fan favorite HK-47 who is now I think funnier than ever before especially if you give him the Pacific chip, you will get a chuckle out of him. You can always influence your partners to be good or bad depends of your Force meter and even train them to be Jedi padawans! Though their attitudes don’t change only when enough “trust” and finish some certain dialogue you can teach them of the force, that’s all.
How about the villains they are great right! Well….one of them, Sith Sion looks so cool with its corpse shape body, don’t feel any pain and just want death! The other with a haunted mask, um…what’s his name again? Half of the play through I completely forgot his name, he had potential he looks like a badass next level villain going on, he is a leech that sucks up the Force and drains it out until the person is dead is sounds so cool-if we get more scenes out of him! Back story I don’t know much about except when I look in Kotor 2 wiki to know more about the guy and I only know little of him in the game, the comic seems to show a bit more backstory and shows more of an actual intimidating villian. Sadly in the game he is an underrated villain that gets a few lines and screenshots like Darth Maul and not the full extend potential this guy could have been. I love him and Sion and I want him to have as much attention as he had but I guess the comic should make it up for it.
Sadly they dumb down the “moral meter” like if you're going for light side, yes you have good moments with people you met but the major characters that will judge you near the end, nope they will treat you like a monster and at the end your effect will be “good” but only through story telling instead of seeing the effects. Want to be dark side, be a prick to everyone with no reason and the major characters will see you the same monster they still sees in you and at the end your effects, same thing story telling that you "feel" the horrid impact but the effect is less than when you are good, show don’t tell is always important. Especially in the “trust” system your partners morals are really one sided, like one of the good character calls you out on doing something bad but next mission she slaughter innocent characters and even encourage the players to do so. There is the flaw of the trust system the inconsistent character moral placements, it just do what it wants to nag you and the characters will have no impact if you did something terribly wrong, they would not question nor abandon you or any, though if you go to the dark side you will get more dark side characters than it is light side characters, but it is the same. Bad characters don’t react on your good behavior on some missions but in one particular simple mission they would go all out on you.

Gameplay is nice and it adds a few elements to it like crafting, new force powers, new partner trust system, they are good but it feels like this game had been rush like it could have add more than just a few treats and that’s what most people had an issue with. Not only cut contents but the bugs is everywhere!  I spot many dialogue glitch problems when talking to an NPC, not to mention some scenes will froze itself or don’t do anything, it is frustrating. Thankfully and I can’t believe I haven’t realize the existing of it, but there is a very good mod called “the sith lord restored content modification (I will link it at the end of the review) it fixes “most” of the issues even add some of the plot holes that was missing, it is like the actual sequel to Kotor 2. At its “vanilla” state I will give a 5/10 (I wish steam has a medium choice option, but as for vanilla state is a no option, but the mod defiinatly a yes on improvment) it had potential but for the “holiday rush” it did show the end result of bugs, missing contents the works. But for the restored mod content if I played it again fully, it could get a 6 or maybe 7 out of 10 but as of now I am moving on to other games so hopefully when I have the time and energy I will play the full version, is a must have to get the full experience.

Nihilumbra has a defined art style, strives for narrative, and deals whimsically with depression. But its narrative does come off as a touch preachy and its narrator is not entirely interesting. There’s also the problem of game play. Nihilumbra is a puzzle platformer with few solid puzzles and irritating platforming that consists of predetermined stages of play. These areas shift as you move along instead of the screen following your character. It’s off-putting at first then it becomes truly annoying as you die to enemies situated directly out of your view or you have to take leaps of faith. The game doesn’t advertise itself with the game play though, but ultimately what it does claim to have falls short. There is great potential here, but it simply falls short for me personally.
Nihilumbra has a good name, interesting art, and a nice soundtrack… That’s about it really. If you like those things go for it. If not, I can’t recommend it. If you're looking for a similar, more flushed out expirance I suggest you look at titles like: Oxenfree, The Stanley Parable, The Beginner’s Guide, Firewatch, Event(0), Undertale and, most specifically, Thomas Was Alone. See, Thomas Was Alone does everything this game wanted to do, but excelled. Where can be Nihilumbra predicatable, Thomas Was Alone had me guessing all the way. Where Nihilumbra suffer’s from poor gameplay, Thomas excels. Where Nihilumbra falls short of my expectation Thomas surpasses them all.

Roughly five years ago, I got my hands on the first Knights of the Old Republic, which also happened to be my first introduction into the RPG genre of gaming. That game gave me such a wonderful experience and didn't think any other game could capture the atmosphere and great story I experienced, considering I was and still am, a huge Star Wars fan. However, at the time, when I looked up Knights of the Old Republic II: The Sith Lords, the overall opinion from the gaming community was to avoid this unfinished, rushed, and bug-ridden game. Years later, I come across an article stating how a dedicated community of modders bravely took on the challenge to restore a great number of content left out of the vanilla game. It is thanks to the people behind the Restored Content Mod (also known as the TSLRCM) that I was able to sink my teeth into this highly anticipated sequel nearly forgotten. Knights of the Old Republic II: The Sith Lords does several things right. For one, the interface feels more intuitive to use and arguably a sharper UI design compared to the first game’s UI. Beyond some minor UI tweaks, however, what truly shines are the companions, and the significance of your main character. I will not spoil anything here, but what I will say is that for the most part, many of your companions have this sense of layered depth. They have flaws, they have hidden and traumatic pasts, they have regrets, they have strengths, humor, and usually comment on what your main character does when applicable. It’s not to say the first KOTOR didn’t have great characters because it certainly did, but KOTOR II definitely has the leg up with the introduction of the Influence System.
The Influence System adds an additional layer to the game by allowing you to experience consequences whenever you interact with your companions when it comes to the dialogue you choose as well the decisions you make. This gameplay element makes multiple playthroughs quite appealing, as you choose which companions(s) to focus more over the others, as it’s difficult to cater to all your companions on one playthrough, not to mention the obvious Light and Darkside paths to explore.
It should be of note that KOTOR II offers a less thrilling Star Wars experience, and instead offers a more personal and critical view on the Force, the Jedi, Sith, and on your actual character as well. Personally, as a Star Wars fan, I found this change of atmosphere completely engaging. Chris Avellone, the lead writer/developer, wasn’t initially blinded by personal attachment to Star Wars; an outsider’s take on the franchise we know and love, gave us fans an unique and fresh perspective rarely explored in the main movies.
I am conflicted how to properly review this game without mentioning the ending. It does still suffer from being rushed and not fully realized due to limited information and resources about how it should have had ended. Yet, oddly enough, I was not bothered by the way it ended, to a degree. For instance, I personally think the conclusion ends on a somber, yet somewhat satisfying note if I chose the Lightside. I knew what my character was going to do, and basically made more sense story wise. However, on the Darkside, it definitely feels much to be desired and I am not impressed of how it ends. This is overall a difficult subject to review, as it tends to be highly polarizing among gamers, understandably. If nothing else, I still highly recommend this game simply because the actual meat of the game, its characters and fresh take on the Star Wars universe, makes this game stand out and arguably more compelling than its predecessor. It ultimately comes down to what you want out of a Star Wars game; an epic heroic (or villainy) adventure full of badass moments, or do you mind a more personal, character-centric, “all about the journey and not the destination” type of story?

I want to preface this by saying I have played OOTP16 for over 200 hours, and gave it a glowingly positive review. Great improvement over OOTP16. The only issue I had with '16 was the slow sim times and overall lagginess of the game. It takes a matter of minutes to sim an entire season in '17, and I find myself spending 99% of my play time making decisions and playing the game rather than waiting for the game to load. The other major improvement I see is the "needs" you can set. It prevents all of those, "I'll give you my 76 year old $30mil/yr first baseman for Chris Sale" type trade offers you would get in previous versions. Now you get offers that are only in the area you want them to be in. I find myself accepting far more trades offered to me by the AI teams than last year.
I suspect that the game has messed with many "under the hood" details as the progression of young players, AI evaluations of players (it seems like prospects are valued wildly different by teams), overall player rating changes seem to be much different in this version. However, take that with a grain of salt as I cannot confirm this is the case. If these changes did occur I like them quite a lot, and you can consider this another positive change.
The only negative thing I can say about this game is the price. For me, the $40 is well spent for the faster load times alone. If you don't mind waiting, I would advise you to not purchase this version, as the changes outside of the performance boost don't warrant a full-price purchase.
Overall, this version of the game had little tweaks, and a huge performance boost, along with updated 2017 MLB rosters. If you liked the previous version, you'll like the new faster version even better.

Currently only played through the first 5 missions, but I can tell it's everything I wanted from it. Scratches my itch for a hard-sci-fi space combat simulator, with highly detailed space flight physics model. Think Kerbal Space Program but in a more turn based setting, except for when you enter combat where it turns into a more tactical combat game, with all the intricacies of what near-future space combat would actually be like.
Weapons are sufficiently varied including lasers, cannons, railguns, missiles, drones, and nukes. The complicated damage model on the spacecrafts' armor and systems makes up for the fact that you don't have much control of individual ships during combat(one of the few shortcomings, but understandable) due to the beautiful way combat looks with tracer rounds bouncing all around your target and each individual damage mark being displayed.
The fact that there is no sound in space also adds to the atmosphere, with the only sounds being heard are essentially what the crew would hear, with the groans of the structure stressing from repeated impacts and decompression of the crew module by a puncture.
The reading material between missions provides some moderately interesting backstory on the world and factions and the basics of space navigation.
I would reccomend it if you are at all interested in advanced space flight and combat mechanics and don't mind the kind of high price point.

This game is everything I've been wanting in "realistic" space combat.  Imagine Kerbal but with non-fantasy weapons, and a pretty decent campaign of scenarios.  This game is NOT easy.  You'll have to get your head around real-world physics, because there is no flying by the seat of your pants.  Everything is a plotted intercept course, and the extremely limited amount of fuel the ships can carry means it's as much a puzzle game as anything.  It's all about timing and altering your orbit to put your ship in position to fire at the enemy.  Intersecting ellipses and last moment course correction burns.  Some ships are carriers for drones, so you use the carrier to line up the intercept and then let the drones burn their own fuel while you stay out of gun range yourself.
This is all very plausible.  The closest I've ever seen this elsewhere is Ken Burnside's "Attack Vector Tactical" board game.  This is NOT Star Trek.  I sincerely hope the developers continue to expand on this game, keep making scenarios, and maybe figuring out how to get some multiplayer into the next iteration. Disclaimer: Received for free during the game's testing phase. Sure, I'm not completely neutral towards this, but this does not mean I was "paid" to give a positive review.
Short version:
CDE is, simply put, a hard-fi space combat simulation I never thought would be made. If you enjoy games like Kerbal Space Program, spacecraft in general, or simply like sci-fi and are looking for something with a bit more detail, have a look at this.
-Gameplay:
The game is very detailed. Everything, from orbital mechanics, to missile fragmentation, to impacts on armour, is managed by a precise physics simulation. As far as actual gameplay goes, the game features a linear campaign with varied missions (some are orbital “puzzles”, some intense fleet battles), as well as a sandbox mode.
When in a mission, there are two separate phases. A turn-based “strategic” phase, focusing on orbital manoeuvres, and a real-time “tactical” phase where actual combat takes place.
Space combat is obviously very different from usual sci-fi strategy games, but it has a lot of depth to it.
There is also a ship editor and module editor. The ship editor is straightforward, but the module editor has a sharper learning curve, and a bit more documentation wouldn't hurt. But even if you prefer not to use those editors, the default ship selection has a lot of variety and is certainly enough to complete the full campaign.
The game is very replayable : getting high scores on the campaign can be a challenge, and the editors and sandbox mode givs a lot of additional playtime.
-Atmosphere
Outside of some great lighting effects, the graphics are not anything special, but the gameplay itself makes that a non-issue. The ships themselves have a unique style.
The story is surprisingly good. Briefings and additional notes explain the game's conflict in a way that makes sense, and there are a few unexpectedly serious thoughts about war in general. This story is not the most central part of the game, but it certainly adds a lot to the experience.
There is also a pretty good soundtrack that fits the atmosphere well.
-Developer:
Qswitched, the game's dev, is very active. He has been very listening during closed testing, and has fixed many of the issues highlighted during this phase.
Support continues, and there are gameplay expansions planned in the future.
Overall, CDE is a great game with amazing potential, and  I would definitely recommend it.

-=ORIGINAL REVIEW=-
So after logging about an hour of the game, this is what I gotta say so far...
PROS:
- Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ it's about time that the gaming market has gotten a game like this. Hard sci-fi fans have been denied a game that they can seriously dig their number-crunching teeth into for YEARS.
- Controlling your ships is very easy and convenient.
- Combat is really fun to watch, and really does highlight all the reasons why practical and realistic space combat is really cool.
- I love the worldbuilding and story that is in this game. I really appreciate that the game also comes with an area where I can simply read over who the different factions are, and what the system's history entails.
- SANDBOX MODE, YEAAAAHHHH!!! SUCK IT, MWO! THIS GAME ACTUALLY HAS A SANDBOX MODE.
- The soundtrack~ Aw yis, this is a very good soundtrack. Not too in-your-face to be distracting, but also active enough to not be boring. The various synths are constructed really well, and are generally very satisfying to listen to. The drums are a very interesting choice, given the theme of the game, but any alternative I would have picked would have been way too aggressive or electronic, and thus distract the player.
- The sound design is really excellent as well. Similar to the soundtrack, it sits between two extremes very nicely, giving that extra bit of feedback without being annoying. (Here, I'm looking at a few games in particular where the sound of your mouse going over a menu button is some super-obnoxious beep that never seems to stop haunting you. This game doesn't have that; it won't haunt you in your sleep.)
- SpeakING OF SOUND DESIGN: NO SOUND IS SPACE, CAN I GET A HELL YES??
- Can I also mention that the actual GAMEPLAY is really unique as well? It kinda works as an real-time and turn-based hybrid, giving you time to think when you need it, but still remaining within a constantly-moving universe.
- Orbital mechanics: yes. Just yes. No botchy estimations. We actually get full physical simulations of orbits, with all the fun traits it brings. We even get to choose our frame of reference, which is really nice.
- I have yet to find a bug in the game.
- Tutorial is included and very clear, thank the galaxy.
CONS:
- I'm really used to the mouse rotating in another direction when I drag it a certain way. It would be really nice to have an option where we can invert certain dragging directions.
- I feel like this is a game that a lot of Hollywood fans are gonna attack because they don't understand what it's actually trying to accomplish here. I'm trying to spread news of this game as far and wide as I can to all the hard sci-fi nerds I know, because this game deserves to have an awesome fanbase.
I may post another review as I get more hours into this, because I invariably will.

FULL DISCLOSURE:  This game was awarded for free for participation in the closed beta.
What is Children of a Dead Earth?
Well, it's like a few other games, but that doesn't do it justice.
It's part Kerbal Space Program (Physics-accurate rocketry sim)
It's part Command: Modern Air and Naval Operations (Fleet-scale strategy game at a realistic scale)
It's part Rule the Waves (warship design with realistic constraints)
and it's part Nuclear Engineering Degree.
So what is it really?
CODE (because it's much easier to type than Children of a Dead Earth) is a fleet-scale strategy game set in the middling-future where, as you might have guessed from the title, we've managed to accidentally break the Earth.  The backstory has something about World War 3 causing a complete ecological collapse, so humanity is scattered to the rest of the solar system.  That's about as much plot as I'm going to get into right now because let's be frank; the story is just an excuse for spaceships to shoot each other.  Oh, it's well-thought-out, and is an interesting read, but it's not really central to the game save as window dressing on why you're shooting lasers and railgun slugs at the other guy.
It is single-player only, with a series of story-driven missions and a sandbox mode.  There are also ship and subsystem design modules unlocked through the campaign, with the mission after each unlock virtually requiring you to play with these modules to succeed.
And it is, near as I can tell, 100% accurate to the physics of space warfare.  I suggest you go over to Atomic Rockets and do some studying if you're at all interested in this game, it will serve you well.
The missions have a variable-length turn-based feel to them, where you plan maneuvers similaar to KSP and set the clock to advance by a certain amount (interrupted if, say, you get close enough to shoot or the enemy launches drones or missiles) with actual combat being real-time and frantically fast.  don't expect micro to do you a lot of good, most enounters are over, one way or another, in under a minute, usually substantially shorter.  High closing speed means a quick flyby engagement which may or may not be decisive (but usually are.  Space warships are eggshells equipped with thermonuclear sledgehammers.)
Ship and module design is painstaking.  It doesn't make you lay out fuel lines and power conduits, but you will be expected to provide radiators for your heat-generating components, supply sufficient power generation, and shield your crew from engine radiation.  You have a LOT of options for armor, how many layers of what thickness and what composition (thin aluminum sheets for whipple shields as defense against high velocity railguns, thicker ceramics to shrug off lasers, and harder metals to turn aside slower but heavier coilgun or gunpowder-fired projectiles, for example) and several built-in options for weapons and engines each with advantages and diadvantages (for example, methane or decane as a propellant may not have the specific impulse of hydrogen deuteride, but it's a lot denser letting you make your ships much smaller and therefore less expensive in terms of mass to armor.)
Module design is going to require you to study some material on the physics of lasers, nuclear reactors, nuclear thermal rockets, railguns, coilguns, and what have you.  It is unlocked significantly later in the campaign than the ship design.
Is it worth it?
Well, I've logged almost 60 hours in the game over the past month.  I'll be honest, this game is extremely niche, but if you salivate reading articles on Atomic Rockets or have ever played and enjoyed a game of Attack Vector: Tactical (a hard-science tabletop wargame ALSO highly inspired by Atomic Rockets) or wish KSP let you shoot at other ships...  You'll probably enjoy it.  For everyone else, the learning curve is rather more like an overhang cliff you must climb with no safety gear.
Can I find out if I enjoy the game within the refund period?
Honestly?  Probably not.  The design modules unlock way too late in the game for you to be able to try them out before you've hit the end of the two-hour refund period.  You'll get to shoot at ships before then though, and that might provide you some clues as to whether you'd find the rest enjoyable.  That said, I'm glad the design modules unlock after you've had sopme practical playtime.
What would you change about the game?
The ability to do slow-mo replays of battles for battle-damage assessment.  Some guided tutorials through the design modules, especially for NTRs.
Is it as-advertised?
Exactly as it says on the tin.
Did you receiving this game for free affect your oinion?
That's a silly question, of course it did.  Though, being involved in the beta, I've seen both the good and the bad.
What about your system specs?
I've played it on both my gaming PC desktop (which is a few years behind the curve) and on my more function-over-entertainment macbook, and both run the game acceptably if I'm not stupid about graphics settings on the laptop.  Certain features in certain missions can cause significant slowdown, (orbit predictions with reference targets where deep gravity wells are concerned, significant numbers of missiles [like, a hundred or more])

Overall, I would just barely recommend this game.
At this point I have only finished the story mode, I have yet to try Void mode, but I wanted to center my review on the base game first.
The first three colours you receive are fun, and slightly reminiscent of Element41, which is a game I really enjoyed. But the last two seemed like they had a vision for the game based on 5 colours and no ideas left. There could also be a much easier way to switch between colours, like using the number keys or cycling through using q and e.
That coupled with what I thought was really weird voiceover work (both the voice acting and the writing) were the two main flaws of the game. The voiceover sounds like the guy from truck commercials trying to sound omniscient and he just came off sounding kinda bored. What made matters worse, voiceover-wise, was the writing. I would say the writing is by far the weakest facet of the game. It's too explanatory. What makes games like Element41 great to play was the simplicity in the explanation, and they didn't overuse the voice to further the plot. Nihilumbra felt the need to explain every metaphor to death and back.
Now for the positives:
The level design was interesting, especially towards the end where there could have been a few different ways to use the colours to move ahead in the level. The atmosphere is very neat, and the creatures from the void had some cool designs.
All in all, I don't regret buying this game on sale for $2.39, I'm not sure I would pay the full $7.99 list price for it as a relatively poor person. Get it on sale if you can, see if you like it.

Although this game is from 2005, it is definitely worth playing. The 2005 graphic's are a bit chunky. The control's are simple, make sense, and are easy to use.
The game play make's up for chunky graphic's. It play's a lot like Mass Effect 1, only less refined. Through adventures, you assemble a team of specialized member's, and build up your skills to defeat a growing evil, save the galaxy, learn a lot of back story, and claim your destiny. The game follows a story line, but you can take several path's to the main goal. There are a lot of side quest's and main quests.
There are only currently 68 mods in the Steam workshop. However there are also many more on the Nexus website.
There are a few bug's. The 2 main bug's, for me, are:
1st
After a cut seen, the view won't stop rotating.
The fix is to, hit esc. save the game, exit the game and log back in to your save. The spin will be gone.
2nd
Crashing when during a cut scene, when you enter the next step in the story line.
This is mostly caused by one or more of the mods I have installed.
This is just my guess. What usually seems to happen is, during a cut scene, The game use's thing's
a character is wearing or using, so the character's look like they did going into the scene. Then the game doesn't find some file, and crash's.
A cut scene looks like a movie, but is not a movie. It is actually a string of event's that happen in the game that get triggered, like when you step on a mine, or trigger a door. The reason it looks like a movie, it is seen from " cinematic view ". When a cut scene can't find a file. The string of events gets broken and you get a crash. That is my guess. I'm no expert.
The fix for this is to REMEMBER to save your game before you leave to a new map, like entering and leaving your ship.
When the game crash's:
Step 1 Remove suspected mods. This is easy enough to do in Steam workshop. Just unsubscribe the mods.
Step 2 Restart Steam. This is so Steam will remove the unsubscribed mods.
Step 3 Relog into the game from your last save. Then play the game, without the mods, until you  get through the cut scene's that crashed.
Step 4 Save your game, log out, and reinstall your mods. If using Steam workshop mods, just resubscribe the mods you want.
Step 5 Restart Steam. This is so Steam will load the mods you just subscribed to use.
Step 6 Relog into the game at your last save, and continue playing.

If you're like me, and you've always played Franchise Mode in sports games but preferred the trading/drafting/etc to playing the actual games, then OOTP is perfect for you. There is an insane amount of depth, which could be overwhelming...except you can autmomate whatever tasks you dont want to deal with or assign them to your coaches, basically allowing you to make the game as deep, complex, and involved as you would like. If you do prefer to be hands on, however, you have an absurd amount of content at your fingertips.
Games can be automated batter by batter, inning by inning, or just skipped/automated entirely.
A crazy amount of players to draft and develop, including International League players.
Very detailed and realistic in ways that most sports games are not (for instance, it is not uncommon for a high draft pick to refuse to sign with the team that drafted him, allowing him to re-enter the draft pool next season).
Insane amount of customization.
Great attention to detail, enjoy the flavor text and play-by-play.
Realistic player development. A seemingly can't-miss prospect can end up being a bust without the proper coaching, playing time, if they're rushed through the minors too quickly, etc etc.. On the other hand, a seemingly average prospect can end up being a stud under the right conditions.
Absolutely recommended for anybody who prefers the GM and coaching aspects of sports games.

I am so glad that this game exists. With so many RTS's out there trying to be AoE or something along the lines of Civilization, this game dares to be different, and even if you don't like it, you can at least agree with that.
Offworld Trading Company is an RTS that instead of being based around fortification and combat, is based around economics, and it works so well!
Admittedly when I first started playing this game, I thought it was going to be a bit slow and tedious. But that was before I started campaign mode. The devs have made the stakes so perfectly weighted in this game that anything can feel rewarding whether it be winning the campaign or coming second on one of the rounds. And the sheer speed of some of the rounds can knock you flat on your butt. You'd think that buying and selling iron and silicon would be the most boring premise of a game but the way it's set up, it feels like your life depends on an opponent buying a little bit of carbon from you.
For anyone who would be deterred from the idea of never actually fighting your opponents, I suggest you give this game a shot. It may not provide the exact same feeling as toppling the final wall of your friend's base, but it'll give you an amazing rush when you screw everyone over by having a monopoly on food.

The Good
1. A couple of interesting puzzles.
The Meh
1. No voice acting (other than some incomprehensible demon gibberish).
2. Sound levels are inconsistent, there are times I thought my speakers were muted, so I turned the volume up, to be nearly deafened in the next area.
3. Easily forgettable story, characters and plot with the mildly cute and amusing daemons literally being the only saving grace.
4. Lazy animations, an example is at one stage you have to build a boat to get to an island and in the transition animation of the boat rowing to the island, there's no one in the boat.
5. The puzzles are either very easy or rather challenging.
The bad
1. Fixed low resolution, bearable at 1080p (just).
2. Buggy (once had a C++ runtime error crash and another time a black screen loaded with just the hud when transitioning).
3. Hidden object game mistakes, most notable a scalpel was actually a pair of tweezers and a lire was actually a lyre.
There's far better HOG games on offer on steam in this price range and I wouldn't recommend this particular game at full price, @50% off however it's worth a punt.
On a final note, please ignore my play time, I was AFK a lot and I also placed the game twice to make a video walkthrough, in reality, expect about 5 hours play, a little for more for those who struggle with logic puzzles and a little less for seasoned HOG players.

Im going to start with the bad 1st since there is so many I need to get that out of the way.

Dont want to be the counselors? Tough luck.
The game does rotate players who want to be Jason but nearly everyone wants to be Jason. If you stay in the lobby long enough or pure luck you may get selected as Jason assuming the lobby doesn't close. This does ensure good que times.
Jason is extremely unbalanced. I hear its intended. A good Jason sucks the fun out of the game. Teleporting right beside you or re-appearing beside you with an instant grab or swing that is near impossible to avoid unless Jason screwed up. Despite the game just coming out a good amount of Jason's are able to perform this most of the time.
There is little to do for the counselors. You will being looking through drawers after drawers hoping to find items you can hopefully slowed down or stun Jason. The only way to prevent Jason from killing you the moment he grabs you is if someone hits Jason soon after or you are holding a pocket knife. You can truggle to break free but you just won't unless the Jason wants to kill you somewhere in which he has to carry you there.
You can try to fight Jason but its not reccommended if hes not distracted by other players. Sometimes you may have to take a chance. Be warn though his grab reach is much longer than it appears. He will grab you before you manage to even finish your attack. Even then, if you do hit him he could just recover in a few seconds and teleport/shift and grab you.
There is fun to be had when players work as a group but there are plenty of times this just doesn't happen.
Hiding is extremely tough to do as a counselor. You could always get into a tent and stay in there at the start of the game and be invisible to Jason. To do this you need to have low or no fear. You don't have a clear indication what your fear level is. When your character is extremely scared your screen will grey out and you won't even be able to see your hud as it all fades away.
This game even has troubles of friendly Jason's working with a few counselors to give away other players positions for safety, whether its temporary or not. The Devs are okay with it. They have even came out and said greifing is and will be part of the game. So get team killed by a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that wants to ruin your experience. Its allowed.
The game gets incredibly repititive.
While throwing people through windows or smashing their heads in is fun amoung other things. Its honestly to easy as Jason. Pub stomps feel very rewarding in most games because you displayed such a degree of skill. Here you could do a pub stomp with almost no skill.
If you do happen to escape or die. Im not sure if you get any experience though if you left. When I left I don't recall seeing my exp go up any but that may be because my level is above 10 and the amount it takes to level up starts to increase around there. Friday the 13th is back!!  Ever since the 1989 video game, we have always wanted a successful follow-up to this franchise.  And now we have it!!  Pulled off extraordinarily by GUN MEDIA & ILLFONIC.
To start off, I have to mention that some of the negative feedback by gaming media is ridiculous.  They're complaining about the game being too difficult, when they aren't even putting in the time with counselors to learn how they play, and how Jason plays as well.
This game's mechanics are a new learning experience for players, just the same as Demon Souls and Dark Souls were when they first released.  You have to really put in the effort to learn how to use Stamina, Fear, and (the one I love the most) YOUR BRAIN, and other various tactics to outsmart and evade Jason.  You must employ avid awareness to your surroundings and what other players are doing, where you've been, and keep a solid view on what you are doing in a match, instead of aimlessly wandering, and you will do awesome!!
This game is fresh, and because of all the awesome mechanics implemented within it... it creates a horror experience recipe like no other.  Playing Kane Hodder's "Jason" is absolutely just the best thing ever I might add.
By far... I hope the gaming industry takes note of this game and learns from it.  I'd love to see other horror franchises make MORE than just another cash grab with the big title names they choose to dip their fingers into... follow GUN MEDIA's example.
UPDATED 9/24/2017
Now that we've all become familiar with how Friday the 13th's mechanics work, I can say now in my review that the developers GUN and ILL have a ton to work on to make Jason "actually scary" in this game.
Because of the mechanics in place and players learning how Jason works, he's no longer scary, but just an annoyance to the objectives.  I think the devs have some adjustments to make in order to keep players fearful of the hockey masked killer, and to drive the immersion home.
In ALIEN: ISOLATION we can play over and over and at least be somewhat fearful of the alien, even tho we learn how he works in some fashion... in this, I see players becoming more agitated with Jason because of mechanics like "SHIFT GRAB" and other small nit picky things, that, instead of immersing the player in *Horror*, instead immerses the player in *frustration*.
I hope to see the devs overcome this hurdle in time!

You will die and lose everything. That's how this game is. Be it getting backstabbed by a "friendly"player, clawed to death by a Nether or walking off a roof due to a glitch, there's no sugar coating. You will die, and then you will laugh about it for minute, cry for the next before hitting respawn.
The world is large and immersive and because it's still in development, it's only going to get better. Nether roam the desolate streets of Chicago; from the agile Crawlers to the powerful yet cumbersome Golems. And at anytime, you might be in the crosshairs of another player. The world is your enemy and it's up to you to survive and fight back.

In
we take the role of Sonya, a young woman who receives a strange invitation with a promise of revealing something extremely important related to her daughter Lisa.
Sonya quickly wishes she didn't accept such invitation, as the Devil himself appears and kidnaps Lisa, leaving behind a mother in tears but also convinced in bringing her little girl back.
This is the journey of a mother to reunite with her daughter and keep her away from darkness once and for all.
Because of such traverse storyline with an interesting middle twist, we get to enjoy a story tangled between the present and the past. In order to uncover the deepest secrets, Sonya must travel between mirrors, to unveil family secrets, and ultimately undo the contract with the devil that ties her daughter to such events.
With such great story development, we end up spoiled with great visuals across this first game by
, that bet all in for a fantastic experience.
In-game options are limited, in particular the lack of resolution choices, as limits the visual quality, which is the main focus of Hidden Object games. Other than that, the quality is as good as expected, and due to extreme diversity the game actually offers a solid visual experience.
As gameplay goes, choosing between the system and game's cursor is a nice option, and in-game vsync is on by default, which is good for some users! Puzzles range from easy to medium difficulty, and HoC are available in the traditional system, and an interesting mode in which the objective is to find pairs of objects, without any hints. Not as hard as it seems, and it was a good feature since there aren't that many HoC sequences.
To make the gameplay even more appealing, we get to collect seven little demons, that represents the seven deadly sins, and lock them in a special small box. Ideas like these are exactly what HoC need, more and more!
Audio-voices aren't available, so cutscenes are displayed with just subtitles, but a new language was created for the seven little demons.
Visiting different locations from past and present, dealing with the devil and a cursed offspring, Sonya sure is a mother of courage, and so is young Lisa.

Good art style, but that's about where is ends. Although the leprechaun and the stupid "demons" are ugly as hell. It's this kind of "cute ugly" like someone would design them if they like those ugly Trolls toys. Makes me want to vomit.
Has no proper widescreen support which is bad if the game was really released in 2015. Game crashed once and stuck on a black screen another time. It seems like it really doesn't like the player to click somewhere if there is an animation playing. Luckily the automatic saves seem to be frequent and you barely lose progress, actually none.
And when will devs learn that cutscene narration and sound effects shouldn't be controlled by the music volume slider? If you turn off the music, you get silent cutscenes. Stupid.
BTW, the animations are the most annoying feature. Normally you can't do anything if an animation is playing. This starts on the start menu where you can't click PLAY until the "devil" is done wiggling the scroll. This destroyed most of the trial and error puzzles for me because I hated waiting for the animation of every little move to finish. Speaking about puzzles, there are very forgettable and, like I said, trial and error, which isn't fun. In the end I skipped most of them.
Hint meter recharges quickly, which actually made me finish the game, because I couldn't be bothered with the "adventuring" in the second half of the game. Some of the steps to advance seem very badly designed and not very logical. I don't mind the adventure part in HO games, but don't make it too convoluted. It also felt very repetitive, because the game is divided into parts and in every part you have to get a demon and charge a mirror.
Some scene transitions are completely unnecessary, i.e. boat and lift. The game has no map or fast travel.
The HO scenes are ok, but nothing to write home about. They are relatively easy with only some badly designed items. The matching pair ones were mostly fine.
Bottom line: get it for the art, but nothing else, if you really have to. Overall not a relaxing HO game: too many annoying things.

This game asks its players what it means to live and what it means to be human.
Despite the strong horror and oppresive atmostphere of the game, SOMA is very inspiring.
While playing this game, I didn't realize my idea and perspective on self-awareness and life were changing.
It was only until I reached the end that everything came together.
What amazes me, is that each encounter is so intense, frightening, and horrific that you tend to ignore the subtle themes throughout the game (or so you think). The characters are developed so well with each event, incident, and conversation, by the end of the game you're just left with your jaw open.
You HAVE to play this to believe it.
Truly a masterpiece. A work of art in the form of video game media.
In conclusion, I personally think this game is better than of this developers other works, including Amnesia: Dark Descent. Amnesia: Dark Descent was horrific and scary in its own rite, but the underlying theme in this game poses DARK and RADICAL questions that make you take a harder look at even the most simplest of life's questions.
"What does it mean to be me?"
Spooky the human acts are also horrifying.

I would recommend this to someone who does not typically play horror games.  The gameplay itself is split up between exploration with plot building and encounters with monsters.  The monsters themselves are a bit underwhelming when compared to other horror games out right now, like resident evil, where enemies will continuously impede your progress.  In SOMA, when you die, you pick up right where you left off, taking away the fear of starting again and with it the fear of the monsters.  Surprizingly, the monsters are not what makes this game scary.
The plot is far beyond most horror games.  This game often times leaves you feeling hopeless.  Not for gameplay reasons, but because of the questions that will inevitably be burned into your mind.  Without giving too much away, the terror is centered around the breakdown of ones identity.  What it would mean if it were possible to continue consciousness outside of the human body, and the struggle of accepting that new identity.
The game is worth the full price tag, and on sale it is a steal.  I haven't played this game in over a year and I still think about it sometimes.  There are only a couple games that have ever had a lasting impact on me.  If you buy it and play it through, then it will stay with you.

Ah, Nihilumbra, another one of those "Cute" games that comments philosophically on the nature of life, the universe, and everything. Yes, a lot of games do this, but I have never been so attached to a character as I have been to Born, so much wanted to see this character grow, and so wanted everything to be okay for the little mite. You really kind of have to put your own spin on the character by nature of what it is, and that's pretty different from most games like this I've seen.
The story is that you (Born) are a shadow being from the Void - the Nothingness, that is - and you, curious about the world outside the Void, break free from it into the world of... Something. Quickly, you learn to become and adapt in this environment, changing it, loving it, only for the Void to come after you time and again, trying to reclaim you. The way Born navigates his environs is through elemental magic of a sort, painting elements onto the environs to solve physics puzzles in a way somewhat reminiscent of Okami/Okamiden. Of course, Okami/Okamiden never left me a crying disaster over a shadow creature just trying to make his way in the world, because puppies generally try not to hurt your heart when they make mistakes. The monsters in the game are terrifyingly designed and (yes I know my reviews say this a lot) really do look like something out of a Lovecraft story. Try looking at a Crawlaggar and NOT seeing something that could reasonably pass as a Hound of the Tindalos, I dare you, especially when it comes chasing after you in packs from off-screen...
That said, this charming game is not everyone's cup of tea - there is a New Game Plus mode after the end of the normal game, a sort of "B Adventure" where you go back through the levels fixing what the Void has destroyed, and it is ABSOLUTELY BRUTALLY HARD. I'm serious, I consider myself a puzzle buff and a fan of rogue-style difficulty, but this is even too much for me. Split-second timing, rather unfair jumps, trial and error, and using elements to deflect bullets into incredibly tough series of enemies - they're all here, often during the chapter-end chases, and they will bend you over a table and go in dry. I am not kidding here, the New Game Plus of this game reaches unprecidented levels of Guide Dang It at points, and that's not even counting the various achievements that aren't related to gameplay itself! I genuinely needed a walkthrough to even make it to the end, and even that was difficult when you look at some of the absolute bull-hocky that this game expects you to do in New Game Plus. To compound that, Born's hitbox sometimes plays oddly with certain enemies - like the Vacuumore - where even being two feet away from the enemy's maw is enough to kill you. This also appears to occur with boxes and spikes on some occasions. I suspect this is a bit of a glitch or oversight, and the game maker did not intend to make the hitbox quite so sensitive, in which case - please fix this, it makes the game quite difficult for the wrong reasons.
At the same time, IMHO, the normal game is almost too easy, with obvious solutions to fairly obvious puzzles. Yes, it gets very clever with them - using the bounce power to ricochet bullets, using the sticky power to stick enemies to walls and ceilings (which is freaking hilarious to watch because they flail around), etc. However, generally any time you need speed, you used the slippery power, making electronics work uses the electronic power, etc. Obvious problem + Obvious power = Obvious solution, and I wish that there was more use of mixing of powers to get to a solution as the New Game Plus does. So, between the main game being too easy, and New Game Plus being too hard (but not impossible), couldn't there have been a bit more of a transition between the two? Maybe like, just add more monsters instead of more difficult puzzles, or add more puzzles but not more monsters? Then you could have an easy, medium, and hard mode for those who wanted to play around with the powers and use new and more interesting power combinations to reach their goals, and you could have had the B Adventure be tougher without being so tough it made me tear my hair out in frustration. At the very least, you could have cut down on the number of timing-sensitive puzzles that are near freaking impossible; there's a difference between Nintendo Hard and Frustrating.
All in all, I do still like this game, a lot, and find it difficult to hate. The scenery and general idea behind it is gorgeous, I love playing Pseudo-Okami with the powers, and obtaining each power was a true pleasure and very satisfying. Burning things with the fire power is amazingly fun, and the puzzles are pretty clever all things considered. I would recommend this game, but only if you like physics platform-puzzlers with a tough streak in its New Game Plus, because seriously - that second half makes you WORK for its achievements...

TLDR:  Bottom line is that i HIGHLY RECOMMEND  this game if you are a fan of the turn based battlefields. (similar to Vandal Hearts/Final Fantasy Tactics in ways)  so let's get to it.
WARNING: The Menu/UI can be very confusing at first. as their is alot of information to be used.  I believe Devs are working to simplify but IMO there will still need to be alot  on the main menu screen so I recommend clicking around and learning it all the old fashioned way. (really wouldn't say more than 20 minutes for a less comprehensive person like myself)
You build squads of 3 out of basically 6 classes (Healer, Paladin, Rogue, Archer, Mage, Warrior) each with their one unique ability, Plus you control yourself (Hero Class, Can use all Gear) Battles can hold up to 48 total units and are played out on a fairly large field with random debris allowing for strategy to take place.

Battles are turn based and use a very solid system to determine turn order, effected by gear type, weapons used on attack, squares moved and turning.  (you can strafe/backpedal but only attack the way you are facing, hence the turn feature.)
Battles can be a little slow, Especially larger scale ones.  This is not a bad thing all of the time, but when you are grinding and aren't at the point that you can let AI battle for you,( there is autobattle option)   you can end up spending alot of time feeling like you've not made any real progression.
There isn't any storyline
The game is PvE heavy, but endgame seems to be PvP guilds. Areas are seperated for Levels and from 5 on you can be attacked without warning by a player(There is some balancing and i believe the player has to be geared similarly to you.) There is no consequence to winning/losing a fight however and you will be shielded afterwards so being harassed seriously should not be a concern.  PvE monsters will also attack you in later levels so PvPer's could really be treated as another encounter.
-Global Market, Completely optional to the game.
-Global Chat is actually chat, Guilds who raid eachother ultimately show respect towards eachother and don't just BM.
-There is a crafting system where you can craft your self/guild gear as you level up and find the resources on the map.
-THE MUSIC IS 10/10.  I mean we're all biased, but for me. seriously great job.
-Battles overall are fun, Looting/gearing/squad building feels immersive enough.
-I have no idea what i'm really doing in my guild, but i really enjoy being in the guild i'm in.
-Level your units, expand your guild, get the best gear.  That is all there really is to ultimately do at the moment but this is a very young game and the devs are seemingly in it for the long-term. I hope the best is yet to come.
Hope the review helps.  The Music inspired me to write it.

Nihilumbra is a unique indie 2D platformer/puzzle game in which you play as an awakened consciousness from the Void that has decided to escape from the dreary and desolate darkness and start life anew, traveling across vast landscapes while the Void lingers slightly behind in pursuit. You, as the Void Creature, traverse across numerous unique and beautiful landscapes to discover your purpose in life while solving puzzles to progress further. The game's light platforming segments are made into unique puzzles based around various powers you acquire from different colored flowers, each with its own special ability and suiting to the environment.
If anything can be properly said about Nihilumbra, is that it does it's tone WONDERFULLY. As you travel across the land, your exploits and thoughts are told by a wisened narrator that offers his thoughts (or rather, narrates your own in second-person fashion) on every instance you find yourself in. The game's atmosphere is finely split between three moods: Wonder, somber, and fear. Every new area you enter, you find yourself experiencing thoughts of wonder and curiosity, amazed at every little thing, from the embracing green of the leaves to the harsh red of fire. However, the mood shifts to somber once you realize that the Void, having been chasing after you on your journey for leaving, will come soon and consume the land. And finally, when the Void shows up, intensity is raked up to twenty, and you are in a state of panic as the narrator continues his tirade about hopelessness and inevitability, some part of you desperatly clinging to the idea that he is wrong and you can prove it!!!
... Wow, that got a little outta hand there, didn't it?
Well! Anyway, Nihilumbra is an artistically pleasing game, good on the eyes, good on the ears, good on the gameplay, and good looking in your game library. I give this game a positive recommendation and a 8/10 rating. Plus, there's always Void mode to play post game, if you're so inclined for the challenge...

As a US Army veteran, it's easy to see the time which was put into this game to make it as accurate as possible (while still keeping it a game). Although the single-player campaign is short, it plays like a movie with you as the main character(s). Aside from giving us a mere glimpse into the skill of our special operations fighting force, it also shows the level of brotherhood these warriors share and the lengths they would go to in order to protect their own.
Although there were a few bugs in the game (respawning into an area where you're killed again in seconds with no way to escape, A.I. trying to walk through walls, shoebox-style gameplay where your movement is limited to a pre-defined area, etc.), these are overshadowed by what I consider to be a great story line. If you're looking for a realistic open-world sandbox style FPS, however, you'd have better luck with the ARMA series.
I didn't (and won't) bother with the multiplayer, but I can tell you that if you're looking for a great story-driven FPS, look no further than this game. In the end, it will pull at your emotions and give you a glimpse, even if only briefly, into the mind a our great defenders and silent warriors.

The setup sounds great, Holmes & Watson inexplicably drawn into a world of fantasy horror... Except the follow-through is a boring and groan inducing embarrassment. It has little to do with either the works of Conan Doyle or Lovecraft and the tonally devoid hot mess that follows is evident of that. Looking at it simply as a game it's a frustrating series of clumsy and broken puzzle mechanics; if you've come for a narrative or engrossing world though then you're really in trouble. The plot attempts to string together kidnappings in England, an asylum in Switzerland, a swamp in New Orleans and finally a lighthouse in Scotland using some vague Cthulhu cult to no definable end. It's all so disjointed you realize about halfway through that none of the developers actually read any of Lovecraft's stories. Professor Sullivan has a blink-and-you'll-miss-it cameo but nowhere in the narrative is Innsmouth (home to The Esoteric Order Of Dagon) or any of the creatures of Lovecraft's mythos. Cthulhu himself is never even mentioned by name! So what you're left with is less a sect and more a social club that stuff dead people full of squid and call it a herald of the apocalypse. It's also really, really ♥♥♥♥ing stupid. It doesn't work as a mystery, it doesn't work as fantasy horror, and it just plain doesn't work as a game.
Now all we need is an open world Jedi Knight RPG with the scale of Elder Scrolls, except with the addition of exploring other planets.
