I've been enjoying the modern reimaginings of Sherlock on CBS (Elementary) and the even better BBC series.  So, when the Sherlock collection went on sale on Steam, I decided to give it a try.  Of course, this game portrays the original Sherlock Holmes.
This is mostly typical point-and-click adventure fare and puzzles, with a little more than the usual pixel hunting due to the forensic nature of the story.  For a game created in 2006 and then "remastered" in 2008, the production values are low, but the voice acting is pretty good.  There are a few brain teasers thrown in, which can be difficult, but there is a built-in hint system.  The game requires a little bit of deductive reasoning, but it falls short of making you feel like Sherlock.  All too often, you gather all the evidence only to have Holmes pull it all together in a cut scene.  The story is kinda slow, but it comes together nicely in the end.  All in all, not a bad game, but not great either.

Sniper Elite V2 is a WW II 3rd person shooter with a linear level design with SP and MP mode.
Graphics:     5/10
Graphics are ok but the textures appear blurred even with the highest settings.
The colors are realistic and suitable. Neither special nor modern.
I like the bulletcam. It gives you the right feeling of hitting someone critically.
Leveldesign:     4/10
Well - I know the scenery is determined by the World War theme but it's extremely monotonous. Always the same destroyed buildings. The levelborders are partly ok since it's not that difficult to design them in a destroyed city.
Gameplay/Handling/Equipment:     7/10
All in all a standard shooter. It annoys me that the bullet hits a cover I never aimed for because the view is odd sometimes. The snipers work fine for me. I didn't really recognize a major difference between them except for the clipsize and manual or semi-auto.
The pistols are kind of useless, but after all the game is named sniper elite.
Trapmines are nice but you will rarely use them.
AI:     6/10
Seeks cover, uses grenades, authentic aiming, reacts when someone gets hit.
But sometimes the AI just randomly runs around inviting the sniper to shoot him right between the eyes.
Sound:     3/10
First the good things: Yes, it sounds like a war. Plenty of bomb explosions from afar, gunshots etc, etc. The weapon sounds are somewhat "ok" but i'm not impressed. The music is very annoying.
There are like 2 or 3 tracks and that's it. And on top of that the soundtrack is boring in the first place.
Storyline:     1/10
I think the problem here is: The developers wanted the story to be kind of realistic. But it is not.
Why? Because you are a super-sniper-soldier, killing hundreds and hundreds of Nazis and Russians.
And your "awesome" mission is: Kill some strange guys who have something to do with the V2-Rockets. Well. Nice. That shows that the priority was set on the word "Sniper".
Because they just needed any random reason to take a gun and shoot people.
Critic summary:     4.3/10
Personal fun rating:     5/10     [mediocre game]
Since I got the game for free I recommend the game to play it at least a few hours.
But I would never buy the game for 10 bucks. Not sure if I would for 5.
It's strange enough to make the game in third-person-view. I didn't finish the story and I think I never will. There is no reason to play the game twice. If you are a Sniper-enthusiast then go for it. But since I write this review for people who consider to buy it:
Don't do it.

I've now put quite a few hours into OOTP 17 now since buying it in July so I can now fairly give a review and also compare to last years OOTP 16.  First thing I noticed different from last year was the design and colors of the screens. Much better imo and easier to read. Something else that is much improved over last years game is the trading. You can actually now make a list of needs you are wanting so the computer makes more offers to you making the game more realistic in that area. Now I'm not saying the trades are easier to make, I still always get the they want two five star players for their 4 star and 3 star thing happening but overall this new function really adds to the game.
Now to just go over the game in general and not comparing to last years game. If you like baseball and sims you will absolutley LOVE this game. The options to starting leagues are never ending. There is almost nothing you can't make your league into with all the options given. You can base a league on current MLB seasons, historical MLB seasons. You can dump all the MLB players into a pool and draft them into new teams. You can start fictional leagues. You can decide on whether its an offensive league, pitching league or neutral league. You can start foreign leagues. It's endless.
The interface can be a bit tricky to learn to start but after a bit it starts to fall into place for you as things are designed well for the most part. My biggest complaint about the game is when setting individual player game strategies you can't always see all the players stats needed to adjust you strategies. Otherwise they have done a great job on making sure you can almost always find what you are looking for easily after a bit of practice.
I highly recommend this game to baseball fans and sim fans, you can't do any better than this game. If you are wanting to learn more about basebal I also recommend this game as well, so much can be learned while playing the game, it won't take long before you know you've improved your baseball IQ.

and

Contract with the Devil has beautiful graphics and an interesting plot, but the atrocious writing, tedious progression, and bad hit detection pretty much ruin it as a hidden object game.
Contract with the Devil shows tremendous effort, but wastes it on a hidden object game where even some of the more fundamental HOG core design aspects are completely wrong.
This game is riddled with issues like terrible hit detection—the main menu can drop your input!—and repetitive item gathering (even by HOG standards), which all come together as boring at best, annoying at worst.
They are the smaller problem compared to the game’s tendency to waste time.  Not only the backtracking is downright ridiculous, but you also need to wait for every single frame of every animation to continue, as if the game is unable to cope with two things at once.
It tries to make up for it with astonishing visuals and the plot is decent for a HOG: we play as a mother trying to save her daughter from a pretty evil person who once made the titular contract with the devil. But, the game messes up even here, with dialogue so childish, so simplistic, it is almost insulting.

If you've played Amnesia or Penumbra you know Frictional Games is a fantastic developer that really knows how Survival Horror works; by taking away your ability to effectively fight and making monsters not play by a simple set of rules they make what was already terrifying truly horrifying. SOMA is no exception to the theme and it adds a lot of variety as well as story depth.
STORY:
The Story is very well told with fantastic voice acting that really adds to the feel of the game and carries the plot in a believable way that balances reveals to keep you in suspense. Not only that but the themes of the story and flavor of the lore you pick up really comes together in a fantastic and yet suitably creepy way. I would say more but i don't want to ruin a great story that really accentuates the cyber sci-fi horror falvor.
MONSTERS:
More than their previous games the monsters are more unique in appearance if not mechanics and match perfectly with the other aesthetics of the game. The sounds, Movement all comes together very well. I've played a number of horror games and these gave me the creeps on  more than one occassion.
GRAPHICS:
The game is beautiful, no arguement there; and the styles really give the feel the rest of the game's elements try to portray. To put it simply the game's appearance is very polished and it comes together very well. however if you don't like underwater things this game may unsettle you, more that it should.
GAMEPLAY:
Like Amnesia is a good way to put it but with a little more emphasis on story and world but more polished and fluid. You know, if that actually makes any sense.
SUMMARY:
It's good, it's beyond great. if you like survival horror and like cyber sci-fi then this is the game for you, no doubts about that; HIGHLY RECCOMEND.

SOMA's story brilliantly succeeded in discussing the idea of existence, which not too many games have done well. Because its narrative rests on several story events, I can't share much except that it was effective. That being said, the game was pretty sad and existentially disturbing, so it helps to be in the right mood.
Some things to note. First, there is no combat. This will upset some players. Instead of combat, you are required to flee or hide from monsters. On the upside of there being no combat, the only important items in the game fall into two categories: (1) key items necessary to progress the story, and (2) secondary items you can view (but not equip or store), such as notes and photos. The upside is that you won't find yourself searching nooks and crannies for power ups, weapons and so on. The story is the main concern; monsters exist for the occasional scare and to leave in the dust.
My only big complaint is that there were a few areas where the monsters were very poorly placed. An example (and there are others): you need to pick up an energy stick thing to power a suit. Problem is, when you get to the location of the energy stick, there's a monster RIGHT in front of the important item. The monster won't move unless you get close enough to it and then it chases you; might even kill you. Eventually you'll get the monster far enough away to grab the stick and leave, but it's frustrating that you're made to go through the effort. This was one of those points where having a weapon or at least a way to distract the monster would have made for a better experience.

This review will cover only the gameplay.  There are a myriad of other reviews that cover the game's story or bugs.
A good way to indicate whether a game is great or terrible (or anywhere in between) is how compelled I feel to continue playing.  There are some games that are so fun to play that I find myself still playing after several hours have passed.
Is KotOR II that kind of game?  Not really, no.  Don't get me wrong, KotOR II's story and characters are far superior to BioWare's original title.  The game's theme is so immersive that I found myself thinking about it all the time while not playing it.
The problem is that when I AM playing the game, it doesn't take long before I quit out of irritation.  I was able to blow through KotOR I in a couple of days and have replayed it many times over the years, but KotOR II takes me much longer, and I have not replayed it as much.  Here's why:
-The game's central premise is that most of your party members can be converted to Jedi.  Sounds great, right?  The problem is that it takes a while to sufficiently influence your party members, and once they become Jedi, you don't get to reroll their skill points and attributes.  You essentially lose what the character was good for and are left with a mediocre Jedi.  Indeed, it's better to not influence them at all purely from a gameplay perspective.
-The various levels of the game feel awfully rushed.  Especially Nar Shaddaa.  There is a brilliant story going on, but you can go from long periods of relative quiet to suddenly being dropped into very difficult situations with little warning.  The flow of the game is simply inferior to KotOR I, which was not any less difficult but always seemed to give me sufficient time to prepare.
This game conflicts me.  It has one of the best stories of any game I've ever played, certainly the best story that has "Star Wars" in its title.  It's just that it's a mediocre game.  If it was a book, it would be the best book ever written.  Nonetheless, I'll recommend it.  I owe it that much, given all the memories I have of it.

Not bad for an actively developed free-to-play title. This is a squad based tactical rpg mmoish that's got enough going for it that I'm landing just on the side of recommending you check it out.
The battle system seems to flow pretty well and is very quick to react. This is a much bigger deal than people realize for this type of a game. Turn-based games by nature are generally lighter on action and can be time consuming. Double that time consuming effect for anything multiplayer and it can make an otherwise enjoyable experience quite a slog trying to get through a map. The Squad size is currently set to 3 units max and this also helps keep the playtime down. For the moment tactical considerations are very limited but it seems like features that will be expansions of the current system are on the way.
It's a decent amount of fun at the moment. Not great or aweinspiring but it's a solid foundation that will hopefully see improvment over the coming months and so on.

Let me preface this by saying I have played every baseball game created in the last decade, and Out of the Park Baseball 17 is the greatest one ever made.
I am a lifelong Mariners, (the pain) and baseball fan. I have a passion in the sport and can rattle off statistics and random info better than I can the Pledge of Allegiance. And I'm not even sorry.
This game has everything the inner baseball fanatic in me wants. Complete control of roster, to player sliders, to creating ballparks, expanding the league, accurate minor league systems, actually accurate simulations, and realistic decision making.
Yes, "all you do is stare at a screen". But it hearkens back to a day of text based Sims that gets me nostalgic just like the great American pastime does.
The only downside I have for this game is that I wish I could actually play the games instead of siming them, as in being the player, not the manager, but it's a small sacrifice.
Some other cons: the game tends to crash semi often. I am talking about once every few hours for me. But I also play the crap out of it, so I may just be too hard.
The salary players demand becomes unrealistic if you max their stats. For example: I traded Mike Trout to my team, and maxed his stats because I wanted to see him crush a bunch of records. He did. But, after his contract was up, he wanted $55 million a year for 10 years. Uhm. My team salary is $200 million lol. That said, you can lower their stats and sign them for cheaper, then raise them again, but I don't like doing that because I want to keep it slightly realistic. The other solution is editing your finances to have a bigger pay roll.
All in all, this is an incredible game that any stat minded player will love. Their are endless statistics to pour through, which I love. If you are a fan of baseball, and like number based Sim games, this is what you have been missing your whole life.

In Sniper Elite V2, you take the role of the worst marksman the collective allied powers could muster who is sent on a high-stakes covert mission by his superiors from within intellegence agencies to destroy progress Nazi superweapons, the V2 Rockets. You know. As a joke. To aid him, you gain access to a wide arsenal of submachineguns that your international assassin can just barely figure out which end is which on, pistols that are all broken and work improperly to some degree and high-power battle rifles with worn-out rifling, thousands and thousands of rounds of reduced power ammunition, and increasingly powerful optics made in the back of a moving truck that are incapable of any adjustment.
Coincidentally, as you undergo your mission, the magnetic field of the earth becomes much more powerful in Europe. Thousands die. This forces the people of Europe to redesign their roadways to only go in straight lines though low-magnetism areas, so there is only one path throughout all of the missions. On top of this added challenge, your projectiles (which are low velocity to avoid radar detection) are being wrestled to the earth, clawing all well-made death machines to an estimation of 3,679 Minute of Angle accuracy. To make up for this handicap, though, your infantry rifles do have anti-tank capabilities and the majority of your opponents are firing at you with fire hoses filled with lead fishing weights.
As far as the plot goes, it's your normal fare. It's a historic fiction game set between 1939 and 1945 very similar to others such as Medal of Honor, Call of Duty, etc. Now I have a bone to pick. These games all rip eachother off in their writing. Their characters all look the same, even have the same names, the games all take place at the same times in the same places. I mean, compare the main antagonist of this game, Adolf "Fuhrer" Hitler, to that of the Adolf Hitler character in any of the games I mentioned previously. What hacks. They even all have the same moustache. Is it really so hard to come up with your OWN setting? How about you call your war something other than "World War Two"? What about the first one? And why Germany? Why not something like Antagonistia or Detroit for a name? Some of the most uncreative writing I've ever found in a video game. Although, later in the game, I do like the twist where your character is bitten by a radioactive Nazi and gains x-ray vision, which reveals that the Nazis were really skeletons all along. It adds a nice twist to the setting and what I think would have actually happened were this a real war.
I would recommend this game for young readers ages 8 to 12 who are hypoglycemic, get in excess of 40 hours of sleep a day, are multilingual, and have chronic vestigial flight capabilities.

I enjoyed this game.  I can be pretty picky when it comes to graphics, which can be a lot to expect with HOG/point & click games sometimes, but this one was great.  I could nitpick on a few things, but overall, it took me over 8 hours to finish it and I had fun.  I liked the "logical pairs" hidden object scenes because it was a refreshing change from the norm.

The game was frustrating due the poor movement of the cursor.  Also I have been "stuck" in areas, where through reading I did not do the "clues" in the corrct manner.  Restarted the game and 3 times this is happened.

I agree with many of the reviews, stating that this game has beautiful graphics complemented by suiting music, even at a lack of voice actors to bring out more personality of the characters, but the storyline wasn't as interesting as the various other games in the same genre.
The puzzles were mostly frustrating, but wasn't impossible to beat. I attempted to use hints on the puzzles, but all it ever did was to point out the (?) which leads to the instruction screen that explained how to play. It would be helpful if a hint or a sparkle lit up the area for those who needed help after a certain time passed, especially for those who played in casual mode.
At times, the animation felt painfully slow. Especially during the hidden object screen (HOS), which would be nice if it didn't take as long as it took choosing one object to another. Talking about the HOS, sometimes the objects' hotspots doesn't register the click, even though it was the same object, proving much harder for a hidden object game to be enjoyable. Another disappointment, though not as frustrating as the other points I've pointed out, was the misclick penalty for all modes. I really don't see any differences between the modes except for hints and skip recharging at a faster rate, when misclick penalty was enabled for all modes. Although I love HOGs, I have a big problem with them from time to time, and the misclick penalty was very much annoying when it clouded my vision every 5? misclicks.
As for the cutscenes, it's alright, but they seemed like cutouts of a painting moreso than a well animated cutscene. Not to mention that the text fade to black too quickly, it was hard to read more than half of the text on screen, before it was changed to a new line and the cycle repeated. It would be much better if the cutscenes can be paused and advanced with a click of a "continue" button, instead of forcing the cutscenes to autoplay itself. This might seem like I'm nitpicking, but honestly, when the cutscenes weren't complemented with voice acting, the most important thing would be the subtitle that explains the story. When I can't even read the text, then all I can do is to stare at the moving pictures, instead of fully grasping the storyline, removing the last sense of immersiveness.
Overall, I think this game is around the average level for a HOG. It didn't have anything surprising to bring to the table, although I do have to applaud the developer for introducing the matching system. However, with all that's said, the restrictiveness and the black screen bug from time to time kinda ruined the game for me, so I do not recommend this game to anyone unless it's on sale.

Hi there!
First of all it is quite interesting how the STEAM rating of the game dropped from "very positive" to "mixed". Most people have problems with connecting and playing the game even me so I guess most people are just upset because servers are down all the time.
Please do not forget even Diablo3 had big problems at launch so you should not judge the game by server connectivity shortly after launch.
The game itself is AMAZING. If you are a fan of the "Friday the 13th" franchise this one is the game for you. There should always a bit scepticism when it comes to movie based video games. Very often they were just bad games using the license to make money out of a game that offers nothing.
Friday the 13th is different. The locations are designed very nicely and look like the real counterparts in the movies. Also there is enough room to hide and the maps are quite large so that it could be very spooky running through the forest where nothing happens and then you see Jason in the distance. This is what the games does really well it takes the atmosphere and the horror from the movies right onto your screen and you feel frightened, scared and run for your life.
Many people say Jason is "overpowered" I don´t think so because you can stun him with pistols, bear traps and even try to fight him but I wouldn´t do that. Jason is a killer he is made for hunting you down so he needs to have some abilities usual players don´t have! Otherwise Jason is not scary anymore.
The game is more about hiding and trying to get away with a car, calling the police and make your way to the camp exit. This is exactly what I was looking for and what CSGO and COD shooters couldn´t deliver - at least imho. The sneaking the hiding this  slower not hectical gameplay this is what I was looking for and this game delivered it.
Hmm is the game better than Dead by Daylight? IMHO I would say yes! Because it concentrates on the "Friday the 13th" franchise and really does a great job delivering the atmosphere, the maps, the characters and Jason at a very very great detail.
Oh yeah you can level up your character e.g. that Jason cannot spot you outside a building anymore so it is much more difficult to find you out in the woods. In a lodge Jasons senses are disabled and you have to search by yourself finding a poor guy waiting to be slashed and killed.
Go ahead give it a try even if the servers make problems at the moment. But when you are connected you have alot of fun! Guaranteed!
You know, it's not Portal, but it's good enough! Actually it's very fun!

So I purchased this game out of nostalgia for the originals, hoping that at the very least, I would get a good 5-10 hours of a mindless linear shooter campaign in which i could unwind by popping skulls, and half paying attention to an unoriginal story.
Unfortunately, it appears that even though my standards were very low, I still set my expectations much too high.  The level design is rather convuluted, and I often found myself trying to figure out where to go.  I guess this shouldn't have been as much of a problem as a lot of the level progression is explained to you by your squad mates.  Unfortunately, for the majority of the game, the entirety of the Dialog was both imperceptable and unitelligable, leaving me feeling lost and confused.
On 3 or 4 occasions, the game got stuck, and failed to load the next mission objective, leaving me confused and frustrated for a few minutes until I figured out what was going on, and re-loaded the game save.
Unfortunately, not even the story was able to redeem this game in my eyes.  Unlike most linear first person shooters, Medal of Honor doesn't try to tell some kind of story with a villan and a hero via dialog and cut scenes, but rather it attempts to give the player a "slice of life experience".  This is all well and good, however it was not executed well.  As most FPS characters are, the subjects of this game are static characters who neither develop as the game goes on, or are given a chance to really set themselves apart as someone for you to care about.  And since you don't care about the characters, you unfortunately are left not caring about what happens to them, causing the "slice of life" arc to fall on deaf ears, and a regretful wallet.

The main problem I did have quite a bit of during the game however was the AI, I played on the hardest difficulty for the extra challenge, (No slow motion aim assist, realistic bullet drop and windage, AI can see you from a greater distance and never forget about you even if you hide) which made the game just that much more challenging and fun. The problem however, was that as I had to account for bullet drop and windage the AI sadly, did not and on many occasions the second I would pop out of cover to even try and take a shot I would get hit and considering it only takes two shots to kill you from a sniper on said difficulty it was an incredible pain to take out the snipers who would know where I was even if I relocated.

Pros
+ Fantastic sniping experience that takes into account gravity, wind direction/speed, bullet velocity, distance, target movement, etc
+ Delightfully brutal x-ray kill cam
+ Focused, believable historical plot line
+ Multiplayer co-op is actually fun
Cons
- Stealth system is broken and unfinished (no takedowns, a silenced weapon that's only accurate when on top on an enemy, non-stealth friendly environments)
- Borderline unrealistically "nerfed" pistols and submachine guns (terrible accuracy, can take an entire magazine to kill an enemy)
- Tripwire grenades and mines are useless due to the AI hardly ever trying to flush you out
- AI in general can be a little wonky
Bottom Line
If you're looking for a more recent shooter to satisfy your WWII urge and/or a solid sniper-centric game you can't go wrong with V2. A broken stealth system and sometimes wonky AI aside it's an enjoyable experience that puts other sniper games like Ghost Warrior to shame (which I guess isn't saying that much...).

SOMA goes places. I expected a game full of jump scares and scary thriller sequences but I was given all that and then some.  The game's story is rich and intriguing with a thrilling concept. The game will make you feel many emotions throughout the experience and each one is presented amazingly. You as the player get to decide just how much you want to engage with the narrative, as the game places (not hides) the details around the environment. The game also never hides your objective and is very straight forward when it wants you to do something.  The controls are also kept simple so there is almost nothing that gets in the way of the story and sequences. These are the things Frictional has done well with in SOMA; keeping the game honest and the story accessible, all the while grabbing the player and keeping them engaged.
The only negatives I could point out is that some of the mechanics of the enemies was very vague. I personally believe this made the encounters more novel as it makes the player confront their fears of the unknown in order to figure out the solution to do what's needed, but I can see this being a negative aspect for others.
Fans of thought provoking narratives should play this game, even if you're not a fan of horror.

- being AZ-Art's only project so far - is a decent HOG with some fascinating art work and promising gameplay, presenting you 5 hours or so fair gameplay + some achievements.
Our protagonist is a single mother called Sonya. She receives a letter from a strange gentleman named John McGraw, inviting her to his mansion to share some urgent information about her daughter, Lisa. Accepting this odd invitation, Sonya visits John alongside Lisa, oblivious to the shocking occurrence that shall soon take place. As they were sharing a cup of tea, John invites Sonya to take a look at an antique mirror in his possession. As soon as the surface of the said mirror is revealed though, an eerie flash of light engulfs the room and John disappears alongside Lisa. Shaken and grief-stricken Sonya takes on a supernatural journey through a collection of mirror realms to take her daughter back to safety. As she progresses, she learns the ominous past of the McGraw family and John's reasons for abducting her daughter which concerns a contract... a contract with the Devil.
Quite Faustian, eh? I must say that I liked the concept of the game - and the design of the said Devil - a lot. Some real labor went into display properties, that's for sure. The art works are fascinating with a rich color palette. CGs and animations are flowingly beautiful. Sadly, there is no voice acting though and written narrative skips a bit fast, making it possible to miss some narration, yet it is always possible to track the story through your diary.
There is the mention of 7 Deadly Sins - a.k.a. 7 Hellish Vices and some quests revolving around some little demonic creatures concerning those vices, yet considering a HOG is supposed to be kid-friendly, their concepts are a bit dumbed down. There is not sin of Lust or Pride for some reason, yet there is Gambling or Power Lust etc. It sure is cute, but wrecks the lore and the authenticity. Then again, one shouldn't expect genuine Catholic lore from a HOG anyhow.
Item collection takes a bit of attention mostly. It is possible to miss an item if you are not careful enough. HOG scenes are various and enjoyable, yet sometimes a bit on the ridiculously hard part. Puzzles are quite challenging and intriguing too. There is no map option, but considering every chapter consists of 4-5 areas, it is not that big of a chore to backtrack.
Considering all sides,
is an enjoyable little HOG adventure with a good story build, nice art work and challenging puzzles. Grab it on sale to spare a lazy afternoon with it, HOG lovers.

Hi there!
First of all it is quite interesting how the STEAM rating of the game dropped from "very positive" to "mixed". Most people have problems with connecting and playing the game even me so I guess most people are just upset because servers are down all the time.
Please do not forget even Diablo3 had big problems at launch so you should not judge the game by server connectivity shortly after launch.
The game itself is AMAZING. If you are a fan of the "Friday the 13th" franchise this one is the game for you. There should always a bit scepticism when it comes to movie based video games. Very often they were just bad games using the license to make money out of a game that offers nothing.
Friday the 13th is different. The locations are designed very nicely and look like the real counterparts in the movies. Also there is enough room to hide and the maps are quite large so that it could be very spooky running through the forest where nothing happens and then you see Jason in the distance. This is what the games does really well it takes the atmosphere and the horror from the movies right onto your screen and you feel frightened, scared and run for your life.
Many people say Jason is "overpowered" I don´t think so because you can stun him with pistols, bear traps and even try to fight him but I wouldn´t do that. Jason is a killer he is made for hunting you down so he needs to have some abilities usual players don´t have! Otherwise Jason is not scary anymore.
The game is more about hiding and trying to get away with a car, calling the police and make your way to the camp exit. This is exactly what I was looking for and what CSGO and COD shooters couldn´t deliver - at least imho. The sneaking the hiding this  slower not hectical gameplay this is what I was looking for and this game delivered it.
Hmm is the game better than Dead by Daylight? IMHO I would say yes! Because it concentrates on the "Friday the 13th" franchise and really does a great job delivering the atmosphere, the maps, the characters and Jason at a very very great detail.
Oh yeah you can level up your character e.g. that Jason cannot spot you outside a building anymore so it is much more difficult to find you out in the woods. In a lodge Jasons senses are disabled and you have to search by yourself finding a poor guy waiting to be slashed and killed.
Go ahead give it a try even if the servers make problems at the moment. But when you are connected you have alot of fun! Guaranteed!

Death Squared is an interesting puzzle game that has blocks that are affected by physics.
I want to start off by saying that I’ve beaten all single player missions, and have not done any of the multiplayer missions because this game only supports local multiplayer. The reason I’ve decided to not dive into any of the local multiplayer is because many people simply can’t play local multiplayer games as such I’ve decided to look at this game only from a singleplayer perspective.
In this game you will control a red and blue cube that you will move by using the WASD and Arrow Keys, you have to navigate these cubes through levels with several obstacles ranging from deathly lasers to spikes and other moving objects. Then at the end you have to move both cubes onto a circular pad in order to complete the level.
Often you will confuse which cube is moved by which keys on your keyboard, I've often failed a level because I instinctively moved with the wrong set of keys.
The game likes to throw random deaths your way by making spikes appear out of nowhere when you stand on a button, this would be fine if the game wasn't adamant about recording the amount of deaths it takes to beat the level, having cheap one-time deaths defeats that purpose.
Due to the game having physics it's pretty easy to cheese some levels by glitching cubes into places or moving into places that don't feel intended.
I had to play with the SFX Music muted because the cubes would make a horrendous noise when they are placed upon the circular pads (check my video for an example).
Background Music is gorgeous and fits really well.
Levels provide some real difficult challenges.
Funny Dialogue between levels.
I can't reccomend this game at full price if you are looking for a singleplayer puzzle game, I'd reccomend you wait for it to go on sale.

Death Squared is basically the game you break out to test your sanity when communicating with your friends. It makes for a fun, rage-inducing puzzle game whereby a ton of shouting is involved . However, if you like puzzle games on thier own and you have a quieter friend to play with, the 1-2 player mode is a calmer, nicer distraction with added value through the mode-exclusive voice acting. The voice acting here is done by Mick Lauer AKA RIcePirate - an animator and voice actor on Youtube. The voice acting and writing itself isn't Portal level but it is solid. The music in this game is also great. Techno beats add tension to the game and make everythine come alive. This is all wrapped up in plenty of levels which range nicely in difficulty as you start with easy puzzles but move quickly to more and more challenging ones later on. What makes the game so rage inducing in co-op mode is getting everyone on the same page to move to the objective perfectly. Communication is required as some players cannot do everything on thier own. Overall it makes for a fun night.
If you enjoy puzzle games on their own and you also want a nice game to break out to incite hatred (the good kind) among your friends; this is worth the 20$. However, if you already have a stack of co-op local multiplayer games and don't care for the single player puzzle solving aspect; i'd wait for a price drop.

So far I've only played with 3 players. It's a blast. Some of the puzzles aren't so bad to solve, but actually coordinating as a team can be tricky. I enjoy the challenge of having to control two myself (and they don't usually move at the same time), but that's not for everyone. I'd say most people would likely prefer even numbers of players.
Anyway, this is, for me, the same kind of fun that Magicka is. Sorta slapsticky. This game isn't goofy or intended to have those sorts of things, but with 4 players moving around, people will mess up, or fall off platforms, and people tend to laugh in a mix of amusement and frustration. THIS is the aspect that makes this a great game.
The puzzles are good, but without that mix of amusement and frustration, this game wouldn't be nearly as good.

Death Squared is a great puzzle Co-Op game to play with almost everyone! It's great fun playing around and exploring the world of death squared and uncovering secrets with my friends. I had the chance to play this at Pax East (2 years in a row) and found the best experiences with this game were with complete strangers! It forces you to communicate with the other players and learn to cooperate with whoever you're playing with.
Another suprising aspect of this game is the story behind it. Anyone could get away with making a 2 or 4 player Co-Op game like this with absolutely no story, and nobody would complain. SMG Studio decided to go the extra mile and add dialogue in between the levels giving the game a plot!
Overall, I'd rate the game 9/10. The downsides being the lack of accessibility to the customization and my good friend Mr.ThirdWheel will have to cycle in our 2 player campaign every few levels.

I really can't recommend this game at all unless you already know how to play this game or have no problem researching on forums how to properly play the game.
The first thing I noticed when I first started the game was that there is no tutorial on how to begin playing the game.  It literally gives you a message saying visit the forums for more information on how to play....really?  Very poor and lazy on the developers part. Also, if you have ever used Windows 3.1 then these boxes will look very familiar.  It looks a bit sharper in the screenshots provided but when you start playing, you will notice the ugly edges on all the charts/messages/etc and it feels incredibly cheap.  I expected quite a bit more polish out of an officially licensed game.  I saw the screenshots but it looks much poorer once you actually start it up and feels like it was meant to be played on an old box monitor instead of on crisp hd monitors.  Some chart boxes looked so poor they almost seemed like they overlapped.  It's like if you took nearly a dozen Windows 3.1 boxes and put them all together and added in some pictures/icons/colored font/etc.
The two things I liked about the game was how in depth it is and the player portraits.  The portraits were all in some kind of weird but somewhat realistic looking shots.  David Ortiz looked almost like a claymation version of himself which I thought was neat and looked closed enough.  This is great for a simulation game since once you progress to a point where you need fake players created as rookies then they can just use any random faces and it won't look weird next to the other real players since there are no real player photos in the game to begin with.
All in all, I honestly can't recommend this game.  I'm a huge fan of sports, sports simulations and tycoon games but this feels much more appropriate for gaming in the early 1990's than an officially licensed game in 2016.  I do like the direction they are going in and I may revisit this series if they release a game in the future that adds a proper introduction to the game, better looking boxes/charts and possibly some larger bolder font.

The Good:
Excellent graphics: This game looks amazing blowing away similar titles such as DayZ and Rust.
Controls are solid: Familiar key bindings make this game easy to jump into and enjoy.
Multiplayer experience: Playing this game with friends is what I like to call a blast in a glass. Enjoy hours of exploring, battling enemies and being killed by other gamers online. The hours of fun times are endless.
Weapons: The arsenal available in Nether is solid offering a large enough collection of weapons to both purchase and scavenge to keep you entertained for a long time.
Developers: As Nether gets closer to be an official release (who knows when that will be) the development team continues to improve upon and expand the game. This is always a great sign.
Environments: The lands are huge, detailed and original. You won’t get bored exploring and you will always be on the hunt for hidden goodies (see: finding a large back pack).
The Bad:
Opponents: You will regularly become disappointed as you leave a safe zone just to run into a hidden sniper waiting for you to take off your head and steal all of your collected and purchased goods. What makes this even worse is that upon your death you lose everything, including the perks which you had ranked up through out that life. This can become extremely frustrating.
AI: we would like to see more diverse Nether in the game. As of now, the human players are more difficult than the Nether.
Weapon glitches: Being that this game is still in beta makes it difficult to mention issues with weapons, but I feel it must be said.
Ammo is valuable in game. Very valuable. There is a glitch which will currently allow you to unload and reload our weapon netting you extra ammo each time you do so. I am sure this will be fixed before the game officially releases, but as of now, it can be an issue.
Stuck on stairs: The current build of Nether often has you getting stuck on the stairs, not allowing you to go up or down.
Clipping: Randomly, your character will sink into the ground in certain areas of the world.
Micro-transactions: I simply have never been a fan.

Nihilumbra is a puzzle platformer, with more emphasis on puzzle and less emphasis on platformer.  I'm usually pretty terrible at platformers, but I'd even classify it as "not hard but fun."  I rarely requires very much precision in timing.  There are places where you might be pressed a bit with timing and precision, but that's certainly not the emphasis.
You play with a combination of keyboard and mouse.  With one hand you control movement (left, right, jump); and with the mouse hand you control the deployment of "colors" which change the characteristics of the terrain around you.  For instance, one of the first colors is blue, which is slippery, and if you apply blue to a surface it becomes slippery, allowing you to go faster and/or build up momentum.  There are secondary effects, such as making your enemies slide also.  Other colors have different effects such as bounciness, stickiness, etc.
Again, I'm usually terrible at platformers and I enjoyed this, so if you're more into puzzle aspects of games, and less into platforming, I'd say give this a go if you're interested.  For those of you who are more hardcore platformers, there is a more difficult void mode of the game that is much more challenging than the regular game that unlocks at game completion.  The more difficult mode is far more difficulty than I was looking for, but it might be good for those looking for something requiring more precision and quickness.

I've got mixed feelings on this game. Overall it was a good experience and a relaxing platformer/puzzler to play over an evening. The puzzles were ridiculously easy (except for a handful that were mainly dependent on perfect timing) for any adult, which normally I'm fine with so long as the story is interesting; however, the story was really nothing interesting at all with awful narration that was horribly redundant and rarely revealed anything interesting. The game mechanics for the puzzles were fun - but they clashed with the way side-scrolling was implemented by sliding in/out each background/scene instead of a single continuous level. Most of the trouble I had with puzzles was due to the mechanics clashing with side-scrolling, but not in a fun way that seemed intended at all. Toward the end I started wanting to just finish the game already, and found myself enjoying it less and less.
Pros
- Nice artwork, and sound was decent
- Fun game mechanics (painting colors on surfaces)
- Relaxing platformer/puzzler gameplay that never left me frustrated
Cons
- Short (I like short games now and then, but I know it will irk others)
- Way too easy (Solutions were always always obvious at first glance without any thought)
- Story was bland and repetitive, if you can even call it a story
- Narrator was getting annoying
- Only challenges were unintended annoyances due to side-scrolling implementation
- Lots of glitches with getting stuck on certain surfaces (causing character stuttering and sound repeating)
Artistic approach on this game blew me away. It's fun and beautiful. Recommended.

I've played for 400 hours in total so far, not through Steam, and I can say this is a fun and challanging game with new challanges being introduced pretty regularly as this game is still being developed. The graphics are not the best of the best, but I like the style and shading method. Other minor tweeks and changes keep the game nice and fresh when playing for so long. But here are some random things about the game:
P(l)ay 2 Win: Many players go look at the market when they first play and straight away see the over priced "high" stat, end game gear, and you could easily say this game is p2w. It's just simply not, the economy is still very young and there's almost no demand for higher level gear, so the prices are very over the top. Chances are those items were found by free 2 play players who challange themselves against leader/deities.
"Grindy": . . .I don't know what people expect, it's an RPG, of course there's going to be a grind, but you can avoid this pretty easily by just letting AI battle for you. You gain less xp (~60% less if the battle was fought with only AI) and decreased loot chances but you can go do something else.
Admins: A game where the admins (dungeon masters) are actually involved, you can chat with them, have some laughs instead of admins being hidden and only appear to deal the ban hammer, how many other games have something like this?

The game eases you into play in the beginning, but it ramps up to be more challenging. You fight as a squad of 3 vs another squad of 3, but you can have several squads of fighters join into one battle. This lets you do 6 vs 6 or more. Multiplayer is possible by joing with friends in the same way. There are guilds to help you out and additional gameplay added when you join through guilds fighting each other.
the world lets you find enemies, do quests (find and kill enemies of a specific faction), find treasure, collect resources, and find relics to enhance your fighters and their gear with a bonus enchantment.
The Devs have made a wiki
, an armory/leaderboards
, and forums
for help and in depth information.

There is a learning curve, but oh it's worth it. Life is feudal is not meant to be played on your own, you NEED at least two other people to be able to do anything past building a shack and a fence.
During the time I played, I learned the basic mechanics for a small week on my own, planting stuff, running around, getting killed by russians, etc, before finding a small clan (maybe 10 people total, from a bunch of different countries). And there the game really began. It's all about building a community, where each person is specialized in something, and everyone thrives to improve the "quality" of the materials and items. Unlike what you may hear from some people, you don't need to play 10 hours a day to enjoy it. We were 3 playing a lot, the rest would just pop by a couple hours a day to do their daily harvesting/crafting/hanging out.
After a month we had a large town, stone remparts, a fort, lots of fields, a lot of horses, and basically every available craftable items. The most time consuming task was terraforming for our walls, but we all chipped in whenever we had a moment, and it probably took us a good week of shovelling total (complaining about it the whole time).
Once you reach this stage with your group, it's a whole new game that opens up again. You get to train your weapon skills, build siege weapons, train warhorses, arm the newbies that live near your town, and attack your mean neighbours.
Back when I played, that was the most flawed aspect of the game, we sieged a castle for a good 6 hours, because our enemies repaired their wall faster than our 2 siege engines damaged it (eventually we climbed on top of eachother and killed everyone). The combat system was also not the best, a naked guy with a pitchfork or a bow was much more efficient than an fully armored one. I hear a lot of it has been fixed now, so that shouldn't be a concern for the mmo launch.
All in all this game is trully excellent, it has some flaws but there just isn't anything on the market that is as realistic and community oriented. I couldn't recommend it more!

Death Squared is a surprisingly clean and competent puzzle game. It can be played solo or cooperatively with both methods of play working smoothly and satisfyingly. It stands well above the average when it comes to indie puzzle games and features a big chunk of content, challenging but not unfair difficulty, and even a surprisngly well voice-acted narration that injects humour and personality into the game.
The aim of the game is to coordinate and move both cubes safely to the end, but obstacles and tricky environments can make that a challenging task.
The game offers:
80 x 'story levels' (can be played solo or local coop)
40 x 'party levels' (intended for 2 to 4 players - but all content is possible solo, if you can coordinate)
10 x '2-player experiments'
10 x '4-player experiments'
Death Squared controls well, I plugged in a controller and controlled one cube using the left joystick and one with the right joystick. You could alternatively use 'wasd' and 'arrow keys' to control the cubes. I also played coop where I used the controller and my partner the keyboard, although you could share a keyboard if you like, every method works.
The puzzles are also satisfying, not so difficult they made me rage but definitely challenging. Death Squared tested the player not just in their wit and puzzle solving abilities, but also in their coordination, cooperation (if played with a partner) and memory. I will say that the puzzles will often be solved using trial-and-error which isn't inheriently a bad thing, but was sometimes less satisfying because of it.
The game also had a tonne of personality (think Portal) which helped to seperate it from its sometimes more clinical competition. One of the few criticisms I had of the game was the inability to access the options menu from the pause screen, needing to instead back out to the main menu. The options also didn't include subtitles which I would have liked to ensure I didn't mishear any of the dialogue, although there are potentially hearing impaired players out there who this will be an even bigger issue for - I'm hoping they patch that in.
Ulimately a fun experience though. If you like puzzle games you will like Death Squared. Coop always makes things more fun and only adds to this experience. It's the perfect entry game for a friend, partner, or family member who isn't usually into gaming to jump in with you.

Download Size: Less than 9 gigabytes
Playtime: Less than 6 hours for single player
Medal of Honor (2010) was my intro to modern First Person Shooter games, so I go back and play it once in a while.  Despite the fact that the game plays nearly identically to the Call of Duty Modern Warfare games, Medal of Honor is actually from EA (makers of Battlefield). If you have this game, you probably got it as part of the Humble Origin Bundle from a year or so back (bunch of great games in that one). Like the Call of Duty games, MOH is split into Multiplayer and Single player installations, which means you can download just one or the other if you’re only planning to play through the campaign (like me). There is a separate Steam entry for each.
The story of MOH follows a couple of Navy Seal teams in Afghanistan trying to root out Al Qaida / Taliban soldiers, mostly taking place in the mountains. You also switch to playing a member of a squad of Army Rangers for a couple of missions, and see the war from a different perspective. MOH is very story driven, and since you’re almost always in a squad, you can count on the other members of your team to support you when you’re under heavy fire. However if you get shot enough you’ll die and reload the checkpoint. Your team doesn’t “revive” you like in some other squad based games (Payday, Left 4 Dead). Gameplay is very much like Call of Duty Modern Warfare where you’re supposed to do most of the heavy lifting while the rest of your team kind of picks off a few enemies occasionally and provides ammo.
MOH has the regenerating health system as expected in most modern first person shooters, with the screen edges turning red as you are taking damage and then clearing up if you don’t get shot for a few seconds. This means that a lot of the time you can risk making a run without cover and take some hits as long as you don’t die. You can also pick up the weapons of fallen enemies, though you should almost always keep your primary assault rifle (with the silencer when available).  An interesting gameplay element as mentioned above is that if you run low on ammo, you can always ask a computer controlled squad mate for more. I don’t remember this being available in many other first person games.
Pros:
+Pretty good graphics and engrossing story. If you like Call of Duty type shooter games, you should like MOH. I believe the game’s story is based on actual events.
+A lot of gameplay variety. You can occasionally control aerial bombardment (as an attack helicopter pilot) or heavy direct fire aircraft (blowing up stuff with big guns!). The sniper/stealth sections are fun as well.
Cons:
-The game is really short. It can take less than 5 hours to beat the campaign if you’ve played the game before. For a game this short it takes up a lot of hard drive space.
-There is at least 1 mission where it can be difficult to tell where you’re supposed to go. Your squad leader gives you an order and it isn’t immediately obvious what you’re supposed to do. Also, more than once I got stuck due to a game bug where an event didn’t trigger the way it was supposed to (marking a spot for air strike).
Overall Medal of Honor is a fun game to go through in a weekend, and get a feel for what highly trained combat soldiers have to do for a living. If you’ve seen the recent Mark Wahlberg movie “Lone Survivor” this game has a similar feel (elite soldiers surrounded by enemies).
Sequel info:
MOH Warfighter is exclusive to EA Origin (no Steam version). I got my copy as a physical DVD so I didn’t have to go through the process of downloading it through Origin.
Install size: Less than 20 gigabytes
Playtime: about 6 hours for single player
In Warfighter, you play a new member of the same group of Navy Seals as in the first game, but with a few new additions to your team. The action takes place in several regions all over the world (Philippines, Middle East, etc.) unlike the first game, where you were in Afghanistan the whole time. There are also a bunch of cutscenes following a few characters in their “off-duty” life in the United States (kind of boring). The general plot of the game though, is chasing down terrorists before they execute their complicated plans of blowing stuff up.
The game is very similar to the first MOH (as expected) and  it uses the Frostbite 2 game engine, which was featured in Battlefield 3. The graphics are VERY good and almost photo realistic at times. Unfortunately, this means that some computers may not be able to run the game at a decent frame rate. I found an issue where I would have horribly low frames per second at certain parts of the game, and it turned out that it was due to Origin downloading free map packs in the background (Zero Dark Thirty map pack was about 900 megabytes). When I stopped the downloads the game sped up. If you liked MOH1, you’ll like Warfighter.

This is surprisingly fast and intense game about economics. The game starts out simple, claim tiles and build on them. But then you add in a fully floated market for each of the resouces in the game, the fact that you have a sevearly limited amount of tiles to buy, and the sabotage options availible and you have a brutally challanging game of resource domination and trading.
People have described this game as being like Catan and I have to say I see the similarities. There's no direct combat, you won't be building armies or anything. You'll just buy tiles and build resouce generators on them plus factories to refine the resources. But it's the dynamic market system that really makes this game special.
Your aim is to buy out your compediters before they buy you out. To do that you need revenue streams, meaning whatever you mine/refine. The prices for everything in every game is floated on supply and demand (or the manipulated states of). And this is the real meta. Dominating one or a few areas of supply and driving up demand while competing against whatever resources you don't have and devaluing them.
10/10 would lose my hair again trying to outcompete Robots at food production.

This review falls into the "great game, but ... " category.
I played a ton of OOTP about 10 years ago. Created a custom league, played a dozen or more seasons, and LOVED IT. Spent a lot of time on their forum, and enjoyed the community. Sure, there were some minor problems with the game, but they were just that -- minor.
I've kept an eye on the title since then, knowing that sooner or later I'd be back for more. The recent mid-summer sale was the final bit of incentive I needed. I took the plunge and bought OOTP 17.
All the new stuff that's been thrown in during the last decade looks damn cool. Problem is, the entire thing seems to be a house of cards. I played 7-8 historical games, and had some problems that took away a lot of the fun. For instance, when starting a new game, and trying to decide on lineups/batting order, the damn game won't show me statistics for one of the teams. (And yes, I've set it to "human" control for both teams.) All I get are a bunch of zeros in the stat categories, no matter how I toggle the display.
Then there's the play-by-play itself. Very frequently (several times a game), the animation will show a ball hit to one side, while the text pbp tells you someone on the other side of the field made the play. Talk about losing that feeling of immersion.
And now the last straw. The third time I tried to open the game, it refused. Turns out this is a fairly common problem, but none of the fixes I found online worked for me. I could keep trying, or wait until the developers work it out (because I'm sure they will, eventually). But there are just too many glitches in the product at this point for me to invest more time in it. Even if I could get it running again, I'm not going to take the chance of getting halfway through a season (or through several seasons) before some other fatal flaw rears its head.
Love the game and what the developer is doing. Not willing to pay for a product with these kind of problems.

I've been looking forward to Friday the 13th since the Beta, which I had a lot of fun with and I pre-ordered on backerkit once the Beta went live to get some keys for friends. Now with the full game out I don't think the $40 is justified if you're looking for a large chunk of content and a strong release weekend.
I won't go into much detail about what the game is but rather, what the game has to offer: 3 maps, 6 Jasons and 8 or so counselors. All of the maps are from the films, immaculately recreated which is awesome but it also makes it all of them feel very samey. I get it, most of the films are in the boonies and the maps should reflect that, but at least we could of had dynamic variations in weather, cloud cover, lighting just to change it up from match to match. The counselors and Jasons don't vary by a lot, but there are considerations for you to take into account which is good, it doesn't make any of the characters feel worthless or overpowered and gives you a wide range of options without feeling like you made a bad choice; your survival really comes down to how you play.
I'm really happy that they added another option to surviving (the boat), but it still feels like there's not much to do as a survivor. Another thing that has been added was the need for a fuse to fix up the phones to call for help, which, adds another layer to getting out but I don't know if that was necessary considering how hard it is to come across the fuse and I don't even know if there can be more than one in a match.
The launch went pretty well at midnight, everything was fine until the next morning. The servers were overloaded and went down and now that there's up it seems like certain accounts have issues with their saved games or even being able to connect at all. My stats will "save" but won't show in the lobby, so I'm always Rank 0 until after a match, and then I don't even think my experience or points save. My friend can't even connect at all to the game servers, but this issue isn't effecting me at all. Also no one has access to their pre-order DLC and the "day 1" patch didn't drop.
I do believe the game has potential and if the devs continue to support it it could be one of the best games of it's genre but as of now things feel a little anemic. The game is a labor of love for sure, with Kane Hodder giving us a ton of gorey kills, Henry Manfredini composing a fantastic score and a very good layer of polish on everything but at $40, unless you love this type of gameplay like me, there's just not enough for most. Coupled with the rocky launch, I'd give it a week.
I'm still going to give the game a recommendation because the foundation laid is sturdy and this should be easy to fix; hopefully.

So this game is, like, really ♥♥♥♥ing good
THE STORY
The story of KOTOR 2 isn't like the first one at all, other than the fact that you're in the Star Wars universe with the force and lightsabers. In the first game, you were fighting Darth Malak, who was indisputably a "bad guy" who would laugh evilly as he blew up planets. The antagonists of KOTOR 2 are much more subtle; using manipulation, assassinations, etc, to achieve their goals. The plot of KOTOR 2 is much more morally gray than that of the first one; with very few adamantly good/bad characters. Now, a flaw with the subtlety of this story is that it can be hard to understand from a first-time player's point of view. So, it comes down to personal taste in storytelling if you like this game over the first or not.
THE CHARACTERS
The characters of KOTOR 2, much like the story itself, are much more complex and morally gray than the first game. Almost all of the party members in the game are of the neutral alignment (or very close to neutral). And, unlike the first game, there is an actual practical use to speaking with and getting to know the personalities of your party members. Instead of just getting a blurb of backstory or a special side quest like in the first game, your party members in KOTOR 2 will often teach you some technique (such as mental Pazaak or "How to Kill Jedi") that will improve your gameplay experience. It also gives you a constant sense of progression and increasing power.
"INFLUENCE"
Influence is probably the greatest improvement KOTOR 2 made to the first game; because it allows the bulk of your party members to ascend from crappy gunners and medieval sword wielders to Jedi or Sith. A huge flaw with the first game (and this one) is the gun combat. It simply pales in comparison to lightsaber combat. So, in the first game, you were stuck with a bunch of party members that were trash compared to the jedi on your team; because they were less versatile in combat. Now, you can have a fully trained team of Jedi or Sith disciples that can use all the same force powers that you can.
GAMEPLAY
As said before, the gameplay of KOTOR 2 is much more intuitive than that of the first game; because it gives you many more options for how you want to play. The only step backward in my opinion is the gun combat, which has taken an even larger backseat to lightsaber combat. Now, you character starts off as a Jedi right off the bat, and makes it almost completely impractical to use blasters (especially late game). There are also certain parts of the game that ramp up the difficulty to insane amounts with little warning. One minutes you're cutting through a bunch of useless wildlife and then get ambushed by 10 Sith Lords. Despite the gameplay system's flaws with difficulty and gun combat, the lightsaber and force combat is very entertaining. Nothing quite beats the feeling of using force storm to clear an entire room or using force crush on the bigger bosses of the game.
"THE EXILE"
The Exile is the main protagonist of the story and the character you play as more often than not. Unlike Revan of the first game (and most RPGs for that matter), you do NOT have amnesia for once! In fact, the Exile's past is crucial to the plot of the game and it is very fun to be given hints about it and to piece together his/her involvement with the Jedi and the Sith. Canonically, the Exile is female, but both male and female playthroughs are very fun and surprisingly different from each other. There is an entire party member that varies depending on the Exile's gender, as well as a subplot with one of the main antagonists, and a subplot with one fo the Jedi masters. The Exile's dark/light side alignment is also very important, as it almost completely changes the tone of the story (and a party member is determined on you alignment). In a light side playthrough, you are the naive Jedi who disregards the dangers of the Sith in order to unite the Jedi as allies, save the Republic, and rebuild the Jedi order. However, playing dark side turns you into a demonic hunter whose goal is to destroy the order on every planet you visit and to cripple both the Jedi and the Sith; forging your own Empire by the end.
KREIA
Kreia is, without a doubt, one of the most interesting star wars characters ever. Her views on the fabled neutral alignment are very compelling and backed up with solid theories and philosophy. Kreia is, arguably, the most essential character in the story, which is surprising due to the fact that she was never mentioned in the first game. To a first-time player, Kreia might appear to be the nagging grandma who berates your every choice regardless of light or dark. With more and more playthroughs under your belt (or good perception), it becomes easy to interpret Kreia's actions and do things that she approves of (if that's your goal). Kreia is interesting because no matter what alignment you ultimately choose, she supports you and trains you in whatever you are interested in. For example, she appears to be a Jedi but has no qualms with you becoming a Sith Lord and hunting down the remianing Jedi. Likewise, though she seems to have vague connections with the Sith in the past, she doesn't care if you become a dark-banishing Jedi master who hunts down Sith Lords. To avoid me rambling any further about Kreia (and I could), I'll just say that you should absolutely give her character a chance and listen to many of the interesting perspectives on the Star Wars universe she has to offer.
I would ramble more but I think I've made my point.

I've been playing Dire since the kickstarter and have enjoyed watching the game mature into a pretty well-balanced turn-based strategy game.  The active development means there are constant changes - some great, some not nearly as good - but the equally active community helps steer the game mechanics into a direction that is best for all players.
The PVE element is well established, with high loot-drop rates that increase with your willingness to challenge yourself.  If you use tactics and patience to defeat tougher NPC opponents you will get a greater chance at a greater reward.  Teaming up with friends to complete quests or just farm gear and experience is easy, and is possible with Guild mates, friends, or even enemies.
The PVP portion is evolving.  At present, there is not much incentive to fighter other actual players beyond rivalry and some low-key battles over resources, but the developers are actively building systems to make PVP more rewarding.
The graphics are amazing and highly detailed.  The soundtrack choice is inspired and the ambient/battle sounds are engaging.  You can also cut all those details out to concentrate on the chess-like mentality that is often required to play the challenging portions.
In all, I think the game is rich and engaging as-is.  The promises of the future are exciting.

It's been almost 5 years since ArmA3 came out, yet for the life of me, I can't feel that ArmA3 was better than its predecessor. ArmA2 offered so many advances and improvements compared to ArmA1, including plenty of additional content and mods, as well as powering several of Bohemia Interactive's other titles. ArmA3 on the other hand, has always felt rushed, incoherent, and lost. It wanted to be a futuristic game, yet it still feels like the 1960s. It wanted to have better infantry combat, yet it remains clunky and difficult. Vehicles only show slight improvements and not significant enough to write home about.
The rough beginnings of the game seems to have hung around and put a curse on it, because every time I play it, I feel like I'd rather play ArmA2. That's a shame because it does offer some marginal improvements that needed to happen, but too much was lost to bring those to the front. There's still a lot of things to do, but one will have to download a lot of 3rd party mods to get them since the base content is considerably poor. Nonetheless, credit must be given to the developers since over the past 5 years, they've kept updating the game and steadily fed improvements, even if it does seem too little, too late.
Overall, ArmA3 can be an enjoyable experience, but only if you're willing to put the effort into it beforehand. It's not a game that you can just pick up and go; it takes considerable investment to adjust to the mechanics. For that reason, I can't recommend it, and can only hope that Bohemia Interactive will persevere and apply lessons learned to their next title.

There was a point in time when Medal of Honor was a series that mattered. A franchise born in a time where WWII shooters were still hot and Allied Assault was blowing players and its competition away. But between then and now bolt action rifles and beach stormings have fallen out of fashion, most of the people who made Medal of Honor a respected name among shooters have long since left for other studios, and 2010’s reboot (for lack of a more appropriate term) is left doing the same thing so many other games were a decade or so ago when the series was first kicking off: attempting to ape its peers in the hope of grabbing a slice of the pie.
Today’s analogical pastry is the impossibly large Call of Duty, which along with its innovations in campaign structures and online play brought itself out of the early 20th century and into modern day. Naturally every other military shooter has followed suit, but Medal of Honor is perhaps the first to really attempt to ground itself in the ongoing conflicts happening in the middle east, a decision that could have given its campaign meaning outside of itself and showcased to its players the very real horrors raging on in Afghanistan which somehow still feel so distant.
Instead we end up with exactly what you’d expect from a modern military shooter, except coming along with the added baggage of playing off actual current events, which for all of developer Danger Close’s intentions has only managed to turn the game into a giant mess. It’s not that I expected Medal of Honor to provide any meaningful commentary on the scenarios its portraying, but by marrying its summer action movie mentality to a war that’s still raging and killing thousands it trivializes the losses of American soldiers and innocent Afghans for mindless entertainment.
Medal of Honor is happy to proclaim itself as being “real” only so far as it can manage to fit in a blockbuster sequence of set pieces and explosions, showing you how horrible the things its replicating are one second while reveling in gory headshots and idiotic “bro-speak” the next. It feels emotionally manipulative and tasteless, unwilling to commit to being anything but a dumb action game with as little nuance in presenting its subject matter as that usually entails.
And what an unbelievably dumb game Medal of Honor is. Below its terribly handled premise, incoherent plot, and attempts at “gritty realism”, there’s a game that’s terrified of letting you play it. It funnels you through levels with gratuitous levels of restriction, placing invisible walls everywhere so as to always be entirely in control of where you are and where you can go even if it intends to let you there later. You move when it tells you to, shoot where it points you, watch the often malfunctioning scripted sequences sometimes when it makes you, and participate in its series of strict directions because that’s all you can do.
Medal of Honor is so obsessed with being in control that I began to ask why I was even there at all. The game clearly didn’t want me there, as I became one more thing needing to be kept on a leash, in case I potentially walk too far ahead and break another scripting trigger or stumble into an area before it’s had time to spawn its enemies, and I didn’t want to be there because the lack of any player agency made it feel like I was watching a very dull movie that I had to keep moving forward.
But it’s probably the incompetency with which the game hides any of this that’s the most insulting. There’s never any question that you’re being moved through egregiously linear environments, shooting enemies with zero tactical awareness that pop up like target dummies with guns that never feel right. The game presents itself entirely as it is, as if it hasn’t even enough pride to try and hide its mind numbing tediousness and genericism; to try and pretend it wasn’t plopped out in the hopes of catching hold of Call of Duty’s momentum because it hasn’t a single original idea left for itself. In a way I kind of appreciate this sort of honesty, if only because it’s the only bit of sincerity the game ever shows.

It is hilarious to me, all this whining about not having dedicated servers.  Yes, the game is peer to peer, but it does peer to peer in a way no other game has done, I'd encourage you to do your own research on how it is handled, but i'll give you a TLDR.
Normal peer to peer: One player hosts the game, has ping advantage by default.
FH peer to peer: Everyone is hosting the game, yet no one is. Everyone is running a simulation of the game, and basically handshakes all the players actions. You will never get disconnected from a game because one player left, there is no ping advantage, because everyone is connected to everyone.
With that out of the way, this is probably one of the most unique and interesting titles out in the past 5 years in my opinion. I've played two closed betas, and the open beta for an extensive period of time. At the time of writing I have 52.7 hours in post release play, but collectively around 120 hours so far (with no intent to slow down, i may add.)
The combat in this game is genuinely unique, offers a LOT of depth, and is HIGHLY gratifying. Anyone that tells you the game is boring is probably among the worst players in the game.  Every character offers a unique playstyle, with varying abilities and attacks. It has many mechanics very akin to fighting games, but does so in such an immersive way.
If you are passing on this game because of peer to peer and you don't live in a place with internet on par with dial up at best, you're shooting yourself in the foot by not playing it.
edit: The devs have already taken to patching balance and technical issues, as well as compensating people for the mm server's down time.
