Tl&dr: my recommendations for M&B variants are as follows:
1. Viking Conquest Reforged
2. Floris mod
3. Warband
4. Any mod you can find, but you can expect some crashes and bugs in some
5. With fire and sword
6. Blood and Gold: Carribean! (only for a 5 minutes laugh)
I assume this M&B version wanted to put the player in a position closer to an army general than the original Warband, but fails to do even that through its own fault. This is why (comparing to Warband):
- no more character attributes design at start of the game. You start with the same point in all attributes and can distribute only a few. You will be a poor fighter, poor trader with a slightly above average IQ; no other choice.
- since the discovery of fire (a.k.a. muskets) any fight can end abruptly if some mediocre rifleman gets lucky and lands a head shot from across the map, no matter how many hit points you have or what head gear you use; but to be honest, this can be avoided 99.99% of the times if you get a horse and run around in circles like a crazy chicken. In short, if you run around buck naked you survive, if you stand still in the best armor in the game, you die.
- although the game almost forces you into a command position, the battle map size doesn't really give you this feeling. Half the times, after you give a few commands and your men start to move into position, the enemy cavalry is already close and charging, turning what should be a clean line-infantry battle into a total mess of men and horses.
- adding to the above point is the battle size limiter to 150, which makes you feel like you are the leader of an oversized gang, rather than some wannabe Napoleon. There are tools to increase this size to 1000, but, considering the small maps, having 1000 men fighting is more of a lottery than some tactical or strategic combat.
- Warband had a questionable AI at best in siege battles, but this one made the step forward. The best result I had against this terrible AI was at a siege 60 attackers vs. 180 defenders. Attackers won with 1 wounded and 1 dead.
- speaking of AI, do not expect any challenges on the global map either. No matter what you do, you can't be outsmarted, the only way to lose anything is through brute force, when you are seriously outnumbered.
- story-line quests are bugged; almost all of them. The only one that works without constantly saving because of the fear of the bugs is the Polish one. However, it has some interesting ways to make the game challenging. One moment you have half of the map, the next half of your cities belong to the enemy without any battles fought or any warnings. Why? Because you talked to some guy and asked him what's wrong. Thank you.
- no more tournaments, lots of quests from Warband removed
- troop upgrade trees are lacking imagination to say the least
- money from fiefs are not sent to you automatically forcing you to make a tour every now and then to collect your taxes
Overall, a M&B with less interesting combat, but in which you can trade and become a tax collector.

SOMA goes places. I expected a game full of jump scares and scary thriller sequences but I was given all that and then some.  The game's story is rich and intriguing with a thrilling concept. The game will make you feel many emotions throughout the experience and each one is presented amazingly. You as the player get to decide just how much you want to engage with the narrative, as the game places (not hides) the details around the environment. The game also never hides your objective and is very straight forward when it wants you to do something.  The controls are also kept simple so there is almost nothing that gets in the way of the story and sequences. These are the things Frictional has done well with in SOMA; keeping the game honest and the story accessible, all the while grabbing the player and keeping them engaged.
The only negatives I could point out is that some of the mechanics of the enemies was very vague. I personally believe this made the encounters more novel as it makes the player confront their fears of the unknown in order to figure out the solution to do what's needed, but I can see this being a negative aspect for others.
Fans of thought provoking narratives should play this game, even if you're not a fan of horror.

I had almost given up on this game and come to write an incendiary review after the first few missions. So let's get it out of the way: this game is far from perfect.
Mouse sensitivity is awkward, it feels fast for small movements and slow for big ones. The AI is pretty weak, as even on hard difficulty, ennemies still seem to think running right in front of you and kneeling before even raising their gun is a good idea (they're not actually surrendering), and they severely suffer from the stormtrooper syndrome (better not shoot the hero). You're the only guy in your squad of elite badass soldiers that really shoots down more than one enemy per encounter. The early missions felt uncompelling and lacking in purpose, with some painfully obvious script checkpoints—that sometimes forget to trigger, forcing you to restart the last sequence. The quad sequences (only one mission) are both eventless and clunky.
It gets much better however, and I'm glad I stuck around for it. You get used to the control awkwardness. You live the extraordinary landscape. The ennemies start to feel like they invariably punish you for leaving exposed body parts stick out. Your squad doesn't feel useless anymore. The missions finally get purpose, and I played through the most engaging and memorable FPS sequences I ever played.
I can't speak for the multiplayer part that I didn't play.
This game is extremely backloaded. It is such a waste that all the bad things about the game appear at the beginning, when it surely drives many players away before they can get to the juicy bits. So if you decide to give this game a chance (and you should), make sure you don't give up on it too easy.
Keep in mind, however, that the campaign is very short—I'd wait for a sale if short games make you feel bitter.

For Honor is a gameplay first driven experience. Many people who review this game take things into account that should barely be considered an issue, such as the microtransactions and season pass. While the game does offer these things, they do not effect the core gameplay experience.
While Ubi Mon. may have intended Dominion, the 4v4 moba/capture gamemode, to be the main gamemode, serious players will recognize that 1v1 duels are where the real game will happen. In 1v1 duels, gear, level, feats, etc DO NOT matter at all. I have played against a Lawbringer who had all of the unlocks, special execution and emote effects, etc, and still handed him his♥♥♥♥♥ You can pay to look cool, but you cannot pay to win. Microtransactions and s. pass are there for people who have more money than time, not for people to get an advantage.
The biggest legitimate issue people have is the peer to peer connection system in place. Unfortunately, while Dominion mode is hosted on servers, everything else is not, including the 1v1 duels. This can go as badly as you might expect (i.e whiffed parrys you thought you should get, stuttering, and flat out disconnects.) I stand with most players and suggest Ubi Mon. pursue dedicated servers for ALL game modes. It is a shame when you get beat by someone because THEY have poor internet, not because they're better than you.
As previously stated, however, the gameplay is solid. It is easy to pick up, and a long road to master. It strikes that great balance of not scaring away casual players and not alienating those who get frustrated, but rather encourages you to become better and better. Definitely watch some streams of high level players and learn some advanced techniques.
If you are passionate about fighting games, I would say pick this game up for sure right now. If you are pretty casual and just think the game looks fun and interesting, consider picking it up on sale. If you are easily tilted and salty, stay away. I know many HATE to hear this, myself included, but it really is the truth: people who dislike the core gameplay loop in this game, I believe, are simply not good enough to find enjoyment in it yet. I thought I was dissapointed in the game at first, but keep pushing and practicing and it will become more enjoyable when you land that heavy into execute, or parry that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ warden playing to aggressive. Good game, just needs a few tweaks.

Even though the servers are very bad, I would still recommend this game. With beautifully stunning graphics, diverse controls and a better playerbase than CS : GO or Dota 2, this game is a very addictive fighting game. Inside the game itself, you are given three different factions. The Samurai, the Viking and the Knight faction. Each faction holds four different characters, each having a very different playstyle from one another. There's the Vanguard, the Heavy, the Assassins and the Hybrids. The Vanguards are the easiest to play (I'd recommend you try this class first), with a considerably fast attack speed  and an average amount of damage that can be dealt, it is definitely the most balanced of all the classes.The Heavy, as you can expect from the name, is the slowest and most durable. However, to compensate for its slow speed, it can deal very high amounts of damage. The next character from the four is the Assassins, a very fast paced character. It is the most nimble and agile from the four and is the deadliest when fighting in close quarter combat (duel or 1 v 1 situations). Despite that, the Assassins are very fragile, they can be dealt with easily and is very hard to play. The last class, the Hybrid, is a mixture of the Heavy and the Assassins. It is both nimble and tanky, making it the most versatile of all the classes. But as you can expect, it is the hardest to use.

Do you remember Amnesia? Heh, there's irony in that question...
But if the answer is yes, and you liked that game, you can safely purchase this one. It's set in the future this time, but the feeling is exactly the same, even though because of the changed setting it doesn't feel like more of the same.
If the answer is no, here's the long description.
First and foremost, it's a horror game that relies on the atmosphere more so than jumpscares. There are (small) puzzles to be solved, but you feel like exploring the environment even though it also tends to scare you. It's hide and seek: no weapons, just you and the stuff around you. I don't think you can wonder off to far, but I never felt there was only one way to go (when that was probably the case anyway, just like with amnesia).
There are monsters, but the main focus is slowly unfolding the story by just... wondering around and trying stuff.
What I liked the most is that this time your character has more text and what he says clearly is in line with the amount of story you have so far. The developpers don't treat you like an idiot in that perspective. What you often see is that the ingame character is not half as far through figuring the story out as the person behind the computer, but with this game it is not the case.
I love amnesia, and I love this game. Apparently it's suddenly very happening to use a futuristic setting, or maybe I'm accidentily drawn towards futuristic settings lately, but it works very well for this game.
Definitely a 10/10

Probrably archery is a complicated archery simulator game.
There is no story.
Gameplay is the selling point here. Basically, you need to shoot an arrow at a variety of targets. The problem is that you need to position your elbows, shoulder and hands in the right position in order to make the shot. This is where things get tricky as you need to do 'trial and error' in order to get the right set up to actually hit your target. There are a variety of game modes including shooting still targets, moving targets, rope and timed trials. There is also a multiplayer component, but unfortunately it is dead. The controls were quite frustrating to get a hang of and I grew bored quickly.
Audio is descent. Music is not memorable and so are the sound FX when shooting. There is no voice acting either.
The graphic suit the game well. Cartoony models fit well into the background, although they do lack detail.
If you want a very challenging 'archery simulator' game and have the patience (or just want cards), then this game may be for you. Else, stay away.

I told myself, let me play this game about 7 days before I write an honest comment about it. 7 days ago I came into this game thinking it would be another Ark simulation, thus the content that I have experienced really blew my mind away. This is so much better than what the critics subjectively acused it of being. To be quite honest and since I have been playing sandbox MMO's for quite some time, since Star Wars Galaxies, I will say that Life is Feudal is not only ambitious and unique, but it is possibly one of the greatest sandbox ideas ever done. People complain about the grindiness, but let me be clear, it is not a game for people who don't enjoy putting in the work. You can't do everything in one day or even one week. You will not be able to experience everything even in one month.
This game is hardcore! You will need to work to level your skills and start from pretty much a primitive savage. Another thing, it is very difficult to play this game alone. You will need a friend (or friends) who will support and care about the game to actually enjoy this. Conan is so broken now, and the mobs are just silly, the combat is clunky and now broken also where when you run you automatically sheathe your weapon. In LiF none of that exist here. The combat is actually one of the greatest things about this game. Two things it reminds me of, and games that are dear to my heart: Mount & Blade Wardband with a ruthless feel of Mortal Online.
Yes! The combat is truly skill based (With first or third person options), probably with more combat ambition ever done in a game; from tactical formations, to siege equipment and mounted warfare. Each combat discipline has skill trees; Cavalryman Knight, Militia, Footman, Slinger/Archer, Assualter/Berserker and so many secondary options birthed from these parent trees. This game finally got combat right! But it is not just combat that is intriguing, but the entire crafting system. You have Carpentry, Masonry, Herbalism, Farming and Hunting with so many skills underneath these parent skills.  The graphics are breathtaking and the nighttime is dangerous and feels like a real forestry.
Also the weather system is very intricate. You actually have seasons that allow you to progress and do things like plant crops, plow and harvest resources. I am not sure how the cycle works, but since we've been playing on our server, every 24 hours is like a month. And you can see the months and days on your map.
Negatives
There are a few things that can be fixed and maybe this will happen in the MMO, when it releases. Character customization is really bad and the race selection in this game is minimal as well. There are pretty much four faces to choose from for everyone. Not much here, but so much better than that other stuff out there. Conan is pathetic and Ark is a waste of money. But Lif is a game for the ages. If you want to play a real game with little bugs and a fun and rewarding experience, with an opportunity to make your mark on a realm, I encourage you to check this game out. Please do it with friends though, because alone this game can be laborous to the point of rage quit.

The game. Well it really reminds me of an advanced, 2 dimensional Wizardry. You know, the one came out for the Apple II back in like 1982? FFFPPP…I mean this in the utmost of positive ways. If you like narrative-driven exploration games, and you're a fan of classic science fiction, then this is a game you need to check out. Reminiscent of games like Dear Esther and Gone Home, this has a more straightforward, traditional narrative arc, while still allowing for some experimentation.
The entire game takes place over one small city block that changes based on the player's exploration and interaction within the environment. This focused environment allows the writing to stand on its own, and as such the story is captivating, rife with conspiracy, paradox, and the paranormal. Each segment of the game explores a different version of the same scene. In addition to a memorable setting, the game is filled with recurring NPCs that are characterized excellently, returning as different iterations of themselves in each segment. Each one you encounter has a unique and memorable voice and design that makes them stand out. Although the voice acting is not the greatest, no character really stands out as obnoxiously bad, and the atmosphere is never lost.
If you're looking for something light on action, and heavy on exploring themes and environments, then I definitely suggest this game. If you're looking for something more traditional, this probably won't be your jam.

Platformer
Nihilumbra is one of the  few 2D platformers to which I could find no deficiency. It is a chain with no weak links. Everything from the way it looks, sounds and plays, feels perfect. Storywise, few platform games leave a more poignant impression in regards to the levels themselves which seem deserted and devoid of any chromatic diversity until the protagonist arrives. Color plays an important role in Nihilumbra (loose Latin translation for “shadow of nothing”), since you will face more puzzles than enemies in this game. The use of colors in altering the landscape and avoiding obstacles bares a powerful contrast to the barren levels. While it never becomes too easy, after completing the first playthrough you unlock the Void mode, which significantly increases the difficulty. The game’s asking price is fully justified and you have both Achievements and Cards. Nihilumbra remains more of a contemplative journey than one filled with action and combat. And that is exactly what sets it apart from generic platform titles which fail to deliver a story.

+ Interesting game concept, storyline and effects.
+ Diversified levels with two game modes.
+ Steam Trading Cards & Achievements.
- None.

Yet, I don't see myself continuing playing after a lot of time invested. And that is not only all shown on Steam. I started weeks before release. I stop because of two following reasons:
1. Lack of challenge. My group is very-well equiped. They all are ascended once. I am able to beat any AI-played group without casualities in many cases. I was able to lead two guilds, one of them founded by me. My collection of titles is very filled.
I didn't win the game. 10 ascends are before me and then, I will still be able to use my fighters for pvp. But it's a grind and could take about 4000 hours.
So is crafting. You need that much ressources you will never have enough of. Except if you are point 2.
2. Kickstarter conservative nobles. I had some ideas how to make hardcore warriors playable. They are not played at all, because you loose too much on death, therefore, pvp is too risky. Nobody buys them and some people stopped playing completely on death. My ideas were progressive concerning pvp aspect that was about to be added. Decreasing greatly the loss on death and making it a percent amount from the exps to the new level.
My second idea was about guilds. It is incredibly hard to found a guild, because you need lvl 20 non-hardcore warriors to guard it, and many players who can move them. This takes time and makes people avoid ascending, so they are still pvp-capable. This system is bad, because new players interested in politics or even old ones if they are alone can't have a guild. Guild encourages friendly factor especially if you play with people you know. The time to needed catch up old guilds would be incredibly high and tiring. My idea was to set guild raids to a level of map, where guild hall is deployed. Everyone would be able to guard well and there would likely be more guilds deployed somewhere else than next to each other in the lvl 22 area.
Both suggestions were to improve game for beginners. Though, rejected by the eldest players. They will not gave up their grind for a good. Perhaps, they would be close to second / third ascend if they didn't stay lvl 20 without ascending. Perhaps, they would prefer playing hardcore if it is changed from 'insane' to actually 'hardcore'. And some say 'Ozy always decided on favor of new players.'
This keeps game backward, because devs can't go directly against their most supportive group, which fund every of their games (Spellbook supporters are permanent community lasting years).
Second problem with them is that their contribution on kickstarter gives an advantage. Devs do everything they can to avoid p2w element, but they can't set silver prices to fit everybody. Those who had two kickstarter account can buy ressources for a high price and craft legendary items in a week. They have non-human fighters, which is advantage, but minor. They were given strong armor, some of them still have it. And most importantly - silver. This abundance can't be reached throw playing easily and you will never have that much for crafting you would need. It's generally impossible to take away silver from them, drops are so low when scrapped. And they reject ideas, which would adapt the game more in favor of new players or just those interested in hardcore.
---
These problems were just major ones. Apart from them, I really recommend this game. Trying to figure out how stuff works, what is the best fighting class combination for 3v3, 6v6, 9v9 and 12v12. Economy. It's fun. But it's not a game to play every day and compete with others, who contributed kickstarter. You really can become competitive, but it takes so much time. So much time...

Game: Nihilumbra
Publisher: BeautiFun Games

Gameplay:
Nihilumbra is a puzzle platformer which heavily depends upon the use of five colours. Your main goal throughout the game is mostly solve the puzzles and kill monsters using the power of your colours which have various different properties like Burn, Stick, Electricity, Slide and Bounce. All the areas in the game has a different colour scheme which requires you to use the given powers in a different manner each time.
Nihilumbra is divided into two parts: A tutorial sort of Story mode, and the Void mode. The story mode is quite short lasting around 4 hours and relatively much easier than the latter. Void mode is where the real meat of the game lies. It is difficult to cross, no one holds your hands during these levels and sometimes it can be brutal to surpass these levels. Overall, Nihilumbra presents a different kind of gameplay which is not seen much in today’s games.
Visuals
The art of Nihilumbra is very unique.  It lends beautifully to the atmosphere created by the gameplay. It helps create a very solid environment which doesn’t let go until the very end. As the gameplay relies mostly on the use of various colours, the visuals do make you feel as if all the different colours are popping on the screen. It also helps that the protagonist is entirely purplish black which shows how much the colours might mean to him. The visuals are sharp and very intelligently done. Nihilumbra sports a visual style which will remain in your minds for quite some time.
Sound and Music
While not as exceptional as the above explained visuals, the sounds still do a good enough job to support the environment of the game with minimal soundtrack while you are doing absolutely nothing and some intense music during the final stages of the game. It really helps set the mood right and helps the game grow to another level where it really shines.
While it is nothing that we haven’t heard before, it still shows that a good soundtrack combined with solid and unique visuals can create a strong atmosphere.
Performance
Nihilumbra has spent time on the shelves and runs buttery smooth with no crashes, screen tearing or freezing at any given point of time. I did encounter a couple of bugs but nothing took me out of the immersion or broke the game. It is a very stable game which might even run on even the lower-end of the computers.
Overall
Nihilumbra is a very good game which captures your attention from the get go and never lets go. It’s unique visual style and a solid gameplay really deserves the applause and it is a game you won’t regret buying. The story mode might be short but the Void mode more than makes up for it.

Way back in the Commodore 64 era, I remember spending hours creating custom rosters for Microleague baseball, mostly comprised of me and my friends with comically high ratings.   We'd gather around the screen, taking on the legends of the game, arguing about who got to hit the button next and making fun of the one member of our group who was 'only' hitting .560.    I bought this game in a fit of nostalgia, hoping to recreate a little of that magic.   I've been pleasantly surprised so far; this game brings the magic like David Copperfield after a Barry Bonds smoothie.
You may initially be overwhelmed by the numbers of screens and info thrown at you, but the user-friendly interface makes it very easy to control.   You can do as much, or as little, as you'd like.  If you wish to rule the world, make yourself Commissioner and have a hand in everything.  If you'd like to earn your way to the top, start as a manager for the Brevard County Manatees or some other minor-league team.  Go back in time and GM the Yankees in the 70's and 80's for the sheer fun of hiring and firing Billy Martin.
OOTP is clearly not a graphics-driven, but anyone who played Microleague back in the day will appreciate the 3D presentation of the individual games. I just recently got interested in Baseball and was looking for a good video game. A friend of mine recommended that I check this out because the level of detail would help me learn about the game and boy was he right. I've played other baseball games and this blows them out of the water. It's not your usual game where you try to use the controller to hit or pitch to the point it's all about your ability to mash buttons. This game really embraces the thinking aspect of baseball that often gets overlooked. I could not recommend this game enough. I will warn you that the learning curve is kind of steep, but thankfully the OOTP Development website is stocked full of useful information.
One interesting example of how this game models baseball so well is that I decided to start a game as Commissioner and GM and picked one of the lowest ranking teams in MLB. I thought it would be fun to stack the team with all the best players from around the league and enjoy the fun of offering low level prospects for superstars and then force the trade. There was just something fun about fleecing some of the best teams of their star players. Once that was done I expected to just run away with the season. Boy was I surprised. Even when simming a game I found myself barely above .500. I had to go back and retool my team because while I may have had bats made of fire that launched balls into the parking lot, my defense was a open as a the US border and let just about everything through.
This game taught me that there is more to baseball than just star players, there are subtle tactics that only true disciples of baseball ever really see. With what I've learned from this game I started looking around the real league and suddenly Managers choices started making a whole  lot of sense.

So, here you are, reaching a major milestone of your life on your 25th birthday. You are given a passport kit that allows to (finally!?) travel outside of your country and monthly allowances that, if used wisely, make your trips less hitchhiking-esque. Isn't this a dream for everyone who sets his/her/their eyes on what's beyond the tiny bubble called "home"? Anyway, you can post on your blog with what I believe to be automatically generated hashtags whenever you travel to a city or spend a good few days there. Though I'm on the rather wary side when it comes social media and often its accompanied whiny, imbecilic "commentators," here in the game you can't steer away from it. This is supposed to be a casual, relaxing game where you go to different places and meet people, the interactions mostly being enjoyable, but the reality is that you can't do much other than click on the name of your destination, fast forward as you travel, and then spend a few days there while basically nothing happens, which makes posting on your blog to get followers one of the only few goals and perhaps the most important goal of the game. But the followers mean nothing but a number to you--there's no interaction or impact at all whatsoever--and, after the first few posts, choosing hashtags becomes a chore.
I understand that the game is still in early access, which is why I'm giving it a tentative yes.The premise is interesting and there is just so much potential in what it can be that I'd be sad to see it fail.

I've never written a review on Steam until this game. Let me just say this - it's fantastic. It's a game that makes you really think about the philosophical meaning of a true apocalypse. Is it better to emulate life after the end? Simulate it? Or is it better to go on and live the best you can, drawing out until the inevitable collapse of humanity? It even goes back to the age old question, what does it really mean to be human?
Frictional Games have a hit on their hands.
Every nook and cranny of this game has been gorgeously rendered down to the smallest detail. Let me say that the atmosphere is excellent and is rarely matched, especially for an independent game. The gameplay makes sense, fits in with the story and is very well captured. This game will be compared to their previous games - Amnesia: The Dark Descent and the Penumbra Series (both of which were very good but had issues of their own). This tops both of them Ten fold.
Even though I have high marks for this game, it is not perfect:
The only real annoyances that popped up for me was occasionally when Simon was forced to make his way around the monsters. I get it - this is a horror game, but sometimes it just felt unnecessary to throw the sequences in; especially when the AI would seemingly find me when I was completely out of sight. Some of it works, and some of it doesn't as  this would break the immersion occasionally. I'd be hiding out of view and somehow a monster managed to see me. They seemingly knew that this would be an issue and the problem was addressed a bit by giving you several hits before you die. However, it would degrade your vision each time you were hit, making it increasingly difficult to see. This made the scary sequences more annoying than scary at times.
Other than that, the game has an story that is very well done. It may come off as confusing to some, but the payoff is competely worth it. When you reach the end of the game, you truly feel like you are contributing what you can in a last ditch effort to save humanity. While there isn't much replayability in this game, you may want to give it another go around to fill in the blanks of the story that you missed the first time. The game really rewards you for exploring with nuggets of the story that you missed.
Anyways, I believe this is one of the best games that I've played in quite some time. It is HIGHLY recommended. Oh, and by the way. BUY IT so they can make a Soma 2.

This is basically ARTIFICIAL DIFFICULTY: THE GAME
The controls are HORRIBLE:
>It forces inverse Y and X axes for your mouse movements. It makes manipulating your wrists and arms very complicated, and that's bad considering this is an aiming game. You know why is there no option to change this? BECAUSE ARTIFICIAL DIFFICULTY.
>Every time you shoot and then grab a new arrow, your right arm does not go back to its previous position. It insists on going somewhere else, and you have to fiddle around with your elbow and wrist controls just to nock the arrow again; AND if you don't position your hand exactly like you did on your previous shot (which is very likely), you will have nocked the arrow in a completely different direction and now you either have to redo it or have to adjust your left arm holding the bow to compensate, which is just as annoying.

One of the best story-intensive games I have ever played. The atmosphere is superb, oppressive, alien and disconcerting, it never stops feeling this way as it keeps introducing new environments and narrative, which I can only admire for being so well writen and thought provoking.
This is a horror game, and the fact that I, being kind of averse to this kind of game, as I do feel genuinely uneasy when playing games of this genre, is already a big compliment. In fact, I've had to exit the game more than once due to being too scared to continue and I will also confess to reading up what was next on walkthroughs, in an effort to make the game less scary for myself. However, I've also always had the desire to get back and continue where I left off, just to learn more about the beautiful and broken world of SOMA.
I definately recommend this, you might have a bit of a rough time I've you're the sensitive type like me, but oh boy is it worth it.

Well, here we are. The game is in season 2 and with new characters, maps and gear system out... I feel like It's time to edit this review.
In short let me tell you what everyone in the reviews is complaining about. *ahem*
"New DLC characters too strong, nerf pls Ubisoft, bad game."
"Still no dedicated servers?! NANI?!"
"For Honor? More like, No Honor."
The characters are new, it's been about a week and a day that they have been out in the time I'm editing this review. They're getting their nerfs. But people also need to understand how to fight against these characters, someone with 5-15 hours won't really understand how to fight them in comparison to someone who has 50-100 hours.
The two new characters are: Centurion for the knights faction and Shinobi for the Samurai faction. Currently as it stands, they are extremely powerful, no denying that. Though you are able to fight your way around them, it's not completely impossible.
A lot of people will over exaggerate this topic. Things like "One in 15 games you will actually be able to complete" from time to time. We all know that peer to peer connectivity is atrocious, but we do not need to exaggerate it this much.
I do hope that Ubisoft does bring dedicated servers to For Honor, but as it stands right now... that might take a while.
Of course! I want more and more people to join this game. Currently, the game has the same problem that rainbow six siege once had, and it saddens me a lot that it does. But I hope that they can fix this.
Do people still complain about 1v4? Yeah, but I don't see this as a problem anymore. These fights can be won if you're the one who is fighting 4 people.
So let me close this review with a... I love this game, it's REALLY good.

A barebones but fun couch game. There isn't a lot of content, but it's fast and hectic without feeling unmanageable, and the content stretches much farther than the few minutes estimated by a some of the reviewers. We've played a few several-hour sessions, and it's still a blast. The VVVVVV-esque gravity switching gives the game some unique flavor, and it controls very tightly.
The game probably doesn't hold up as well as some bigger-budget party games, but its gravity-swap mechanics give it its own flavor and it easily merits the tiny asking price. At time of writing, it's on sale for $1.24, and I'd recommend it to anyone with a couch gaming setup for that price.

This may be the single most underrated video game of all time. In fairness, the original version (as I played it on my Xbox) was indeed a bit of a mess. I have no idea why this game was recently updated with full modern game amenities (steam cloud, achievements, controller support, workshop, etc) but it's one of the happiest gaming surprises I've ever experienced. Playing through this game again - this time with the restored content mod - was an awesome opportunity I never thought I would have.
If the philosophy of Star Wars has ever interested you in a deeper way, this game was written for you. The way the story deconstructs the Force - what it means to be a Jedi, a Sith, what generalizations those titles reflect, and what meaning they contain is infinitely fascinating, and I find myself reflecting on the scenarios and characters introduced in this game more so than any other Star Wars property (and most science fiction in general).
If you want to unravel the true mysteries of the Force - or just want to find out what happens after the first KotOR - this game is definitely worth your time.

This is a deeply flawed, incomplete game that also is a strong contender for the best CRPG ever made and made me remember why I like Star Wars in the first place.
I’m going to first discuss the game as it was released on steam, without any of the history or additions to the game, and then more complete thoughts and history after.
Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic II - The Sith Lords is a direct squeal to the first Knights of the Old Republic (called KOTOR from this point on), taking place five years after the events of that game. It’s not required to play the previous game, but some story elements are brought up and the main protagonist of that game has a huge impact on the story of this one, as well as smaller cameos and returning characters from the previous game. The game uses the same d20 RPG system from the first game, with most of the combat being dice rolls and progression mirroring that on a pen and paper RPG. This can make combat somewhat “boring” for people who are newer to the genre, as you’ll generally be using the same buffs/debuffs/attacks through the game. The upgrade system from the previous game has been improved and the crafting system in this game allows for a great deal of creativity with how you want to equip your character. Most of the best items/weapons/armor in the game is created from this aspect, and instead of having to farm for materials or find rare recipes, you learn better creations by leveling up your other skills (Security, Demolitions, Stealth, ect), giving some previously less useful skills a chance to shine.
The game’s main issue is it’s technical faults. A vanilla installation will be riddled with bugs that range from shaders making the screen blurry after the effects of a specific spell (which is very useful) wear off (this can persist through cut-scenes), characters getting stuck behind objects, events and cut-scenes repeating themselves, achievements randomly unlocking (I got the max Persuasion and Computer Use feats just by getting into the ship for the first time?) and overall a lack of polish. The UI seems less clean than KOTOR 1. Voice lines for characters will sometimes be missing. The game seems to have chunks of it missing, creating minor plot holes that blemish what is otherwise an amazing story (see below). In the state the game’s in at this point, I’d still recommend it.
ALL OF THAT BEING SAID
KOTOR 2 was developed by Obsidian Entertainment (the same people behind Fallout: New Vegas and Neverwinter Nights 2) in an extremely short time-frame, due to pressure from Lucasarts to release it in the 2004 holiday season. This game probably should have gotten a full additional year of development, and the amount of content they scrapped was immense. A fan patch, which you can now easily install with one click using the Steam Workshop, was released that fixes over 500 bugs and readds most of the lost content. The amount that this helps this game is only comparable to something like “DSFIX” for the PC port of Dark Souls. In fact, I’m not even sure that’s comparable, this is a labor of love that fixes a broken game and tells a fantastic Star Wars story.
The way it tells this story is superb. Your character isn’t a fresh recruit, he’s a former Jedi, returned to known space from exile. The game assumes that your character would know information, and you can respond accordingly to not only shape the future of the game, but the past as the universe knows it. At first, I thought I liked the game because it wasn’t like a Star Wars story before, but upon reflection it’s actually distills everything that makes Star Wars great. Jedi are rare, mystical beings and even though in the events of the game they haven’t been gone long, people aren’t exactly sure how they work. There is black and white morality behind the two major groups that wield the force. The worlds feel grimy, dingy, lived in and yet not unwelcoming and the characters that you gather in your party through the game feel like characters you could see in episodes IV, V or VI. They even surpass those, however, as when you get to know them they start to become representations of the “grayest” concepts the Star Wars universe has to offer, like the price of loyalty, love on the battlefield, the nature of the force and if it’s sentient, should we accept it’s malevolence, where does honor truly come from, what constitutes the “greater good”, ect. Your quest, while on the surface, appears to be a “go around, find the Jedi and save the _______” storyline, it actually becomes more of a philosophical pilgrimage, with your character learning the true meaning of what it means to be a Jedi or Sith, and imparting those teachings to those that follow him. Also, there are at least 4 instances of recurring main party members from KOTOR 1, and 2 of them even join your party (and as someone who didn’t play KOTOR 2 until very recently and grew up with KOTOR 1, I really enjoyed this, they nail the characters perfectly). And that’s not even saying anything on Kreia, who’s easily worth the price of admission alone, with the only close comparison being the dynamic between Naked Snake and The Boss from MGS3 (and even then, I feel this surpasses even that).
Without the restoration patch, this game is worth the Steam asking price. With it, it’ll give you the best ride we’re probably gonna get in the Star Wars universe. More than any VR lightsaber game or Battlefront sequel EA churns out, this makes you feel like a goddamn Jedi.

Whenever people discuss KotOR II, the word “deconstruction” is used a lot, referring to Chris Avellone's interpretation and criticism of SW as a whole, The Force, how the Jedi are perceived by civilians, Dark Side/Light Side, the infamous “Are you an angel?” easter egg, etc. but the deconstruction doesn't stop there.
KotOR II is a critique of the entire RPG genre, in the way it deals with common occurrences and cliches seen in most RPG's. How can you stop your very important main quest, even momentarily, to fetch some irrelevant piece of junk to a random nobody? Why do your party members follow your lead and attack whoever you attack? Why is it okay to loot corpses? Do you have to be good to everyone in a “good” run, and conversely, do you have to butcher little rabbits in an “evil” run? (Not that Light Side/Dark Side is the equivalent of good/evil in other games, just follow me here.)

You solve the puzzles, deal with various purple monsters and progress by painting parts of the platform with 5 different colours, each of which has its own property: slide, bounce, sticky, burn and electricity. There are 5 areas in the game, each with its own environment and colour scheme. Within each area you can take your time until the last level which is always a speed run where you are chased by the Void (a purple wave covering the whole screen).
The graphics are beautiful and the gameplay itself adds to the beauty as you paint the scenery. The devs are clearly proud of their work, and rightly so, as their gallery of rough sketches and gameplay development is gradually unlocked throughout the game.
Steam trading cards and achievements are included and it's cross-platform (I'm a Linux user so that's a big plus for me).
No performance issues or glitches at all. Very stable and smooth.
Nearly all of the negative reviews of this game show less than 4 hours of gameplay, which means they are only reviewing the Story Mode part of the game, of which there are 41 levels that seem endless. The gameplay at this stage is very easy, I would say the first 70% is child level. The whole time you are subjected to an extremely irritating narrator droning on about hopelessness and death and giving clues to the gameplay, as if it wasn't easy enough already. I was sorely tempted to throw in the towel like so many other reviewers but I wanted to get all the achievements so I carried on. I'm so glad I did!
As it turned out, this is a 'game of two halves'. Void Mode is properly challenging, one of the best puzzle platformers I've ever played. I'm talking 50+ attempts at some levels involving timing and accuracy, and that's after you've worked out how to solve it in the first place which isn't easy either. The narrator has disappeared by this point too, replaced by a subtle background tune, just what you need for concentration. Many of the solutions took a lot of brainpower but none were impossible if I thought about it for long enough.
After beating Void the 'polyglot language' is unlocked. All the menus etc are slang/internet speak. You can play through Story Mode again and this time there are funny comments from the developer and interesting insights into the game concepts. It's strange because after Void Mode it seems to take no time at all to speed through the entire game (this is the same playthrough that seemed to take forever the first time!) If you reach the 'True End' you will find out what the Void represents.
Finally, I cleared up half a dozen of the remaining achievements which, having completed Void, were entertaining but not too difficult (but would have seemed impossible without all my previous experience).
In retrospect the Story Mode is nothing more than an extended tutorial. If the developers left Void Mode open from the start instead of forcing you to play through the entire Story Mode to unlock it then players who were getting bored of Story would attempt Void and go scurrying back to Story because they would realise they need the practice and that there is a decent game ahead. I'm sure doing this simple thing would prevent most of the negative reviews.
Fullscreen only, no windowed mode.
No controller support, although this may have been left out deliberately. It would be better for moving around but the painting side of it just wouldn't be feasible with a controller, it needs a mouse.
64-bit Linux doesn't upload achievements to your profile but there's a workaround - it's Linux, of course there is :)
This is excellent value considering the low price vs amount of gameplay. Apart from the initial Story Mode section (which I now understand was a necessary evil), the vast majority of the 32 hours I've spent playing this game have been fun and rewarding. I highly recommend it as long as you have the patience to work through the 2-4 hours at the beginning before you get to the meaty part of the game.
Hot tip: use right-click to quickly erase - it's much easier than selecting it and you will need to know this for some of the quick-fire later levels.

This is a very deeply flawed game with a tremendous amount of charm.
Mechanically, it's barely even a puzzle game.  The majority of gameplay is just wandering around in these 3D spaces, searching for a fixed number of hidden symbols in each space.  Generally you can find a symbol by looking at it from just the right place, or by seeing clues that become apparent once you're in the right place and looking in the right direction.  In any case, gameplay is basically all about looking everywhere in each space from every location possible, which is, let's face it, a
tedious prospect.  To make things worse, there are technical issues with the game (flickering/jittery movement, bizarre object collision) that specifically make wandering around looking in every direction deeply irritating.
But that's the bad part.  The good part is that the 3D spaces you're methodically combing have a tremendous amount of character and charm.  The graphics— particularly the colors— are stunning.  You get lines of dialogue by approaching the cardboard-cutout like other characters that populate these spaces, and some interesting narratives emerge.  The fact that the "reward" for finding each symbol is another visually-arresting window into another reality makes these spaces dynamic.  And if you're into Philip K. D
ck, by which I mean the entire
, not just the dizzingly weird fiction but the enigmatic and contradictory personality at its core, the paranoia of his Hacienda Way days and the esoteric religiosity of his final decade...  well, the designers built a world that's kind of like a big beautiful diorama celebrating of all of that, and it's worth seeing.

Fun game, addicting even. BUT , there are a few things you should know. A top 5 pro/con is below.
PRO:
1: Open world, lots of willing players to help you learn the game
2: Pretty nice graphics, makes you think you're in the medieval times (mostly).
3: Guild/PVP/Open world mechanics are pretty small and closeknit
4: The ability to directly influence the terrain and affect how you make a moat, or defenses
5: Hours will go by before you realize it, it's pretty fun.
CON:
1: VERY steep learning curve at the start for the most mundane of things (like how to make a simple stone axe)
2: The skill tree system doens't make any sense; You have to learn to craft roads/build towers before knowing how to farm
3: Combat mechanics are clunky (you have to "go into combat stance" and then selecting weapons is a chore) .
4: Controls are clunky You have to right click everything virtually to interact, plus you cant just change the way it works
5: The "world" isn't big by any stretch, but a decent size for a server of 64 tops. Normally guilds rule the server and love to "raid" smaller groups or integrate into a kingdom and get all mad when you play "unfair" to combat their uber armor/weapons/horses. Enforcing rules are relished to the few admins on servers but can be a gamble as a newbie on a new server with known abusers of power (bans, god mode , they come wipe your town you invested 50hrs building). More players on less servers would help with this power vacuum.
As it stands the game is "Fun" if you need something new to enjoy for approx 200 hours. But beyond that get ready to restart on servers when the hosts get bored of their current world and total server wipe it all (there goes your huge keep you JUST COMPLETED) frequently. The learning curve has to be explained by trial and error or kind players, simply don't assume. The tech/learning tree has no sense or thought put in, you have to farm X many points to be able to be a glass blower, or you have to be skill level 60 in swords to be able to wear basic chain armor in the chivalry skill....Yeah the skil tree has zero sense, and couple that with a low skill amount then you'll never be able to at least own a bow (by the way you need to have like 60 skill in crossbows before you can pick up a bow and string one apparently last I played)...Lots of common sense is abandoned in this game I feel and it'll be a long time (if ever) that you'll see any justice on the reworkings (while they fudge up the Beta MMO process currently).

This is almost a good game.  When I first played this game, back when it first came out, it was plagued with bugs and it was very easy to say this game wasn't worth playing.  There are a lot of fan made fixes these days, even a lot of restored content and so my decision to not recommend this game is much harder.
What makes me hesitate is the story, there are great characters in this, great back stories, but sadly there are aspects of the  story that fail badly and they are partly to blame for me not recommending this.  This is a long epic game, you'll get a lot of game time out of this, but the endings are . . . well, the pay off just insn't there IMO.  KotoR had a great pay off with an epic fight with a villain you'd grown to hate, KotoR 2 has multiple bosses, including one that nears Darth Malak, but they pay off just isn't there.  I didn't feel any satisfaction from defeating this foe.  If anything I felt annoyed at my lack of choices.
Another terrible aspect of the game is that it forces you to play NPC characters.  The first hour of the game, which I'm including the tutorial, you'll be playing as a T3 droid more than your own character.  I made a character that's supposed to represent me.  That's who I should play.  That's who I want to play. Sadly, not only are you repeatedly forced to play NPCs, made to include them in your group for certain sections (something KotoR did, but I liked all of those NPCs so it never seemed a pain), and that leads to another flaw in the game: the narrative isn't being told from your character's perspective.  Because you're playing as NPCs, getting cut scenes with NPCs talking amongst themselves, you've given this disjointed narrative that makes the story far far less immersive.   I'll give an example:
Fairly early in the story there's a light side quest that has you breaking into the mainframe of an evil cooperation, and there's an option to use a protocol droid to do it.  Naturally the game makes you play as the protocol droid.  However this mission intersects with a side mission where you're hunting bounties on two escaped criminals, and somehow this droid, who's only been in your group for this mission, who wasn't party to any of the bounty hunter mission, instantly recognises the two criminals and you're forced to choose between two dialogue options where you recognise the two and demand that they stop.  Both flee instantly.  Then you go on with the rest of your mission.  How does the droid know they were wanted criminals?  How do you learn they escaped to the planet surface?  None of these questions have an in game answer and so you're forced to think about it out of the game which is not good for the whole immersion thing.
However, those problems have nothing on the biggest most terrible flaw in the game: the influence system.  Let me just say that if this system had worked it would have been amazing, the ability to make good characters bad, make evil characters good, it would be a player's dream, but ultimately the way it works is that your player is the one who has to change to gain influence with the NPCs.  You have to act how the NPC wants, choose dialogue that they like so that you can gain influence with them.  It's a backwards system.  It's more like they're influencing you to appease them.  You want to play a good character?  Well there are NPCs that you simply can't bring with you.  Want to be evil?  Well don't bring any good NPCs on missions with you or you're going to lose influence.
One last point on NPCs: I really liked most, we had some return from the first game, the two droids, and one other who I won't spoil, but most of the new ones were pretty fun.  Bao-Dur, on the other hand, is one of the most horribly voiced NPCs I've ever had forced on me in any RPG game I've ever played.  You end up with this grating monotone NPC fairly early and even though I was a light side character I instantly wanted to force choke him to death.  Sadly we're forced to play this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ a number of times throughout the game.  Another problem with the NPCs is that two of the NPCs join based on the gender of the PC you pick, if you're male you get the awesome Handmaiden of Atris, a kick♥♥♥♥♥character who has tons of fan art and pages of information on, if you're female you get some dude called "the Disciple" . . . a character so bland that even wookipedia could barely write three pages on.  Darth Vader's glove, a Mandalorian Crushgaunt has more information on it.  Speaking of wookipedia, the gender, name, and appearance of the PC was added (because wookipedia needs pages and pages of pointless information) and the exile, your character, is supposed to be female.  Which means the Handmaiden should accompany you, but the game has very ridged romance story lines written into the game and same sex romances were strictly forbidden.
And one final note: there are a ton of powers added to the game.  The original KotOR had a lot of power selection, but this game has tons more!  The only problem though is that at the higher levels I found a power I liked, force push, and found that it was more than effective for nearly every encounter afterwards.  Having a lot of choice isn't that useful when you only need one answer.
KotOR is my favorite Star Wars game ever.  This game is likely being unfairly compared to that classic, and admittedly if this were a standalone game I might even have given it a reluctant recommendation but the fact that it bares the KotOR name forces me to not recommend this game, the first one was so much better, and two is too much of a mess for me to recommend.  However, I will say that it's far from the worst Star Wars game I've ever played and if you're a rabid fan you really can't go wrong at the price the game is currently selling at.  Even bad games might be worth playing at that price, and, it's worth noting that there is a moding community and there have been changes and restored content add via fan made mods.  The choice added back into the game from these mods would allow me to recommend the game if they were part of the initial release so with that in mind, and if you don't have any fears of modifying your game, it's worth picking up if you like RPGs or Star Wars.  I can't justify giving a thumbs up to a game that I needed to modify to enjoy however, so while I can't recommend the game as is, there is a relatively decent game once modified to something playable.

Former Microleague player, yea back in the mid 80's I started getting into that game. I had all the floppy disk and finally the editor so I could edit and add all the major league players individually, which I did.  Played a whole season with each individual team then.  I can tell you that was a lot of games I had to play and I loved every minute.  This is just to tell you how dedicated I was to simming a entire one season of baseball.  Then came Tony Larussa Baseball, and then OOTP, where I can sim entire season in one day instead of one year of my life.
Last OOTP I played was OOTP 11 which was  few years ago.  Enjoyed the game but it had a few faults in it, especially the not so friendly interface.   I haven't bought baseball sim game since, thinking my joy for the game had faded.
So you ask why I bought this game?  Well it peeked my interest from the high reviews I have read about it.  So I said to myself why not, lets see if we can spark that old flame again.  It not only sparked the flame, it has caused a three alarm fire.  This game is going to be a classic.   It has surprassed any of my expectectations I had for it.
The Quick Sim is now extremely fast because of the 4 processor support.  No more simming and waiting for few minutes, just a quick click and a few seconds delay and the day is done.   I love how technology has made it this easy, instead of the days of me individually going to play each game for each team.
One thing I truely love and pretty much look forward to is the unique things that pop in a season.  Things can put your player out, not just basic injuries either.  You might have caused one of your players to be overworked one game, for example a pitcher.  That said pitcher you push him to his limits trying to get him a complete game and his arm figuratively falls off with a tired arm syndrome. So you loss him for few starts.   Stuff like that and players being suspended for fighting is all in this game. Also players age as years go by and you can see how this effects them on thier portrait.  Aging also has effect on how well and bad they play.  Like a upcoming player  starting to reach thier potential or a aging star fading away during his twighlight of his career.  There is soo much content in this game,  I am only skimming the surface of what this game has.
If you want to be just a coach for minor league team, you can.  If you want to control every aspect of your franchise you can too.  The choice is yours,  if you want to relive your childhood and see your favorite heros from the past play, you can.  Having every authentic player from both minor leagues and majors makes this game so realistic.
I am probably just babbling now.  But for me this game has been enlightening and has taken me back to when I was a kid and when I was playing Microleague,  I had wished a computer game just like this.  I mean some of the extra stuff they did to this game is stuff I never thought off back then, but boy I am enjoying each and every new surprise each day.
Buy it if you love Baseball, buy it if you like micromanaging, buy it if your a strategy fan, buy it if you like history, and  buy it if you like gaming.  This is just a game, but its more then game.  If you get my meaning.  This is the Best and I mean "The Best Sim Game" out there bar none.

This game is too cheaply made to really be worth your time. The story is cookie fodder -- early -- Final Fantasy fare, the chosen hero has to save the world yadda yadda yadda.
The only unique feature which tries to set it apart from other RPGMaker games is the cheesecake portraits of female characters, which heavily feature in the store front screenshots.
The main problem is easily seen in all the random battles: there is absolutely no art consistency in this game. Backgrounds are pixel paintings, player characters are minute chibi sprites and as for the enemies, they are without exception several times larger than the player sprites and of various differing art styles, ranging from generic slime to highly detailed soldier. Battles use RPGMaker default rules and there isn't even a selection cursor showing just which of the many enemies on screen is 'Soldiers A' and which is 'Soldiers D' -- note the plural.
The game text has multiple grammar and spelling errors, and even complete novice errors such as referring to a DESCENDANT of someone as ANCESTOR.
Other problems include the complete lack of indicators on sprites that are affected by status impairments such as poisoned, while with player characters there is some indicator in the battle screens, there is no such info for enemies. Combine with the lack of identification of individual enemies and you have to remember which enemy has which status...
There is also no health bar for enemies, or even any indication that they may be close to death. Fortunately (?) they are all very easy. Without grinding, I only died once during the entire game, and that was a scripted loss. Even the optional bosses are extremely easy to beat.
On top of all that, the game ends on a clfifhanger with a 'to be continued'.
All in all, if this were a free RPGMaker game I'd be supportive of it as the game creator does have a good idea of what makes a decent oldschool RPG game, but for a commercial release that is sold for money, I expect more. So I just can't honestly recommend it.

A very, very paint-by-the-numbers kind of RPG. There's just so little going on here. This game has a very low price point, which is the only true saving grace about it, but that's literally it. I suppose I should say that as a first effort, it's not THAT bad, but it's pretty forgettable as a whole. Keep in mind it also ends with a bland cliff hanger and a 'to be continued...' screen, but more attention should have been paid into making this one rather than any intent on going to a sequel. There's not much to recommend.
Disappointments about Chosen:
1. Possibly the most generic RPG I've ever played. Forgettable non-personality characters with run of the mill anime names (Edge, Serenity, Akuma). Tired order versus chaos storyline. Even the 'twist' at the end is utterly predictable.
2. Super easy. I never needed to grind. Enemies, including the special bosses and the final villain, all hit like wet socks. Had decent gear by the end, but not anything great, nor did I need anything better. A quiz at the end of the game has no penalties, you just keep answering different things until you get it right. A few pushing boulder puzzles that I could do in my sleep.
3. No character has any personality. They speak a few lines, but they're all honestly interchangable and faceless. Only the main character has anything that can be described as a motivation. Heck, one of the party members even shares the same image as her ruler's full image, except the latter has a dress and a tiara.
4. Lack of a navigation system. There's no map feature and if you miss or forget the quick blurb between story events about what direction to go to, good luck. The overworld has limited defining features at best. They're just empty islands with one, occasionally two enterable places at best. I spent more time wandering around between playing sessions trying to figure out where I was supposed to go than anything else.
5. The whole experience... it's just lazy. Words running off the screen, with frequent grammar mistakes. Incomplete maps, numerous empty traveling screens with no monsters or anything to do on them. Generic bikini clad party members for quick eyecandy sales. If you want some cheesecake, play Huni Pop, because you won't see much of anything beyond the screen shots above. Numerous NPCs in the last town don't speak whatsoever, unlike ones from previous towns. Oh, and the last area? There's no wandering monsters. In fact, you can pay gold to literally buy experience points.
A couple of acceptable points...
1. The aforementioned low price point. Mind you, this was also on sale when it came out...
2. Music is generally good...? Not certain how much is RPG maker (the game makers use a ton of common RPG maker assets) and how much was custom made, if any.

To be honest, I was hoping that there'd be more of a game under all the cheesecake, but unfortunately, what's there just isn't very good. It's an RPGMaker-born game, and oh boy, does it show. I think the gratuitous skin is to distract from the fact that this game really, really isn't ready for much of anything resembling launch. It needs more than just a spit-shine; it needs rebalancing so very badly- some of the moves can simply allow you to cheese the game. For example, we'll look at the most egregious example: Serenity's "Tackle" skill.
Most RPGs have several different status effects- you know, poison, paralyze, slow, etc.- the usual ones that we all know and loathe. Chosen introduces us to a new one: off-balance. Essentially, a target affected by off-balance cannot take another action until they are no longer off-balance, essentially turning them into a punching bag for the duration. It usually wears off after a turn or two, but you can essentially just layer it every single turn if you get lucky enough. It's game-breaking: believe me when I say that nothing in the game is immune to it- not even the final boss. Yes, as long as you keep Serenity alive during the final battle, you stand a darn good chance to just wreck him by abusing the cheezburgers out of her "Tackle" skill. The only saving grace is that it requires ten tech points to use, and the only way you can get those is by either attacking the enemy, or being attacked. You get five per successful attack... and, of course Serenity gets two attacks a round right off the bat and, of course, TP is figured per strike rather than per command.
It means that, well... you can alternate Tackle every turn with the regular attack and eliminate plenty of difficulty from the game, because "Tackle" is the first technique that Serenity learns. You'll have it before you're finished with the first dungeon. Every other technique that she learns is outshined and not even needed. Other abilities are overly costly, others are just useless. You can simply use three abilities aside from regular attacks (Edge's "Strong Attack", Serenity's "Tackle" and Trinity's "Aura Blade" (has a chance to silence the target) along with a decently-sized nuke from Myste) and not use another attack pattern, apart from using Trinity to drop item heals on targets that need it.
The game is unfinished- there are missing walls that are not coded in (most observable in Volcano Village- in which there is someone living in a tent, where you can walk past the boundaries of the tent and all over the screen without hitting an invisible wall. The exit was programmed in, the invisible walls were not. The text is making my inner English major throw a fit worthy of my three-year-old niece, and I wholeheartedly say that she could have done a better job on editing the script than whoever was hired to do it. It's full of errors that a run through spellcheck would have caught, and there's no real excuse for something like that.
All in all, it appears the dev is hoping that plentiful cheesecake will distract from the myriad of shortcomings, errors and mistakes currently present in the game- while I have nothing against cheesecake, you can't just hide the fact that this game's nowhere near done and really shouldn't have been released in this condition without much more time in development.
The only real thing the game has is the cheesecake, and if that doesn't float your particular boat, I honestly can't recommend this game.  I'd pay no more than fifty cents for this clunker of a game- I hope the dev takes note and does better with the next installment and irons out the mistakes and errors.

Probably Archery is amusing.  The controls are pretty horrendous, but that's kind of the point.  You struggle and try as hard as you can to figure it out, then fail miserable and fire an arrow straight into the ground... or the sky... or you accidentally drop it because you let go of the wrong button.
I spent just under an hour playing the game.  In that time, I went from struggling to grasp what was needed and having trouble grabbing the bowstring to being able to fire off arrows rapidly (but with no accuracy or sense of direction).  After some practice, I was able to complete the basic targets.  I tried shooting the hangman's rope, but couldn't get the accuracy down in the short time you have to succeed.  I tried shooting an apple off of a person's head like William Tell.  It did not go so well.  Fun, but I managed to sink an arrow into the target's head and its neck instead of the apple.  I also tried shooting flying eggs in a china shop.  I managed to hit 6 before I was fired for breaking too much stuff.  I strongly recommend using a controller for the game.  I found it to be less frustrating than the keyboard/mouse.
The primary reason I purchased it, however, was for the VR support.  Unfortunately, the game will not detect the Rift (DK2) and I have been unable to fix it.  The development team has also been quiet on and future support or updates, so it is hard to know if they will be doing anything about it.  I cannot recommend the game without knowing if bugs or issues will be fixed.
So short version:
Fun, frustrating game, but VR support is not working with DK2.  If you bought it for a fun, frustrating game like Surgeon Simulator, you'll be happy.  If you bought it for VR support, you'll be disappointed.

For Honor is a hybrid of a fighting game and mount-and-blade style melee combat game, with a little Souls thrown in. At early and intermediate skill levels, there's quite a lot to enjoy for all types of players, though the game's systems can be intimidating to new players. Once you reach a certain skill threshold, however, you quickly realise that at its core For Honor's combat system is weighted very heavily towards playing defensively, creating quite a rigid style of play that dominates.
It features a fair number of maps, modes and classes on release, as well as a decidedly acceptable singleplayer campaign. It features deep character customisation, though cosmetic and gameplay-affecting options are gated by an obscenely long grind. It also features microtransactions, because the triple A games industry is hell.

If, I could summerize my experience so far with this game. The only word that could do it any justice at all would be "exhilirating". -John Wayne
-This game offers a wide map to traverse alone or with friends. The odds of being killed are great without a steady hand and a decent weapon. I will also state that this game offers (in terms of its multiplayer aspect) a DayZ feeling as no player can be trusted unless you are in a party. In my opinion this only adds to the thrill of looking for loot and exploring the map.
-The game also offers a level up system for your character and account. Whenever your current character kills something or someone you get experience. You will level up and choose from a perk system. Nothing that breaks the feel of the game but adds a little variety to those of you who want to play a different sort of style. That being said, upon death you will lose these levels and everything in your backpack. This makes death a severe consequence and adds to the thrill of PVP.
-Nether also has its' own banking system. At any of the safe zones (while they aren't being invaded) players can access their own global inventory and store a certain amount of items in there. This softens the harshness of death and makes getting back on your feet much easier to the experienced players.
-Let's talk about the npc's. Nether, as they are called in this game, are teleporting baddies that try their best to make your life points hit zero.
-The enemies themselves are not hard to beat if you have the right equipment. Now while this may technically be a con to the game I may remind you it is still in beta, I digress, the game offers a small selection of weaponry including but not limited to: assault rifles, smg's, sniper rifles, and shotguns. While this makes some of the weapon balancing rather off in my own opinion, I still think the weapons work great on players and npc's without being very over powered.
-Curious about the looting system? Loot is found throughout the wasteland and city area in a variety of containers. You may find food, water, gun parts, ammo, and even cash. Now, there are such a thing called golden containers which require keys to open. You may buy these keys with in-game money or you may purchase gold with real life money and use the gold to purchase said keys. What makes these golden containers special is that you may find such items like cosmetics like masks and other things as well as big money drops or loots of valuable supplies. That being said there is a possibility of also finding nothing. However, since you can buy these keys with in-game gold, that doesn't really justify as a con.
-Wanna party up? Good news! Nether comes with a faction system. Before setting off on your journy to the wastes, I recommend you posse up before you dive in! There is a decent variety of factions to choose from. These factions will control points throughout the map and make it easier for you, the player, to treverse the lands and hunt for loot.
-The gun mechanics work nicely as to compensate for the lack of fire arms in the game right now.
-The game is still in beta so beware that there are bugs. The servers go down sometimes. Nothing completly game breaking but keep in mind that it is what it is.
-Game isn't very demanding in the hardware section. I have a very outdated GPU and run the game on high detail just fine.
-Overall, this game took me by complete suprise. I did not expect the game to be this immersive. I would recommend this game any day of the week.
