The only true problem with this game that people can unanimously agree on is the developers themselves. The game itself is, in my opinion, a work of art. The beauty of a desolated city, the post-apocalyptic landscape that makes my skin tingle and the creatures that still cause fear for any player, no matter how veteran.
The thrill of survival makes the blood coursing through my viens boil.

The idea of slipping into the role or a scavenger, a psycopath, a savior, or anyone inbetween and interacting with the environment and people as such. Be friend or foe, be wrong or right, be whatever you want to be. No one will stop you and if they try, kill them until you're happy again.
In the end, I'd just like to say: The game is great as it is, the developers are terrible, and the game only gets better as more people join. Please try the game if you haven't, please give it another shot if you have.

Sniper Elite V2 is a third person shooter that takes place during World War 2. The game is less of a run and gun shooter and more on stealth. I never did get into any multiplayer gaming and just played the solo campaign (I am not much for multiplay when the game offers an excellent campaign play through).
I was one of the lucky people to get this game when Steam was offering it for free (for a 24 hour period) so I figured I would try the game out. Why not if its free right?
I was impressed with the use of history and how it made for the story line during my first few minutes of play. I liked how the bullet cam worked as well. Taking aim at a very long shot after controlling your breathing then firing your rifle you will see your bullet travel all the way from your barrel to the target.
What I was most impressed with was the X-Ray kill cam. At certain moments when you have a shot and fire you get an X-Ray of the target and get to see the skeleton and organs get damaged as the bullet travels through. Its pretty gruesome and for my first time seeing this I was amazed at the effects and coolness of it. I wouldn't say its true to life but well done for a video game.
I didn't notice any issues with the game while playing but I did find that it relied on triggered events. For instance, I get in a building and hang back then use my sniper rifle scope to check the area ahead and don't notice anyone around. I fire a shot and nothing, so I creep up to the doorway and then the enemy's spawn.
Setting yourself up to a vantage spot is very useful. In a solo campaign where you camp at a good spot and peg off anyone around is a good tactical move for playing a sniper in any game or any game mode.
You do have other tools at your disposal like trip mines. Setting on up in a door way then heading up to the second floor and getting some kill shots off only to hear the trip wire go off makes me smile. Its an easy kill plus a good method to alert you to move to another spot.
The main campaign story was also good. At the beginning of every mission there was a briefing as to the scenario to play out and what was needed to be done, all of it was voiced.
I played the game with the Xbox 360 controller and Sniper Elite V2 is very friendly for controller support. I can't see myself playing this game with the keyboard and mouse.
I have to admit this game was addicting and I did spend allot of time trying to get the X-Ray kill cam to happen. If it wasn't for that I don't think the game would offer all that much. The bullet cam is cool but its the X-Ray kill cam that really makes the game interesting.
Now I got this game when it was free so I can't really say if its worth the price because when something is free of course its worth the price. However the game is currently $29.99 and although thats not a bad price I would wait till its on sale or the price drops to $9.99. You may also want to wait till the game and the DLC come bundled together for $29.99. Either way the game is fun and worth a play.

This game deserves a way higher rating IMO.
There seem to be roughly 2 main reasons for negative reviews:
1. "This is not the strategy/management game I expected". I think the developers are quite clear on what you can expect. This is NOT a Civilization ripoff. You should expect 20-30 minute games that revolve about supply/demand of goods and stocks. If you are not into finance, but you want a nice and slow strategy game, then don't buy this game. The game is easy to learn for everyone, but nearly impossible to master. And I can't stress enough that you must like finance!
2. "The game is not complete without the dlc's". I can only say, I don't own any dlc's for this game (yet), but there is definitely enough to play without them. Also, I've read a lot about the dlc's that are currently available and I've pretty much only read positive feedback. They have a fair pricetag of 5 euros each in the Netherlands. I only think the soundtrack dlc, which costs 10 euros, should be in the main game.
Finally, I want to point out that the developers are very active. The designer mentioned in the game summary, Soren Johnson, responds to a lot of threads in the forum, is active on Discord and regularly streams the game on Twitch where he also responds to questions about strategy choices or gameplay balance.
This is one of the first games of its kind that I'm aware of and I'm very happy I gave this one a shot.
EDIT: I think it is important to mention that almost all negative reviews I read had less than 20 hours into this game. Now, for some games you've seen it all after 10 hours and there is no replay value. This one is different. I now have almost 70 hours into this game and I'm a complete newb. I've just won my first multiplayer after 60+ hours. Maybe because I'm a strategic failure, but probably because it takes some time to fully learn and appreciate the game mechanics. I'd say you can't judge this game after just playing the tutorial and a skirmish on lowest difficulty. Just take a quick look at the gametime difference between positive and negative reviewers. The more you play this, the more you'll appreciate it.
IMO you should at least won 1 multiplayer match before you can say whether the game is boring or not. Which does not mean you can't have fun in single player. The game offers a whole lot for its pricetag.
And for the dlc's, you don't need them to enjoy the game. I personally like the fact that the game is not too expensive and if you like it you can add options you want through dlc's, instead of a high pricetag with all dlc's in the base game.
This game is not intended for 10 hours of fun; it is for players that like a challenge and those who are not affraid of losing the first 50+ games or so because the game is just so damn hard.

I am in the 20th year of my fictional league.   It is bottom of the ninth in the 7th game of the 2036 world series and my team is down by three runs.
First up to the plate is my catcher Okuma.  This guy has been a big disappointment.  He was a great player who I signed to a big $ long term deal.  But he has had a bad year - so bad I brought up a minor leaguer at the end of the year to catch.  But I put him into my playoff roster as cover and my manager has decided to use him.  He gets a hit.
Next we have Rodriguez.  He is my 'moneyball' guy.  Just great at getting onto base and on minimum wage.  My scouts hate him as does my manager.  But I have forced him to be used as a starter and he has put up great numbers.  He walks.
Herrara now comes to the plate.  I picked him up as a throw-in on a big trade many years ago and he has been pretty good (although the guy I traded has been better).  However my owner has set me a goal to get a better centre fielder, so keeping him on is risky.  He gets a walk.
Bases loaded and Koot comes up.  This guy is Mr Mediocre. He is only on my playoff roster because I had one space left and could not think of a good reason not to use him.  I have never really paid him much attention - he is one of those guys you have to rest your real players.  Why my manager has put him into the game in the bottom of the 9th is a mystery.  And then he hits a walk off Grand Slam home run to win the World Series.
No doubt Mr Koot will soon be playing elsewhere, I will still be annoyed at the money I am wasting on Okuma, I will still be battling my manager to use Rodriguez as a starter, and Herrara will have gone to make my owner happy.
But I will remember those guys...

Respectable effort, aesthetically this is probably more true to PKD than most of the movie adaptations out there (A Scanner Darkly coming closest). The themes are semaphored rather than fully developed, and I wouldn't say no to a more adventure-game treatment with a bit more depth, but I found the final chapter strangely moving and effective nonetheless, the music was a very nice touch. Thanks to the devs for this brief trip into the mind of my favourite author ever.

This is a grind game.  You will sink hours into this game making or gathering one thing for enough materials to build another thing, or to make food so you survive long enough to make the things.  It is not an action packed thrill ride for the ages.  Once your settlement turns the corner and is self-sustaining, a whole new world of crafting opens up as you can concentrate more on smithing, masonry, and other jobs instead of having to hunt for food.
Combat is almost identical to Mount & Blade games.  I find it clunky and unsatisfying when engaged in fights with other players.  A lot of the exploits used by players have been squashed, but the actual combat system itself rewards players with the heaviest armor.
The only way to defend against a player in full plate with a tower shield and a hand-and-a-half sword is to have the same and hope that your swings register as you try to run around their shield and hit them before they do the same to you.  Lighter armors are pretty much useless on direct hits with any weapon and smaller shields are harder to block with as the player has to place the shield in front of the blow to stop the damage.  That's not easy when your opponent is rubber banding and teleporting around you.  This is strictly speaking 1v1 fights.
When you build a settlement, walls will not protect you.  On most servers it's common practice for d... players to build barkboxes, stack them on top of each other and climb over the wall, killing every living thing in sight.  If you're on the recieving end of this type of raid, you better you hope you have armor and weapons on and your friends are online and similarly geared, or you will all die.  The good news is, unless it's judgement hour, they can't take any of the stuff on your claim.  Can't even operate the gates.
P.S.  Raiders usually have grenades to throw at you and your friends from the parapets you built.

Finally, and this is a tetchy subject, the devs still update the game and hit bugs, but there seems to be a lot less focus on this game now that the devs have diverted funds and effort to the MMO version.  NPC enemies and monsters still haven't been introduced, some crafting minigames set for this version were instead added to the MMO.  That's all I have to say about that.

Final Fantasy VI is probably my favorite entry in the series.
Story
Satisfactory Narrative, nothing ground-breaking, it has the same plot that many other Final Fantasy games have. Evil empire, people fight that empire, empire stops being the bigger threat, everyone gets together and kills a god. While it isn't going to win points for originality, it is certainly well executed in Final Fantasy VI, and I find that to be infinitely more important.
Most of the plot significant characters that receive development are generally likeable. I do wish that some of the less plot-relevant characters received more screentime, although most of the actual story content provided is enjoyable. The antagonist in the series is easily the strongest and most interesting one the series has offered.
There is a section late into the game in which your time with the game will become much more focused on exploration and side quests, and less about furthering the narrative along. This has been a section that has been criticized by many, although I didn't find it to be much of a problem. This section does have some tonality problems. In a time for the world in which things are supposed to be dark and bleak, there seems to be a lot of areas that are quite pleasant and are getting along fine. This is a criticism of the game I have, although it is a relatively minor one.
Gameplay
The gameplay is pretty much your standard fair Final Fantasy experience. ATB based combat system, and a basic progression system. Most of the game is incredibly story heavy, so there will be lots of reading, and in the later sections of the game, there will be much more exploration going on. If you like Final Fantasy already, you are probably used to this. Ultimately, it is nothing fans of the series hasn't already seen, but it executes the series' formula effectively.
Presentation
The Steam version can easily be the best way to play Final Fantasy VI, if you install the mod that replaces the new spritework with the old SNES/Gameboy/PS1 versions. I find the hyper cartoony look of the game clashes horribly with the more serious moments of the game. Fortunately mods for this game are incredibly easy to install.
As expected, Final Fantasy VI does have an excellent soundtrack, composed by Nobou Uematsu, one of the signature composers for the franchise. Many pieces contain an incredible amount of personality, and it always effectively creates the atmosphere and the tone of the situation. Those that have played the game are fully aware of the excellence of the final boss theme.
Final Verdict
Buy it, and start demanding that Square makes a current-gen remake.

Bought the game solely because Philip K.♥♥♥♥♥♥was mentioned in the description and went in blind. Californium can be considered as a tribute to PKD's works -- A collection of weirdness familiar to readers of his books. In essence, Californium is a walking simulator where the sole gameplay element revolves around finding glitches in your reality: Items flickering in and out of existence, TV sets sending out secret, subversive messages only you can hear.
In♥♥♥♥♥♥s fiction, reality is always malleable, and such is the case also in Californium. Once you start peeling back the wool over your eyes, alternate realities begin to ooze into current ones. A sunny California baked in red turns into a grey, dystopian police state governed by the spirit of a long-gone president. Even you seem to change into a different person, but you still hear the omnipresent, self-aware narrator inside your head, and think the same thoughts you always did.
It doesn't stop there, though. The alternate realities keep on coming and the world gets progressively more out of joint. Californium is a very Dickian experience in the way that for most of the time, you have absolutely no idea what is going on. The game evokes paranoia and drug-induced delusion to the point where you cannot be certain about anything anymore.
In that way, the game probably nails a "true" PKD storyline better than any other game before it. I just wish the gameplay would be more interesting, because now the only thing you do is hunt for hotspots. Some of these are quite well hidden, and since you have to find them all to progress, frustration can occur if you get stuck. Diversity would have been more than welcome.
Aesthetically, Californium sits at a happy medium. People are represented as flat sprites in an otherwise 3D world; A decision that is probably budget-induced but which I actually found being a nice touch (it spares us from possibly cartoony 3D models). Some of the voice acting is definitely off, but isn't too distracting at the end of the day. I did also run into an unfortunate bug that forced me to replay an entire section, which is a shame.
Overall, Californium is a hard game to recommend, but after weighing all of the aspects of the game I'm going to do that anyway. It's a very short experience with annoying gameplay mechanics and a few technical difficulties, but it also stays true enough to PKD's work to be worth checking out if you have a chance. But I'm probably biased; After all, Ubik is my favorite book.

For example, PKD had all sorts of "interesting" ideas about parallel worlds, alternate realities, artificial intelligence, robots, and mind-alterting drugs/technologies.
The game mechanics are simple (find the Sigils and click on them -- that's basically it!), but the overall tone and theme are very engaging. There are clues to the location of the Sigils if you pay close attention to lighting and audio cues, or to apparent visual "glitches" (not all of which are bugs!). The art and music are excellent, and the "other world" portal effect is very nice too.
Caveats: there *are* a few genuine bugs (dodgy collision etc.), and the only save-points are automatic ones at the start of each chapter.. so give yourself time to play a whole section in one sitting (each of the 3 main chapters takes about an hour to get through).

Final Fantasy VI is commonly regarded as one of the greatest games of all time, and it earns that title. The cast of characters, excepting a few, is excellent, and the story makes full use of them. Combat features another version of the series' signature Active Time Battle system, which remains just as entertaining a twist on turn-base combat as ever. The game also does a good job of allowing you to customize characters to an extent without making them all feel samey, a pitfall the series has fallen into a few times. Each character has their own unique fighting style and special abilities, but the player can control which spells they learn. It's not nearly as innovative a system as the Job System in Final Fantasy V, but it still allows for some sense of player control while also forcing you to explore each character's style to form superior strategies. I will mention a few disappointing elements, however. Firstly, this port of the game features redesigned sprits and a rather obtuse new battle interface. This can be distracting for fans of the original version, but does not by any means make the game unplayable. The soul of the game is still there, even if it looks a little funny. Secondly, as mentioned above, this game has a pretty character driven story, something that has been praised over the years. While the first half of the game is a treasure trove of ambitious ideas and great character moments, the latter half can quite live up to it. Perhaps this is because the game is largely overshadowed by a major twist at the halfway mark which leaves the deliciously mad villian mostly absent from the proceedings. Perhaps it's due to the fact that the game just has too many characters to give them all their due. Either way, as grand as this game is and as commendable its ambitions, it does peter out every so slightly by the end.

TL:DR - Fun adventure, puzzle, hidden object game.
The first thing that struck when when I loaded this game was how much I liked the music and graphics.  My first thought on the graphics where that they were in the style of Steampunk, but upon further reflection, the graphics are more closely related to scenes from DaVinci's workbook.  The voice acting is during cutscenes is, thankfully, very well done.  The cutscenes themselves are pretty fun to watch.  Without getting into spoilers, it is quite fun watching the story unfold throughout the game.
This is at its core a puzzle game - similiar in style (but not setting!) to games such as Shadowgate or Kings Quest.  This genre of game will succeed or fail, in my opinion, on the quality of the puzzles.  You wander from room to room picking up items, fitting them together and solving puzzles.  Luckily, the puzzles are logical unlike some other games (I haven't run across any "microwave the hamster" puzzles or nonsense like that).  The puzzles from the items you pick up make sense:  sweep up the sand, light the lamp, follow the recipe.
Every now and then another puzzle opens:  such as fighting blocks into a shape or figuring out a code.  These are all very well done.
Overall, the game is pretty great.

SINGLE-PLAYER REVIEW
From the serie that "started it all", that led the way for cinematic FPS games, I expected more than this. I played the whole MoH serie since the ps1 games, so I know how it was born and grew.
The story is the usual, recycled, already seen soup, which is quite boring and you can skip with no regrets. The problem is that you can only skip movies and not cutsecenes, so if you want to replay the game, you'll have to watch them again and again, and they last for about 50% of the level time.
The real problem is the gameplay, though. Being used to games that tells you everything you need to push in order to even move, so much that it gets annoying, I was surprised that this game tells you nothing at all. Well, it tells you what to push to move and jump, the basics that everyone already knows, but not how to use the special equipment you're supposed to use in the "mini-games". Ok, there's no mini-games here, but there's special sequences where you need to use a special binocular to mark targets for bombing, a sequence where you use the weaponry of an helicopter, and some sniper sequences. Well, on the first 2 modes you have more than 1 firing mode but the game doesn't tell you that, and you end up wondering why certain targets don't blow up, or why the game keeps telling you to do something that you're already doing.
The actual FPS mode is sub-par, too. You can't choose what weapons you start the mission with, and you can only collect enemy weapons (not ammo to refill your one, unless it's the same model) or ask your friends for ammo, if they use the same one as yours.
The action has so many little breaks because you either have to climb a 1.5 meters step with the help of a teammate, something exploded near you and you take a whole 15 seconds to get on your feet again, a whole lot of enemies arrived at a near position (so it's better to just look at them instead of firing, right?), the teammates has something to tell you, and so on. It's frustrating. The fact that the game is also an on-rail shooter, with no space for exploration and only one way from point a to point b, makes the SP experience feel so restricting and unsatisfying, that the fact that it only last 3 hours won't bother you so much at the end.
Yes, you've read it right, 3 hours. That is about how much it took me to complete this game.
It wasn't even so much fun for those 3 hours. The game plays the compassion card for all the soldiers that actually went into those places, risking their life for our freedom. Well I'm sorry, but there's already movies for that and when I buy a game I want a game, not a barely interactive movie. I'm sorry for those people and I really appreciate their work, and I think it's not honest to use their sacrifice to make bad games.
The only thing that barely saves this game from being a complete disaster are the graphics. I get a solid 60fps in full-hd and everything at max, with vsync on, but it only looks good during daylight missions (like with most games anyway), and even there there's part of the graphics that is too blocky and/or has bad textures, but it's overall pretty good looking.
The audio is a mess, though. The sound can barely be heard and you have to increase the volume at almost maximum in your audio equipment.
Oh yeah, there's an additional game mode in SP, where you fight your way in a selected level for leaderboard score. Such fun.
If only they added coop, that could have marginally saved this terrible game, but as it is, it's the usual EA game: just bad.

Maybe I just have slow internet (thanks Abbott) but seeing other players move around without even an attempt at leg animation is disconcerting.
Following on, the servers are slow as all hell. If you do manage in a semi timely fashion to find and log onto a server, assuming the slow response time hasn't basically frozen your mouse, you will be greeted with some of the worst lag you've ever seen. Be forewarned fair traveller, you will think it's a one-off lag problem. Verily it is not. I have never actually tolerated this much lag in a game and it seems to be a pretty standard part of Nether so there's that. This of course makes combat a frantic button mash with little to no skill.
At first I thought this might be why I can't seem to move smoothly, but then I realised that the entire world has been put together so half-assedly that physically conected land elements (like a floor and a ramp) might require you to jump over some imaginary partition holding them together. Clipping is, as you can imagine, basically just part of the ambience at this point.
Then there's the game itself. It seems to have no idea how games are meant to work. There are safezones where you spawn when you die. In theory, in a safezone you can't use weapons, can't die, and the nether can't get in. This will periodically cease to be true and you have to run around repairing the anti nether devices. As a noob, you will be the ONLY one running around repairing anti-nether devices. Everyone else can survive without them just fine. When you aren't running for your life from aliens, which teleport by the way, utterly ruining the point of a zombie survival game, you're couriering parcels from A to B in the vain hope that you can scrounge enough bits and pieces from these transactions to craft a semi decent weapon. None of this is immediatley obvious to you as the game has basically no explanation of anything at all.
Upon undertaking a task outside the safezone, you will rapidly become aware of the fact that the difficulty of the nether around you will in no way be tempered to suit your skill level or armoury leading me on my first run to take on a small nether army which included a golem (try to guess what they're like) with nothing by a can gun (one shot shotgun made from a spray can) and a sword. Needless to say I died.
On subsequent attempts I found fewer nether, which was great for me, but alas this came at the price of having other players around me. It turns out that the average nether player is cut from the same cloth as a day Z player, and will galdy follow a n00b out of the safe zone for the explicit purpose of killing them and looting the $10 dollars they have. Fortunately for them, since they tend to already have automatic weapons and heavy body armour, this is an enetertaining and low-risk sport. For those of us trying to figure out the game, it is not.
In short, I have yet to find any element in this game which I think is good. You find eclectic items throughout the world, all of which are terribly rendered and usually look like an entire stash of discrete items, much to your chagrin. You sort of have to guess which ones can be combined at the weapon smith and into what. Until then, you're lugging around 50kg of♥♥♥♥♥♥with no way to use it. Things pop up on the screen which I'm sure are meant to be informative, but mean absolutely nothing if you haven't had it explained before, and when you start out, your chance of survival is approximately 0. Since you spawn with nothing but what you could put into a global stash (I assume, this bit is a bit fuzzy) after dying, it makes it nigh on impossible to ever advance to any reasonable level. Statistically any level of enemy can appear anywhere (except the reapers) and players have trained themselevs to see all non-tribe-members are walking goody-bags/piñatas. The game has a decent idea behind it, and if it were designed by competent designers and hosted on semi-decent servers, with a reasonable how-to guide, and some mechanism giving new players are fair shot, it'd be worth the $15. At this point though, I wouldn't even waste the bandwidth on it if it were free.

Do you like survival horror games with large guns? Overwhelming amounts of ammo? Body armor so thick that bullets ricochette off you like pebbles? Then don't buy Nether.
Nether's method of survival is much harsher.
Every bullet counts, and scavenging is vital.
PROS:
+Atmospheric - beautiful landscapes and environments
+Harsh Survival Standards - people will kill you for bags of chips
+Tense Player Interaction - Are they bandits or will they help you?
+Immerisive - play smart, crouch in bushes, cross streets between cars, duck into buildings
+Tribe Suppport - get together with tribemates to do objectives, and stay alive
+Semi-Permanent Death - dying means your ammo, food, and everything else you gathered is lost (excluding your Global Inventory and Vanity items), along with reseting your level (and thus losing  stat boosts)
+No "Pay to Win" - Buying items using real money are vanity only.
+ "Fair" PvP - heavily armed players still die eaily enough, if you score the hits. No one is impervious to harm
+Nether Swarms - simple supply runs can get heated and can lead to death if you fire off your gun like a maniac
CONS:
-Hard to Start - You'll often find yourself outgunned
-Hostile Players - expect to be mauraded often
-Endgame is Easy - stockpiling weapons, supplies, and ammo make dying inconvientent at best
-Endgame is Bland - after you've leveled tasks become mundane
SUMMARY:
Playing Nether is hard. Dying is easy. Surviving is hard. Thi game can be a challenge when you're starting out but this makes it fun. This isn't Resident Evil or DOOM, where you just outgun everything after a few levels. Expect a challenge.
SHOULD YOU PLAY IT: If you like a survial game with decent amounts of realism (scarce food, harsh conditions, hostile people) you'll like Nether.
RATING: 7.5/10 (remember it's still in development)

Please, let me save you, and your wallet...
This game is NOT full release, despite what the "developers" and rabid few fans (likely because of how easy the game is to hack, dupe items, camp, etc.) may say. Just drop by the forums for a few and take a look at what people are saying there.
The game is, in my opinion (for what it's worth, I have participated in 19 different alphas / beta's of various games) still in alpha stage, NEARING beta, but not nearly there yet. The claim of being "full release" is utter nonsense, and you WILL be disappointed if you spend money on this game.
Specifics you say ? terrible hit detection, terrible, non intuitive crafting system, terrible "quest" system (consists of running from point A to point B to deliver a cardboard box. over ... and over ... and over again.)  TERRIBLE inventory management. there is a space and weight system, neither of which correlates with reality or common sense (its being used to essentially keep people from carrying more than a standard load of weapons, which is a huge hinderance when trying to gather loot)
Typical F2P pricing scheme in marketplace where the in game currency vs cash currency is monumentally lopsided, which is to be expected.
water kills you. and by kills you I mean this alpha state game is so glitchy, if you go into the water and try to swim, you have something like a 90% chance of getting stuck on invisible geometry, and unable to escape the water which you just found out damages you slowly. The solution offered by a helpful player in game ? "bunny hop across the water" yes indeed, because the programmers couldn't do water without making it a deathtrap, you get to bounce giddily about as you frantically mash the space bar in order to skim the surface without getting stuck and slowly withering away in a pond of what i presume must be toxic sludge that just looks like water.
did i mention invisible geometry ? its not just in the water folks! thats right, randomly whilst walking about, you get to discover the myriad number of invisible dirtbike ramps strewn about, suddenly hovering 10 feet above the ground on some mystery object you cant see. Which is nowhere near as enjoyable as the stairs, steps, and ladders EVERYWHERE that you cant walk up without first wiggling your way past the invisible forcefield at the first step. Best technique ? mash that space bar while moving back and forth!
Some of you may have read a review a while back, when the game was first submitted for early access, talking about he "verticality" of the game, and how it added a whole new depth to the game, sneaking your way in terror through vast skyscrapers, nether creatures shrieking nearby! spooky! ... Guess what ? complete and utter bull****! MOST of the buildings you cant even enter, the ones you can, 90% of them have a single floor, which would be the ground floor. 8% of the remaining have ... *gasp* two stories! the second of which you might have to struggle for 5 minutes with those darned invisible forcefields to get to, but when you do, gosh! the verticality of looking 10 virtual feet to the ground! Its almost as if you're soaring with the eagles! or mutant bats in this case. the remaining 2% ? i think i've found maybe 5 buildings, total, so far, which have more than 2 floors. and these exciting buildings are literally just one giant open room on each floor, with a giant plank ramp leading to the next floor, over and over and over. Verticality must mean something along the lines of "uninspired and unoriginal" the level design literally looks like CS_Mansion, and i'm talking about the one from Counterstrike beta 3.1 ish ... like ... what ... 5 ? 6 ? 8 ? how many years ago was it ?
I could keep going, theres a LOT more to complain about, as this  game is fundamentally broken and unintuitive in just about every way you can imagine... except for the subways ... those are nifty... and spooky for about 5 minutes till you realise that for some reason, the creepy scary nethers apparently dont like creepy, dark abandoned subways ... which makes the subways a lot less creepy.
Other positives ? ... the guns feel relatively distinctive for the most part, although theres not much in the way of variety. And despite the fact that they "feel" different, there are basically only two worth trying to get, and stock up on, for pvp (which is what this game IS, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but be aware if youre thinking of buying that the nethers are just background noise, similiarly to DayZ these days, the other players are the real monsters) annd ... well ... thats about it ... I got about ... 5 nice "ohS***!!" crap my pants moments, all in the first 30 minutes or so... the problem is, after that first 30 minutes, i had literally already done EVERYTHING this game has to offer. Theres such a draught of content that once you realize theres really nothing else to do, you end up just looking for some poor helpless newbies to lure out of the safezone and then promptly execute ...
I want to keep going ... I want to write a book about how unfinished this game is... but i know most wont even make it this far
TL:DR,
This game has VERY few redeeming qualities ... i think like .. two ... maybe. other than that, its terrible, feels, plays and crashes like an alpha, not a "full release" title, and i think steam better start considering refunds for those of us who got duped. At the same time, it has its funnish moments ... but theyre just not worth the pain. Stay away!
Overall rating ? 2.5/10
Graphics: 6/10
Sound: 4/10 (some sounds are fantastic! the screams of the nethers are pretty great ... but most are terrible)
Design: 1.5/10 (Most repetitive game world i've seen since ... literally ... the 90's ... we're talking Playstation 1 fps level design     here, its just sad)
Content: 1/10 (like mentioned above, I literally did EVERYTHING there is to do in the first hour or so of playtime.
Fun!: 3/10 (for the first couple hours, I kept pretending not to notice all the glitches and rough edges, after the first couple of hours, my soul had been crushed to the point that I couldn't pretend anymore, and now here I am writing my very first review ...)

Californium is not for everyone. It's more of a postmodern art piece than a game, which makes sense, since it was funded as an art project. It's a
strange game,
it's a walking simulator (which I personally enjoy, but I realize isn't for everyone).  But if you like surrealism and you're open to more "non-traditional" sorts of games, you'll likely have an enjoyable experience.
The game does suffer a bit from what little gameplay it does have - you search around the environment finding hidden theta symbols that create bubbles of alternate reality, but some of them can be pretty difficult to find. Nothing ever kept me stumped for too long, but I feel it almost would have been better as a "pure" walking simulator without trying to shoehorn a hidden object game into it. It doesn't detract from the overall experience though.
If you're looking for a short, cheap, and certainly unique experience, you should give Californium a try.

Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic II is one of the most underrated RPGs of all time while also being one of the greatest RPGs ever made. Hands down. This game has been plagued with an undeserved negative reputation all across the internet for reasons I can only assume must be both malicious and blatantly fraudulent.
Heres my take on KOTOR2 and it's bad rep.
1. MAJOR BUGS and GLITCHES
I have never EVER suffered a single game killing bug playing KOTOR2 unlike what is said from everyone else which leads me to believe it's all either collective disinformation or people need to stop playing on Win95 PCs, I have beat it 12 times with no mods and twice with many mods on multiple different PCs with both Windows and Linux (WinXP, Win7, Win10, Ubuntu 12.04, Peppermint 4, Lubuntu 16.04) using the DVD version, the Steam version and even the original Xbox version on both the original Xbox and Xbox 360. No game crashes, no freezes, no game killing bugs of any kind, not once, ever. Either I am very lucky, people do not know what they are doing or the internet is full of♥♥♥♥♥♥ I have had resolution issues in the past but that was because AMD drivers suck and because the game was simply not made in the era of HD but it has since been updated to accommodate this very issue amongst other minor things.
2. THE ENDING WAS TERRIBLE
The ending was a goddamn cliffhanger, KOTOR 3 was already in the works to directly follow the game and got canceled. In other words, the story was not finished, it was to be continued on so in that the ending was actually really good in terms of what it was trying to accomplish which was, once again, a cliffhanger ending in preparation for a sequel that no one at the time knew would never happen. This is also perfectly in line with the Star Wars franchise, In "A New Hope" it had a cheesy dumb ending (like in KOTOR1) and in "Empire Strikes Back" it had a cliffhanger, a fairly dark cliffhanger (like in KOTOR2) in preparation for "Return of the Jedi" so imagine if Star Wars Episode 6 never happened and you were just left with the first two films and a cliffhanger ending of the second... Thats what it's like and people would call you dumb if you said "Empire Strikes Back sucks because the ending was just so gosh darn terrible!" If those people knew the facts behind the ending and why it never got explained, they'd call you and idiot and they'd be right.
3. KOTOR1 WAS BETTER
In what way? Story? Gameplay? Quality? To my mind it depends on what you want. Kotor1 was very basic, very to the point but yes was well written, well acted and overall well made. No question. BUT what did it lack?
- Depth in both story and character development.
- It, like all of Star Wars, had a very black and white view of good and evil both visually and in the ways it told the story.
- The gameplay had less game mechanics than Kotor2.
- The game had far less dialogue options than Kotor2.
- It had far less options in terms of how one completes a mission, granted not too much less... to be fair.
- Kotor1 in no real way branched off from the rest of the Star Wars universe in any way that would separate it from the rest of the franchise.. In other words, unlike Kotor2, it never questions the philosophical foundations of Star Wars and thus neatly fits within the Star Wars motif, some people may actually see that as a good thing... Whatever floats your Death Star.
- Kotor1 has a giant evil military machine floating in space. Kinda getting tired of giant Sith machines.
- Kotor1 contains too many damn Star Map dreams.
- In Kotor1 your choices do not directly affect your teammates except when you choose the dark side and only near the end of the game.
- Kotor2 actually tells you when♥♥♥♥♥♥is ♥♥♥♥ing empty.
- Kotor2 allows you to build/upgrade far more items.
- Kotor1's story was NOT written by Chris Avellone.
I'm sure I could go on but these are just a few things that Kotor1 doesn't have that Kotor2 did that made it far more interesting, immersive and fun.

I really wanted to like this game, but it is honestly one of the most boring survival games I've ever seen. There is no conflict unless you create it. There is no "survival" aspect to speak of. Really its an AFK grinding simulator. Want to level a skill? Yeah, you're going to be AFKing while your character automatically picks grass for hours. Not even joking. That's how you level your Nature's Lore skill. You set your character to automatically pick grass, then leave your computer. To give an example, in the 5 hours I played with friends, I completed one building. That's it.
The game is 95% AFK grinding, 4% Pretending To Role-Play out of boredom, and 1% incredibly clunky Mount and Blade style combat. Not to mention the absolute least intuitive UI I've ever seen. I wants to be an MMO, but it is not only abandoned by the dev's so they can actually make a REAL MMO, but it fails at the MMO style its attempting to go for.
Music: 1/10: Literally just Greensleeves ad other recognizable 'medieval style' classic songs over and over again.
Sound: 3/10: Thudding while grinding. Occasionally people scream for undescernable reasons. Congratulations. You are now deaf.
Graphics: 8/10: Only good thing about the game.
Gameplay: 3/10: Digging simulator. One section of digging takes 10 seconds. You must do the same section a dozen times to make any change on a very small cell. Your buildings are 30x30 cells.
Learning Curve: 4/10. There is a tutorial and tutorial videos, but the videos leave a lot to guess work, and the UI is incredibly difficult to manage.
Replayability: 3/10, if you're in to that sort of thing.

So just finished the game...
I started playing this game the first day it came out, and as you may have read in other comments, it had a lot of bugs. I was actually discouraged to continue, then saw that the Development team are taking their jobs seriously and fixing the bugs less than 24 hours after they're found, which allowed me to finish the game on day 2.
The art is strange yet appealing, and is difficult to associate to anything else I've ever seen. The music is simple yet completely appropriate to what's going on in the game. The story will make you wonder and feel uneasy.
Is this game perfect? No.
Is it crazily addictive? Absolutely not.
You also shouldn't buy this game if you're looking for a great gameplay, a huge open world or if you like multiplayer.
That being said, I still do recommend this game, because I value original thought. You can feel that the developers of this game want to innovate and have taken the risk of exploring a new type of game, more of an interactive psychedelic storyline, almost as if you were reading a comic strip. This is not just another FIFA, Assassin's Creed or CoD. This is definitely the strangest gaming experience you will have had in a while... if you're willing to explore off the beaten path, that is.

The game itself is cool, if you are NOT familiar with the Mount & Blade titles I suggest you to start either with the regular one (which is only single player) or Warband (which has an expanded single player more + the multiplayer battles), or if you have just With Fire and Sword and can't get the other titles, I think you should lower all the difficulties, because this game can get cruel really fast with you.
Which brings to my downpoints. Mount and Blade has always had an unfair start in my opinion. Too unfair against the enemies or against you. You ALWAYS have a horse right at the beginning, meaning that you learn how to fight on a horse really fast, but the regular enemies (Lowest tier: Looters) almost won't stand a chance against you. But then as soon as you face the second-lowest tier of enemies (Bandits) almost all of them have firearms with decent accuracy, meaning they can one-shot you or your lowest tier recruits really fast. Contrary to the other titles, I believe that this game has the hardest start of them all, specially because I didn't see any Tournaments. BUT I believe this was intended as a challange because like I said the start of the other titles was kind of unfair to your favor, now it's kind of unfair against you. For some, this may be part of the project, but for me, this was not well thought.
The second downside I found was that with some low spec computers running everything in the lowest setting possible the game is running pretty good, but during some points, specially melee fights, the fps just drops to the floor, it goes from 60+ to 1 or to weird chokes in a second, and that may occur when you are aiming at someone who is also aiming at you but then you can't be fast enough in the trigger because of fps lag, then you get killed. This has annoyed me the most in this game, something that I did not observe in Warband.
Aside from that, it's a decent game! Graphics are kinda ugly for its time but not that bad if you raise some settings, and because battles can get quite big they needed to make things simpler. I don't think I would recommend getting this game out of a sale, though. I totally would for Warband, it's a great experience (sandbox, tactics, commanding, fighting, etc), but not for With Fire and Sword.

Ignore the negative reviews about this game as they are less about the game itself, and more about people feeling entitled. The game has had a rough launch, but what first time publisher hasn't had issues? The thing to appreciate is that it's been less than 24 hours since the game was available and they've already addressed server isues, and are working hard on the few other superficial issues.
As for the game itself - I think it really captures the spirit of the films, while being just random enough that each round plays out slightly different from the last. I do wish it had a bit more of a tutorial, but after you play a few rounds - and especially after you play a round as Jason - you get the mechanics of the game and how they interact. This leads to you looking for the counselor that plays to the way you want to play - aggressive, sneaky, quick to repair things, able to outrun Jason, etc. It's never a gurantee that you'll survive a round, but then it wouldn't be much fun if you were always winning either. Having that cat and mouse chase with Jason feels excellent on both ends of the combat.
As counselor, you feel mostly helpless but with some map awareness, and some luck - you can evade.
As Jason, you feel all powerful but not invincible. Counselors CAN and WILL escape you.
I'll agree that there are things that can be improved on - keybinding is an obvious oversight, as is some of the lobby mechanics. But these are things that can be addressed, and in the meantime what you still have is a very fun game to play.

When you match 3 Reindeer, all tiles surrounding the Reindeer you placed are destroyed, clearing space, and you gain a power-up tile that can be placed at any time. These either clear the entire row, entire column, row+column, adjacent diagonals, or all surround adjacent tiles depending on which you get.
My only gripes are that you can get all 118 achievements in like 5 minutes, though I think the Letter Achievements were a bug. And that you can't save and quit, which I find annoying.
I definitely recommend this to any puzzle, match 3, or 2048 fan.

Mount & Blade: With Fire and Sword is based on award winning novel of the same title (With Fire and Sword) This novel, and later film series, was loved and is still loved by millions in Poland. I believe the game immerses you beutifully into this world (based on historical happenngs storyline wise) and although of course it's not the same as in novels, it is very nice to play for anyone that enjoyed the novels.
On a purely gaming point of view, it's good ol' M&B with guns and historically accurate troops. To have access to better troops you need to recruit them from a faction so at the start the best you can do is hire mercenaries. It features some unique aspects like attacking caravans or defending from a camp if you set one up. I believe the troop trees are fairly balanced and all have their strengths and weaknesses. The different countries kinnda fit in with M&B:WB divison of factions strengths (Poland having the best cavalry etc.) It gives a great experience and that's about it. I don't want to spoil the storyline, so I can't say much else.

As of 2/20, I would like to say that the combat of this game is very genuinely unique. The combat is fantastic, and I adore reaction based games like this. Duels and brawls (1v1 and 2v2) are my favorite modes in this game, as it feels like the connection feels pretty solid. From a viewers standpoint, I could understand how it seems like a boring game, but when you get your hands on the controller, it's very different. Blocking, dodging, parrying, reflecting, all very important mechanics to the game.
I will say that it seems like match making is very poor. I feel like most of my battles are always either a huge stomp, or a huge loss. There's a very rare inbetween. This is also really apparent in 4v4 where gear/feats matter. Speaking of which...
4v4 is where it gets messy, as it seems like players are constantly dropping, and I'm waiting for the game to start back up again. But it's not the worst thing in the world. I may have gotten lucky, as I've only dropped from a game about twice over the course of 35+ hours. People will also straight up leave from matches that aren't in their favor, and they won't get punished for it.
There is a downside to the gameplay though. As you move up to higher tiers of gameplay, it seems like everyone just waits for the opponent to swing first, allowing them to parry/feint/etc. What seemed like a very aggressive game, starded to go towards a route of just the waiting game.
Another huge downside is how the menu in this game works and how the client deals with certain issues is overall a huge downfall. You can't look through character customization while you're waiting for queue. In fact, you can't do anything while you wait in queue, you're just looking at a loading screen. Also, when you're in a party with friends, and there's not enough people in the lobby, it will automatically kick you and your buddies out of the match, disbanding the party. Which means you have to reinvite everyone again. If you play by yourself, and the lobby you're in decided to leave, you don't automatically go into another queue. No, you have to
. It's extremely frustrating to deal with.
I've also had times where I would wait a few minutes in queue, only to get an error message stating: "Couldn't join lobby, since lobby was full," then it would kick me out, and I would have to queue up again. Why would any game search for full lobbies?
Uplay is also pretty infamous as well. I've had lots of issues sending invites to my friends, and being able to accept friend invitations. Until a lot of these things get fixed, I wouldn't strongly recommend it.

When most hear the term RTS they think of gathering resources to build armies to throw at enemies until one eventually overtakes the other or for some other victory condition, and in the case of Offworld Trading Company this is largely untrue. Instead you have a completely economic focus here that is a mad scramble for resources and cash in order to put yourself on top and screw over the competition.
Despite the economic focus it's very fast paced and strategic as you only have so many claims to tiles so you have to be smart with how you set yourself up, more than that every resource is available to buy and sell regardless of whether or not you are actively harvesting it at the moment. Plus there is the black market which is full of little tools that can throw a wrench in the plans of the competition, and if you don't take advantage of it you can bet your opponents will. There are also various things you can build that can give you other sorts of advantages, or inflict disadvantages on you competition.
Overall it's a fun game with a rather unique premise that I definitely recommend.

As a sci fi economic RTS, Offworld Trading Company is a niche game, but for the right kind of player there's really nothing like it and I can't recommend it enough.  Single player, assuming you take advantages of saves and pauses, it plays like a tough simulation or even turn based game where you try to build a profitable company in a hostile environment before your AI opponents do.  But multiplayer is a whole different animal, it is fast and frantic, with split second strategic and economic decision making.  I played single player for months (on another platform), and stiil wasn't really ready for multiplayer, but I am having the time of my life trying to keep pace.  The music is also incredible.
For those who familiar with the game but not the DLCs, the one to check out is Ceres, which is OTC but with some rule changes, new buildings, patents, etc.  The newest one, Io aka Jupiter's Forge is the same type of thing.  It's a lot of fun to see what works in these new environments and what doesn't.

Game is not worth it's asking price, especially when things like difficulty is a DLC. Even the map editor is a DLC. But let's forget about that for a second, after all, the quality of a game isn't defined by it's studio's greedy practices.
So is OTC a good game? Well, it's average. You play as a CEO of a company, and your job is to setup a production pipeline on Mars. Along the way you'll have to compete with rival companies, and should you win, you basically monopolize Mars. Sounds pretty cool on paper, but in reality it's underwhelming.
Some people might say there's a deep tactical aspect, but that is a lie. The company mechanics will dictate your playstyle, and it won't be long untill you figure out that there is only ONE playstyle, and that's the intended one. Robots pump out power, Scavangers can build with ductape and gum, Expansive can, well, expand faster, and Science are nerds that think they can do things better by skipping resource mining, when in reality they are gimped.
The way this works is that every "race" has their strengths in different stages of the game, scavengers take the early, bots take the mid, expansive take late, and science take endgame. Obviously depending on the map and resource availability, this changes depending on the player. Unfortunately that's as far as the depth of this game can take you.
At the end of the day, every game plays, and ends, the same way. Even after buying some DLC's (things that should be features of the base game) that added some variety to the game, it was hardly engaging. A lack of units hurts the gameplay, at times forcing you to sit and wait, even if you max out the play speed. The endgame is another thing that never changes, eventually the local market gets saturated by all the companies producing pretty much everything, requiring you to build some rockets and export your stuff offworld.
Whoever buys the most shares at a colony/oposing company, be it by building modules, fullfilling wholesale orders, or by burying your competition in debt, wins the game. Along the way you can utilize some special "skills" which will cost you depending on how often it's used. The price of these skills is shared between players, so if everybody decides to nuke each other's resources pools, the price will skyrocket pretty fast. This is probably the first game that made a NUKE, boring. Like everything, these skills are mostly underwhelming, so don't expect to be blasting things to bits, or building an army. Your one and only weapon is the market, and while certainly a capable and formidable weapon, it's not enough to hold this game against other, more fairly priced and more feature packed products.
So ultimately, is the game FUN? That's after all, what counts. Assuming you don't buy any DLC's, you'll have it all figured out in about 4-5 hours of gameplay. It'll take you about 6-7 with the DLCs. After that, it's rinse and repeat. The rest depends on how much endurance you have for the same thing over and over again.

Love this game; the title is a give-away to how charming and innocent this game is. You're a young girl and are attempting to help your monster friends save their home. And reclaim lost furniture.
What carries this game is its charm; there's something likable about the characters and setting. It feels "Studio Ghibli-ish"; those that know the studio and have watched a few of their movies know exactly what I mean. There's a child-like whimsical nature encapsulated in the experience which the character designs, music, art style, and the totality of the visual helps convey. It makes for an entertaining experience everytime you boot it up; but that just might be me since I believe unique visual flairs to titles add to the experience and make them uniquely their own. This is one of those titles that people would place in that, "I would enjoy a cartoon series or short episodes of this being made" because what's here is fantastic.
The game itself is no slouch: whilst clearly targetted at children its still quality. It's on the easier side, but you'll still see the game over screen a few times and get damaged plenty, especially when you're attempting to get used to the game during the initial stages. The title is a mixture of platformers, light puzzle game, but is mostly a 1 button fighter with a few special moves and a drill that can be charged in battle. The charge is required against most enemies as they have armor, and the armor needs to be obliterated through a charged attack. You have an attack button, a dodge button, and a jump button. Simple.
My only complaint is the inclusion of the critical system in the game. At the top of the screen there is a bar and musical notes coming from the left and right side of the bar meeting in the middle. If you attack anything when the musical notes meet in the middle of the bar, you get a critical hit. Critical hits build up your drill's power and inflict more damage. The mechanic is interesting, but you will never realistically be stopping your attacks to time hits better. As it stands, criticals are incidental more than anything, as no one stops in the middle of striking opponents to get the timing down properly. It's like telling you you can juggle during matrix fights-its impractical. It's a superfluous mechanic.
Also worth noting is the weak sauce that is some of the "worlds" having levels that are just mirror versions of previous levels. Feels like padding and lazy as hell. It's not a lot of levels, and some are interesting, but still worth noting.
I'd place this game in the same categories as some of the Kirby Titles and Starfy: games that look to have a certain target market but bely an experience that can be enjoyed by all. Although the comparison is a little unfair, as the aforementioned franchises tend to have titles that usually lack any semblance of a challenge. This game may be targetted at younger audiences but it will still trip you up here and there. Additionally, the plot has depth that you otherwise wouldn't expect.
All in all, recommended. The game isn't particularly *amazing* or anything PHENOMENAL, but it has so much charm and the totality of the package makes for an enjoyable experience. The ending was bitter sweet for me as I wanted to see more of these characters and wished for it to continue. You get a solid game with characterization reminiscent of a child's movie that adults can enjoy even moreso than children due to its innocence that is lost on those that lack the ability to place nostalgic value on it.

Having played and been suitably impressed with OOTP 16, I re-signed for another year when I learned that OOTP 17 had negotiated with the MLBPA to use actual names instead of random ones, as well as making other, incremental enhancements. As I'm heading into my sixth OOTP 17 sim-season, I felt it was time to share my thoughts on the game while it's fresh. In general, my thoughts are overwhelming positive. Still, it has some rough edges.
Pros:
- The big one: "Is it fun?" Yes, especially if you're a real fan or a serious nerd. (If you're not, it might be overwhelming.)
- Incredible level of depth and detail, with deep financial and roster rules that are there if you want to use them, but that can be turned off or delegated if you don't.
- The game engine runs from values that are generated from statistics instead of directly from statistics. This is superior to older stat-based systems as they can be more easily adjusted by the game for stat anomalies. It also allows the system to more easily project career stats forward for players who want to use multi-season fictional leagues based on real players.
- The AI plays a pretty good game, both when you're against a sim manager and when you're letting the game auto-play. (Just don't let the AI do too much, or you might come back after a month and find out that you have a totally different team than the one you drafted.)
- As a GM, you can delegate almost anything you want to your staff. You can choose your level of micromanagement. However, beware ceding control to the AI...
- The "owner goals" option allows you to work for a fickle bonehead like George Steinbrenner if you want the challenge. (Just be aware that the AI might ask you to do something that truly is impossible, like most real bosses.)
Cons (AKA room for improvement):
- Like many niche games, the graphics are functional. They're fine for baseball sim grognards, but they won't win many design awards.
- The likelihood of anomalies cropping up seem a little higher than they should be in real life, and some things seem to be impossible (I don't think that a Lou Gehrig or Cal Ripkin could ever make their historical streaks).
- The UI could still use some optimization.
--- I find myself having to click to transition between screens often, and sometimes, the process involves several screen transitions to move back and forth. I think it either needs more keyboard shortcuts (with mouseover tooltips so you can learn them) or perhaps a user-configurable "most used" button bar or something.
--- There are a number of terms used in the UI that required googling outside of the online documentation to find the answer.
--- It's often difficult to find things when you need them, and (see above) the online manual does not have entries for all the screens/options you might need. The game is complex, so it's not surprising, but it's nonetheless annoying at times.
--- It took me about five tries to get my fantasy league set up. Using the wizards provided make it easier to do if you want all the defaults, but some of the options I wanted to use lay in the advanced options, and there was no way to enable them if you used the wizard.
- The AI trading algorithm could use some work. I had to disable it and run trades manually because my assistant GM kept trading off my key players for minor league prospects in the middle of the season. I can´t really decide whether I would recommend this game or not.
The game is cool, no question and you can see that the developers are trying to get rid of the main issues of survival focused apocalyptic games such as the SOS (Shoot on Sight) syndrome.
They tried to do that by just increasing the outgoing danger from the Nether mutants (not really zombies) which might have worked, if it would have worked.
The thing is now: You´re still getting shot as much as before (although I definitely got less player-related deaths in here than in DayZ) but now you also have very dangerous mutants around you.
What left a bad taste in my eyes is, that you have a store where you can buy stuff with premium currency. (I´m just calling it premium currency. It´s basically currency you mostly get through investing real money)
You can´t buy any weapons with it, as far as I have seen, mostly just medkits and food and whatnot so the amount of impact this has on the game is relatively low.
Further, I don´t understand how this game supposedly reached a gold status.
The game still has two of the main bugs it had in the Alpha.
They are rather small bugs, but due to their frequency can become gamebreaking very quickly.
Basically, your character gets stuck whenever you crouch and try to move over the border of an object, a street, or a wall.
Example: You jumped onto the brim/ledge of a window. You´re crouching and watnt to get down onto the street. When you want to walk off the brim so you can fall off onto the street below you, your character will get stuck and not able to walk off the brim, unless you stand up.
Now you might think "Well this doesn´t sound too bad" but this happens with EVERYTHING your character can touch. You get stuck on the street, on rails, when you are too close to a wall next to you your character will be stuck, when there´s a fence too close, you will get stuck.
So the collision in this game is pretty messed up and always has been ever since the Alpha.
Gamebreaking because I can´t see that ending good, when you´re in a firefight or something similar.
The game needs more improvement but overall it´s cool. If the developers would pull this one off and market it properly, it would brush DayZ off of the survival-apocalypse-throne easily.
Your character has perks and can level up. Your character gains XP for killing Nether mutants (not players, as far as I remember) and also a load of XP for every 60 minutes your survived.
Further, there´s a Global inventory, where you can save some of your things so that you don´t have to start completely from scratch when you die. The stuff you carry with you will be gone forever though.
So the Global inventory only slightly affects the survival instinct.
The game is not easy, especially regarding weapons.
At first I gathered an arsenal of weapons very quickly, but the developers understood that wasn´t the intention behind a survival game and patched that - now I can be glad if I find two parts of a simple pistol.
Personally, what is annoyiny me is that the mutants just randomly spawn somewhere.
That is pretty stupid, considering that you might be sneaking across a street you checked out from a safe distance before to see if there are any mutants, and then you´re there and one of these mutants spawns 5 meters away from you. Tough luck if it discovers you.
But aside from that, I would mainly recommend playing this game with friends.
I was able to survive the longest when I played alone, but it´s just better with friends. Everything is better with friends.
My overall score for this game:
6.5/10

Absolutely phenomenal game. Frictional Games is best known for 3 things so I'll rank these here: Horror, Puzzles, and Story.
8/10 Horror
Not the scariest game ever, but it had very unique ways of building atmosphere and tension and it could scare you in unique ways other than simple jump scares; certainly a unique horror game in terms of its mechanics and story.
5/10 Puzzles
Puzzles weren't challenging, and despite being able to pick up everything, you will almost always know what objects are useless to you, and which ones will help you complete a puzzle.
11/10 Story
This game is not only an amazing narrative, but a thought experiment about what it means to be alive, and what it means to be conscious. Many philosophical and ethical issues are presented in the game in interactive ways that really get you to think about your actions.
The story is very subtle and easy to miss as it is not shoved in your face. Story is delivered mostly in the form of written notes scattered about, emails on computers, and "memories" stored in corpses. There are many interconnected story lines involving many different characters; they are gradually revealed as you progress in the game. All of them culminate to deliver an absolutely amazing ending.

In Amnesia: The Dark Descent you play as Daniel. You awake in a dark gloomy castle and shortly after find a letter written by your former self telling you one thing. Kill Alexander, the Baron of Brennenberg castle. In your quest to kill Alexander, you descend into the depths of the castle and beneath the very stone of Brennenberg where you discover twisted things about the harrowing abominations that stalk you but also about your own past.
Your best bet at dealing with the enemies is to stay quiet and avoid them at all costs. You cannot shoot or fight back. This makes for some incredibly intense moments which are broken up by sections where you don’t feel as threatened and must complete some puzzles which the control system of using the mouse to grab and move objects and open doors makes very engaging. This helps reset the tension ready for the next terrifying section. There is a lot to interact with and explore in the world of Amnesia and you will be scrounging around in places you would rather not be for much needed light sources. You must manage your resources well as you don’t want to be left in the dark to go insane with those things.
The Dark Descent is hands down the most atmospheric game i have ever played and that is largely due to the incredible soundtrack. The ambient music sounds natural like screams coming from the depths of the castle and gives you that constant feeling of dread whether there is something there or not. This game MUST be played with headphones and in the dark for full effect. I have never been so on edge playing a horror game and had to stop after just 20 minutes sometimes so i didn’t have a stroke. I was careful and only actually died 2 or 3 times but you always felt like you were about to die. Looking around you constantly getting that feeling like the boney fingers of death himself were on your shoulders. Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic II is an absolutely great game. But as many games do, it does have problems. And even though these problems are small and inconsistent, they are still a flaw in the game. And while it might not be as good as its predecessor, it still is an amazing game.
Pro's: Compelling main storyline, great characters, beautiful worlds, and the modding community.
Con’s: Bugs, and the starting planet.
Storyline:
The storyline of SWKOTOR 2 is a little complicated, but once you get to the nitty gritty, you can see it for its entirety. And while I would love to tell you how intriguing it is, I’m afraid that I will unwillingly tell you what the story is about. But once you start to play the game, and when you do get to the grit of the story, you will be more than interested in it.
Characters:
The characters, my god the characters. Never in my life had I felt so much hate, love, and understanding for characters. Not even with most of modern games today. Every character you meet, either side characters or companions, all feel fleshed out. And while there are a stray or two that feel like they are cardboard cutouts, it’s not enough to detract from the world of this game. And your companions are probably the most interesting people you are going to see in this game.
They all have their own agendas. One of them just wants to get out of the situation, one just wants to be in the situation, and they’re all just so damn interesting. Not a single one of your companions are the same. If you were to rob someone blind, one of your companions will tell you that it was worth it because we need the caps. While the other one will scold you and tell you off. The game finds a way for it to work, and it works beautifully.
Worlds:
The worlds in this game are absolutely stunning, and not a single world feels the same. If you go to Nar Shaddaa, you’ll feel crowded, claustrophobic, and lost. While on a forest world, you’ll feel like you're in the depths of a jungle. The world’s are portrayed outstandingly, and are an absolute charm to be in.
Modding:
The modding community in this game is ferociously great. There are so many mods for the game that I can’t even count. And no, not just the Steam workshop. There are mods that fix the game, make it look better, and make every single part of the game feel much more fleshed out.
Bugs:
And even though the game is great and has been patched multiple times, there are still so many damn glitches. One of these glitches, for instance, is a glitch that happens when you play the game for over 3-6 hours. And what basically happens is that is automatically skips dialogue for you. And while this is probably a must for speedrunners, the people who are more than interested in the game's narrative will find this a little more than annoying. But thankfully all you would need to do is simply restart the game to fix it.
But that still doesn’t mean that there aren’t some other bugs. I came to experience one of these bugs via teleportation. One minute I was walking down the hall and the next I was talking to one of my companions, and then the game crashed. And I lost everything that I have done up to that point. It was annoying but it only happened once while playing the game, so it wasn’t that big of a deal.
First World:
The starting planet is boring as all hell. The first time while I was playing the game felt like I was about to fall asleep while playing it. I don’t think I can explain it anymore than I have. It’s boring, plain and simple.
Verdict:
The game is amazing and it coulnd't be any more so. And it does have a few bumps here and there, but other then that, I couldn't recomend this game any more than I am.

Star Wars were pretty simple and straightforward science fantasy action movies. Mostly. Except for those needlessly convoluted, idiotic prequels.
KotOR takes the whole world of Star Wars and puts things into perspective; it's no longer just a story about wacky aliens and robots, sassy space pirates, talking carpets and laser-sword-wielding wizards who rally under the banners of Good and Evil so that they might distinguish who's fighting who and whether they like sand or not.
Gameplay-wise, KotOR is an action RPG, resemblant of Neverwinter Nights and other D&D-based RPGs. Upon character creation you pick one of the three classes, resembling the Warrior, Rogue and Mage archetypes, each with their own array of skills. Dialogue system gives you several options on how you can handle the talking with the game characters, you have to weigh your options and sometimes put your skills to use to achieve the desired results. The combat consists of round after round of skill/power/item usage or simply watching your characters trade auto-attacks with the enemy. As solid as the gameplay may be, the story and the writing is where KotOR really shines.
In KotOR, even the most basic RPG mechanics such as murdering thousands of creatures, and assembling a party to become stronger, are questioned. What moral right do you have to take people's lives, even if you seek to protect others?
Why certain characters are drawn to you, seemingly eager to follow your orders? What events will you set in motion by touching with their lives? What gives you the right to shape the world around you as you see fit?
Is it the mysterious Force, an ability to wield a lightsaber and throw things with the sheer power of will?
No. It's not just about the Force. It works in numerous, mysterious ways, and it is a great ally. However, it is just a part of what life really is.
Lightsaber is not your life either, it's just an instrument. Or perhaps, a weapon. Lightsabers, codes of Jedi, teachings of Sith, the Force — these things alone do not shape a person.

The Force may be the single greatest power in the universe. And sometimes, you have to turn yourself away from the Force to see the world around you for what it really is.

Story
The story of Amnesia starts with… Well you do not remember anything, but find yourself trapped in a huge castle. Only after a few collected notes you find out that you drank an amnesia potion on purpose which makes no sense at all at the beginning. If you read all the notes you will find out what happened, though you can decide not to do so and only walk from level to level, which I don’t recommend since the story in Amnesia is a nice companion to the gameplay and Atmosphere.
Gameplay
The first person horror game has neat controls and the gameplay does not get repetitive, at least not if you prepared for a horror game where you have to repair a ton of stuff, due to low quality mechanisms that open the next area. Amnesia provides a lot of interaction with your surroundings, for example can you barricade a door by dragging nearby objects in front of it. There are of course monsters in the game that will chase you, but beware that you have absolutely no chance of fighting back. The only options you have is running or hiding.
Graphics
On highest graphics settings the game looks good and if it is only about graphics for you, Amnesia might not be perfect compared to Outlast, but for a 2010 game it satisfies all needs.
